units.la: COgitanti de eo, in cuius nomine parvum hoc opusculum meum apparere velem, O Rex, quidni debebat M. tua potißimum in mentem mihi venire, quæ primitias laborum meorum, cuiuscunque demum ij sint sint generis, suo quodam jure sibi vendicat: & cui primitiæ primi illius generis laborum & scriptionum mearum, hoc est, commentationum, à me jam sunt oblatæ: An non igitur par erat, ut eidem quoq; primitiæ secundi hujus generis laborum nostrorum, quod cernitur in locis Theologiæ communibus tradendis, offerrentur. Ab hoc instituto, etsi multa erant quæ me deterrebant, inter quæ imprimis obversabatur mihi Majestas Regia, & ea quidem, ut ingenuè dicam, singulari quadam cognitione rerum diuinarum adornata, Majestas
units.tr: Pondering on the one in whose name I wished this little work of mine to appear, O King, why should Your Majesty not have come most readily to mind? Your Majesty claims for yourself, by a certain right, the first fruits of my labours, of whatever kind they may be. To you I have already offered the first fruits of the first kind of my labours and writings, that is, my commentaries. Was it not therefore fitting that the first fruits of this second kind of my labours, which consists in setting out the common topics of theology, should be offered to the same person as well? Although many things deterred me from this undertaking, among them above all the Royal Majesty stood before me, and that Majesty, to speak frankly, adorned with a singular knowledge of divine things, Majesty

units.la: DEDICATORIA.
units.tr: DEDICATORY.

units.la: iestas, inquam, cujus magnitudinem ferre non poterant, tenuitas ista mea, simul & opusculi hujus mei mediocritas: Tam ẽ cum memoria repetebam, quanta semper esse soleat humanitas illa & clementia tua, cum erga omnes, tum vero imprimis erga me; decreui potius in suspitionem audaciæ aliquam incurrere, quã officium erga M. tuam meum, aut potius pietatem humillimam, non testatam facere, vel hac ipsa hujus opusculi mei, quantulumcunq; illud sit, dedicatione. Accipe igitur, O Rex, non tam opusculum hoc parvum, quàm testimonium animi M. tuæ in Domino addictissimi, & paratissimi, pro eo ac debeo, & pro modulo mearum virium, ad obsequendum M. tuæ quacunque in re, & quàm potest fieri, submisse. Sed quid est in quo ego M. tuæ queo inseruire magis, quàm in eo, vt assiduis & seriis cum Deo meo precibus agā, vt tu ipsius gratia ac beneficio singulari, virorum qui hoc nostro sæculo doctrina & pietate excellunt apud exteras gentes, opinionem illam præclaram, quam non immeritò sustines, ad extremum usque tueari: vt, & in præsenti hac vita fœliciter regnes, & in altera illa socius sis cœlestis illius regni (Præ cuius gloria, ut hoc dicam obiter, ego non ita pridem audiui te terrena ista regna omnia despicere, cum, inter alia, de Christo, deque precibus ad eum solum, non etiam ad Angelos, aut sanctos homines, qui hac vita defuncti sunt, concipiendis, in familiari quodam sermone, & non nisi paucis aliquot præsentibus, multa erudite (Dicam ad Dei gloriã, absque vlla assentatione, quod res est) & pie suauiterque differebas.) socius, inquam, sis cœlestis illius regni, ac cohæres cum
units.tr: Majesty, I say, whose greatness my littleness could not bear, and the modest scale of this little work of mine. Yet when I recalled how great that kindness and clemency of yours has always been, towards all people and especially towards me, I decided that I would rather incur some suspicion of boldness than fail to bear witness to my duty towards Your Majesty, or rather to my most humble devotion, even by the dedication of this little work of mine, however slight it may be. Accept then, O King, not so much this small work as a testimony of the mind of Your Majesty, most devoted and most ready in the Lord, in accordance with what I owe and to the best of my powers, to serve Your Majesty in whatever matter, and as humbly as possible. But what is there in which I can serve Your Majesty more than in this: that with constant and earnest prayers to my God I may pray that by his grace and singular kindness you may maintain to the end that famous reputation which you rightly bear, among foreign nations, as one of the men of this age who excel in learning and piety; so that you may reign happily in this present life and be, in that other life, a companion of that heavenly kingdom. (Before whose glory, to say this in passing, I not long ago heard you despise all these earthly kingdoms, when, in a familiar conversation with only a few present, you discussed at length, learnedly, piously and pleasantly, among other things, Christ, and that prayers should be addressed to him alone, not also to angels or to holy men who have departed this life. I say this to the glory of God, without any flattery, as the truth is.) I say, may you be a companion of that heavenly kingdom, and a co-heir with

units.la: [D]Um opusculum hoc D.Roberti Rolloci de efficaci vocatione typis committerem, venit forte in manus D. Theodori Bezæ epistola, ad Scotiam D.Iohanni Iohnstono missa, quæ operum quorūdam ab eodem hoc authore editorum, et a me excusorum, commentarii, inquā, in Epistolā ad Ephesios, & Analyseōs Epistolæ ad Romanos, commendationem continebat. Eam itaque huic operi præmittēdam censui, vt tu (benigne Lector) quodnā viri illius in universa doctrina Theologica exercitatissimi, & de Ecclesia optimè meriti, de hujus Authoris scriptis judicium fit, perspiceres; & ex eo de cæteris ejus laboribus, vel hactenus exaratis, vel impostèrum ad Ecclesiæ vsum exantlandis, æstimares: Deum (cum D. Beza) precatus, vt hunc hominem novis subinde donis auctum fœliciter conservet, & alios, quando ipsi visum fuerit, huic similes operarios in vineam suam emittat. Vale.
units.tr: When I was about to send this little work of Master Robert Rollock on effectual calling to the press, a letter of Theodore Beza, sent to John Johnston in Scotland, happened to come into my hands. It contained a commendation of certain works published by the same author, and printed by me, namely his commentaries on the Epistle to the Ephesians and his Analysis of the Epistle to the Romans. I therefore thought it fitting to prefix it to this work, so that you, kind reader, might see what judgment that man, most practised in the whole of theological teaching and most deserving of the Church, passes upon this author's writings, and from that might estimate his other labours, both those already written and those yet to be undertaken for the use of the Church. I pray, with Beza, that God would keep this man safe, enriching him from time to time with new gifts, and send out other workers like him into his vineyard, when it shall seem good to him. Farewell.

units.la: SPECTATAE TVM PIETATIS, TVM DOCTRI- NAE VIRO, D. IOANNI IOHN- STONO amico summè ob- servando.
units.tr: TO THE MAN DISTINGUISHED ALIKE FOR HIS PIETY AND HIS LEARNING, MR JOHN IOHNSTONE, MY MOST HONOURED FRIEND.

units.la: Eriùs ad tuas literas, vt ferò mihi redditas, respondeo, mi Iohnstone, ex quibus pergratum mihi fuit intelligere te salvum ad tuos reversum, Ecclesias vestras in beato & tranquillo statu comperisse, quem illis perpetuum & securum in longos annos exopto. Et quidni sic futurum confidam? Quum & tàm praclarè iam inde ab initio fuerint à magnis illis & verè fidis servis Dei iacta earum fundamenta: & qui supervenerunt, non stipulas, neque fœnum; sed aurum & argentum, & lapides verè pretiosos superstruxerint: immò sanctis eorum laboribus sic Deus manifestè faverit, ut quicunque ad hoc Dei ædificium impegerunt, non modò suis conatibus excciderint; verùm etiam procul, velut ipsius Dei manu, sint dissipati, & iam quasi in tenebras exteriores proiecti. Ad hoc accedit rarissimum & pretiosissimum illud Dei donum, quo vos est idem ille Deus dignatus, concesso vobis eo Rege, & in tot, tantisque periculis admirabiliter conservato, qui ad illud singulare pietatis tuendæ, & conservandæ puritatis Ecclesiarum studium, tantam Christianæ Religionis ex ipsis fundamentis cognitionem adiunxerit, ut in eo pene Dominus, & Regiæ Maiestatis, & sacri ministerij dignitatem videri possit simul contulisse, ut Scotiæ iampridem nihil decesse videatur, unde optima & maxima quæque sint illi speranda, si modo, quod sane suturum non immerito confidimus, tanta hæc dona agnoscere, & sicut adhuc fecit, illa pergat ad rectum illum summum finem & scopum, idest, ad ipsius omnium bonorum auctoris gloriam dirigere.Hanc vero tam beatam sortem, tibi, caterisque ibi venerandis fratribus, hisce literis gratulandi gaudeo præbitam mihi occasionem, tum abeo vestrate, D. Davide Dromenio, viro pio, & non indocto, cuius præsentia aliquot dierum nobis hic fuit iucundissima, ad vos revertente, cui has literas comisi; tum ex eo quod hoc ipso tempore mihi contigit thesaurum nancisci, qui nescio quo siniistro fato quamvis hic in omniomnium aliorum conspectu versaretur, me tamê adhuc subterfugerat: thesaurum enim cur non appellem, & quidem pretiosissimum, illos honorandi summè fratris D. Rolloci, tum in Epistolam ad Romanos, tum in Epistolam ad Ephesios, utramque inter Apostolicas omnes Epistolas celebratissimam, commentarios? Sic enim ego quidem de iis apud me statuo (quod absque ulla specie adulationis dictum velim) nihil adhuc legisse me in hoc interpretationis genere breuius simul, & tum elegantius, tum iudiciosius scriptum, ut ipse me iis inspectis continere nequeverim, nec etiam, opinor, debuerim, quin & Deo, de hoc utilissimo proculdubio quamplurimis futuro labore, gratias magnas agerem, & tantum hoc vobis bonum, vel toti potius Ecclesiæ concessum gratularer, Deum precatus ut hunc hominem novis subinde donis auctum feliciter conservet, hoc præsertim tempore, in quo propter tantam operariorum in excolenda Dei nostri vinea raritatem, & paucissimos ex veteranis illis exercitatissimis superstites, triumphare iam sibi de oppressa veritate Sathan cum suis videbatur. Caeterum, quod ad huius Ecclesiæ & Scholæ statum attinet, perstamus quidem adhuc illa vere, ipsis etiâ nostris hostibus admirabili, omnipotentis Dei, et Servatoris nostri manu velut ut ex ipsis mortis faucibus erepti, sed solis adhuc καὶ ἀυθρώπου inducijs cū hoc anno finiendis freti, & ab ijs necessario pendente nostro statu, quæ tandem in illo nunc Rothomagi coacto cætu, vel de bello, vel de pace, (in qua & nos æquis conditionibus comprehendamur) inter ipsum Gallia Regem & vicinum nobis principem brevi decretum iri sperամus. In hoc autem tam incerto statu illud nos plane solatur, quòd sciamus istud quantumvis tenue & fragile filum, à quo veluti suspensi nunc pendemus, ipsius Dei nostri manu teneri, nunquam passuri ut falsum comperiatur quod, & ex Apostolo didicimus, & toties reipsa sumus experti, Omnia videlicet eorum qui Deum diligunt bono cedere. Vos autem interea nostri in assiduis vestris precibus memores esse quaso pergite. Ego vero iam ab aliquot mensibus, etsi neque febri, neque calculo, non denique podagra, vel acribus illis malis vexor, quæ senectam ferè consequuntur: tamè ita me sentio debilitatum, ut ab utroque publico munere meo pene cogar prorsus abstinere, me domi continens, & totus ad ἀναλυσιν illam optatissimam intentus: quo me 78. annum iam agetem, ætas ipsa vocat: qua in re tuas & piorum omnium fratrum preces requiro, & quidem nominatim venerandi mihi fratris D. Melvini, itidemque D. Petri Iunij, quæ quem, nisi me fallit memoria, D. Scrimgerus beatæ memoriæ, sibi cognatum hic olim appellabat: quibuscum, adiunctla meo nomine officiosissima salutatione, peto ut has tibi communes esse literas velis: Deum precatus, mi suavissime frater, ut vos ipsi hic omnes quam potentissime & felicissime adversus omnia pericula domi & foris tueatur. Bene vale. Genevæ, Calendis Novembris, veteri nostro calculo.
units.tr: I reply at last to your letter, which I am told was delivered to me, my dear Iohnstone. It gave me great pleasure to learn that you have returned safely to your own people and found your churches in a blessed and peaceful state, which I pray may last for many years, secure and unbroken. Why should I not trust that it will be so? Their foundations were laid from the beginning so splendidly by those great and truly faithful servants of God, and those who came after them have built upon them not straw or hay, but gold, silver and truly precious stones. Indeed God has so plainly favoured their holy labours that whoever has run against this building of God has not only failed in his own attempts but has been scattered far off, as if by the hand of God itself, and is now cast out, as it were, into outer darkness. To this is added that most rare and precious gift of God, which the same God has deigned to bestow on you: a king, preserved wonderfully through so many and such great dangers, who has joined to his singular zeal for defending piety and keeping the churches pure such a knowledge of the Christian religion from its very foundations that in him it seems nearly as if the Lord had bestowed both the dignity of kingship and the dignity of the sacred ministry together. So nothing seems to be lacking to Scotland for which the best and greatest things may be hoped, provided that, as we confidently trust (and not undeservedly), you acknowledge these great gifts and, as you have done until now, continue to direct them to that highest end and goal, that is, to the glory of the author of all good things. I rejoice that this letter gives me the opportunity to congratulate you and the other venerable brethren there on so blessed a lot. The occasion comes partly through Mr David Dromenius, your countryman, a godly man and not unlearned, whose presence here for some days was most pleasant to us, and who is returning to you and to whom I have entrusted this letter. It also comes from the fact that at this very time I have happened upon a treasure which, by some unlucky fate, had escaped my notice although it was lying in plain view of everyone else. Why should I not call it a treasure, and indeed a most precious one: the commentaries of our most honoured brother Mr Rollock, both on the Epistle to the Romans and on the Epistle to the Ephesians, the two most celebrated of all the Apostolic Epistles? For this is my own judgement of them (and I would have it said without any appearance of flattery): I have never read anything in this kind of interpretation that is at once briefer, more elegant and more judicious. Having looked at them, I could not restrain myself, nor, I think, ought I to have done so. I give great thanks to God for this labour, which will undoubtedly be most useful to very many, and I congratulate you, or rather the whole Church, on this good thing, praying God to keep this man safe and to keep adding new gifts to him, especially in this time, when, because of the great scarcity of workers in the cultivation of our God's vineyard, and because so few of those veteran and most experienced men survive, Satan with his followers seems already to be triumphing over the oppressed truth. As for the state of this Church and School, we still hold on, by the wonderful hand of Almighty God and our Saviour, as men snatched from the very jaws of death, even in the eyes of our enemies themselves. But we rely only on a truce, a human one [καὶ ἀνθρώπου], which is to end this year, and our state depends necessarily upon it. We hope that soon it will be decided, at the assembly now gathered at Rouen, whether there is to be war or peace between the King of France himself and the prince who is our neighbour, and whether we shall be included in the peace on fair terms. In this so uncertain state, this alone consoles us: we know that this thread, however slender and fragile, from which we now hang as if suspended, is held in the hand of our God, and he will never allow what we have learned from the Apostle, and have so often proved by experience, to turn out false: that all things work together for good for those who love God. Meanwhile I beg you to continue to remember us in your constant prayers. For my own part, for some months now, although I am not troubled by fever, nor by the stone, nor finally by gout or those sharp ailments that commonly accompany old age, I feel so weakened that I am almost forced to give up both of my public duties altogether. I keep at home, wholly intent on that most desired departure, to which my age, now nearly seventy-eight, calls me. In this matter I ask for your prayers and those of all the godly brethren, and in particular those of my venerable brother Mr Melville, and likewise of Mr Peter Junius, whom, unless my memory fails me, the late Mr Scrimgeour of blessed memory used to call his kinsman here. To them, adding my most respectful greetings in my name, I ask you to allow this letter to be common to you all. I pray, my most sweet brother, that God may keep all of you there safe and most prosperous against every danger at home and abroad. Farewell. From Geneva, on the Kalends of November, by our old reckoning.

units.la: VT INTELLIGAT LECTOR quem locum habeat sequens tractatus De Vocatione efficaci in doctrina theologica, placuit Methodi locorum Theologiae haec quasi prima et rudia quaedam lineamenta ducere.
units.tr: THAT THE READER MAY UNDERSTAND what place the following treatise, On Effectual Calling, holds in theological doctrine, I have thought fit to set down these, as it were, first and rough outlines of a Method of theological commonplaces.

units.la: 1. DOctrinae Theologicae summa & generalissima capita duo sunt, 1.de Deo. 2.de operibus Dei.
units.tr: 1. The chief and most general heads of theological doctrine are two: 1. concerning God; 2. concerning the works of God.

units.la: 2. Capiti primo generalissimo de Deo subalterni sunt loci, 1. De natura Dei & ejus attributis, quae vocantur, essentialibus, ut Misericordia, Iustitia, potentia, Sapientia &c.
units.tr: 2. Subordinate to the first and most general head, concerning God, are the commonplaces: 1. concerning the nature of God and his so-called essential attributes, such as mercy, justice, power, wisdom, etc.

units.la: 2. De Trinitate sive tribus in unica Deitatis essentia personis
units.tr: 2. concerning the Trinity, or the three persons in the one essence of the Godhead.

units.la: 3. Caput secundum generalissimum, quod est de operibus Dei, habet sub se locos speciliores 1. De opere Dei quod ab aeterno est, cujusmodi est generalis providentia & decretu Dei generale de omnibus creaturis, quod inde ab aeterno est. 2. De opere Dei quod in tempore est, quodque cernitur in executione aeterni illius Decreti & providentiae divinae.
units.tr: 3. The second and most general head, which concerns the works of God, has under it more specific commonplaces: 1. concerning the work of God which is from eternity, of which kind is the general providence and the general decree of God concerning all creatures, which is from eternity. 2. concerning the work of God which is in time, and which is seen in the execution of that eternal decree and of divine providence.

units.la: 4. Sub loco de executione decreti, continentur speciales alij 1. De creatione rerum omnium. 2. De administratione rerū omnium creatarum.
units.tr: 4. Under the commonplace concerning the execution of the decree, there are contained other, more specific ones: 1. concerning the creation of all things. 2. concerning the governance of all created things.

units.la: 5. Sub loco generali de creatione continentur speciales alij de particularibus creaturarum speciebus, nominatim vero loci de rationalibus creaturis 1. De Angelo. 2. de homine.
units.tr: 5. Under the general commonplace concerning creation there are contained other specific ones, concerning the particular kinds of creatures, and especially the commonplaces concerning rational creatures: 1. concerning the angel; 2. concerning man.

units.la: 6. Ad locum de homine pertinent inferiores alij 1. De innocentia. 2. De lapsu & peccato primo. 3. De reparatione ipsius.
units.tr: 6. Under the commonplace concerning man belong further, subordinate ones: 1. concerning innocence; 2. concerning the fall and first sin; 3. concerning the restoration of man.

units.la: 7. Ad locum de reparatione pertinet locus De Christo Mediatore in quo facta est reparatio.
units.tr: 7. To the commonplace concerning restoration belongs the commonplace concerning Christ the Mediator, in whom the restoration was made.

units.la: 8. Ad locū de Christo Mediatore pertinēt loci subalterni alij 1.
units.tr: 8. To the commonplace concerning Christ the Mediator belong subordinate commonplaces, namely:

units.la: 1. De natura ejus. 2. De personali unione duarum naturarum 3. de officio ipsius triplici. 4. de beneficiis ipsius, sive benedictionibus spiritualibus quibus nos benedicit Deus pater in Filio suo Iesu Christo.
units.tr: 1. concerning his nature; 2. concerning the personal union of the two natures; 3. concerning his threefold office; 4. concerning his benefits, or the spiritual blessings with which God the Father blesses us in his Son Jesus Christ.

units.la: 9. Ad locum de beneficiis sive benedictionibus Dei in Christo Iesu pertinent inferiores loci de particularibus beneficiis,
units.tr: 9. To the commonplace concerning the benefits or blessings of God in Christ Jesus belong the more subordinate commonplaces concerning particular benefits,

units.la: 1. De praedestinatione hominis ad vitam, sive electione in Christo quae fuit ante tempora saecularia. 2. De vocatione Dei in Christo, quae est in tempore. 3. De justificatione Dei in Christo. 4. De Dei in Christo nostri glorificatione.
units.tr: 1. concerning the predestination of man to life, or election in Christ, which was before the ages of time; 2. concerning the calling of God in Christ, which is in time; 3. concerning the justification of man by God in Christ; 4. concerning the glorification of God in us through Christ.

units.la: 10. Ad locum de Praedestinatione hominis ad vitam pertinet locus de praedestinatione hominis ad mortem, sive de reprobatione
units.tr: 10. To the commonplace concerning the predestination of man to life belongs the commonplace concerning the predestination of man to death, or reprobation.

units.la: 11. Ad locum de Vocatione pertinent plures subalterni alii 1. De Verbo Dei, sive de foedere Dei utroque, tam operum, quam gratiae. 2. De Scriptura sacra. 3. De peccato. 4. De fide. 5. De spe. 6. De Charitate. 7. De resipiscentia. 8. De libero arbitrio, sive de natura hominis. 9. De gratia Dei.
units.tr: 11. To the commonplace concerning Calling belong several subordinate ones: 1. concerning the Word of God, or the covenant of God, both of works and of grace; 2. concerning Holy Scripture; 3. concerning sin; 4. concerning faith; 5. concerning hope; 6. concerning charity; 7. concerning repentance; 8. concerning free will, or the nature of man; 9. concerning the grace of God.

units.la: 12. Ad locum de glorificatione pertinent loci 1. De Regeneratione. 2. De bonis operibus. 3. De merito operum.
units.tr: 12. To the commonplace concerning glorification belong the commonplaces: 1. concerning regeneration; 2. concerning good works; 3. concerning the merit of works.

units.la: 13. His omnibus locis de benedictionibus Dei in Christo Iesu, subjecti sunt loci,
units.tr: 13. Subject to all these commonplaces concerning the blessings of God in Christ Jesus are the commonplaces:

units.la: 1. De Sacramentis, quasi superiorum omnium sigillis. 2. De Ecclesia Dei, quae ex superioribus benedictionibus unacum Sacramentis suis consurgit, & ad quam eae omnes pertinent.
units.tr: 1. concerning the sacraments, as it were the seals of all the foregoing; 2. concerning the Church of God, which arises from the foregoing blessings together with its sacraments, and to which all of them belong.

units.la: 14. Ad locum de Ecclesia spectat locus De Disciplina Ecclesiastica.
units.tr: 14. To the commonplace concerning the Church pertains the commonplace concerning church discipline.

units.la: TRACTATVS DE VOCA- tione efficaci, deq; particularibus aliquot locis theologicis sub ea comprehensis.
units.tr: TREATISE ON EFFECTUAL CALLING, AND ON CERTAIN PARTICULAR THEOLOGICAL TOPICS COMPREHENDED UNDER IT.

units.la: De Vocatione efficaci.
units.tr: On Effectual Calling.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: VOCATIO Dei efficax est qua Deus præscitos ab æterno & prædestinatos ad vitā, ex mera sua gratia per promulgationem fœderis gratuiti sive Evangelij prædicationem,vocat ex tenebris in lucem suâ admirabile,à potestate Satanæ ad Deum,in Christo Iesu ; vocati autem eadem Dei gratia respondent,creduntq; in eum per Iesum Christum. Responsio hæc fidei est, quæ reipsa est conditio promissionis quæ est in fœdere gratuito. Quare efficax vocatio consistit in promissione fœderis quæ fit sub conditione fidei,& in fide, quæ nihil aliud est quā implectio conditionis.
units.tr: God's effectual calling is that by which God, out of his mere grace, calls those foreknown from eternity and predestined to life, by the proclamation of the covenant of grace, or the preaching of the Gospel, from darkness into his marvellous light, from the power of Satan to God, in Christ Jesus. Those who are called, moved by the same grace of God, respond and believe in him through Jesus Christ. This response is faith, which is in fact the condition of the promise contained in the gracious covenant. Therefore effectual calling consists in the promise of the covenant, which is made under the condition of faith, and in faith, which is nothing other than the embracing of that condition.

units.la: Vocationis igitur efficacis duæ sunt partes, prior est externa Dei vocatio prædestinatorum ad vitam, à tenebris ad lucem, idq; ex sola Dei gratia, & per promulgationem fœderis gratuiti sive prædicationem Evangelij. Posterior est interna fides ex eadem Dei gratia sive per Dei Spiritum, à Satana ad Deum: nam posterior Vocationis pars quomodo à fide differat reipsa non video.
units.tr: There are therefore two parts of effectual calling. The first is the external calling of God, by which the predestined are called to life, from darkness to light, and this from the grace of God alone, and through the proclamation of the gracious covenant, or the preaching of the Gospel. The second is the internal faith, from the same grace of God, or through the Spirit of God, by which we turn from Satan to God. For I do not really see how this second part of the calling differs from faith.

units.la: In priore parte Vocationis efficacis primum consideramus personas, vocantem & vocatam; Vocans est Deus proprie solus, qui solus promittit in fœdere suo, qui vocat ea quæ non sunt tanquam sint Rom.4.17. Persona vocata, sunt ij quos præcognovit Deus & prædestinavit ad vitam: Nam quos prædestinavit eos vocavit.Rom. 8. Secundo in prima parte vocationis efficacis habemus causam quæ movit Deum ad vocandum nos. Est autem sola ipsius gratia; nam causa omnium beneficiorum Dei erga nos, est in ipso Deo: Vt enim prædestinavit nos in sese pro benevolo affectu voluntatis suæ. Ephes. 1. 5. Sic vocavit nos in sese, justificavit in sese, glorificavit in sese, ad laudem gloriæ gratiæ suæ, vt ipsi in solidum sit omnis gloria. Tertio habemus instrumentum vocationis, quod quidem est fœdus promulgatum, vel Evangelium prædicatum. Quartò in priore hac parte vocationis efficacis habemus terminos, à quo, et ad què: Terminus à quo sunt tenebræ, potestas Satanæ, miseria illa nostra conditio, quę est extra Christum, posita in peccato & morte: Terminus ad quem est lux, Deus ipse, deniq; beata hominis in Christo conditio. Ex his videmus locum de verbo Dei, item locum de peccato & miseria, subalternos esse loco de vocatione tanquam capiti generalissimo.
units.tr: In the first part of effectual calling we consider first the persons, the one calling and the one called. The one calling is properly God alone, who alone makes promises in his covenant, who calls those things that are not as though they were (Rom.4.17.). The persons called are those whom God foreknew and predestined to life, for whom he predestined, those he also called (Rom. 8.). Second, in the first part of effectual calling we have the cause that moved God to call us. It is solely his grace; for the cause of all God's benefits toward us lies in God himself. For as he predestined us in himself according to the benevolent purpose of his will (Ephes. 1. 5.), so he called us in himself, justified us in himself, glorified us in himself, to the praise of the glory of his grace, so that all glory may belong wholly to him. Third, we have the instrument of calling, which is indeed the covenant proclaimed, or the Gospel preached. Fourth, in this first part of effectual calling we have the termini, from which and to which. The terminus from which is darkness, the power of Satan, that wretched condition of ours which lies outside Christ, placed in sin and death. The terminus to which is light, God himself, and finally the blessed condition of man in Christ. From these points we see that the locus on the Word of God, and likewise the locus on sin and misery, are subordinate to the locus on calling, as to its most general head.

units.la: In posteriore efficacis vocationis parte habemus hæc capita notanda. Primum causam responsionis siue fidei nostræ in Deum, ipsius Dei gratiam, qui fidem hanc intus operatur in nobis per Spiritum sanctum suum cum verbo suo communicatum: Vt enim Deus ex gratia sua vocat nos exterius ad se, ita ex eadem sua gratia in Christo Iesu accendit in nobis fidem eam, qua nos ipsi respondemus.
units.tr: In the second part of effectual calling we have the following heads to note. First, the cause of our response or faith toward God is the grace of God himself, who works this faith within us through his Holy Spirit, communicated together with his Word. For just as God by his grace calls us outwardly to himself, so by that same grace in Christ Jesus he kindles in us that faith by which we ourselves respond.

units.la: In secunda parte vocationis quam in fide ponimus, si lubet eam subtilius distinguere, duplex est Dei gratia sive operatio in cordibus nostris: Prima est dum per Spiritū suum sanctum creat novam & cælestem lucem in mente prius obtenebrata, quæ nec vidit, nec videre potuit ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei. 1.Cor. 2. 15.
units.tr: In the second part of calling, which we place in faith, if it pleases us to distinguish it more finely, there is a twofold grace or operation of God in our hearts. The first is when by his Holy Spirit he creates a new and heavenly light in a mind previously darkened, which neither saw nor could see the things of the Spirit of God (1.Cor. 2. 15.).

units.la: 1.15. Animalis homo non est capax eorum quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, sunt enim ei stultitia, nec potest ea cognoscere. In voluntate prorsus perversa ac a Deo aversa creat rectitudinem, denique in omnibus affectibus novam sanctitatem. Ex hac creatione existit illa nova quæ vocatur creatura, ille novus qui vocatur homo, qui secundum Deum conditus est ad justitiam & sanctimoniaveram. Ephe.4.24.
units.tr: 1.15. The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know them. In a will utterly perverse and turned away from God he creates uprightness, and finally in all the affections a new holiness. From this creation comes that new thing which is called the new creature, that new man who is called man, who is created according to God in righteousness and true holiness (Ephe.4.24.).

units.la: Papistæ hanc primam in fide gratiam et Spiritus sancti operationem vocant non creationem novæ alicujus creaturæ, quæ antea non fuit, sed exsuscitationem bonitatis & sanctitatis, quam dicunt etiam mansisse in natura hominis post lapsum illum primævum, & quam libertatem arbitrij vocant, quam in lapsu non plane interijsse dicunt, sed attenuatam modo & debilitatam fuisse. Atque hæc, quam vocant, libertas arbitrij, nihil est aliud profecto, quam naturæ illa sanctitas & vita Dei, lux spiritualis, quacum creatus est jam olim homo in principio. Sed de ea suo loco erit dicendum. Dicunt igitur post lapsum hominis mansisse non solum facultates animi, sed etiam qualitates sanctas facultatum, sed læsas ac debilitatas. Atque hæc est ipsis illa arbitrij libertas quam dicunt excitari per prævenientem sive operantem gratiam, quam definiunt motionem foris quasi stantem ad ostium cordis, ipsumque pulsantem. In prima gratia, quam dicimus creationem sanctarum in anima qualitatum, homo habet se tantum pathetice, & est tanquam materia. In illa enim prima creatione sive redintegratione omnis boni & sancti in facultatibus animi, quae sancta qualitas esse potest cujus beneficio cooperetur animus cum Spiritu Dei, cum gratia operante? Non tamen dicimus hominem in nova illa creatione habere se ut truncum aut stipitem, quum in anima hominis sit potentia passiua, ut sic dicam, ad recipiendam illam sanctam qualitatem & vitam Dei, sit facultas ac vita rationalis, quae quidem potentia non est in trunco aut stipite. Adversarij autem dicunt in excitatione libertatis arbitrij cooperationem esse ipsius libertatis, quae vel recipit & admittit, vel rejicit illam gratiam, quam dicunt operantem sive praevenientem. Ergo operationem tribuunt gratiae, cooperationem vero libero arbitrio.
units.tr: The Papists call this first grace and operation of the Holy Spirit in faith not the creation of some new creature which previously did not exist, but the rekindling of goodness and holiness, which they say also remained in the nature of man after that first fall, and which they call the freedom of the will. They say that this freedom was not wholly lost in the fall, but only weakened and enfeebled. And indeed this so-called freedom of the will is nothing other than that holiness of nature and life of God, that spiritual light, with which man was created long ago in the beginning. But this will be discussed in its proper place. They say, therefore, that after the fall of man there remained not only the faculties of the soul but also the holy qualities of those faculties, though injured and weakened. And this, they say, is that freedom of the will which is stirred up by prevenient or operating grace, which they define as a motion standing as it were outside the door of the heart and knocking upon it. In the first grace, which we call the creation of holy qualities in the soul, man has himself only passively, and is like matter. For in that first creation, or restoration, of all good and holy things in the faculties of the soul, what holy quality could there be by whose benefit the soul cooperates with the Spirit of God and with operating grace? Yet we do not say that man in that new creation stands like a trunk or a log, since in the soul of man there is a passive power, so to speak, for receiving that holy quality and the life of God, and there is the faculty and rational life, which certainly is not in a trunk or a log. But our opponents say that in the stirring up of the freedom of the will there is a cooperation of that very freedom, which either receives and admits or rejects that grace which they call operating or prevenient. Thus they attribute the operation to grace, but the cooperation to free will.

units.la: Secunda gratia sive secunda Spiritus Dei operatio in secunda vocationis nostri parte, sive in fide, est ipse actus fidei, vel actio promanas a nova illa creatura, metis illuminatae actio in cognoscendo Deum in Christo, voluntatis sanctificatæ actio in amplectendo vel apprehendendo Deum in Christo. Hic agens principalis, siue principaliis operans, est ipse Dei Spiritus, qui potest primam illam gratiam & creatione manet ac habitat in nobis, at manendo non otiatur, sed perpetuò aliquid boni agit & operatur in nobis & per nos. Secundarius agens siue cooperans est ipse animus humanus, vel potius novus homo, et in animo ac facultatibus animi ipsa nova creatura. Per hanc Spiritus S. vt sic dicā, cognoscit, vel quod idem est, in cognoscendo Deum Spiritus sanctus vtitur nova creatura: per hanc Spiritus sanctus Deum in Christo amplectitur atque apprehendit. Sic loquitur Paulus Rom. 8. Spiritus sanctus, inquit, interpellat pro nobis suspirijs inenarrabilibus. Ecce actionem suspirandi Spiritui tribuit, tanquam principali agenti. In hac secunda gratia quæ est actio sive opus fidei, non jam habemus nos ipsi mere pathetice, sed acti per Spiritum sanctū agimus, excitati ad credendū credimus, vno verbo cū operante Spiritu S. cooperamur, ac Spiritus sancti συνεργοι sumus.
units.tr: The second grace, or second operation of the Spirit of God, in the second part of our calling, that is, in faith, is the act of faith itself, or an action proceeding from that new creature: an action of the enlightened mind in knowing God in Christ, an action of the sanctified will in embracing or apprehending God in Christ. Here the principal agent, or principally operating one, is the Spirit of God himself, who, having given that first grace in creation, remains and dwells in us; yet in remaining he is not idle, but continually does and works some good in us and through us. The secondary agent, or cooperating one, is the human soul itself, or rather the new man, and in the soul and faculties of the soul the new creature itself. Through this, the Holy Spirit, so to speak, knows; or, what is the same thing, in knowing God the Holy Spirit makes use of the new creature. Through this, the Holy Spirit embraces and apprehends God in Christ. So Paul speaks (Rom. 8.): "The Spirit himself," he says, "intercedes for us with groanings that cannot be uttered." See how he ascribes the act of groaning to the Spirit as the principal agent. In this second grace, which is the action or work of faith, we are no longer merely passive, but, moved by the Holy Spirit, we act; stirred up to believe, we believe; in a word, we cooperate with the operating Holy Spirit, and are fellow-workers of the Holy Spirit [συνεργοί].

units.la: Adversarij dicunt secundam gratiam in fide esse actionem liberi arbitrij, qua nos per libertatem arbitrij nostri disponimus nos ipfos,& præparamus ad gratiam justificantem, credendo,iperando,pœnitendo.In hac actione principalem agëtem dicunt non Spiritum quidè, vel motionem, vt ipsi loquuntur, Spiritus; verùm libertatem arbitrij,quam dicunt in agendo præire & operari,cum illa motio Dei subsequatur & cooperetur. Nihil hic loquuntur de Dei Spiritu,fiue in prima, fiue in fecunda gratia,qui revera agens est in vtraque sicuti diximus, sed motionem nescio quam foris stantem & pulsantem Spiritus fanêti loco substituunt. Hanc motionem dicunt excitare libertatem arbitrij,hanc dicunt cooperari cum libertate arbitrij jam operante,nofq; ad gratiam justitiæ præparante. Hæc eorum doctrina peregrina est, neq; sapit Scripturam Dei sanctam aut Scripturæ phrafin.Hactenus de gratia Dei in fide,fiue fecunda vocationis nostri parte duplici.
units.tr: Our opponents say that the second grace in faith is an action of free will, by which we, through the freedom of our will, dispose and prepare ourselves for justifying grace, by believing, hoping and repenting. In this action they say the principal agent is not the Spirit, or the motion of the Spirit as they call it, but the freedom of the will, which they say goes before and operates in acting, while that motion of God follows and cooperates. Here they say nothing about the Spirit of God, either in the first or in the second grace, who is in truth the agent in both, as we have said; instead, they substitute in place of the Holy Spirit some motion I know not what, standing outside and knocking. They say this motion stirs up the freedom of the will, and that it cooperates with the freedom of the will already operating, and prepares us for the grace of justification. This doctrine of theirs is foreign, and it has no taste of the holy Scripture of God or of the phrasing of Scripture. Thus far concerning the grace of God in faith, or the twofold second part of our calling.

units.la: Deinde in ea considerandi sunt termini, qui ijdem sunt,qui in vocatione eam antecedente fuerant. Ad hanc fecundam efficacis vocationis partem pertinet Doctrina fidei, quæ reipfa videtur eadem cum ea. Fidem fequuntur Spes, Charitas, Refipifcetia; Resipifcetiæ fubalternus est locus de libero arbitrio.
units.tr: Next, the terms that were in the calling that precedes it must be considered in it. To this second part of effectual calling belongs the doctrine of faith, which in fact seems to be the same as the calling itself. Faith is followed by hope, love and repentance; the topic of free will is subordinate to repentance.

units.la: De verbo Dei siue fœdere in genere, & de fœdere operum in specie. CAP. 2.
units.tr: On the Word of God or covenant in general, and on the covenant of works in particular. CHAP. 2.

units.la: LOco generalissimo de vocatione subalternus est primùm locus de verbo Dei siue fœdere, deinde locus de peccato & miseria hominis, tertio locus de fide, quâ sequuntur spes, charitas, et resipiscentia. Quare nunc de verbo sive fœdere Dei erit dicendum, si primùm de hoc admonuerimus, quod totum verbum Dei ad fœdus aliquod pertineat: nihil enim loquitur Deus homini extra fœdus: Unde à fœdere sive testamento Dei utraque Scriptura & vetus & nova, quæ continetur universum verbum Dei, appellationem suam est sortita.
units.tr: Under the most general topic of calling, the first subordinate topic is the Word of God or covenant, then the topic of sin and the misery of man, and third the topic of faith, which is followed by hope, love and repentance. So now we must speak of the Word of God or covenant, if we first remind ourselves of this: the whole Word of God pertains to some covenant, for God says nothing to man outside a covenant. Hence both Scriptures, the Old and the New, which together make up the whole Word of God, have received their name from the covenant or testament of God.

units.la: Fœdus Dei in genere est promissio sub certa aliqua conditione. Est autem duplex, primum: fœdus operum; secundum, fœdus gratiæ. Paul. Gal. 4. 24. duarum pactionum diserte meminit, quæ in veteri Testamento adumbratæ sunt per duas fœminas tanquam typos, nempe, Hagaram ancillam & Saram liberam. Nam hæ, inquit, sunt duæ illæ pactiones. Nunc igitur de duplici hoc fœdere dicamus quædam, ac primùm de fœdere operum.
units.tr: The covenant of God in general is a promise under some definite condition. It is twofold: first, the covenant of works; second, the covenant of grace. Paul, in Gal. 4. 24., expressly mentions the two agreements which in the Old Testament were foreshadowed by two women as types, namely Hagar the slave woman and Sarah the free woman. For these, he says, are the two agreements. Now, therefore, let us say something about this twofold covenant, and first about the covenant of works.

units.la: Fœdus operum, quod & legale siue naturale vocari potest, fundatum est in natura quæ fuit in creatione pura sanctaque, & in lege Dei, quæ in prima creatione insculpta fuit hominis cordi. Postquàm enim Deus naturam hominis creavit ad imaginem suam puram & sanctam, legemque suam insculpsit menti ipsius, percussit cum homine fœdus, in quo promisit ei vitam æternam sub conditione operum sanctorum & bonorum, quæ nimirum responderent naturæ creatæ sanctitati & bonitati, legiqueipsius essent conformia. Quòd autem natura informata sanctitate, justitia, & legis notitia, fit fundamentum fœderis operum vel ex eo apparet, quòd non stetisset cum justitia Dei percutere fœdus sub conditione bonorum operum & obedientiæ legis perfectæ, nisi ipse naturam priùs creasset bonam sanctamq; , eiq; legem suam insculpsisset, ex qua bona illa opera proficisci oporteret. Quamobrem etiam cum populo Israelitico repetiturus esset fœdus illud operum, primùm dedit legem insculptam tabulis lapideis, deinde percussit cum populo fœdus suum, Facite hæc, inquiens, & vivetis. Ergo fundamentum fœderis operum erat, non quidem Christus, non gratia Dei in Christo, sed natura hominis in prima creatione sancta integra & legis notitia informata. Fœderis enim operum nullus fuit in principio mediator qui intercesssit inter Deum et hominem, ad hoc vt in ipso tanquam mediatore Deus percuteret fœdus suum cum homine. Cur autem mediatore non fuerit opus in causa est, quòd etsi duæ fuerint partes contrahentes, tamen non fuerint inter se diffidentes ita vt ad reconciliationem faciendam opus habuerint mediatore aliquo: Nam in fœdere operum pangendo Deus tanquam amicus cum hominibus tanquā amicis pactus est: In creatione enim fuimus deo amici, non autem inimici. Hactenus de fundamento fœderis operū.
units.tr: The covenant of works, which can also be called legal or natural, is founded on the nature that was pure and holy in creation, and on the law of God, which was engraved on the heart of man in the first creation. For after God had created the nature of man pure and holy in his own image, and had inscribed his law on man's mind, he made a covenant with man, in which he promised him eternal life under the condition of holy and good works, which of course would correspond to the holiness and goodness of created nature and would be in conformity with its law. That nature, endowed with holiness, righteousness and knowledge of the law, is the foundation of the covenant of works is clear from this: God could not in justice have struck a covenant under the condition of good works and perfect obedience to the law, unless he had first created nature good and holy and inscribed his law on it, from which those good works ought to proceed. Therefore, when he was about to renew that covenant of works with the Israelite people, he first gave the law inscribed on tablets of stone, and then struck his covenant with the people, saying, "Do this, and you shall live." So the foundation of the covenant of works was not Christ, nor the grace of God in Christ, but the nature of man, holy and whole in the first creation and informed with knowledge of the law. For in the covenant of works there was at the beginning no mediator who came between God and man, so that God might strike his covenant with man through him as mediator. The reason there was no need of a mediator is that, although there were two contracting parties, they were not at enmity with each other, so that they needed some mediator to bring about reconciliation. For in making the covenant of works God contracted with men as a friend with friends; for at creation we were God's friends, not his enemies. So much concerning the foundation of the covenant of works.

units.la: Quod in fœdere operum promittitur, est vita æterna primùm, non justitia: quia homo in creatione jam justus fuit & integer, cum originali illa, quam vocant, justitia; nisi dicas promissam esse in fœdere operum justitiam factorum & operum, qua Deus homine postquam jam benè operatus esset, justum pronunciasset ac declarasset: Duplex enim est justitia consideranda in fœdere operum, prima est justitia originalis, quæ nihil aliud est quā naturæ sanctitas et habitus quidam. Hæc justitia extra controversiam non est promissa in fœdere operū: fuit enim fœderis fundamentum. Altera justitia est quæ sequitur bona opera naturæ sanctæ & justæ,vocarique potest Iustitia factorum:Postquam enim homo jam bene justeque fecisset secundum justam bonamque naturam, tum iterum quasi justus fuisset, & Deus eum declarasset justum ex bonis operibus factifq; suis Deo gratis & acceptis, atque sic jam justificato dedisset vitam æternam. Paulus enim ad Romanos docet imputationem aliquam justitiæ ex operibus bonis esse,si modo sint opera perfectè bona: Vnde vsurpatæ sunt hæ loquutiones: Abraham non est justificatus ex operibus: Ex operibus nulla caro justificabitur. Hactenus de fœderis operum promissione, siue de rebus promissis in fœdere operum.
units.tr: What is promised in the covenant of works is first eternal life, not righteousness, since man in creation was already just and whole with that so-called original righteousness; unless you say that the righteousness of deeds and works was promised in the covenant of works, by which God, once man had already acted well, would have pronounced and declared him righteous. For there are two kinds of righteousness to consider in the covenant of works. The first is original righteousness, which is nothing other than the holiness of nature and a certain disposition. This righteousness, beyond controversy, was not promised in the covenant of works, for it was the foundation of the covenant. The other righteousness is that which follows good works done by a holy and just nature, and it can be called the righteousness of deeds. For once man had already acted well and justly in accordance with his good and just nature, then in turn he would have been, as it were, just, and God would have declared him righteous on account of the good works and deeds done by him, acceptable and pleasing to God; and so, now justified, God would have given him eternal life. For Paul in the letter to the Romans teaches that there is some imputation of righteousness from good works, provided that the works are perfectly good. Hence these expressions have been used: "Abraham was not justified by works"; "by works no flesh shall be justified." So much concerning the promise of the covenant of works, or the things promised in the covenant of works.

units.la: Nunc videamus ipsius conditionem. Fœderis operum códitio est operum bonorum; operum, inquam, bonorum proficiscentium non à Christo vel gratia Christi, sed à natura sola integra, legis notitia informata,perfectèque bona, qualis fuit in creatione: proficiscētium videlicet ab ipso fœderis operum fundamento. Ergo opera merè naturaliter bona duntaxat requiruntur, tanquam conditio in fœdere operum.
units.tr: Now let us see its condition. The condition of the covenant of works is good works: good works, I say, proceeding not from Christ or the grace of Christ, but from nature alone, whole, informed with knowledge of the law, and perfectly good, such as it was in creation; that is, proceeding from the very foundation of the covenant of works. Therefore only works that are purely naturally good are required, as the condition in the covenant of works.

units.la: Ergo hac conditione excludis fidem Chrifti? Excludo. An excludis quoque hac conditione à fœdere operum, opera gratiæ & regenerationis? Excludo quoque. At fœdus operum passim in Evangelio proponitur ijs qui sunt sub gratia & in Christo Iesu? Quoties enim benefacientibus promittitur merces vitæ æternæ? Ergo in fœdere operum intelligenda quoque sunt opera Regenerationis, quum istiusmodi opera requiruntur ab ijs qui sunt sub gratia? Respondeo, antecedens salsum esse: Nam si quando audimus vel legimus in Evangelio gratiæ, bona opera requiri ab ijs qui in Christo sunt, & ab ipso jam justificati sunt, in eum scilicet finem ut vitam consequatur æterna, non est putandum agi cum ijs ex formula fœderis operum; quia in Evangelio ab ijs qui in Christo sunt, requiruntur bona opera, non quæ ex natura vel naturæ viribus proficiscuntur, sed tantum quæ promanant ex gratia regenerationis. Nusquam enim legimus in novo Testamento eos qui in Christo sunt vrgeri ad opera illa fœderis operum quæ naturaliter bona sunt, aut ijs etiam proponi fœdus illud operum ut per ipsum & ipsius opera quæ naturaliter bona sunt vitam consequantur. Non enim leges vsquā dictum iis qui sunt in Christo: Facite hoc vestris viribus freti ut vivatis: quæ revera est sententia fœderis operum.
units.tr: Do you then exclude faith in Christ by this condition? I exclude it. Do you also exclude from the covenant of works, by this condition, the works of grace and regeneration? I exclude them too. But the covenant of works is set forth everywhere in the Gospel to those who are under grace and in Christ Jesus. For how often is the reward of eternal life promised to those who do good? Therefore in the covenant of works the works of regeneration must also be understood, since such works are required of those who are under grace? I answer that the antecedent is false. For when we hear or read in the Gospel of grace that good works are required of those who are in Christ and have already been justified by him, namely in order that they may obtain eternal life, we should not think that this is done according to the formula of the covenant of works. For in the Gospel the good works required of those who are in Christ are not those which proceed from nature or its powers, but only those which flow from the grace of regeneration. For we never read in the New Testament that those who are in Christ are urged to those works of the covenant of works which are naturally good, nor that that covenant of works is set before them, so that through it and its works, which are naturally good, they may obtain life. For nowhere do you read that it is said to those who are in Christ: "Do this, trusting in your own strength, that you may live," which is indeed the sense of the covenant of works.

units.la: Nam quod ad illum locum, Math. 19. 17. in quo Christus dixit juveni cuidā, qui compellavit eum dicens: Magister quid boni faciam ut habeam vitā æternam; respondit autem Dominus ac dixit, Si vis ad vitam ingredi serva mandata: fateor equidem illo in loco agi de fœdere operum, et à Domino ibi propositam esse juveni fœderis operum formulam. Verùm sic respondit Dominus ei qui quærebat sibi vitam ex lege, & adhæsit fœderi operum, imò præsidebat operibus tanquam meritis. Cuivis autem qui est extra Christum, quæritque justitiam ex lege & operibus legis, proponenda est pactio operum legalium simul & norma legis operum, eo scilicet fine, ut si possit fieri, præparetur sensu peccati & miseriæ suæ ad fœdus gratiæ in Christo amplectendum. Dixit enim Iuvenis ille Domino, ut ad verba ipsius redeam, Quid boni faciam? Ergo quærebat vitam æternam ex factis, non ex fide Christi. Respondit itaque Dominus accommodate ad quæstionem ab ipso propositam: Fac hoc & vives: Quæ formula nunquam proponi solet in Evangelio ijs, qui semel Christum
units.tr: As for that passage, Matt. 19. 17., where Christ said to a certain young man who addressed him, "Teacher, what good shall I do that I may have eternal life?", and the Lord answered and said, "If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments": I grant that in that place there is a discussion of the covenant of works, and that the Lord there set before the young man the formula of the covenant of works. But the Lord answered in this way the man who was seeking life for himself from the law, and who clung to the covenant of works, indeed who relied on works as merits. But to anyone who is outside Christ and seeks righteousness from the law and the works of the law, the agreement of works and the rule of the law of works must be set forth, with the aim, if it were possible, that he be prepared, by a sense of his sin and misery, to embrace the covenant of grace in Christ. For that young man said to the Lord (to return to his words), "What good shall I do?" So he was seeking eternal life from deeds, not from faith in Christ. The Lord therefore answered in a way suited to the question he had put: "Do this and you shall live." This formula is never set before those in the Gospel who have already embraced and professed Christ. For from them those natural good works are never required by the formula of the covenant of works, nor are promises made to them under the condition of those works.

units.la: { } ftum sunt amplexi & professi: Nam ab ijs opera illa naturæ bona nunquam requiruntur ex formula fœderis operum, neque etiam promissiones sunt ijs factæ sub conditione istorum operum.
units.tr: ...who have embraced and professed (Christ). For those works of nature are never required of them under the formula of the covenant of works, nor are promises made to them on condition of those works.

units.la: Requiruntur quidem fateor bona opera ab ijs qui jā in Christo sunt, & justificati sunt: sed ea sunt opera gratiæ & Regenerationis omnia, & quidem solius gratiæ, non etiam liberi, vt vocant, arbitrij, vel naturæ bona opera: vt scias ijs qui jam in Christo sunt hactenus abolitum esse fœdus illud operum, quatenus per id vel justificatio vel salus obtinetur. Manet quidem, fateor, lex quæ est norma illorum operum proprie & primò, eorum, inquam, quæ requirebatur in fœdere operum; sed jam alium quendam vsum habet, manetque nunc vt norma & regula operum gratiæ & sanctificationis: Cessavit ergo lex, vt norma est operum naturæ ex formula fœderis operum, manet vero ijs qui in Christo sunt vt est regula operum gratiæ. Eadem enim Dei justitia perpetuò manet sui similis: Lex autem Dei est imago quædam justitiæ divinæ: Ergo lex Dei necesse est maneat in perpetuum, licet non semper eundem vsum obtinens, & eorundem operum regula & norma permanens, mens. Sed de hoc postea fufius erit dicedum.
units.tr: I admit that good works are indeed required of those who are now in Christ and justified; but all of these are works of grace and regeneration, and indeed of grace alone, not also of so-called free will or of good works of nature. You should know that for those who are now in Christ the covenant of works has been abolished, so far as justification or salvation is obtained through it. I admit that the law, which is the rule of those works properly and primarily (I mean those that were required in the covenant of works), remains; but it now has another use, and it remains as the norm and rule of the works of grace and sanctification. So the law has ceased as the norm of the works of nature under the formula of the covenant of works, but it remains for those who are in Christ as the rule of the works of grace. For the same justice of God remains ever like itself, and the law of God is a certain image of divine justice. Therefore the law of God must necessarily remain forever, though not always holding the same use, and remaining the rule and norm of the same works. But this will be discussed more fully later.

units.la: Hic quaeritur, an in foedere operum requisita sunt ab homine opera bona in creatione prima, tanquam vitae promissae meritoria? Respondeo, minime id quidem: sed requisita sunt ab homine in creatione tantum vt officia gratitudinis erga Creatorem, propter illud creationis bonum, ad glorificandum videlicet Deum Creatorem. At inquies, Paulus ad Rom. quum disputat adversus opera naturae, (nam in illa ad Rom. Epistola praecipue adversus hoc genus operum disputat) disputat, inquam, adversus ea vt merita, non tantum vt gratitudinis officia ac testimonia. Ergo verifimile est praescripta fuisse homini in creatione vt meritoria? Respondeo, Paulus ibi exagitat quidem ea vt merita, sed id facit non ex sensu suo, verum ex hypothesi Iudaeorum, qui eo caecitatis sunt prolapsi, vt opera naturaliter bona putarint non tantum bona esse & justa: sed etiam meritoria esse justitiae & vitae. Sed de hac caecitate Iudaeorum dicemus postea fufius. Haftenus de conditione foederis operum, et omnino de foedere operum pro ratione nostri instituti.
units.tr: Here the question is whether, in the covenant of works, good works were required of man in the first creation as meritorious of the promised life. I answer: certainly not. They were required of man in creation only as duties of gratitude toward the Creator, on account of that good of creation, namely to glorify God the Creator. But you will object that when Paul in Romans argues against the works of nature (for in that Epistle to the Romans he disputes chiefly against this kind of works), he argues against them as merits, not merely as duties and evidences of gratitude. Is it therefore probable that they were prescribed to man in creation as meritorious? I answer: Paul there indeed assails them as merits, but he does so not from his own view, but from the hypothesis of the Jews, who had fallen into such blindness that they thought naturally good works were not only good and just, but also meritorious of righteousness and life. But we shall speak more fully of this blindness of the Jews later. Thus far concerning the condition of the covenant of works, and in general concerning the covenant of works as far as our purpose requires.

units.la: mens. Sed de hoc postea fufius erit dicedum.
units.tr: mind. But this will be discussed more fully later.

units.la: De Fœdere gratuito. CAP. 3.
units.tr: On the Gratuitous Covenant. CHAP. 3.

units.la: IN Fœdere quod vocant gratuitum vel Evangelicum, fundamentum primum est Mediator Iesus Christus, atque is crucifixus & mortuus: vel, quod idem est, sanguis mediatoris, cujus quidem efficacia est duplex: prima est ad satisfaciendum justitiæ & iræ Dei adversus peccata nostra, & propter violatum jam fœdus illud operum. Secunda est ad promerendum novam Dei gratiam & misericordiam erga nos. Atque hæc gratia sive misericordia Dei quæ profluit ex sanguine mediatoris secundum est fundamentum fœderis gratuiti, quo reconciliamur Deo, & cum eo in gratiam redimus. Fundamentum igitur proximum & immediatum fœderis gratuiti, est mera Dei gratia vel potius misericordia, quæ præsupponit hominum miseriam, non autem natura, aut aliquid in natura boni: cum naturæ bonitas jam post violatum fœdus illud operum plane perdita sit, hoc est, natura quod ad sanctitatem, justitiam, & sapientiam attinet amissa est: Nam libertate arbitrij, hoc est, naturæ bonitatem & sanctitatem, attenuatam tamen & debilitatam, ut isti loquuntur, in natura ra corrupta non agnoscimus. Atque hæc de fundamento fœderis gratuiti. Super hoc fundamentum primùm sanguinis Christi, deinde misericordiæ Dei, exstructum est fœdus illud quod vocant gratuitum.
units.tr: In the covenant which they call gratuitous or evangelical, the first foundation is the Mediator Jesus Christ, crucified and dead; or, which is the same thing, the blood of the Mediator, whose efficacy is twofold. The first is to satisfy the justice and wrath of God against our sins, and because that covenant of works has already been violated. The second is to merit for us a new grace and mercy of God. This grace or mercy of God, which flows from the blood of the Mediator, is the second foundation of the gratuitous covenant, by which we are reconciled to God and brought back into favour with him. The proximate and immediate foundation of the gratuitous covenant, therefore, is the sheer grace, or rather mercy, of God, which presupposes man's misery and not nature, or anything good in nature; for the goodness of nature was utterly lost after that covenant of works was violated; that is, nature has lost what pertains to holiness, justice and wisdom. For we do not acknowledge in corrupt nature a freedom of the will, that is, a goodness and holiness of nature, though, as they put it, attenuated and weakened. These things are said concerning the foundation of the gratuitous covenant. Upon this foundation, first the blood of Christ and then the mercy of God, that covenant which they call gratuitous has been built.

units.la: Promittitur in fœdere gratuito primùm justitia, quam quidem necesse fuit primùm promitti, quia jam violato fœdere operum plané amissa & deperdita fuit originalis illa, quam vocant, justitia, & in ejus locum subingressa est injustitia. Iustitia autem ea quæ primùm omnium in fœdere gratuito promittitur, non est inhærens aliqua, qualis fuit illa originalis: sed justitia est ipsius mediatoris Christi, quæ nostra fit per fidem & imputationem Dei, unde justitia Dei vocatur ab Apostolo: Nam sine hac justitia quâ imputatam dicimus non possumus omninò consistere coram illo tribunali: per hujus autem justitiæ imputationem justificari dicimur coram Deo. Post hanc justitiam quæ consistit in imputatione, in fœdere gratuito promittitur deinde inhærens quædam justitia, & naturæ sanctitas atque bonitas, qualis in lapsu hominis deperdita est, in hac quidem vita inchoanda, in altera verò perficienda. Atque justitia hæc inhærens nihil aliud est quam vita nostra æterna, quæ in terris inchoatur, in cœlis autem perficitur: fluitque vita hæc cœlestis & spiritualis ex illa Christi justitia quæ nobis per fidem imputatur: nam Christi illa justitia ad vitā æternam in nobis est efficax per Christi Spiritum sanctificantem & vivificantem. Atque hæc de promissione quæ est in fœdere gratuito.
units.tr: In the gratuitous covenant, first of all righteousness is promised. This had necessarily to be promised first, because that original righteousness, as they call it, was utterly lost and destroyed once the covenant of works was violated, and injustice has entered in its place. But the righteousness which is promised first of all in the gratuitous covenant is not some inherent righteousness, such as that original one was; it is the righteousness of the Mediator Christ himself, which becomes ours through faith and the imputation of God, whence the Apostle calls it the righteousness of God. For without this righteousness, which we say is imputed, we cannot at all stand before that tribunal; and through the imputation of this righteousness we are said to be justified before God. After this righteousness, which consists in imputation, there is promised in the gratuitous covenant, next, a certain inherent righteousness and the holiness and goodness of nature, such as was lost in man's fall: to be begun in this life, but to be perfected in the next. And this inherent righteousness is nothing other than our eternal life, which is begun on earth and perfected in heaven; and this heavenly and spiritual life flows from that righteousness of Christ which is imputed to us through faith, for the righteousness of Christ is efficacious in us for eternal life through the sanctifying and quickening Spirit of Christ. These things are said concerning the promise which is in the gratuitous covenant.

units.la: Reliquum est ut videamus fœderis gratuiti conditionem. Nomen ipsum fœderis gratuiti nullam videtur fœderis conditionem præ se ferre: nam fœdus gratuitum ideo dicitur quòd Deus gratis, hoc est, ut videtur, citra omnem conditionem promittat nobis justitiam & vitam, nam qui gratis se daturum aliquid promittit, is nullam conditionem stipulatur. Sed verbum gratuiti, vel particula gratis, non excludit plane omnem conditionem: verùm eam tantùm conditionem excludit quæ est in fœdere operum, hoc est, conditionem virium naturæ, & operum naturaliter bonorum ac justorum, quæ omninò non possunt consistere cum gratia Dei in Christo Iesu. Neque enim libertas ista arbitrij, quæ importat aliquam naturæ puritatem & sanctitatem, neque etiam opera liberi arbitrij, quæ vocant, possunt cohærere cum gratia Dei in Christo Iesu. Quam igitur, inquies, admittit illud verbum (gratuiti, vel gratis) conditione in fœdere gratuito: Respondeo non aliam profecto quam eam, quæ potest consistere cum Christo & mera Dei gratia: Ea autem sola est fides, quæ & ex gratia est (gratuitum enim est Dei donum. Philip. 1.29. datum est vobis non solum in eum credere, sed etiam pro eo affligi) & pro obiecto suo habet, primum Christum, deinde misericordiam Dei in Christo Iesu: Fides enim amplectitur misericordiam Dei in Christo, & in nobis facit Christum efficacem ad justitiam & ad vitam. Ideo Paulus Rom. 4. 6. ex fide dicit hereditatem esse, ut sit per gratiam: & Ephes. 2. 8. Gratia estis servati per fidem, idque non ex vobis: hoc est, ut ipse exponit postea, non ex operibus: Ex quo colligit salutem, quia ipsa est ex gratia Dei per fidem, merum Dei donum esse. Quamobrem cum gratia & misericordia Dei fides optime consistit, utpote sine qua non posset Christus & misericordia Dei in ipso efficax esse ad justitiam & ad vitam: Nisi enim fide recipiatur Christus & Dei in ipso misericordia, Christus & misericordia Dei in ipso nihil nobis ad justificationem & vitam prodesse possent.
units.tr: It remains for us to see the condition of the gratuitous covenant. The very name "gratuitous covenant" seems to show no condition of the covenant: for the covenant is called gratuitous because God promises us righteousness and life freely, that is, as it seems, without any condition at all; for whoever promises to give something freely stipulates no condition. But the word "gratuitous," or the particle "freely," does not exclude every condition altogether; it excludes only that condition which belongs to the covenant of works, that is, the condition of the powers of nature and of works that are naturally good and just, which cannot at all cohere with the grace of God in Christ Jesus. For neither that freedom of the will, which implies some purity and holiness of nature, nor the so-called works of free will can cohere with the grace of God in Christ Jesus. You will ask, then, what condition that word (gratuitous, or freely) admits in the gratuitous covenant? I answer: certainly none other than that which can stand together with Christ and the sheer grace of God; and that is faith alone, which also comes from grace (for it is the gift of God: Philippians 1:29, "it has been given to you not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him"), and which has for its object, first, Christ, and then the mercy of God in Christ Jesus. For faith embraces the mercy of God in Christ, and in us makes Christ efficacious for righteousness and life. Therefore Paul says (Rom. 4.6) that the inheritance is of faith, so that it might be by grace; and (Eph. 2.8) "By grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves": that is, as he himself explains afterwards, not of works. From this he concludes that salvation, because it is of the grace of God through faith, is the pure gift of God. Wherefore faith agrees very well with the grace and mercy of God, since without it Christ and the mercy of God in him could not be efficacious for righteousness and life. For unless Christ and the mercy of God in him are received by faith, Christ and the mercy of God in him could profit us nothing for justification and life.

units.la: Hic tamen notandum est Deum, qui promittit justitiam & vitam sub conditione fidei, non tam habere rationem fidei quae in nobis est, idque ex Dei dono, quam objecti, hoc est, Christi & misericordiae ipsius Dei, quae fide apprehendenda est: Nam non tam fides nostra apprehendens, quam Christus ipse, cum misericordia Dei in ipso, fide apprehensus, causa est cur Deus impleat foederis promissionem in nobis justificandis & servandis. Quare conditio foederis gratuiti non est fides sola, nec objectum fidei solum, quod est Christus, sed est fides cum Christo, hoc est, fides Christum apprehensura, vel Christus cum fide, hoc est, Christus fide apprehendendus.
units.tr: Here, however, it must be noted that God, who promises righteousness and life under the condition of faith, has regard not so much to the faith that is in us (though that too is God's gift) as to its object, namely Christ and the mercy of God himself, which is to be laid hold of by faith. For it is not so much our faith laying hold of Christ as Christ himself, with the mercy of God in him, laid hold of by faith, that is the cause why God fulfils the promise of the covenant in justifying and saving us. So the condition of the gratuitous covenant is not faith alone, nor the object of faith alone, which is Christ, but faith together with Christ, that is, faith that is about to lay hold of Christ, or Christ together with faith, that is, Christ to be laid hold of by faith.

units.la: Quamobrem illud semel notandum, idem esse re hęc tria, foederis gratuiti fundamentum, foederis gratuiti conditionem, denique causam cur impleat Deus foederis gratuiti promissionem: Ratione tamen differentia est inter haec aliqua: Nam Iesus Christus est fundamentum ut absolute consideratur, citra applicationem aliquam quae fit ad nos; Est autem conditio foederis Christus ut ad nos applicandus & fide apprehendendus est: Conditio enim omnis est rei futurae & praestandae: Causa denique cur impleatur promissio foederis, est Iesus Christus ut jam per fidem applicatus est & apprehensus. Quum igitur dicit nos Paulus fide justificari, sensus est, nos justificari per Christum fide jam applicatum nobis in efficaci vocatione, quæ beneficium justificationis ordine naturæ antecedit.
units.tr: On this point we should note once for all that these three things are the same in reality: the foundation of the gratuitous covenant, the condition of the gratuitous covenant, and finally the cause why God fulfils the promise of the gratuitous covenant. Yet by reason of difference there is some distinction between them. For Jesus Christ is the foundation considered absolutely, apart from any application made to us. Christ is the condition of the covenant insofar as he is to be applied to us and laid hold of by faith, since every condition concerns a thing future and still to be performed. Finally, the cause why the promise of the covenant is fulfilled is Jesus Christ as already applied and apprehended through faith. Therefore, when Paul says that we are justified by faith, the sense is that we are justified through Christ, already applied to us by faith in effectual calling, which in the order of nature precedes the benefit of justification.

units.la: Quæritur hîc, an non in conditione fœderis gratuiti aliquam partem habeant opera gratiæ & regenerationis, quæ vocatur: exclusa enim jam sunt opera naturæ bona omnia. Respondeo ne opera quidem regenerationis contineri in conditione fœderis gratuiti. Primum enim fœdus gratuitum percutitur cum injustis & non regenitis; quæ autem possunt esse opera injustorum & non regenitorum bona & justa? Deinde in fœdere gratuito promittitur ipsa regeneratio vnà cum omnibus bonis sanctisq; suis operibus: nam in fœdere gratuito promittuntur omnia dona Christi, promittitur omnis gratia credentibus: Promissio autè fœderis necesse est differat à conditione fœderis.
units.tr: Here it is asked whether the works of grace and of regeneration, as it is called, have no part in the condition of the gratuitous covenant, since all the good works of nature have already been excluded. I answer that not even the works of regeneration are included in the condition of the gratuitous covenant. First, because the gratuitous covenant is struck with the unrighteous and the unregenerate; but what good and just works can the unrighteous and the unregenerate have? Second, because in the gratuitous covenant regeneration itself is promised, together with all its good and holy works; for in the gratuitous covenant all the gifts of Christ are promised, and all grace is promised to believers. But the promise of the covenant must necessarily differ from the condition of the covenant.

units.la: At, inquies, pluribus in locis novi Testamenti promittitur vita æterna siue merces, vt vocatur, vitæ æternæ, sub conditione bonorum operum, hoc est, operum Regenerationis, vt 1.Timoth. 4. Pietas ad omnia est vtilis, habens promissiones et hujus et futuræ vitæ, Retribuetur tibi in resurrectione justorum. Merces vestra est copiosa in coelis. Non perdet mercedem suam. Bonum faciendo non fatigemur, tempore enim suo metemus non defatigati. Scientes quod quisque fecerit boni, hoc reportabit à Deo. Non injustus est Deus ut obliviscatur operis vestri, & dilectionis quam ministrastis sanctis. Tamen justum est apud Deum retribuere ijs vicissim qui affligunt vos, afflictione: vobis vero qui affligimini relaxationem nobiscum.
units.tr: But, you will say, in many places of the New Testament eternal life, or what is called the reward of eternal life, is promised under the condition of good works, that is, of the works of regeneration; as in 1.Timoth. 4. "Godliness is profitable for all things, having promises of this life and of that which is to come." "It shall be repaid to you at the resurrection of the just. Your reward is great in heaven." He will not lose his reward. Let us not be weary in doing good, for in due time we shall reap, if we do not faint. Knowing that whatever good each one does, he will receive the same from the Lord. God is not unjust, so as to forget your work and the love you have shown to the saints. Yet it is just before God to repay with affliction those who afflict you, and to give relief to you who are afflicted, along with us.

units.la: Ad haec respondeo: Ut quidem mihi videtur, in novo Testamento tria promissionum genera distincta sese offerunt. Primum est ipsa promissio foederis operum, in qua promittitur vita aeterna sub conditione operum ex naturae viribus proficiscentium. Secundum est promissio foederis gratuiti quae fit sub conditione fidei. Tertium genus promissionum efficiunt promissiones, ut sic eas appellem, particulares & subservientes foederi gratuito, quae passim inveniuntur in Evangelio sub conditione operum gratiae & regenerationis factae.
units.tr: To this I answer: as it seems to me, in the New Testament three distinct kinds of promises present themselves. The first is the promise of the covenant of works itself, in which eternal life is promised under the condition of works proceeding from the powers of nature. The second is the promise of the gratuitous covenant, which is made under the condition of faith. The third kind of promises consists of promises, if I may so call them, particular and subordinate to the gratuitous covenant, which are found everywhere in the Gospel under the condition of works of grace and of regeneration.

units.la: Haec tria promissionum genera differunt primum conditione, secundo proprietate, tertio tertiò subjecto, quartò fine & vsu. Primùm igitur conditione differunt,quia promissio in fœdere operum fit sub conditione operum naturæ & naturæ virium; in fœdere gratiæ promissio fit sub conditione fidei in Christum;in promissionibus illis quas dixi particulares, conditio est operum quidem, sed operum gratiæ & regenerationis, non autem naturæ vel virium quarumcunque naturæ.
units.tr: These three kinds of promises differ first in their condition, second in their property, third in their subject, and fourth in their end and use. First, then, they differ in condition: the promise in the covenant of works is made under the condition of works of nature and of natural powers; in the covenant of grace the promise is made under the condition of faith in Christ; in those particular promises which I have mentioned, the condition is indeed of works, but of works of grace and regeneration, not of nature or of any natural powers whatsoever.

units.la: Deinde proprietate differunt,quia promissio in fœdere operū, est merè legalis atq; habet conditione operum quæ tantùm existunt ex naturæ viribus,quæ lege præcipiuntur,& quorum Lex Dei norma est atq; regula: Opera autem naturæ vel naturalium virium, dicuntur proprie opera legis. Rom.9.32. Promissio autem in fœdere gratuito non est legalis,sed merè Evangelica,quia conditio in fœdere gratuito non est operis alicujus moralis & naturalis,sed fidei in Christum, adeòq; ipsius Christi fide apprehendendi. Denique promissiones illæ particulares partim sunt Evangelicæ,partim legales: Nam conditio est operum quæ sunt ex gratia & regeneratione, ac proinde quæ ratione sui principij Evangelica vocari possunt: quia tamen eorum ipsorum operum norma est lex moralis, ideo legalia etiam opera vocari possunt.
units.tr: Second, they differ in property, because the promise in the covenant of works is purely legal and has as its condition works that exist only from the powers of nature, which the law prescribes, and of which the law of God is the norm and rule. Works of nature, or of natural powers, are properly called works of the law (Rom.9.32.). But the promise in the gratuitous covenant is not legal but purely evangelical, because the condition of the gratuitous covenant is not any moral and natural work, but faith in Christ, and so the laying hold of Christ himself by faith. Finally, those particular promises are partly evangelical and partly legal.
