For their condition is works that arise from grace and regeneration, and which, by reason of their principle, can therefore be called evangelical; yet because the moral law is the norm of those very works, they may also be called legal works.

units.la: Differunt subjecto, quia promissio in foedere operum proponitur ijs qui post violatum illud primum foedus, quod est operum, jam mortui jacent in peccatis & offensis suis, interea autem nullum adhuc sensum habent peccati & mortis. Promissio vero in foedere gratiae proponitur quidem ijs, qui mortui quidem sunt in peccatis & offensis, sed sensum habent peccati, mortis, & miseriae, excitatum jam per legem & foedus legale. Denique promissiones illae particulares proponuntur jis qui jam per fidem Christi justificati sunt & renati.
units.tr: They differ in subject, because the promise in the covenant of works is put forward to those who, after that first covenant, which was of works, had been violated, lie dead already in their sins and offences, and meanwhile have as yet no sense of sin and death. But the promise in the covenant of grace is put forward to those who are indeed dead in sins and offences, but have a sense of sin, death and misery, already stirred up through the law and the legal covenant. Finally, those particular promises are put forward to those who have already been justified and born again through faith in Christ.

units.la: Postremo differunt usu & fine, quia foederis operum propositi & expositi finis est, ut peccatores & miseri qui sine sensu sunt peccati & miseriae suae, excitetur ad agnoscendum & sentiendum peccatum & miseriam suam, hoc est (quod dicit Paulus Rom. 7. p. 10.) ut peccatum revivisca t, ipsi vero moriantur, id est, sentiant se mortuos esse in peccatis & ofsensis. De hoc fine leges plurimis aliis in locis, ut Rom. 3. 19. 20. & 11. 32. Gal. 3. 22. & 5. 23. Hic enim usus est foederis operum, ad ingignendum sensum peccati & miseriae, & ad homines ad gratiam recipiendam praeparados. Ideo doctrina evangelica initium sumit a doctrina strina fœderis operum & legis moralis; Frustrà enim in fœdere Evangelico justitia & vita credentibus proponitur,nisi priùs sensu injustitiæ suæ & præsentis mortis præpārētur ad audiendum & recipiendum fœdus Evangelicum. Ideò ipse Christus primùm Math. 5.17. & deinceps, legem vindicat, expurgatque à fermento Pharisæorum & ipsius ἀκριβείας exponit,eo videlicet fine,vt homines primùm omnium agnoscerent ex doctrina fœderis operum & legis moralis quàm miseri essent natura, & hoc cognito præparārēntur ad fœdus gratuitum. Math. 19. Christus sic juvenem illum divite, qui ad ipsum venit discēdi causa,vt præ se ferebat, præparavit ad fœdus gratiæ recipiendum; Vis, inquiens, ad vitam ingredi serva mandata. Paulus doctrinam suam in Epistola ad Romanos à fœdere operum & legis exorsus est,in eaque doctrina tria fere prima Epistolæ suæ capita insumpsit, in eum scilicet finem, vt omnes sub peccato & condemnatione concluderet, atque ita præpararet ad doctrinam fœderis gratuiti, quam inchoat Rom. 3.21. Gal.4.21. Galatas qui voluerunt esse sub lege,vt ipse loquitur,docet servitutem illam miseram,& tandem ejectionem ex regno Dei eorum omnium, qui sunt sub lege: eo, videlicet, fine, vt Galatæ renuncian< tes justitiæ quæ est ex lege et fœdere operum, consectarentur justitiam, quæ est ex fide & fœdere gratuito. Sed multa occurrunt hujus rei documeta quib. nos nunc supersedemus.
units.tr: Lastly, they differ in use and end, because the end of the covenant of works, as set forth and explained, is that sinners and wretched persons, who have no sense of their sin and misery, should be roused to acknowledge and feel their sin and misery, that is (as Paul says, Rom. 7. p. 10.) that sin might revive, while they themselves die, that is, feel themselves to be dead in sins and offences. Concerning this end you may read in many other places, such as Rom. 3. 19. 20. & 11. 32. Gal. 3. 22. & 5. 23. For this is the use of the covenant of works: to beget a sense of sin and misery, and to prepare men to receive grace. Therefore the evangelical doctrine takes its beginning from the doctrine of the covenant of works and of the moral law. For it would be in vain for justification and life to be offered to believers in the Evangelical covenant unless men were first prepared, by a sense of their own unrighteousness and of their present death, to hear and receive the Evangelical covenant. Therefore Christ himself first vindicates the law (Math. 5.17.) and thereafter cleanses it of the leaven of the Pharisees and expounds its strictness [ἀκριβείας], clearly with this end: that men might first of all learn from the doctrine of the covenant of works and of the moral law how wretched they were by nature, and, this being known, be prepared for the gratuitous covenant. In Math. 19. Christ thus prepared the rich young man, who came to him, as he professed, for the sake of learning, to receive the covenant of grace: "If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments." Paul began his doctrine in the Epistle to the Romans from the covenant of works and the law, and in that doctrine he took up nearly the first three chapters of his Epistle, with this end: that he might shut up all under sin and condemnation, and so prepare them for the doctrine of the gratuitous covenant, which he begins at Rom. 3.21. Gal.4.21. In Galatians, those who wished to be under the law, as he himself puts it, he teaches that wretched servitude and at last the expulsion from the kingdom of God of all who are under the law; clearly with this end: that the Galatians, renouncing the righteousness which is from the law and the covenant of works, might pursue the righteousness which is from faith and the gratuitous covenant. But many proofs of this matter present themselves, which we now pass over.

units.la: Finis deinde vsusque promissionis in fœdere gratuito, est vt homines jam dejecti & prostrati sensu peccati & miseriæ suæ, per legem & fœdus legale, erigantur & consolationem accipiant, audita illa justitia & vita, quæ gratis promittitur et offertur credentibus, in fœdere gratuito. De hoc fine lege. Rom.5. Iustificati ergo ex fide pacem habemus erga Deum. Hic finis Evangelicæ doctrinæ proprius est; ideoque secunda et potissima pars Evangelicæ doctrinæ cernitur in doctrina fœderis gratiæ, quæ etiam proprie & præcipue doctrina Evangelica appellanda est, vt quæ sit de Christo mediatore, de ipsius humiliatione primum, deinde glorificatione, denique de beneficijs Christi, de vita & justitia per ipsum, in quibus cernitur Evangelium, & læetum illud salutis nuncium.
units.tr: The next end and use of the promise in the covenant of grace is that people already cast down and prostrated by the sense of their sin and wretchedness, under the law and the legal covenant, should be raised up and receive consolation, once they hear that righteousness and life which are freely promised and offered to believers in the covenant of grace. On this end see Rom.5. "Therefore, being justified by faith, we have peace with God." This end is proper to the Evangelical doctrine. Hence the second and chief part of the Evangelical doctrine is found in the doctrine of the covenant of grace, which should also properly and especially be called the Evangelical doctrine, since it concerns Christ the Mediator: first his humiliation, then his glorification, and finally the benefits of Christ, and life and righteousness through him. In these the Gospel and that joyful message of salvation are found.

units.la: Denique promissionum particularium finis est, vt justificati, renati, erecti, & pacati jam conscientijs, gratitudinem suam sanctis bonisque operibus testatam faciant. Hunc finem nem ostendit Apostolus, Tit. 2. 11. 12. Illuxit enim gratia illa Dei salutifera omnibus hominibus, erudiens nos, vt abnegata impietate & mundanis cupiditatibus, temperàter, juste, et pie vivamus in præsenti sæculo.' Hic cum sit finis harum promissionum, habet ipsæ locum in tertia parte doctrinæ Evangelicæ, quæ est de sanctis & Christianis moribus; vnde videas promissiones has passim commisceri cum exhortationibus, admonitionibus, & præceptionibus, quæ fiunt in doctrina illa paraenetica quę est de moribus: vt Gal. 6. postquam versu 6. præcepit vt qui instituitur in sermone, communicet ei qui ipsum instituit omnia bona: deinde versu 7. & 8. subjicit promissionem simul & comminationem. Ibidem versu 9. postquam præcepit non esse segnescendum benefaciendo, subjecit promissionem; Tempore suo, inquiens, metemus si non elanguerimus. Sic Eph. 6. postquam servis præcepit sincerum famulitium, verf. 5.6.7. subjecit promissionem versu 8. Quicquid boni fecerit quisque hoc eum reportaturum à Domino. Hujusmodi testimonia passim occurrunt, in quibus videas præceptiones, exhortationes, cum promissionibus & comminationibus, conjunctas esse. In hoc itaque genere sunt il-
units.tr: Finally, the end of the particular promises is that those already justified, regenerated, raised up and pacified in conscience should show their gratitude by holy and good works. The Apostle indicates this end in Tit. 2. 11. 12. "For the saving grace of God has appeared to all men, teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously and godly in this present age." Since this is the end of these promises, they have their place in the third part of the Evangelical doctrine, which concerns holy and Christian conduct. Hence you may see these promises scattered everywhere mixed with exhortations, admonitions and precepts, which occur in that parenetic doctrine which concerns conduct. Thus in Gal. 6., after the precept in verse 6 that whoever is taught in the word should share all good things with the one who teaches him, in verses 7 and 8 he adds a promise and a threat together. In the same chapter, verse 9, after the precept that we should not grow weary in doing good, he adds a promise: "In due time," he says, "we shall reap, if we do not faint." So in Eph. 6., after he commands servants sincere service (verses 5, 6, 7), he adds a promise in verse 8: "Whatever good each one does, he will receive the same from the Lord." Testimonies of this kind occur everywhere, in which you may see precepts and exhortations joined with promises and threats. To this class belong

units.la: lę le omnes promissiones à nobis supra citatę, quę diligenter distinguendę sunt, primùm à fœdere operum, deinde à fœdere gratię, sicubi occurrunt inter legendum novum Testamentum.
units.tr: all those promises cited by us above, which must be carefully distinguished, first from the covenant of works and then from the covenant of grace, wherever they occur in reading the New Testament.

units.la: De quibus postremò hæc admonenda sunt. Primùm, conditionem operum regenerationis & gratię in ijs requiri, non vt meritorum, sed vt officiorum duntaxat, & testimoniorum gratitudinis in Deum redemptorem: quemadmodum conditio in fœdere operum non est meritorum, sed officiorum duntaxat, & testimoniorum gratitudinis in Deum creatorem. Sunt quidem, fateor, ad vitam illam æternam quę promittitur, opera ista regenerationis necessaria; sed non tanquâ merita aut causæ meritoriæ, verùm tanquam media, per quę progrediendum est à justificatione & regeneratione, ad gloriam & vitam æternam. Causę quidem etiam dici possunt suo quodâ modo & loco; placent enim Deo in Christo, eumque suo quodam modo movent, verùm non vt merita, sed vt solius meriti Christi effecta quędam, de Christi merito testantia. Sed de his alius erit dicendi locus.
units.tr: On these matters the following should finally be noted. First, the condition of the works of regeneration and grace is required in these promises not as merits but only as duties and tokens of gratitude toward God the Redeemer, just as the condition in the covenant of works is not of merits but only of duties and tokens of gratitude toward God the Creator. These works of regeneration are indeed necessary, I admit, for that eternal life which is promised; but not as merits or meritorious causes, rather as means through which we must advance from justification and regeneration to glory and eternal life. They may also be called causes in a certain sense and place; for they please God in Christ and in a way move him, yet not as merits, but as certain effects of the sole merit of Christ, bearing witness to Christ's merit. But this will have its own place for discussion.

units.la: Deinde secundum est de quo admonemus in hoc tertio promissionum genere, nempe, quod in eo conditio fit operum regenerationis & quidè perfectissimorum ; Iustitia enim Dei summa & exquifitiffima non potest ferre, vel vnius apicis, aut vnius jota defectum. Regula autem omnium operum est justitia Dei, cujus imago quedam in lege morali expressa est. Quare conditio est operum quidem perfectissimorum, verùm non in sese, sed in Christo, & in perfectione satisfactionis ac meriti ipsius.
units.tr: Second, we note in this third kind of promise that the condition is the works of regeneration, and indeed the most perfect works; for the supreme and most exact righteousness of God cannot bear a defect of even a tittle or a jot. The rule of all works is the righteousness of God, of which a certain image is expressed in the moral law. Therefore the condition is of the most perfect works, yet not in themselves but in Christ, and in the perfection of his satisfaction and merit.

units.la: Si objicias. An non Lex præcipit & requirit operum perfectionem eam, quæ fit in ipsis operibus? Respondeo: Ab ijs quidem qui sunt sub foedere operum, sub lege, & extra Christum, eam, fateor, perfectionem postulat lex, quæ fit in ipsis operibus. At ab ijs qui sunt sub foedere gratiæ, & in Christo, eam perfectionem quæ fit in ipsis operibus regenerationis non postulat: Verùm contenta est inchoatis duntaxat in sese operibus, perfectis verò in Christo Iesu: Vt enim nos nondum juftificatos & renatos, justificavit ex mera sua mifericordia, in Christo ipsiusque merito: ita, vel multò magis, jam justificatos & renatos, nos ipsos, & opera nostra pariter, acceptabit in Christo ipfiufq; merito. Sic enim argumentatur Apostolus Rom. 5.9. Iustificati igitur ejus sanguine, servabimur nunc multò magis per eum ab ira. Atque hęc de tribus illis promissionum generibus quę distinctè inveniuntur in novo Testamento.
units.tr: If you object: does not the Law prescribe and require that perfection of works which is found in the works themselves? I answer: from those indeed who are under the covenant of works, under the law and outside Christ, the law, I admit, demands that perfection which is found in the works themselves. But from those who are under the covenant of grace and in Christ it does not demand that perfection which is found in the works of regeneration; rather it is content with works that are only begun in themselves, and perfect in Christ Jesus. For just as he justified us, not yet justified and regenerated, out of his mere mercy, in Christ and through his merit, so, or much more, he will accept us, now justified and regenerated, together with our works, in Christ and through his merit. For the Apostle argues thus in Rom. 5.9. "Being justified therefore by his blood, we shall be saved much more now through him from wrath." And these are the three kinds of promises which are found distinctly in the New Testament.

units.la: De quibus postremò illud quęri potest: An non etiam hęc ipsa quoque distincta inveniantur in veteri Testamento? Respondeo id quidem ita esse, sed non sine discrimine aliquo: vetus enim Testamentum potissimum inserviebat præparandis hominibus ad Christum venturum suo tempore. Lex enim pædagogus erat ad Christum ducens. Gal. 3. Ideòque maxima pars veteris Testamenti insumpta est in proponendo, repetendo, explicando fœdere operum; Quia autem Christus nondum manifestatus est in carne, ideò in veteri Testamento obscurior, & parcior suit doctrina fœderis gratuiti. Postremò in veteri Testamento, ijs qui sunt amplexi Christum, fœderis gratuiti mediatorem, utcunque adumbratum typis & figuris, ijs, inquam, tanquam justificatis jam in eo venturo, & renatis, factę sunt promissiones vitę æternę, sub conditione operum regenerationis; ut est hęc promissio facta Abrahamo. Gen. 17. 1. Continenter ambulato coram me, & esto integer, & faciam fœdus meum tecum; promissio hęc facta est, jam per fidę justificato, & renato. Hujusmodi promissiones inspersę sunt doctrinę parenetice & morali, quę habetur in veteri Testamento, vt est doctrina Proverbiorum, & Ecclesiastes, &c. Atque hęc hactenus dicta sunto, de fœdere gratuito, ejus fundamento, ejus promissione, ejus conditione.
units.tr: Concerning these finally one may ask: are these very things also found distinctly in the Old Testament? I answer that it is so, but not without some difference. For the Old Testament served mainly to prepare men for the coming of Christ in his time. For the law was a schoolmaster leading to Christ, Gal. 3. Hence the greater part of the Old Testament was taken up with setting forth, repeating and explaining the covenant of works. But because Christ was not yet manifested in the flesh, the doctrine of the covenant of grace was therefore more obscure and sparing in the Old Testament. Finally, in the Old Testament, promises of eternal life were made, under the condition of the works of regeneration, to those who embraced Christ, the Mediator of the covenant of grace, however much he was foreshadowed by types and figures; to them, I say, as already justified in him who was to come, and regenerated. Such as this promise made to Abraham, Gen. 17. 1. "Walk before me continually, and be upright, and I will make my covenant with you." This promise was made to one already justified and regenerated through faith. Promises of this kind are sprinkled through the parenetic and moral doctrine found in the Old Testament, such as the doctrine of Proverbs and Ecclesiastes, and so on. So much then be said so far concerning the covenant of grace, its foundation, its promise and its condition.

units.la: Nunc restat vna aut altera quæstio de fœdere hoc gratuito discutienda ac dissolvenda: Prima est, an ijs qui sunt sub fœdere gratuito, jam abolitum sit fœdus operum? Respondeo, duplex est fœderis operum finis, & vsus: Prior est ac proprius magis fœderis operum, vt homines per ipsum justificentur, ac serventur; secus condemnentur: Hunc vsum habuit in Adamo fœdus operum ante lapsum, vt per ipsum Adam justificaretur & viveret: Post lapsum Adami eundem obtinet in non renatis, siue electis illis, siue reprobis, nempe, vt eos vel justificet & servet, vel condemnet: cum autem servare non possit & justificare propter carnem. Rom. 8.3, reliquum est vt condemnet: Atque hanc condemnationem nondum credentes & renati in sese ipsi sentiunt. De vsu hoc lege Rom. 3. 19. vbi dicit per legem obturari omne os, & obnoxium sieri condemnationi Dei. De experientia ipsa sa hujus condemnationis lege Rom.7.10. Ego inquit, mandati adventu mortuus sum ; hoc est, conscientia mea condemnatus sum, sic ut in meipso sentiam praesentem condemnationem & mortem.
units.tr: Now remains one or another question concerning this covenant of grace to be examined and resolved. The first is whether the covenant of works has now been abolished for those under the covenant of grace. I answer: the covenant of works has a twofold end and use. The first and more proper use of the covenant of works is that men may be justified and saved through it, or otherwise condemned. The covenant of works had this use in Adam before the fall, that Adam might be justified and live through it. After the fall of Adam it keeps the same use in the unregenerate, whether they are elect or reprobate, namely, that it either justifies and saves them or condemns them. But since it cannot save or justify because of the flesh, Rom. 8.3, it remains that it condemns. And this condemnation the unbelieving and the unregenerate feel in themselves. On this use see Rom. 3. 19. where he says that by the law every mouth is stopped and becomes subject to the condemnation of God. On the actual experience of this condemnation see Rom.7.10. "I died," he says, "when the commandment came"; that is, I was condemned in my conscience, so that I feel in myself the present condemnation and death.

units.la: Etsi hic vsus prior foederis operum communis sit quibuscunque non renatis, sive electis illis, sive reprobis; tamen id fit non sine aliquo discrimine: Nam in electis peccati agnitio, et condemnatio, quae fit per foedus operum, praeparatio est ad foedus gratuitum : In reprobis vero via est ad extremam desperationem.
units.tr: Although this former use of the covenant of works is common to all who are unregenerate, whether elect or reprobate, it does not happen without some difference. For in the elect the recognition of sin and the condemnation that comes through the covenant of works is a preparation for the covenant of grace; but in the reprobate it is the road to final despair.

units.la: Haec de priori usu: Posterior foederis operum usus est, in vrgendis hominibus ad progressum in fide, & sanctitate continuum faciendum. Hunc usum habet in credentibus et renatis, qui in lege morali, & foedere legali sive operum, tanquam in speculo quodam, continuo vident primum sanctitatem, majestatem, & justitiam Dei. Rom.7.12. Itaque lex ipsa quidem sancta, et mandatum sanctum, justum, bonum. Vident deinde sanctitatem hominis & justitiam, quam vocant, originalem: nempe eam, quae fuit in creatione ad imaginem Dei, quam definimus justitia, sanctitate, & sapientia. Vident tertio vitam illam aeternam
units.tr: So much for the former use. The latter use of the covenant of works is to press men on to make continual progress in faith and holiness. It has this use in believers and the regenerate, who in the moral law and in the legal or works covenant see, as in a certain mirror, first the holiness, majesty and justice of God (Rom. 7.12): so that the law itself is holy, and the commandment holy, just and good. Then they see the holiness and justice of man, which they call original: namely that which existed at creation in the image of God, which we define as righteousness, holiness and wisdom. Thirdly they see that eternal life...

units.la: Rom.7.10. Ego inquit, mandati adventu mortuus sum. poscebat poenam & mortem peccatoris, vel certè ejus vice mediatoris. Quòd si omnia bona sanctaque mediatoris opera non satisfecissent iræ, & justitiæ Dei, adversus peccata nostra, profecto sequitur ea non potuisse promereri nobis novam aliquam Dei gratiam & misericordiam.
units.tr: Rom. 7.10: "I died when the commandment came." The law demanded the punishment and death of the sinner, or else of his mediator in his place. But if all the good and holy works of the mediator had not satisfied the wrath and justice of God against our sins, it surely follows that they could not have merited for us any new grace and mercy of God.

units.la: At, inquies, bona sanctaque opera Christi mediatoris confecerunt saltem partem aliquam satisfactionis, qua satisfactum est divinæ justitiæ; & meriti, quo procurata est Dei misericordia? Respondeo nullam proprie partem vel satisfactionis vel meriti ea consecisse, quum mors Christi, & passio ipsius proprie sola, & justitiæ Dei satisfecerit, & misericordiam ipsius promerita sit.
units.tr: But, you will say, did not the good and holy works of Christ the mediator at least accomplish some part of the satisfaction by which the divine justice was satisfied, and of the merit by which the mercy of God was procured? I answer that they accomplished properly no part either of satisfaction or of merit, since the death of Christ and his passion alone properly satisfied the justice of God and merited his mercy.

units.la: At, inquies, an non licet partiri satisfactionem & meritum Christi inter ea quæ fecit, & ea quæ passus est, sic ut dicamus Christum passione sua ac morte satisfecisse Dei justitiæ, operibus vero sanctis bonisque promeritum esse misericordiam Dei, ut satisfactio tribuatur morti, meritum vero operibus, ut justitia nostra qua nos justificamur coram Deo, partim fit satisfactio, quæ mortis fuit, partim meritum, quod operum Christi fuit? Respondeo solius passionis Christi & satisfactionem et meritum fuisse, si proprie loquamur, & justitiam nostram esse, vel mortem Christi satisfactoriam & meritoriam, vel satisfactionem quæ per mortem fuit, vel meritum ejusdem mortis, vel obedientiam Christi, qua obediens factus est patri ad mortem, mortem autem crucis, vel denique justitiam illam Christi, quā sibi tum acquisivit cum passione sua satisfecit iræ Dei. Imputari enim nobis dicitur ad Justitiam vel ipsa mors Christi, vel satisfactio, vel meritum, vel obedientia, vel denique Iustitia: Hæc enim omnia per eodem accipiuntur.
units.tr: But, you will say, may we not divide the satisfaction and merit of Christ between what he did and what he suffered, so that we say that Christ satisfied the justice of God by his passion and death, while the mercy of God was merited by his holy and good works; so that satisfaction is ascribed to his death and merit to his works, and our righteousness, by which we are justified before God, is partly satisfaction, which belongs to his death, and partly merit, which belongs to the works of Christ? I answer that, speaking properly, both satisfaction and merit belonged to the passion of Christ alone, and that our righteousness is either the satisfying and meriting death of Christ, or the satisfaction which was made through his death, or the merit of that same death, or the obedience of Christ by which he became obedient to the Father unto death, even the death of the cross, or finally that righteousness of Christ by which, when he suffered, he both acquired it for himself and satisfied the wrath of God. For it is said that either the death of Christ itself, or the satisfaction, or the merit, or the obedience, or finally the Righteousness is imputed to us for righteousness: for all these are taken in the same sense.

units.la: At dices, quòd si Christi actiones, neque satisfactionem, neque meritum, neque partem aliquam vel satisfactionis vel meriti, proprie constituerint, tum quis eorum usus fuit, aut est? Respondeo sanctitatem personæ Christi & naturarum, divinæ, inquam, & humanæ, simulque operum ipsius, fundamentum fuisse satisfactionis & meriti, quæ in passione ipsius fuerunt, hoc est, dignitatem illam & virtutem, quæ fuit personæ ipsius & operum, effecisse ut passio esset satisfactoria simul & meritoria: nisi enim tam sancta, tam digna persona, tam sancte viveus exstitisset persona ea quæ passa est, profecto ipsius personæ passio, nec satisfactoria, nec meritoria fuisset. Unde Apostolus Heb.7.26. dum de fundamento passionis satisfactorię & meritorię, deque dispositione futuri sacrificij loquitur: Talis, inquit, nos decebat pontifex, pius, innocens, impollutus, segregatus à peccatoribus, & sublimior coelis factus. Atque hęc hactenus de Christo, quod fuerit sub fœdere operum.
units.tr: But you will say: if the actions of Christ did not properly constitute satisfaction, nor merit, nor any part of satisfaction or merit, then what use were they, or what use are they? I answer that the holiness of the person of Christ and of his natures, divine, I say, and human, and at the same time of his works, was the foundation of the satisfaction and merit which were in his passion; that is, that dignity and virtue which belonged to his person and works made his passion both satisfactory and meritorious at once. For unless the person who suffered had been so holy, so worthy, and had lived so holy a life, the passion of that person would surely have been neither satisfactory nor meritorious. Hence the Apostle (Heb. 7.26), when he speaks of the foundation of the satisfactory and meritorious passion and of the arrangement of the future sacrifice, says: "Such a high priest became us: holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, and made higher than the heavens." So much for Christ, as to what he was under the covenant of works.

units.la: Quod autem non fuerit sub fœdere gratiæ, res est manifestior quàm vt disputatione egeat; nam & fœdus gratię est percussum in eo, atque in ipsius sanguine sancitum, & promissio in fœdere gratię facta est ijs qui injusti erant ac mortui, vtpote violatoribus primi illius fœderis: Denique, conditio in fœdere gratię, fides est in Christum mediatorem. Quare si gratuiti fœderis vel fundamentum, vel promissionem, vel denique conditionem respicias, Christus non poterit dici sub fœdere gratuito fuisse. Hactenus de vtroq; fœdere, deque ijs qui sunt sub fœdere Dei, vel operum vel gratię.
units.tr: That he was not under the covenant of grace is more evident than it needs argument. For the covenant of grace was struck in him and ratified in his blood; and the promise in the covenant of grace was made to those who were unrighteous and dead, namely the violators of that first covenant. Finally, the condition in the covenant of grace is faith in Christ the mediator. Therefore if you look at the foundation, the promise, or finally the condition of the covenant of grace, Christ cannot be said to have been under the covenant of grace. So much on both covenants, and on those who are under the covenant of God, whether of works or of grace.

units.la: Comparatio nostrę & adversariorum sententiæ de fœdere hoc vtroque. CAP. 5
units.tr: Comparison of our opinion and that of our opponents concerning this twofold covenant. CHAP. 5

units.la: NVnc comparatio quędam facienda est nostri & adversariorum, videndumque vtri nostrum rectius sentiamus de fœdere dei, & fœdere operum, & fœdere gratię. Regula, ad quam exigenda est sententia & nostra & adversariorum, alia melior inveniri non potest, quàm doctrina Pauli, quę habetur præsertim in Epistola illa ad Romanos, & in illa nominatim disputatione quam habet de Iustificatione primis illis capitibus, adversus Iudęos illius temporis. Quod si comparatione facta viderimus nostram doctrinâ consentire cum Pauli mente & doctrina, adversariorum verò sententiam eandem esse cum Iudęorum illórum qui tum vixerunt, mente & sentetia, prosecto manifestum erit, nos rectius sentire de fœdere Dei, quàm adversarios.
units.tr: Now a certain comparison must be made between our view and that of our opponents, and we must see which of us holds the truer opinion concerning the covenant of God, the covenant of works, and the covenant of grace. The rule by which both our opinion and that of our opponents must be tested cannot be found better than the teaching of Paul, which is found especially in his Epistle to the Romans, and in the particular discussion of justification that he conducts in the first chapters of that letter, against the Jews of his time. If, once the comparison is made, we see that our doctrine agrees with the mind and teaching of Paul, while the opinion of our opponents is the same in mind and sentiment as that of those Jews who lived at that time, it will surely be plain that we think more rightly about the covenant of God than our opponents do.

units.la: In hac itaque disputatione Pauli confiderabimus primùm mentem & institutum Pauli, tum ex doctrina Pauli colligemus quę fuerit sententia Iudęorum illorum quibuscum Paulo res erat, postea applicabimus vtramq; sententiam, & Pauli, & Iudęorum, ad nos qui hodierno die vivimus, & ad nostras sententias, quas nunc defendimus de fœdęre Dei vtroque. Applicatione hac jam facta, si viderimus nostram sententiam consentientem esse Pauli sententiæ, adversariorum verò consentientem esse Iudæorum menti, profecto illud sequetur, vel ipsis adversarijs confitentibus, nos rectius sentire de fœdere Dei, quam adversarios.
units.tr: In this disputation, then, we shall first consider the mind and purpose of Paul; next, from the teaching of Paul, we shall gather what the opinion was of those Jews with whom Paul had to deal; afterwards we shall apply both views, that of Paul and that of the Jews, to us who live in the present day, and to the opinions we now defend concerning the twofold covenant of God. Once this application is made, if we see that our opinion agrees with the opinion of Paul, and that the opinion of our opponents agrees with the mind of the Jews, it will certainly follow, even by the admission of our opponents themselves, that we think more rightly about the covenant of God than they do.

units.la: Vt igitur rem ipsam aggrediamur, Paulus ad Romanos pugnat adversus eos Iudeorum qui obstinati erant & contumaces, pugnat, inquam, primùm pro Christo ipsiusque merito, quod est primum fundamentum fœderis gratuiti: Deinde pro gratia siue misericordia Dei, quod est secundum fundamentum fœderis gratuiti: Tertiò pro fœdere ipso gratuito fundato in Christo & Dei gratia: Quartò pro justificatione hominis, ex eaque salute, quæ est secundum fœdus gratuitum: pugnat, inquam, pro his adversus naturam primùm, quod est fundamentum fœderis operum; deinde adversus fœdus ipsum operum in natura fundatum: Tertiò adversus justificationem hominis, ex eaque salutem, quæ est per naturæ opera bona ac justa, secundum illud fœdus operum. Expresse quidem, fateor, oppugnat justificationem ipsam & conservationem quę est per opera naturæ, quæ requirit fœdus operum, pugnatque pro justificatione fidei, quam requirit fœdus gratuitum; sed vna eademque opera oppugnat naturam & fœdus ipsum operum, pugnatque pro Christo, pro gratia Dei in co, pro fœdere ipso gratuito: Nam doctrinam antecedentium in consequentis doctrina includi necesse est.
units.tr: To come, then, to the matter itself: Paul in the Epistle to the Romans contends against those Jews who were obstinate and stubborn. He contends, I say, first for Christ and his merit, which is the first foundation of the covenant of grace; second, for the grace or mercy of God, which is the second foundation of the covenant of grace; third, for the covenant of grace itself, founded in Christ and the grace of God; fourth, for the justification of man, and the salvation that follows from it according to the covenant of grace. He contends, I say, for these things against nature, first, which is the foundation of the covenant of works; then against the covenant of works itself, founded in nature; third, against the justification of man, and the salvation that comes through the good and just works of nature according to that covenant of works. Expressly, I admit, he opposes the justification and preservation that come through the works of nature, which the covenant of works requires, and he contends for the justification of faith, which the covenant of grace requires. But by the same works he opposes nature and the covenant of works itself, and he contends for Christ, for the grace of God in him, and for the covenant of grace itself. For it is necessary that the doctrine of the things going before be included in the doctrine of what follows.

units.la: Ex hoc Pauli instituto potest colligi quodnam fuerit Iudæorum aduersariorum consilium, & quæ eorum sententia quibuscum Paulo res erat in Epistola ad Romanos: Iudæi illi contrà pugnarunt pro natura, vtpote fundamento fœderis operum; pro fœdere ipso operum siue naturæ; pro justificatione & salute quæ sunt per opera, & secundum formulam fœderis operum; pugnarunt, inquam, pro his aduersus Christum, aduersus gratiam Dei in Christo; aduersus gratuitum fœdus; denique aduersus justificationem & salutem hominum, quæ est ex formula fœderis gratuiti. Fateor, vt dixi, quæstio fuit de hoc postremo, hoc est, de justificatione, sed quæstio de postremo hoc, inclusit in se superiora illa, vt supra admonuimus. Itaq; nos veterem illam controversiam repetimus à fundamento suo.
units.tr: From this plan of Paul we can gather what the purpose of the Jewish opponents was, and what their opinion was, with whom Paul had to deal in the Epistle to the Romans. Those Jews, on the contrary, fought for nature, as the foundation of the covenant of works; for the covenant of works itself, that is, of nature; for justification and salvation through works, and according to the formula of the covenant of works. They fought, I say, for these things against Christ, against the grace of God in Christ, against the covenant of grace; and finally against the justification and salvation of men, which come from the formula of the covenant of grace. I admit, as I have said, that the question was about this last point, that is, about justification; but the question about this last point included within itself the earlier points, as we have noted above. So we are renewing that old controversy from its foundation.

units.la: In hac controversia obiter observandum est, quanta fuerit primis illis temporibus Iudæorum illorum cæcitas: Primùm non viderunt naturam humanam post lapsum perditam esse, nemo è, quò ad bonitatem; non viderunt naturam suam, neque vllo sensu peccati et miseriæ suæ sunt affecti: deinde non viderunt Christum mediatorem et misericordiam Dei in ipso: Tertiò quum hæc non viderent, non viderunt pariter abolitum in Christo fœdus illud naturæ siue operum. Quartò non viderunt cum homine percussum fœdus illud gratiæ in Christo Iesu: Quintò opera illa naturæ per quæ justificari volebant ex præscripto fœderis operum non viderunt duntaxat officia esse, & testimonia gratitudinis, secundum illius fœderis primam institutionem, sed meritoriam, nescio quam, vim ijs præterea attribuerunt: unde Paulus adversus opera naturæ tanquam merita disputat ex hypothesi Iudæorum. Quod autem pro meritis ea habuerint, apparet ex ea eorum gloriatione in operibus, quam Paulus cohibet, & cujus non vno in loco meminit. Vbi igitur gloriatio? Exclusa est. Rom. 3.27. Si Abraham ex operibus justificatus fuit habet quòd glorietur. Rom.4.2. Non ex operibus ne quis glorietur, Ephes.2.9. Nam qui gloriatur is putat se non accepisse id à Deo, in quo gloriatur, ac proinde meritorium esse putat: Quid habes quod non acceperis: quod si etiam accepisti, quid gloriaris vt qui non acceperis? 1.Cor.4.7 Hactenus de controversia quæ fuit olim inter E Paulum & Iudæos illos veteres de fœdere Dei. Quàm similis est huic controversiæ ea quæ est hodierno die inter nos & Pōtificios: Nos pugnamus hodierno die pro solo Christi merito, pro sola meraque Dei gratia & misericordia, pro fœdere gratuito, pro justificatione & salute, quæ est per solum Christum, per solam gratiam, per solā fidem, (hæc enim idem sunt) pugnamus, inquā, pro his, adversus naturæ vires, siue libertatem arbitrij, hoc est, naturæ bonitatem & sanctitatem, adversus fœdus operum, adversus justificationem, quæ est per opera & ex præscripto fœderis operum. Pontificij hodierno die pugnant pro natura quidem in se sancta, læsa tamen, attenuata, & debilitata (hoc enim est eorum liberum arbitrium) pro fœdere operum naturalium, proficiscentium ex libertate arbitrij, pro justificatione etiā ex operibus liberi arbitrij, juxta fœdus operum, etiam meritorijs: Nam meriti siue sit de congruo, siue de condigno, vt ipsi loquuntur, fundamentum statuunt liberum arbitrium; pro his, inquam, pugnant, adversus solum Christum, ipsiusq; meritum, adversus meram Dei gratiam, & in Christo misericordiam, adversus solum fœdus gratuitum, adversus justificationem, quæ est per solum lum lum Christum, per solam gratiam Dei, per solam fidem: hæc enim re idem sunt.
units.tr: In this controversy it should be observed in passing how great was the blindness of those Jews in those early times. First, they did not see that human nature after the fall is lost, and that no one is good in respect of goodness; they did not see their own nature, nor were they affected by any sense of their sin and misery. Second, they did not see Christ as mediator, nor the mercy of God in him. Third, since they did not see these things, they likewise did not see that the covenant of nature or of works was abolished in Christ. Fourth, they did not see that the covenant of grace in Christ Jesus had been struck with man. Fifth, they did not see that those works of nature by which they wished to be justified, according to the prescription of the covenant of works, are merely duties and tokens of gratitude, according to the first institution of that covenant; instead they also attributed to these works a certain meritorious power, I know not what. Hence Paul argues against the works of nature as if they were merits, on the hypothesis of the Jews. That they regarded these works as meritorious appears from their boasting in works, which Paul restrains, and which he mentions in more than one place. Where, then, is boasting? It is excluded. Rom. 3.27. If Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast of. Rom. 4.2. Not of works, lest anyone should boast. Eph. 2.9. For he who boasts thinks that he has not received from God that in which he boasts, and so he thinks it is meritorious. What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it? 1 Cor. 4.7. So much concerning the controversy that once existed between Paul and those ancient Jews about the covenant of God. How similar to this controversy is the one that exists today between us and the Papists! We today contend for Christ's merit alone, for the mere and sole grace and mercy of God, for the covenant of grace, for justification and salvation, which come through Christ alone, through grace alone, through faith alone (for these are the same thing). We contend, I say, for these things against the powers of nature, or the freedom of the will, that is, the goodness and holiness of nature; against the covenant of works; against justification that comes through works and according to the prescription of the covenant of works. The Papists today fight for a nature that is indeed holy in itself, yet wounded, weakened, and enfeebled (for this is what they mean by free will); for the covenant of natural works, arising from the freedom of the will; for justification also by works of free will, according to the covenant of works, even meritorious ones. For whether the merit is of congruence or of condignity, as they themselves put it, they establish free will as the foundation. They fight, I say, for these things against Christ alone and his merit, against the mere grace of God and his mercy in Christ, against the covenant of grace alone, against justification that comes through Christ alone, through the grace of God alone, through faith alone; for in fact these are the same thing.

units.la: Vide igitur hic obiter Papistarum hodierno die quæ sit admirabilis illa in tanta luce cæcitas: Primum non vident naturam hominis plane perditam, quod ad sanctitatem attinet: Secundo non vident meram solamque Dei in Christo gratiam & misericordiam, ut neque magnitudinem meriti Iesu Christi. Tertio non vident jis qui in Christo sunt plane abolitum fœdus illud operum quoad justificationem: Quarto non vident solum illud fœdus gratiæ cum hominibus post lapsum perculsum esse, præsertim post Christi adventum, in Evangelio suo, idque ad justificationem & vitam æternam: Quinto non vident opera, quæ ipsi vocant libertatis arbitrij, si quæ essent hujusmodi, officia duntaxat esse & testimonia gratitudinis, secundum primam illam institutionem fœderis operum, quæ fiunt ex naturæ viribus; sed & vim quandam meritoriam jis asscribunt. Ergo colligimus eos, etsi non idem plane sentiant quod Iudæi illi veteres, quibuscum Paulo res erat in Epistola ad Romanos, tamen ex parte aliqua stare ab ijs, pugnareque pro natura ex parte bona & sancta, adversus meram gratiam, & partiri quasi justifi-
units.tr: See here, in passing, what a wonderful blindness the Papists today have in such a great light. First, they do not see that the nature of man is utterly lost as far as holiness is concerned. Second, they do not see the mere and sole grace and mercy of God in Christ, nor the greatness of the merit of Jesus Christ. Third, they do not see that the covenant of works, as regards justification, has been utterly abolished for those who are in Christ. Fourth, they do not see that the covenant of grace alone has been broken with men after the fall, especially after the coming of Christ, in his Gospel, and that this is for justification and eternal life. Fifth, they do not see that the works which they call works of free will, if there are any such, are merely duties and tokens of gratitude according to that first institution of the covenant of works, which are done by the powers of nature; yet they also ascribe to them a certain meritorious power. Therefore we gather that they, although they do not think exactly the same as those ancient Jews with whom Paul had to deal in the Epistle to the Romans, nevertheless stand on the same side in some respect, and fight for a nature that is in part good and holy, against mere grace, and divide justifi-

units.la: [Marginal notes: none legible.] justificatione & salutem humana inter Christum gratiaq; Dei, & naturæ vires naturæque opera, quum tamen nullo modo possint consistere in opere salutis humanæ natura & gratia: & quisquis naturam vel naturæ partem aliquam associat gratiæ is plane destruat gratiam necesse sit, quæ vel sola est vel nulla. Rom. 11 Quod si per gratiam, jam non ex operibus, alioqui gratia non erit gratia: & in Epistola ad Galatas ex professo disputat adversus eos Iudeorum qui legè sive naturæ vires & opera, in negotio justificationis & salutis humanæ conjunxerunt cum Christo, gratia Dei, & Evangelio: quibus Iudæis simillimi videtur mihi Papistæ: De jis Iudæorum loquor adversus quos disputat Paulus ad Gal. Nam ad Rom. disputat adversus Iudæos qui Christum plane oppugnarunt, atque eum aperte rejecerunt: ad Gal. vero disputat adversus Iudæos, qui Christo solo non contenti, cum eo legem conjunxerunt. Hactenus fuit comparatio Pauli & nostri, Iudæorum veterum & Papistarum.
units.tr: ...in justification and human salvation between Christ and the grace of God on the one hand, and the powers and works of nature on the other. Yet nature and grace can in no way coexist in the work of human salvation. Whoever joins nature, or any part of nature, to grace clearly destroys grace, which must be either wholly alone or nothing at all. Rom. 11: "But if it is by grace, it is no longer by works; otherwise grace is no longer grace." In the Epistle to the Galatians he argues openly against those Jews who, in the matter of justification and human salvation, joined the law, that is, the powers and works of nature, with Christ, the grace of God, and the Gospel. To those Jews I think the Papists are very much alike. I am speaking of those Jews against whom Paul argues in Galatians. In Romans he argues against Jews who openly attacked Christ and plainly rejected him. In Galatians, however, he argues against Jews who were not content with Christ alone but joined the law with him. So far the comparison between Paul and us, and the old Jews and the Papists.

units.la: Nunc quia de operibus Regenerationis quæri potest quid senserit Paulus, quid nos sentiamus, quid denique Adversarij sentiant, ideo hanc quæstionem paucis expediam. An igitur, dicat quis, Paulus oppugnavit in illa sua disputatione quæ est ad Romanos, item ad Gal. opera quoque gratiæ & regenerationis? Respondeo, oppugnabat præcipuè Paulus in sua disputatione opera naturæ, quæ Iudæi putarunt bona & justa, etiamque meritoria: opera autem regenerationis non rejecit, vt sunt debita, officia, & testimonia gratitudinis in Deum, quin potius eatenus, ea commendavit, Rom.6.7.8.cap. & alijs in locis. Verum in negotio justificationis, & ea quoque quæ vocamus regenerationis opera noluit Paulus cum Christo, cum Dei gratia, cum fide, tanquam causam aliquam, vel partem causæ meritoriæ conjungi. Vide Rom. 4. neque Abrahamum ipsum jam regenitum ex operibus suis regenerationis justificatum fuisse dicit coram Deo: & Rom.6. postquam commendavit sanctificationis opera, tandem versu.23. vbi mortem tribuit peccati merito, non tamen vitam æternam tribuit operum sanctificationis merito, sed postquam dixit stipendia peccati mortem esse, diserte pronunciavit donum Dei esse vitam æternam in Christo Iesu: Quo loco si putasset vllam meriti partem in operibus regenerationis fuisse, non tacuisset profecto de ea laude operum regenerationis, præsertim quum eorum commendatione ex profesìo instituisset. Ergo Apost. ad Rom, quū rejiciat opera præsertim naturę, quę requirit fœdus illud operum, tamen omnia simul ac semel operum genera rejicienda censet, sive moralia & naturalia, quæ antecedunt gratiam & fidem, sive ceremonialia, sive denique regenerationis opera, quæ sequuntur gratiam & fidem, ut uni Christo, merę gratię, soli fidei locus sit. Hactenus de sententia Pauli.
units.tr: Now, since it may be asked about the works of regeneration what Paul thought, what we think, and finally what our opponents think, I will settle this question briefly. Someone may ask: in that argument of his in Romans, and likewise in Galatians, did Paul also attack the works of grace and regeneration? I answer that in his argument Paul chiefly attacked the works of nature, which the Jews thought good and just and even meritorious. He did not reject the works of regeneration, which are duties, offices and evidences of gratitude toward God. Rather, he commended them as far as that goes: Rom. 6, 7, 8, and in other places. But in the matter of justification, Paul did not want even the so-called works of regeneration joined with Christ, with the grace of God, or with faith, as some cause or part of a meritorious cause. See Rom. 4: he does not say that Abraham himself, already regenerate, was justified before God by his works of regeneration. And in Rom. 6, after he has commended the works of sanctification, at verse 23 he assigns death as the wages of sin, but he does not assign eternal life to the merit of the works of sanctification. Rather, after saying that the wages of sin is death, he plainly declares that the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus. If he had thought that any part of merit lay in the works of regeneration, he would surely not have kept silent about that praise of the works of regeneration, especially since he had deliberately set out to commend them. Therefore the Apostle in Romans, while he rejects the works of nature especially, which the covenant of works requires, nevertheless judges that all kinds of works must be rejected together and at once: moral and natural works, which precede grace and faith; ceremonial works; and finally the works of regeneration, which follow grace and faith. So that only Christ, pure grace, and faith alone may have a place. So far the view of Paul.

units.la: Nos hodierno die idem plane cum Paulo sentimus de operibus regenerationis. Adversarij nostri, ut ea admittunt, ita ijs plus nimio tribuunt; neque enim volunt esse officia & testimonia gratitudinis nostrę in Deum duntaxat, sed etiam meritoria esse dicunt ejus justificationis, quam secundam ipsi appellant. Porrò sciendum opera regenerationis adversarijs non tantum proficisci a gratia, quam ipsi infusam vocant, & prima justitiam, sed etiam a natura & libertate arbitrij, quæ simul cum justitia operatur, & cujus etiam respectu, ut supra monuimus, meritoria volunt esse opera bona, quæ partiuntur inter primam illā gratiam & libertatem arbitrij. Atq; hæc hactenus de hac comparatione, ex qua videmus vtri, nosne an Adversarij rectius sentiamus de foedere Dei vtroque, de vtriusq; fundamentis, natura, gratia, Christo; denique de vtriusq; effecto, quod vocamus justificationem hominis. Et cum haec religionis verae fundamentum constituant, videmus vtri, nosne an adversarij, religione & cultum Dei melius solidiusq; fundatum habeamus.
units.tr: Today we think exactly the same as Paul about the works of regeneration. Our opponents, while they admit these works, attribute too much to them. For they not only say that they are duties and evidences of our gratitude toward God, but also say that they are meritorious of that justification which they themselves call the second. Moreover, it must be understood that for our opponents the works of regeneration arise not only from the grace which they call infused and primary justice, but also from nature and free will, which works together with justice. With respect to these, as we noted above, they want good works to be meritorious, and these they divide between that first grace and free will. So far on this comparison, from which we see which side judges more rightly about the covenant of God in both its forms, and about the foundations of each, namely nature, grace and Christ, and finally about the effect of each, which we call the justification of man. Since these things make up the foundation of the true religion, we see which side has religion and the worship of God better and more solidly founded, we or our opponents.

units.la: De verbo sive foedere Dei scripto.
units.tr: On the written Word or covenant of God.

units.la: CAP. 6.
units.tr: CHAP. 6.

units.la: VErbum vtriusque foederis longo tempore inde ab Adamo usque ad Mosen in mundo non scriptum exstitit, sed traditum fuit quasi per manus, & viva voce propagatum; nihil enim nunc disputamus de illis quae Iosephus ante diluvium columnis incisa fuisse refert, neque de Apocryphis scriptis Henoch.
units.tr: The Word of both covenants did not exist in writing in the world for a long time, from Adam until Moses. It was handed down, as it were from hand to hand, and propagated by the living voice. For we are not now discussing those things which Josephus reports were inscribed on pillars before the flood, nor the apocryphal writings of Enoch.

units.la: Cum vero per traditiones, exorientibus subinde corruptelis, puritas doctrinae foederis non conservaretur, & Deus no vellet amplius illa tantum ratione vti, tum alia ratione tempore Mosis ipse instituit, & ostendit: vt scilicet scriptis, divina authoritate & testimonio approbatis & confirmatis, puritas doctrinae caelestis conservaretur & propagaretur; quoque magis scriptum commendaret hominibus omnium ætatum, ipse Deus verba decalogi, hoc est, fœdus legale, suis digitis primus exaravit in tabulis lapideis: Mosi deinde mandatum dedit vtreliqua ex ore ipsius Dei excepta conscriberet; et vt populus Dei certus esset scripturam illam Mosis non humana voluntate allatam, sed divinitus inspiratam esse, Deus valde multis stupendis miraculis scripto Mosis authoritate conciliavit, & ante scriptionem, & post scriptionem, & in ipsa scriptione. Scripsit quidem Moses vtriusque fœderis verbum, & legalis, & Evangelici; verùm cum fœderis Evangelici lineamenta quasi quædam prima duxerit, fœdus legale ad vivum depinxit. In scriptis enim Mosis aperte vrgetur fœdus legale, obscurè verò fœdus Evangelicum. Vnde tota doctrina Mosis legalis vocata est. Lex per Mosen data est, Ioh. 1.
units.tr: But when, because corruptions kept arising, the purity of the doctrine of the covenant was not preserved by tradition, and God no longer wished to use that method alone, then at the time of Moses he himself instituted and showed another method: namely, that the purity of heavenly doctrine might be preserved and propagated in writings approved and confirmed by divine authority and testimony. And so that writing would recommend itself more strongly to men of all ages, God himself first engraved with his own fingers the words of the Decalogue, that is, the legal covenant, on tablets of stone. Then he commanded Moses to write down the rest, which he received from the mouth of God himself. And so that the people of God might be certain that this writing of Moses had not been produced by human will but was divinely inspired, God, by many astonishing miracles, gave authority to the writing of Moses, both before the writing, after the writing, and in the writing itself. Moses indeed wrote the Word of both covenants, both legal and evangelical. But while he drew the outlines of the evangelical covenant, as it were in first sketches, he painted the legal covenant to the life. For in the writings of Moses the legal covenant is clearly urged, but the evangelical covenant obscurely. Hence the whole teaching of Moses is called legal. "The law was given through Moses," John 1.

units.la: Post Mosen Deus subinde excitavit Prophetas, quorum doctrinæ & testimonio ipsę ingentibus miraculis fidem et authoritatem conciliavit: Illi verò licet miraculis essent confirmati, non tamen habebant potestatem vt de doctrina Patriarcharum & Mosis alia, vel diversa, vel contraria afferrent, quàm quæ in libris Mosis consignata erant, sed ex divina revelatione addebant interpretationes illustriores, prout ille lucifer novi Testamenti magis magisque appropinquabat: Totius vero doctrinae suae summam & capita, quantum Deus posteritati necessarium judicabat, ipsi conscribebant: quae conscripta ad sacros libros Mosis, hoc est, in latere arcae reponebantur. Iof. 24.
units.tr: After Moses, God from time to time raised up prophets, to whose doctrine and testimony he gave faith and authority by great miracles. Although they were confirmed by miracles, they did not have the power to bring forward any other or different or contrary doctrine from that which was recorded in the books of Moses. Instead, from divine revelation they added fuller interpretations, as that morning star of the New Testament drew ever nearer. They themselves wrote down the sum and heads of their whole doctrine, as far as God judged necessary for posterity. What they wrote was placed beside the sacred books of Moses, that is, in the side of the ark. Josh. 24.

units.la: Denique post manifestationem Christi in carne, doctrina Evangelica sive novi foederis primum aliquot annis a Christo ipso, postea ab Apostolis sine scripto viva voce tradita & propagata est. Postremo vero ab Apostolis scriptis est comprehensa. Urgentur quidem in scriptis quoque novi Testamenti opera legis Dei & naturae, adeoque lex ipsa a Christo et Apostolis est explicata, & quasi purgata a fermento Pharisaeorum: sed urgentur opera legis & naturae non eo fine ut homines per ea justificentur & serventur, verum urgentur, vel ut praeparetur homines ad gratiam inchoandam, vel ut stimulentur ad progressum in gratia faciendum, sicuti jam antea a nobis dictum est. Urgentur etiam opera regenerationis, sed non quibus justificemur, verum quibus testemur justificationem illam nostram quae est per fidem, et erga Deum gratitudinem. Unde Paulus postquam jam tradidit doctrinam ƈtrinam fidei ad opera legis solet descendere, requirereque vitam & conversationem dignam vocatione illa, qua vocati fumus in Christo Iesu: vide Ephef.4. 1.Theff.2.12. Quod autem vrgetur præcipuè in scriptis novi Testamenti, fides est in Christum. Atq; hæc in genere de verbo fœderis scripto.
units.tr: Finally, after the manifestation of Christ in the flesh, the Evangelical doctrine, or the doctrine of the New Covenant, was at first handed down and propagated without writing by the living voice, first by Christ himself for some years, and afterward by the Apostles. At last it was comprised in writing by the Apostles. Indeed, in the writings of the New Testament too, the works of the law of God and of nature are urged, and the law itself was explained by Christ and the Apostles and, as it were, cleansed of the leaven of the Pharisees. But the works of the law and of nature are urged not for the purpose that men may be justified and saved by them, but they are urged either to prepare men to begin in grace, or to stir them on to make progress in grace, as we have already said. The works of regeneration are also urged, but not as that by which we are justified; rather, they bear witness to that justification of ours which is through faith, and to our gratitude toward God. Hence Paul, after he has set forth the doctrine of faith, usually descends to the works of the law, and requires a life and conduct worthy of that calling by which we have been called in Christ Jesus. See Eph. 4, 1 Thess. 2:12. What is chiefly urged in the writings of the New Testament, however, is faith in Christ. So much in general about the written covenant-Word.

units.la: De numero controversiarum quæ sunt de verbo scripto: deque prima controversia. An Scriptura sit Dei verbum.
units.tr: On the number of controversies concerning the written Word, and on the first controversy: whether Scripture is the Word of God.

units.la: CAP. 7.
units.tr: CHAP. 7.

units.la: DE Scriptura sacra omnino duo sunt controversiarum genera. Primum est earum controversiarum quæ magis sunt, vt sic dicam, essentiales, hoc est, de essentia ipsius Scripturæ. Secundum est earum quæ accidentales sunt magis, & non tam prope attingunt ipsius Scripturæ essentiam. In primo genere controversiæ sunt numero decem. Prima omnium est, An sit Scriptura Prophetica et Apostolica verbum Dei. 2. Qui constet eam esse verbum Dei. 3. est de ipsius antiquitate. 4. De ipsius perspicuitate. 5. De ipsius simplicitate. 6. De ipsius vita vel vivacitate. 7. De ipsius simplici necessitate. 8. De ipsius persectione & sufficientia, quòd ea sufficiens sit et perfecta per se, sine traditionibus non scriptis. 9. An penes Scripturam sit omnium controversiarum judicium. 10. An summa sit Scripturæ Propheticæ & Apostolicæ præstantia, ac major ejus authoritas quàm sit Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Concerning Holy Scripture there are two kinds of controversy in general. The first kind concerns what are, so to speak, its essentials, that is, the essence of Scripture itself. The second kind concerns accidental matters, which do not touch the essence of Scripture so closely. In the first kind there are ten controversies: (1) the first and foremost, whether the Prophetic and Apostolic Scripture is the Word of God; (2) whether it is established that it is the Word of God; (3) its antiquity; (4) its perspicuity; (5) its simplicity; (6) its life or vitality; (7) its absolute necessity; (8) its perfection and sufficiency, that is, whether it is sufficient and perfect in itself without unwritten traditions; (9) whether the judgment of all controversies rests with Scripture; (10) whether the Prophetic and Apostolic Scripture has the highest excellence, and a greater authority than the Church.

units.la: Quod ad octo illas controversias quæ sequuntur primas duas, sunt eç quidem de proprietatibus Scripturæ sacræ, quæ postquàm jam ostensum & demonstratum est, quòd Scriptura sit verbum Dei, sua sponte omnes sequuntur, & ex demonstrato illo quasi Theoremate, necessariò inferuntur.
units.tr: As for the eight controversies that follow the first two, these concern the properties of Holy Scripture. Once it has been shown and demonstrated that Scripture is the Word of God, these properties follow of their own accord and are necessarily inferred from that demonstrated proposition, as from a theorem.

units.la: Hoc enim accepto, quod Scriptura sit verbum Dei, sequitur primùm eam esse antiquissimam. 2. Clarissimam. 3. Simplicissimam. 4. Maximè vivam. 5. Maximè necessariam. 6. Perfectissimam. 7. Judicem omnium controversiarum omni exceptione majorem. 8. Præstantissimam. Sed quum adversarij has ipsas proprietates, quæ octo sunt numero, negent & oppugnent, de ijs singulis sunt singulæ controversiæ, ut diximus.
units.tr: For once it is granted that Scripture is the Word of God, it follows first that it is most ancient; second, most clear; third, most simple; fourth, most living; fifth, most necessary; sixth, most perfect; seventh, the judge of all controversies, greater than any exception; eighth, most excellent. But since the adversaries deny and attack these very properties, which are eight in number, there is a separate controversy about each of them, as we have said.

units.la: Has itaque controversias ordine prosequemur, ac primùm omnium tractabimus eam quæ natura prima est: An Scriptura sit verbum Dei. In genere fatentur adversarij Scripturam sacram esse verbum Dei, sed cum ventum est ad speciem, dissentiunt à nobis. Rem sic apertius expono: Duplex hodierno die verbum Dei in Ecclesia est. 1. immediatum. 2. mediatum. Immediatum dico, quod procedit ex ipsiusmet Dei ore: mediatum vero quod Deus pronunciat per praeconem sive ministrum aliquem suum. Nos itaque affirmamus Scripturam sacram esse immediatum & primarium illud Dei verbum, saltem nobis esse vice primae, immediatę, ac vivę ipsius Dei vocis: Imo vero nobis esse vice non modo vivae Dei vocis, sed internae & inscrutabilis Dei mentis, ac notionum quae sunt in mente divina. Rationes sunt. 1. quia haec est voluntas Dei. Habent, inquit, Mosen & Prophetas, hoc est, scripta Mosis & prophetarum. Luc. 16. 29.
units.tr: Therefore we shall take up these controversies in order, and first of all we shall treat the one which is first by nature: whether Scripture is the Word of God. In general the adversaries admit that Holy Scripture is the Word of God, but when it comes to the particular they disagree with us. I set out the matter more plainly as follows. Today there is a twofold Word of God in the Church: (1) the immediate, and (2) the mediate. I call it immediate which proceeds from the very mouth of God; mediate is that which God proclaims through his herald or some minister of his. We therefore affirm that Holy Scripture is that immediate and primary Word of God, which for us stands at least in place of the first, immediate and living voice of God himself. Indeed, it stands for us not only in place of the living voice of God, but of the inward and unsearchable mind of God, and of the conceptions that are in the divine mind. Our reasons are these. (1) Because this is the will of God: "They have Moses and the Prophets," that is, the writings of Moses and the prophets. Luke 16:29.

units.la: 2. Quod si nihil haberemus vice vivae vocis Dei, profecto deteriori loco essemus quam suit vetus illa & Iudaica Ecclesia, quae habebat oracula Dei: Atqui hoc est dictu absurdum.
units.tr: (2) If we had nothing in place of the living voice of God, we would certainly be in a worse position than that old Jewish Church, which had the oracles of God. But this is absurd to say.

units.la: 3. Ratio est. Fides nostra necesse est pro primo suo fundamento habeat, vel ipsammet Dei vocem vivam, & ipsammet Dei mentem, vel certe aliquid vice vivae vocis ipsius Dei, et ipsius mentis Dei, quod nobis non minus certum sit ac firmum, quam si ipsum Deum Loquentem audiremus, & ipsam mentem Dei ac
units.tr: (3) The reasoning is this. Our faith must necessarily have as its first foundation either the living voice of God himself and the mind of God himself, or certainly something in place of the living voice of God and the mind of God, which is no less certain and firm for us than if we heard God himself speaking and beheld and read the very mind of God and

units.la: ac sententias in mente divina inscriptas inspiceremus ac legeremus. Atqui nunc non audimus ipsammet Dei viva vocem, neq; mentem ipsam Dei intuemur. Ergo necesse est habeamus aliquid quod nobis vivæ vocis & mentis Dei vice sit. Vivæ autem Dei vocis & mentis vice nihil habere possumus, præter sacram hanc Scripturam. Ergo nobis sola Scriptura sacra est vice, tum vivæ vocis, tum mentis Dei. 4. Ratio: Continet Scriptura ea omnia quæ Deus ipse loquutus est jam olim, & quæ Deus mente cogitat de salute ac vita nostra: Ergo &c. Hactenus de immediato Dei verbo. Mediatum Dei verbum dicimus esse Ecclesiæ sanctæ & puræ vocem, quia etsi homines sunt qui loquuntur, tamen verbum quod loquuntur est ipsiusmet Dei.
units.tr: and the judgments inscribed in the divine mind. But now we do not hear the living voice of God himself, nor do we look upon the mind of God itself. Therefore we must necessarily have something which stands in place of the living voice and mind of God. Yet we can have nothing in place of the living voice and mind of God except this Holy Scripture. Therefore Holy Scripture alone is for us in place both of the living voice and of the mind of God. (4) The reasoning: Scripture contains all those things which God himself spoke long ago, and which God in his mind intends concerning our salvation and life. Therefore etc. So far concerning the immediate Word of God. We say that the mediate Word of God is the voice of the holy and pure Church, because although it is men who speak, the word they speak is nonetheless that of God himself.

units.la: Hic insurgunt adversarij, contendunt; vocem Ecclesiæ principalem esse vocem, magisque supplere vivæ vocis Dei & mentis Dei vicem quam Scripturam; quia, inquiunt, vox Ecclesiæ est scriptura in corde Ecclesiæ exarata ipsius Dei digito, non autem amanuensis alicujus opera: Quare vocem Ecclesiæ oportet esse principalem Dei vocem; nam est vox viva, profecta à vivo corde Ecclesiæ, in quo Deus ipse digito Spiritus sui inscripsit & exaravit ravit omnem veritatem; quum Scriptura hęc Prophetarum & Apostolorum dictata quidē sit à Deo, ac exarata sit, non digitis ipsius Dei, verùm Prophetarum & Apostolorum, i. amanuensium digitis, non in vivis hominum cordibus, sed in chartis & tabulis: Vnde sequitur Scripturam quę est in corde Ecclesię esse principalem illam scripturam Dei, & Ecclesię sanctę vocem esse principalem illam vocem Dei, & debere esse nobis vivę & immediatę Dei vocis & abditę etiam Dei mentis loco?
units.tr: Here the adversaries rise up and contend that the voice of the Church is the principal voice, and that it supplies the place of the living voice of God and the mind of God more than Scripture does. For, they say, the voice of the Church is Scripture written in the heart of the Church by the finger of God himself, and not by the labour of some amanuensis. Therefore the voice of the Church must be the principal voice of God; for it is a living voice, proceeding from the living heart of the Church, in which God himself with the finger of his Spirit has inscribed and engraved every truth. Whereas this Scripture of the Prophets and Apostles, although indeed dictated by God and written down, was written not by the finger of God himself but by the fingers of the Prophets and Apostles, that is, of amanuenses, not in the living hearts of men but on paper and tablets. Hence it follows that the Scripture which is in the heart of the Church is the principal Scripture of God, and the voice of the holy Church is the principal voice of God, and ought to be for us in place of the living and immediate voice of God and of the hidden mind of God as well?

units.la: Respondeo ad rationem eorum: Vox Ecclesię viva quidem est, fateor; & proficiscitur à vivo & sanctificato corde per Spiritum sanctum; (de vera enim Ecclesia loquor) sed primùm dico Scripturam hanc propheticam & Apostolicam solam habendam pro Scriptura ipsius Dei digito exarata, & pro verbo ipsius Dei immediato. Deinde dico cor Ecclesię sanctificatum esse et informatū per Spiritum Scripturę, et scripturam quę est in corde Ecclesię nihil aliud esse quàm (vt sic dicā) transsumptum et transscriptum quoddam, quod Spiritus sanctus ad archetypum et authenticum illud exemplar, nempe Scripturam sacram, inscripsit cordibus nostris. Spiritus e-nim nim sanctus nihil docet nunc Ecclesiam, praeter id quod scriptum est, & per Scripturam quodammodo Ecclesiam gignit; & Scriptura mater est, Ecclesia filia; Scriptura magistra, Ecclesia discipula. Tertio dico informationem illam veritatis, quae fit in corde Ecclesiae per Scripturam sacram, non tam plenam perfectamque esse quam est ipsa Scriptura. Postremo dico Ecclesiam, cum imperfecte illuminata & renata fit, posse etiam in rebus gravissimis a veritate aberrare, & aberrare quidem reipsa, quoties discedit a Canone illo & regula Scripturae sacrae.
units.tr: I reply to their argument. The voice of the Church is indeed living, I grant; and it proceeds from a living and sanctified heart through the Holy Spirit (for I am speaking of the true Church). But first I say that this prophetic and Apostolic Scripture alone is to be held as the Scripture written by the very finger of God, and as the immediate Word of God. Next I say that the heart of the Church is sanctified and informed by the Spirit of Scripture, and that the scripture which is in the heart of the Church is nothing other than (so to speak) a certain transcript and copy, which the Holy Spirit has inscribed on our hearts from that archetypal and authentic exemplar, namely Holy Scripture. For the Holy Spirit now teaches the Church nothing except what is written, and through Scripture he in some measure begets the Church; Scripture is the mother, the Church the daughter; Scripture the teacher, the Church the disciple. Thirdly I say that the instruction in truth which takes place in the heart of the Church through Holy Scripture is not so full and perfect as Scripture itself. Lastly I say that the Church, since it is imperfectly enlightened and reborn, can also go astray from the truth in very weighty matters, and indeed does actually go astray whenever it departs from that canon and rule of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Ratione eorum sic confutata, sequitur Ecclesiae vocem (de vera loquor, non de adultera illa Romana) non esse primarium & princeps Dei verbum, neque nobis esse vivae & immediatae Dei vocis, neque etiam mentis divinae loco, verum hanc praerogativam esse solius Scripturae sacrae. Addo praeterea, quod si primum non tam respicias veritatem ipsam, quam loquitur Ecclesia, quam instrumenta loquutionis, quae sunt homines; deinde si comparetur vox Ecclesiae loquentis, cum ipsa Scriptura sacra, ne verbi quidem Dei ipsam merei nomen; sed vocari magis proprie verbum & testimonium humanum. Ipse enim Christus
units.tr: With their argument thus refuted, it follows that the voice of the Church (I speak of the true Church, not that adulterous Roman one) is not the primary and chief Word of God, nor for us in place of the living and immediate voice of God, nor even in place of the divine mind; rather this prerogative belongs to Holy Scripture alone. I add besides that if one looks first not so much at the truth which the Church speaks as at the instruments of speech, which are men, and then if the voice of the speaking Church is compared with Holy Scripture itself, it does not even deserve the name of the Word of God; it should rather be called, more properly, a human word and testimony. For Christ himself

units.la: Iohannis Baptista de se testimonium, hominis testimonium vocavit. Ego, inquit, ab homine testimonium non capto: Ioh. 5. 34. Esto verum & Scripturæ sacræ consentiens testimonium Ecclesiæ, nihilominus vocatur testimonium hominum, siue homines ipsos loquentes respicias, sive eorum testimonium compares cum testimonio procedente ex ipsius Dei & Christi ore.
units.tr: called the testimony of John the Baptist about himself the testimony of a man. "I," he says, "do not receive testimony from man." John 5:34. Granted that the testimony of the Church is true and agrees with Holy Scripture, it is nevertheless called the testimony of men, whether you look at the men themselves who speak, or compare their testimony with the testimony proceeding from the mouth of God and Christ himself.

units.la: At, inquies, Prophetæ & Apostoli qui ipsi homines fuerunt, hæc omnia quæ in Scripturis habemus & loquuti sunt & scripserunt. Ergo hæc omnia quæ scripta sunt pro testimonio hominum habenda sunt? Respondeo me nō plane negare id quod objicis, si vel dictum vel scriptum Prophetæ aut Apostoli alicujus æstimetur ex instrumentis & ministris, vel si etiam cum ipsa Dei vel Christi viva voce comparetur. Nam habita ratione ipsorum instrumentorum, & facta comparatione dicti vel scripti eorum cum dicto vel scripto ipsius Dei, jam illud dictum vel scriptum inferiori loco est, & vocatur testimonium hominis: & ipsius Iohannis Baptistæ testimonium, ratione instrumenti, & comparatione cum Christo ipso habita, vocatum est testimonium hominis. Sed dum nos Scripturam propheticam cam & Apostolicam dicimus vocem esse & testimonium ipsius Dei immediatum, extra comparationem ipsiusmet vivæ vocis Dei loquimur, neque considerabamus à quibus demum instrumentis exarata sit Scriptura; verum ponderabamus rem ipsam & sententias quæ scriptæ sunt, & considerabamus quo loco velit ipse Deus Scripturam sacram à nobis haberi, nempe loco & vice non quidem Scripturæ vel sermonis hominum, sed loco & vice Scripturæ & sermonis ipsiusmet Dei; consideramus denique eam in comparatione cum Ecclesia facta. Nam comparatione cum Ecclesia facta, vox Scripturæ est vox ipsiusmet Dei; Rursus facta hac comparatione vox Ecclesiæ Christi vocatur testimonium hominum, quemadmodum sermo vel Scriptura Prophetæ & Apostoli comparatione vivæ vocis ipsiusmet Dei appellatur testimonium hominis, teste Christo. Ioh. 5. Atque hæc hactenus de prima controversia dicta sunto.
units.tr: But you will say: the prophets and apostles were themselves men, and they both spoke and wrote all the things we have in the Scriptures. Therefore must all that is written be regarded as the testimony of men? I answer that I do not wholly deny what you object, if the saying or writing of some prophet or apostle is judged by its instruments and ministers, or if it is compared with the living voice of God or Christ himself. For once we take account of the instruments themselves and compare their saying or writing with the saying or writing of God, that saying or writing is already in a lower place and is called the testimony of man. So too the testimony of John the Baptist himself, considered as an instrument and compared with Christ, was called the testimony of man. But when we say that the prophetic and apostolic Scripture is the voice and immediate testimony of God itself, we speak apart from any comparison with the living voice of God, and we are not considering by what instruments Scripture was in fact written. Rather, we weigh the matter itself and the sentences that have been written, and we consider in what place and office God himself wishes the holy Scripture to be held by us: not in the place and office of the writing or speech of men, but in the place and office of the Scripture and speech of God himself. Finally, we consider it in its comparison with the Church. For when the comparison is made with the Church, the voice of Scripture is the voice of God himself. Conversely, when that comparison is made, the voice of the Church of Christ is called the testimony of men, just as the speech or Scripture of a prophet or apostle, compared with the living voice of God himself, is called the testimony of man, as Christ bears witness in John 5. So much, then, has been said so far on the first controversy.

units.la: Qui constet Scripturam esse verbum Dei.
units.tr: How it is established that Scripture is the word of God.

units.la: CAP. 8.
units.tr: CHAPTER 8.

units.la: ALtera controversia est de Argumento, quo scitur Scripturam esse verbum Dei; ut igitur prima quæstio fuit an sit Scriptura verbum Dei, ita hæc quæstio est cur sit, quo argumento constet Scripturam esse verbum Dei. Ad hanc quæstionem sic respondemus, non opus quidem esse simpliciter & per se aliqua alia luce, quàm quæ sit in ipsa Scriptura ad hoc docendum. Est enim Scriptura, (quum sit verbum Dei primum & immediatum) αὐτόπιστος, natura sua notissima, & clarissima, & causa lucis illius quæcunque est in Ecclesia & cordibus hominum. Vt enim Solis lux alia quavis luce non est demonstranda, quum ipsa omnem aliam lucem corpoream infinitis partibus exsuperet; ita lux illa Scripturæ spiritualis non eget, sua natura & per se, quavis alia luce qua ipsa demonstretur, quum ipsa sit lux omnium limpidissima, & clarissima: Verùm quòd requirantur alia argumenta, et quasi lumina, quibus ostendatur Scripturam esse verbum Dei, hoc est, lucem ipsam, in causa fumus nos, qui natura cæci fumus ac lippi.
