Quare argumenta et adjumenta quæ afferri possunt alia ad hoc docendum, nihil quidem lucis afferunt luci Scripturæ, quæ per se ac sua natura notissima est, cuique nihil addi potest ad hoc vt magis luceat, sed tantùm eò pertinent omnia, vt quæ per se notissima est, nobis quoque nota sit, & aperiantur oculi nostri ad videndum longè plenissimam & clarissimam illam Scripturæ lucem; hoc est, ad videndum ipsum Deum in Scriptura sacra lucentem & loquentem. Vt qui cæcum docere lucere solem, jam afferret in medium, non ea quidem quibus magis illustraret solis luce, sed ea quibus, si posset fieri, queat aperire cæco oculos, ad hoc vt posset videre solis lucem in se splendidissimam. Ergo, vt dicamus verbo, argumenta ea omnia quæcunque quæruntur à nobis ad hoc vt ostendatur Scripturæ lux, quæri debent, non causa ipsius Scripturæ, quæ per se notissima est; sed nostra causa qui cæci sumus, quibusque opus est argumentis quibuscunq; & adjumentis, per quæ quoquo modo fieri potest, vt oculi nostri aperiantur, & acies oculorum in videndo acutior reddatur.
units.tr: The second controversy concerns the argument by which we know that Scripture is the word of God. As the first question was whether Scripture is the word of God, so this question is why it is so, and by what argument it is established that Scripture is the word of God. To this question we answer as follows: it is not necessary, simply and in itself, to have any other light besides that which is in Scripture itself for teaching this. For Scripture, since it is the first and immediate word of God, is self-authenticating [autopistos], most known by its own nature and most clear, and it is the cause of whatever light there is in the Church and in the hearts of men. Just as the light of the sun need not be demonstrated by any other light, since it surpasses every other bodily light by infinite degrees, so that spiritual light of Scripture does not need, by its nature and in itself, any other light by which it might be demonstrated, since it is the most limpid and clearest of all lights. But that other arguments are required, as it were lamps, by which it is shown that Scripture is the word of God, is because we are the ones who are blind and bleary-eyed by nature, not because the light itself lacks anything. Therefore the arguments and aids that may be brought forward for teaching this add nothing of light to the light of Scripture, which is in itself and by its nature most known, and to which nothing can be added to make it shine more. Rather, they all serve only this purpose: that the Scripture, which is most known in itself, may also be known to us, and that our eyes may be opened to see that most full and clear light of Scripture, that is, to see God himself shining and speaking in holy Scripture. It is like someone teaching a blind man that the sun shines: he would not bring forward things by which the sun's light might be made brighter, but things by which, if it were possible, he might open the blind man's eyes so that he could see the sun's light in all its splendour. Therefore, to put it in a word, all the arguments that are sought from us to show the light of Scripture ought to be sought not for the sake of Scripture itself, which is most known in itself, but for our sake, who are blind, and who need whatever arguments and aids there are, by which in any way our eyes may be opened and the keenness of our sight in seeing may be sharpened.

units.la: Argumenta & adjumenta quibus aperiri possunt oculi nostri ad videndum Scripturæ lucem, vel Deum in ipsa Scriptura loquentem & lucetem, non sunt vnius generis, sed varia afferri solent à viris doctis & pijs; Sed nisi idè ille Spiritus sanctus, qui in Scriptura loquitur, primùm omnium insinuet se in animos nostros, et aperiat oculos mentis nostræ, qui solus eos aperire potest, profecto frustrà quis loquatur de alijs quibusvis argumentis. tis & adjumētis, hoc est, nisi simus Θεοδίδακτοι, doƈti à Deo et Spiritu ipsius sanƈto, nihil profutura sunt alia. Quamobrem prima omnium ac principalis causa quæ efficit vt Scriptura in se nota, nobis quoq; innotescat, erit Spiritus sanƈtus intus nos docens, aperiendo oculos mentis nostræ, ad hoc vt videamus lucem illam Scripturæ, et agnoscamus in Scriptura Dei ipsius & Christi vocem. Spiritus autem sic nos docendo nihil quidem lucis addit Scripturæ, quæ per se abūdè lucet, sed illuminat mentes nostras ad hoc vt lucem illā Scripturæ sacræ abundantem intueamur. Spiritus autē sanƈtus, dum illuminat mentes nostras, id quidem facit per media quædam et quasi organa, quorum ministerio operatur in mentibus & cordibus nostris.
units.tr: The arguments and aids by which our eyes may be opened to see the light of Scripture, or God speaking and shining in Scripture itself, are not of one kind; rather, various ones are commonly brought forward by learned and godly men. But unless that Holy Spirit who speaks in Scripture first of all insinuates himself into our minds and opens the eyes of our understanding, which he alone can do, surely it is useless to speak of any other arguments and aids, since they will profit nothing unless we are theodidaktoi [θεοδίδακτοι], taught by God and by his Holy Spirit. Wherefore the first and principal cause that makes Scripture, which is known in itself, become known to us also will be the Holy Spirit teaching us inwardly, opening the eyes of our mind, so that we may see that light of Scripture and acknowledge in Scripture the voice of God himself and of Christ. The Spirit, however, in teaching us in this way adds nothing of light to Scripture, which shines abundantly of itself, but illumines our minds so that we may look upon that abundant light of holy Scripture. Yet the Holy Spirit, when he illumines our minds, does this through certain means and, as it were, organs, by whose ministry he works in our minds and hearts.

units.la: Mediorum siue instrumentorum Spiritus sanƈti duo sunt genera. Primum est internum, secundum est externum. Internum voco medium quod est in ipsa Scriptura: externum quod est extra Scripturam. Internum medium est principale medium Spiritus sanƈti, estque illa ipsa lux quæ in Scriptura lucet. Ergo Spiritus sanƈtus primùm omnium per Scripturæ lucem aperit mentes nostras, ad videndum illam ipsam Scripturæ lucem, in se quidem dem clarissimam, nobis vero ignotam. Aperit autem mentes ad videndum Scripturę lucem per Scripturam ipsam et ipsius lucem, non vno modo sed varijs. Partim enim quędam loca ex ipsa Scriptura affert quę clarè loquuntur de luce ipsius Scripturæ, & de Deo in ipsa Scriptura loquente, vt est ille, Omnis Scriptura est θεόπνευστος. 2. Timoth. 3. 16. Partim monet vt intueamur res illas spirituales quæ ibi sunt descriptę; partim monet vt respiciamus voces spirituales, quibus res illæ spirituales sunt expressæ, & pronunciatæ; partim jubet intueri veritatem oraculorum & vaticiniorum eventu comprobatam; demonstrat etiam nobis harmoniam illam pulcherrimam veteris & novi Testamenti, qua fit vt de se invicem testentur; non praetermittit illa miracula quæ etiam scripta sunt, quibusque suo tempore confirmata est cælestis illa doctrina; profert etiam Martyres qui sanguine suo veritatem illam obsignarunt, de quibus in eadē illa Scriptura legimus. His & aliis modis nos docet Spiritus ex ipsa Scriptura sacra Scripturam esse verbum Dei, demonstratq; in Scriptura illam lucem omni exceptione majorem.
units.tr: There are two kinds of means or instruments of the Holy Spirit: the first is internal, the second external. I call internal the means that is in Scripture itself; external, that which is outside Scripture. The internal means is the principal means of the Holy Spirit, and it is that very light which shines in Scripture. Therefore the Holy Spirit first of all, through the light of Scripture, opens our minds to see that very light of Scripture, which is indeed most clear in itself but unknown to us. He opens our minds to see the light of Scripture through Scripture itself and its own light, and not in one way only but in several. For partly he brings forward certain passages from Scripture itself which speak clearly of the light of Scripture and of God speaking in Scripture, such as that one: "All Scripture is God-breathed [theopneustos]" (2 Tim. 3:16). Partly he admonishes us to look upon those spiritual things which are described there; partly he admonishes us to regard the spiritual words by which those spiritual things are expressed and pronounced; partly he bids us look upon the truth of the oracles and prophecies, confirmed by their fulfilment. He also shows us that most beautiful harmony of the Old and New Testaments by which they bear witness to one another. He does not pass over those miracles which are also written, by which that heavenly doctrine was confirmed in its time. He also brings forward the martyrs who sealed that truth with their blood, of whom we read in the same Scripture. In these and other ways the Spirit teaches us from holy Scripture that Scripture is the word of God, and he demonstrates in Scripture that light which surpasses every objection.

units.la: In his denique numeranda est dignitas & sanctitas eorum virorum, quorum opera visus est
units.tr: Finally, among these must be counted the dignity and holiness of those men through whose work God seems to have been pleased

units.la: Deus in scribendo verbo suo, quæ ipsa conspicitur in Scriptura. Atq; hoc est internū illud & principale medium & organo Spiritus sancti, per quod nos docet & fidem ingignit in cordibus nostris, qua certò credimus Scripturam hanc esse Dei verbum.
units.tr: to write his word, which is itself seen in Scripture. This is that internal and principal means and organ of the Holy Spirit, through which he teaches us and kindles faith in our hearts, by which we firmly believe that this Scripture is the word of God.

units.la: Sunt & alia media extra Scripturam, quibus id ipsum docet Spiritus, vt est constantia Martyrum, qui suo sanguine quotidie veritatem illā cælestem obsignant; vt est perfequutio hostium Ecclesiæ; vt est Scripturarum oppugnatio ab ipso Satana; vt est conservatio Scripturarum in Ecclesia ad nostra vsq; tempora; vt est denique testimonium verę Ecclesię. Hęc omnia sunt extra ipsam Scripturam, & efficiunt secundarium quoddam argumenti genus, per quod etiam suo modo efficax esse solet Spiritus Dei Sanctus ad aperiendum oculos mentis nostræ, nosque illuminandos, ad hoc vt videre & audire possimus Deum ipsum in Scriptura loquentem ac lucentem.
units.tr: There are also other means outside Scripture by which the Spirit teaches this very thing: such as the constancy of the martyrs, who daily seal that heavenly truth with their blood; such as the persecution of the Church's enemies; such as the assault on the Scriptures by Satan himself; such as the preservation of the Scriptures in the Church down to our own times; and finally, such as the testimony of the true Church. All these lie outside Scripture itself, and they form a kind of secondary class of argument, by which the Holy Spirit of God usually works in his own way to open the eyes of our mind and enlighten us, so that we may be able to see and hear God himself speaking and shining in Scripture.

units.la: Notandum tamen Spiritum sanctum fidem in cordibus nostris, per secundum hoc genus mediorum externorū proprie ac præcipuè non ingignere, (quum proprium ac præcipuum instrumentum fidei sit verbum ipsius Dei; vel enim necesse est sit ipsa vox viva [?]ua Dei, vel certè sit Scriptura sacra, quæ sola nobis est pro viva & primaria voce Dei agnoscenda) verùm corda nostra duntaxat vel præparare ad fidem per verbum ipsius Dei postea ingignendam cordibus, vel certè fidem jam ingenita per verbum Dei aliquo modo confirmare.
units.tr: It must be noted, however, that the Holy Spirit does not properly and principally engender faith in our hearts through this second class of external means (since the proper and principal instrument of faith is the very Word of God; for it is necessary that it be either the living voice of God, or certainly the holy Scripture, which alone is to be acknowledged by us in place of the living and primary voice of God). Rather, these external means only prepare our hearts to receive faith afterwards through the Word of God, or else confirm in some way faith already engendered through the Word of God.

units.la: Quare hoc secundum genus mediorum nonnunquam solet præcedere ipsam Scripturam & Dei vocem, & per id Spiritus sanctus solet nonnunquam præparare aliquorum animos, priusquam per ipsam Scripturam fidem ingignat. Id quod Augustino factum legimus, ipso dicente ac sic loquente. (Non crederem Evangelio nisi me commoveret Ecclesiæ Catholicæ authoritas) Quibus verbis significat se, quum Manichæus esset, præparatum per authoritatem & testimonium Ecclesiæ, ad credendum Evangelio; postea tamen idem Spiritus sanctus qui præparavit Augustinum per testimonium Ecclesiæ; idé, inquâ, Spiritus in corde Augustini per Scripturam ipsam Evangelij fidem eam ingenuit, qua credidit Evangelium esse ipsius Dei verbum: Idque de se ipse alibi fassus est. Et eos, inquit, sequamur qui nos invitant priùs credere quod nondum valemus intueri, ut ipsa fide valentiores facti, quod credimus intelligere mereamur,non jam hominibus,sed ipso Deo intrinsecus mentem nostram firmate atque illuminante.Sic Samaritana mulier Ioh.4. tanquam membrum & testis Ecclesiæ,præconio quodam suo præparavit Samaritanos reliquos ad fidem Christi, qui ipsi postquam jam ipsum Christum audiverunt, dixerunt mulieri,Non amplius propter sermones tuos credimus, ipsi enim audivimus & scimus hunc esse verum servatorem Christum. Qua voce plane fignificarûnt fe testimonio mulieris duntaxat præparatos ad fidem, fidem autem cordibus ipsorum ingenitam per vocem ipsiusmet Christi efficacem. Nonnunquam igitur,vt dixi, antecedit fidem ingignendam hoc genus medij & argumenti ad nos præparandos,nonnunquam sequitur, & fidem jam ingenitam confirmat, nonnunquam deinque & antecedit hoc argumenti genus & fequitur;antecedit in præparandis, sequitur in confirmandis. Varijs enim modis docet nos Spiritus, & accommodat sese alio atque alio modo,ad alios atque alios, prout ipse vult, & infirmitas eorum postulat.
units.tr: Hence this second class of means sometimes precedes Scripture itself and the voice of God, and through it the Holy Spirit sometimes prepares the minds of some people before he engenders faith through Scripture itself. We read that this happened to Augustine, who himself says so in these words: "I would not believe the Gospel unless the authority of the Catholic Church moved me." By these words he signifies that, when he was a Manichaean, he was prepared to believe the Gospel through the authority and testimony of the Church; afterwards, however, the same Holy Spirit who had prepared Augustine through the testimony of the Church engendered in Augustine's heart, through Scripture itself, that faith in the Gospel by which he believed the Gospel to be the very Word of God. He confessed as much about himself elsewhere: "Let us follow those," he says, "who invite us to believe first what we are not yet able to see, so that, made stronger by faith itself, we may deserve to understand what we believe, God himself firmly and illuminating our mind from within, no longer by men." Thus the Samaritan woman in John 4, as a member and witness of the Church, by her proclamation prepared the rest of the Samaritans for faith in Christ; and they, after they had heard Christ himself, said to the woman: "We no longer believe because of your words; for we ourselves have heard and know that this is truly the Saviour, Christ." By these words they plainly signified that they were prepared for faith by the woman's testimony alone, but that faith was engendered in their hearts through the effective voice of Christ himself. Sometimes, then, as I have said, this kind of means and argument goes before the engendering of faith, to prepare us; sometimes it follows and confirms faith already engendered; and sometimes it both goes before and follows: it goes before in preparing, and follows in confirming. For the Spirit teaches us in various ways, and adapts himself in one way or another to different people, as he wills and as their weakness requires.

units.la: Notandum denique secundarij hujus generis argumenti, quòd externum est minufq; principale, non esse absolutam aliquâ necessitatem fitatem ad fidem faciendam. Satis enim nobis esse debet, si nos doceat. Spiritus per ipsum ac solum quidem verbum Dei, sed infirmitatis nostrae causa adhibet idem Spiritus illud alterum & secundarium genus argumenti: Idquod plane docet Christus Iohan.5. vbi dicit Iohannis Baptistae de se testimonium non simpliciter necessarium fuisse, sed ita suisse consultum eorum infirmitati & incredulitati, his verbis verf. 15. Iohannes testimonium dedit veritati, ego autem ab homine testimonium non capto: sed haec dico vt vos servemini. Deinde quod testimonium Iohannis secundarium duntaxat fuerit, primarium autem ipsius Christi de se testimonium paulo post aperte docet: At ego, inquit, testimonium habeo majus testimonio Iohannis: opera enim quae dedit mihi Pater testantur de me. Atque haec est sententia nostra de argumento quo constat Scripturam esse verbum Dei, & responsio nostra facta ad quaestionem quam diximus, cur sit.
units.tr: Finally, it must be noted of this secondary kind of argument that, since it is external and less principal, there is no absolute necessity for it in producing faith. For it ought to be enough for us that the Spirit teaches us through the Word of God alone; yet because of our weakness the same Spirit also employs this other, secondary kind of argument. Christ clearly teaches this in John 5, where he says that the testimony of John the Baptist about himself was not simply necessary, but was so arranged for their weakness and unbelief. He says in verse 15: "John bore witness to the truth, but I do not receive testimony from man; but I say these things so that you may be saved." Then, that John's testimony was only secondary, while Christ's own testimony about himself was primary, he clearly teaches shortly afterwards: "But I have a testimony greater than John's testimony; for the works which the Father has given me bear witness of me." This is our view concerning the argument by which it is established that Scripture is the Word of God, and our answer to the question we have mentioned, why it is so.

units.la: Quid Papistae sentiant facile est ex eorum tum dictis tum scriptis colligere: Haec autem est, vt paucis dicam, sententia Papistarum. Medium et argumentum principale, ac fere vnicum quo conltare volunt Scriptura esse verbum Dei, est testimonium Ecclesiæ, non tantum Catholicæ, vt ipsi loquuntur, sed et eorum qui per continuas successiones ab Apostolis ad nos vsque fidem propagarùnt: intelligunt Pontifices maximè, qui, vtaiunt, successerunt Petro ipsiusque Cathedræ. Hanc Ecclesiæ quam dicunt sententiam, omnium Scripturarum judicem & interpretem volunt esse, à cujus judicio ad alium judicem non liceat cuiquam provocare: dignitatem autem hanc & prærogativam testimonio Ecclesiæ ideò tribuunt, quòd velint Scripturam eam quæ est in corde Ecclesiæ primariâ esse Scripturam, & vocem Ecclesiæ nobis agnoscédam & habendam esse vice vivæ vocis Dei ipsius. Quasi verò Deus nunc præcipuè ac primariò in Ecclesia, & per Ecclesiam loquatur. Quod si testimonium Ecclesiæ volunt primariam esse Dei vocem, & primariam Dei Scripturam, sequitur eos velle pariter summâ lucem esse in Ecclesiæ voce, & eam non tantùm nobis, sed & per se notissimam esse, ac proindè præbere lucem ipsi Scripturæ sanctæ, non tantùm ratione nostri, sed etiam ratione sui. Vnde quidâ ex ijs dixit nihilo plus valere Scripturam siue Ecclesiæ authoritate, quàm fabulas Æsopi. Quum enim sit vox Ecclesiæ illis primaria vox Dei ad omnia respondens, quum viva sit ac vocalis, proindeque non solum natura, sed etiā nobis notissima, sequitur ex eorum sententia eam ministrare lucem Scripturæ, non tantum quoad nos, sed etiam quoad ipsam Scripturam, quæ secundaria quædam Scriptura est, & secundaria quædam vox. Est enim Ecclesiæ vox illis quasi Dei ipsius vox è cælis reddita, vocem Scripturæ, quæ hominum modo est vox, & Scripturam, quæ amanuensium digitis tantum est exarata, confirmās, ratam & authenticam faciens. Ex illis illorum principijs, hoc sequatur necesse est, licet alij aliter loquantur.
units.tr: What the Papists think is easy to gather from both their sayings and their writings; and this, to put it briefly, is the view of the Papists. Their chief and almost only means and argument by which they wish it to be established that Scripture is the Word of God is the testimony of the Church: not only the Catholic Church, as they call it, but of those who through continuous succession from the Apostles have propagated the faith down to us. The Popes especially are meant, who, they say, succeeded Peter and his chair. They wish this Church, as they call it, to be the judge and interpreter of all Scriptures, from whose judgment it is not lawful for anyone to appeal to another judge; they attribute this dignity and prerogative to the testimony of the Church because they want the Scripture which is in the heart of the Church to be the primary Scripture, and the voice of the Church to be acknowledged and held by us in place of the living voice of God himself. As if God now speaks chiefly and primarily in the Church and through the Church! And if they want the testimony of the Church to be the primary voice of God and the primary Scripture of God, it follows that they equally want the highest light to lie in the voice of the Church, and that this voice is most known not only to us but also in itself, and so it gives light to holy Scripture not only with respect to us but also with respect to itself. Hence one of them said that Scripture has no more value by the authority of the Church than the fables of Aesop. For since the voice of the Church is for them the primary voice of God, answering to everything, since it is living and vocal, and therefore known not only in its nature but also to us, it follows from their view that it gives light to Scripture, not only as regards us but also as regards Scripture itself, which is a kind of secondary Scripture and a kind of secondary voice. For the voice of the Church is for them as it were the very voice of God rendered from heaven, confirming the voice of Scripture, which is only human in manner, and making Scripture, which is merely written by the fingers of amanuenses, valid and authentic. From their principles this must necessarily follow, although others speak otherwise.

units.la: Nos quidem vt illorum sententiam quam ex ijs principijs inferunt negamus, ita principia ipsa rejicimus: Negamus enim illud eorum principium primum, nempè, vocem Ecclesiæ habēdam esse pro viva voce ipsius Dei, & Scripturam, in corde Ecclesiæ inscriptam, habendam esse pro Scriptura ipsius Dei digito exarata: affirmamusque pro viva voce Dei habendam esse solam hanc Scripturam propheticam & Apostolicam, & vice Scripturæ exaratæ Dei digito solam hanc propheticam & Apostolicam: Imò addimus præterea eam esse nobis vice sententiarum quæ in mente Dei sunt ab ȩterno: Hȩc enim est voluntas Dei vt ipsum quasi viva voce loquentem in hac Scriptura audiamus. Habet, inquit, Mosen & Prophetas. Luc. 16. 29. hoc est, Mosis & Prophetarum scripta: & Scriptură hanc vult Deus non alio loco habendam atque habita fuit olim illa Scriptura quam ipse digito suo exaravit in tabulis lapideis. Vox autem Ecclefiȩ (de vera loquor, non de Papistica illa & mendaci) est vox ministra, & quasi prȩconis, quȩ promulgat atq; explicat hominibus vocem illam Dei loquentis in Scriptura omni exceptione majorem: & Scriptura in corde Ecclefiȩ, hoc est, sententiȩ veritatis quȩ sunt in cordibus fidelium, nihil aliud sunt quàm secundaria quędam Scriptura exscripta per Spiritum sanctum ex primaria illa &αὐτοπιστα Scriptura, & inscripta hominum mentibus. Quota tamen pars quæso illius tam plenæ Scripturæ Propheticæ & Apostolicę exscripta est, & inscripta mentibus nostris? Imò ne in omnium quidem hominum fidelium cordibus, etiamsi sumas omnes confertim, tamen ne in omnium quidem cordibus inscripta sunt omnia illa plenè & perfectè, quæ habentur in Scriptura hac Prophetica & Apostolica: Neque enim Ecclesia Catholica, quantifper in terris versatur, capax est totius illius lucis quæ splendet in Scriptura Prophetica & Apostolica. Convulso hoc principio primo, alterum illud principium eorum, quod vox Ecclesiæ sit notissima & sua natura & nobis, sua sponte corruit: Labefactato utroq; principio, conclusio eorum quam ex ijs inferunt vltrò collabascit.
units.tr: We indeed, just as we deny their conclusion which they draw from those principles, so we reject the principles themselves. For we deny their first principle, namely, that the voice of the Church is to be held as the living voice of God itself, and that Scripture inscribed in the heart of the Church is to be held as Scripture written by the finger of God himself. We affirm that only this prophetic and apostolic Scripture is to be held as the living voice of God, and that only this prophetic and apostolic Scripture takes the place of Scripture written by the finger of God. Indeed we add further that it is for us in place of the thoughts which are in the mind of God from eternity: for it is God's will that we hear him speaking, as it were with a living voice, in this Scripture. "They have Moses and the Prophets," he says (Luke 16:29), that is, the writings of Moses and the Prophets; and God wishes this Scripture to be held in no other place than that in which that Scripture was held long ago, which he himself wrote with his finger on the stone tablets. The voice of the Church (I speak of the true Church, not that Papist and lying one) is a ministering voice, as it were of a herald, which proclaims and explains to men that voice of God speaking in Scripture, which is greater than any exception; and Scripture in the heart of the Church, that is, the sentences of truth which are in the hearts of the faithful, are nothing other than a kind of secondary Scripture, copied out by the Holy Spirit from that primary and αὐτόπιστος Scripture, and inscribed in men's minds. Yet, I ask, what small part of that so full prophetic and apostolic Scripture has been copied out and inscribed in our minds? Indeed, not even in the hearts of all the faithful taken together are all those things inscribed fully and perfectly which are contained in this prophetic and apostolic Scripture; for the Catholic Church, as long as it dwells on earth, is not able to receive the whole of that light which shines in the prophetic and apostolic Scripture. With this first principle overthrown, their other principle, that the voice of the Church is most known both in its nature and to us, collapses of its own accord; with both principles shaken, their conclusion which they draw from them collapses of itself.

units.la: De Scripturæ sacræ prima proprietate: de qua Controversia tertia.
units.tr: On the first property of Holy Scripture: the third controversy.

units.la: CAP. 9.
units.tr: CHAP. 9.

units.la: DEmonstrandum nunc est Scripturam esse antiquissimam tempore, quæ ex proprietatibus, quæ à nobis suprà Scripturæ sunt attributæ, prima est. Primùm omnium discutienda est nobis vocabuli Scripturæ homonymia. Scripturæ nomen capi potest vel pro re tantùm ac substantia ipsa quæ literis est consignata; vel non modò pro re & substantia, sed etiam pro scriptione ipsa, siue forma qua illa substantia nobis est expressa. Iam si hoc nomine substantiam ipsam intelligas, illud est extra controversiam Scripturam esse antiquissimam, quum substantia sit sententiarum earum, quas non modò loquuti sunt Patriarchæ et Prophetæ, sed etiam ipsemet Deus, quæq; etiam in mente Dei sunt ab æterno. Sin intelligas hoc nomine non tantùm substantiam, sed etiam scriptionem ipsam, et hac quoque ratione Scriptura dici potest antiquissima. Nam Scripturam hanc Propheticam & Apostolicam, etiam ratione scriptionis & formæ revelationis, jam non semel diximus ex Dei voluntate agnoscendam esse à nobis, non tantùm pro viva voce ipsorum Prophetarum & Apostolorum, neque tantùm pro viva voce ipsius Dei, aut etiam Scriptura exarata ipsius Dei digito, qualis erat illa decalogi, quam constat exaratam fuisse ipsius Dei digito in tabulis lapideis; sed etiam pro sententijs illis, &, ut sic dicam, notionibus, quæ in mente Dei inscriptæ sunt ab æterno.
units.tr: It must now be shown that Scripture is the most ancient in time, which is the first of the properties we have earlier attributed to Scripture. First of all we must examine the homonymy of the word "Scripture." The name Scripture may be taken either merely for the thing and substance itself that has been committed to writing, or not only for the thing and substance but also for the writing itself, that is, the form by which that substance is expressed to us. Now if by this name you understand the substance itself, it is beyond controversy that Scripture is most ancient, since the substance consists of those sentences which were spoken not only by the Patriarchs and Prophets but also by God himself, and which are also in the mind of God from eternity. But if by this name you understand not only the substance but also the writing itself, then in this sense too Scripture can be called most ancient. For we have said more than once that this prophetic and apostolic Scripture, even as to the manner of writing and the form of revelation, must be acknowledged by us as the will of God: not only in place of the living voice of the Prophets and Apostles, nor only in place of the living voice of God himself, or of writing inscribed by the very finger of God, such as the Decalogue, which is known to have been written with God's finger on tables of stone; but also in place of those sentences, and, as I may say, notions, which were inscribed in the mind of God from eternity.

units.la: Ut rem hanc paulò altius repetam: Veritas illa quæ est in mente Dei ab æterno, revelata est in tempore pluribus modis; partim enim revelata est ipsiusmet Dei viva voce, partim ipsiusmet scripto, partim voce Patriarcharum, Prophetarū, & Apostolorum, ut hic nihil de Angelis dicam, partim denique scripto Prophetarum & Apostolorum. Cessavit jam à multo tempore viva illa & immediata Dei ipsius vox; non habemus Dei ipsius scriptum; desierunt loqui Patriarchæ, Prophetæ, Apostoli stoli; manent sola scripta Prophetarum & Apostolorum: Quamobrem ad fidem necessarium est ut hæc scripta habeamus nos vice primùm vivæ vocis Prophetarum & Apostolorum; deinde viuæ vocis ipsiusmet Dei; tertiò Scripturæ ipsiusmet Dei digitis exaratæ; quartò denique veritatis ipsius, & notionum ac sententiarum quæ sunt in ipsa Dei mente, quibus cum nihil sit antiquius, sequitur hanc ipsam scriptionem propheticam & Apostolicam esse quodam modo antiquissimam. Nam quæ de viva voce ipsius Dei, vel de sententijs quæ sunt in mente Dei prædicari possunt, illa aliquo modo prædicari possunt de Scriptura hac, quæ supplet eorum vicem: Si enim sic aliquo modo verè enuncio, Scriptura est viva vox Dei, annon aliquo modo verè dico, Scriptura est antiquissima, quum viva vox Dei sit antiquissima? Sed satis est ad ostendendum antiquitatem Scripturæ, si ipsa considerem us substantiam Scripturæ, quæ extra controversiam antiquissima est. Scriptio tamen ipsa suâ habet dignitatem, quum Scriptura ratione etiam scriptionis dicatur θεόπνευστος. Nullum enim est in ipsa scriptione jota quod non sit à Deo inspiratum.
units.tr: To take up this matter a little more deeply: that truth which is in the mind of God from eternity has been revealed in time in several ways. For partly it was revealed by the living voice of God himself, partly by his own writing, partly by the voice of the Patriarchs, Prophets and Apostles (I say nothing here about the Angels), and finally partly by the writing of the Prophets and Apostles. That living and immediate voice of God has long since ceased; we do not have a writing of God himself; the Patriarchs, Prophets and Apostles have ceased to speak; only the writings of the Prophets and Apostles remain. Therefore, for faith it is necessary that we have these writings in place first of the living voice of the Prophets and Apostles; then of the living voice of God himself; thirdly of Scripture written by God's own fingers; and fourthly, finally, of the truth itself and of the notions and sentences that are in the very mind of God. Since nothing is older than these, it follows that this prophetic and apostolic writing is in some way most ancient. For what can be predicated of the living voice of God, or of the sentences that are in the mind of God, can in some way be predicated of this Scripture, which takes their place. If I may truly say in some sense, "Scripture is the living voice of God," do I not also in some sense truly say, "Scripture is most ancient," since the living voice of God is most ancient? But it is enough to show the antiquity of Scripture if we consider the substance of Scripture, which is beyond controversy most ancient. Yet the writing itself has its own dignity, since Scripture is called God-breathed [θεόπνευστος] even with respect to its writing. For there is not a single iota in the writing itself that has not been inspired by God.

units.la: Hic insurgunt adversarij, &, vt alias semper, ita & hic Ecclesiam suâ Scripturæ pr_ferunt, dicuntque Ecclesiam antiquiorem & vetustiorem Scriptura: nam, inquiunt, fuit Ecclesia ante Mosen, qui primus scriptor extitit, annos totos bis mille. A Christi autem adventu per annos multos fuit Ecclesia sine Scripturis. Sed ex his quæ diximus facilis est solutio: Si enim Scripturæ nomine no intelligamus characteras literarum, & volumina, sed substantiam illam & materiam quæ literis his, characteribus, & voluminibus certo quodam modo comprehensa est (in Scripturis enim habemus loquentes Prophetas & Apostolos & viuam ipsorum vocem, habemus ijs comprehensam vivam ipsius Dei vocem, habemus deniq; ijs expressam Dei mentem) si, inquâ, substantiam hanc accipiamus hoc nomine, jam negari non potest Scripturam esse non modo antiquiorem Ecclesia, quæ ex verbo Dei tanquam semine incorruptibili nata est, 1. Pet. 1. Renati non ex femine mortali, sed immortali, per sermonem viventis Dei, & manentis in æternum: Non tantum, inquam, videbitur Scriptura Ecclesia esse antiquior, sed & rerum omnium antiquissima, & cum ipso Deo ab æterno esse. Sin hoc nomine accipias & rem & scriptionem, etiam hac quoque ratione nihil incommodi est fi ipsa antiquissima, non modò Ecclesia antiquior, prædicetur, vt supra fusius diximus. Atque hactenus de prima proprietate Scripturæ sacræ, deque controversia tertia.
units.tr: Here our adversaries rise up and, as always elsewhere, here too they put the Church before Scripture, and say that the Church is older and more ancient than Scripture: for, they say, the Church existed before Moses, who was the first writer, for a full two thousand years. And from the coming of Christ, for many years, the Church existed without Scriptures. But from what we have said the solution is easy: for if by the name Scripture we understand not the letters and volumes, but that substance and matter which is comprised in a certain way in these letters, characters and volumes (for in the Scriptures we have the speaking Prophets and Apostles and their living voice, we have in them the living voice of God contained, and finally we have the mind of God expressed in them), if, I say, we take Scripture in this sense, then it cannot be denied that Scripture is not only older than the Church, which has been born of the word of God as of an incorruptible seed (1 Pet. 1. born again not of corruptible seed but of incorruptible, through the word of the living God, who abides forever), but that Scripture will appear not only older than the Church but also the most ancient of all things, and to have been with God himself from eternity. But if you take the name in the sense of both the thing and the writing, then even in this way there is no inconvenience if it is declared most ancient, and not merely older than the Church, as we have said more fully above. And so far concerning the first property of Holy Scripture and the third controversy.

units.la: De secunda proprietate Scripturæ, de qua Controversia quarta.
units.tr: On the second property of Scripture, which is the fourth controversy.

units.la: CAP. 10.
units.tr: CHAPTER 10.

units.la: SEcunda proprietas Scripturæ sacrę jam semel ostensa est in tractanda secunda controversia: Est autem quòd sit apertissima per se ac intelleƈtu facillima: quum enim sit verbum Dei, & verbum Dei necesse sit omnes fateantur in se clarissimum, manifestissimum, maximè perspicuum esse, sive verba, siue res verbis significatas respicias, nisi velint Spiritum sanƈtum summa afficere injuria, profecto sequitur Scripturam sanƈtam in se & per se apertissimam ac clarissimam esse, & totam & secundum omnes sui partes. De hac summa perspicuitate Scripturæ multa sunt ipsius Scripturæ testimonia. Psal. 119. Verbum Domini lucerna pedibus meis, Psal. 19. Præceptum Domini lucidum, & illuminans oculos appellatur. Proverb. 6. Mandatum lucerna, & lex lux. Dominus per Esaiam testatur se non in abscondito fcondito loquutum 45. 2. Pet. 1. dicitur fermo Propheticus sermo cui tanquam lucernæ lucenti in loco caliginoso fit attendendum. Ergo tota Scriptura et omnia Scripturæ loca, per se & in se sunt manifestissima, apertissima, & accommodata etiam ad captum vulgi, & rudissimorum quorumcunque. Nam certum est Dominum in Scripturis balbutire nobiscum. Iohan. 3. 12. Si terrena dixi vobis & non creditis, hoc est, terreno & crasso quodammodo vobis loquutus sum, accommodaviq; me ad captum verstum, &c.
units.tr: The second property of Holy Scripture was already shown when we treated the second controversy. Scripture is most plain in itself and very easy to understand. Since it is the Word of God, and everyone must admit that the Word of God is in itself most clear, most manifest and most perspicuous, whether you look at the words or at the things signified by the words, it certainly follows that Holy Scripture is in itself and by itself most plain and clear, both as a whole and in every part. Scripture itself bears many testimonies to this great perspicuity. Psalm 119: "Your word is a lamp to my feet." Psalm 19 calls the commandment of the Lord "clear, enlightening the eyes." Proverbs 6: "The commandment is a lamp, and the law is light." The Lord testifies through Isaiah that he has not spoken in secret (Isa. 45. 2). In 2 Pet. 1, the prophetic word is called a lamp shining in a dark place, to which we must attend. Therefore the whole of Scripture, and all its passages, are in themselves and by themselves most manifest and plain, and adapted even to the grasp of the common people and of the most unlearned. For it is certain that the Lord, in the Scriptures, speaks to us as to infants. John 3. 12: "If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, I have spoken to you in a somewhat earthly and coarse manner, and adapted myself to your capacity," and so on.

units.la: Dixi Scripturam sacram per se apertissimam & intellectu facillimam esse, quia si hominum, quà homines sunt, hoc est, ψυχικοί, & carnales, ratione habeas, Scriptura sancta quæ est de rebus spiritualibus tota obscura est: Animalis enim homo nō est capax eorum quæ sunt Spiritus Dei. Sin respicias πνευματικῶς & θεοδιδακτῶς, adhuc etiam ijs obscura est ex parte, nempe, qua ex parte sunt ψυχικοί. Hinc sunt illæ assiduæ piorum, (in quibus etiam adhuc hærent reliquiæ cæcitatis illius & natiuę corruptionis,) preces ad Deum, vt velit aperire oculos mentis ipsorum, ad hoc vt videant lucem illa Scripturarum, & locorum quorumcunque Scripturæ, alioqui in se clarissimam.
units.tr: I have said that Holy Scripture is in itself most plain and very easy to understand, because if you consider men as men, that is, as psychikoi [ψυχικοί], and carnal, Holy Scripture, which deals with spiritual things, is wholly obscure. For the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God. But if you look at it pneumatikōs [πνευματικῶς] and theodidaktōs [θεοδιδακτῶς], it is still obscure to such people in part, namely in so far as they are psychikoi [ψυχικοί]. Hence come the constant prayers of the godly (in whom remnants of that blindness and native corruption still cling) to God, that he would be pleased to open the eyes of their minds, so that they may see the light of the Scriptures, and of every passage of Scripture, which is otherwise clear in itself.

units.la: In precibus suis pij quiqúe longè absunt ab eo vt imputent difficultatem & obscuritatem ipsi Dei verbo, verùm omnem culpâ in se, cæcitatem, ac hebetudinem suam transferunt.
units.tr: In their prayers the godly are far from imputing difficulty and obscurity to the Word of God itself. Rather, they transfer all the blame to themselves, to their own blindness and dullness.

units.la: Etsi autem illud verum sit, Scripturam & omnia Scripturæ loca simpliciter & per se manifestissima esse & facillima intellectu, ratione autem nostri & cæcitatis nostræ obscura esse ac difficilia, tamen illud negari non potest alia Scripturæ loca aliis clariora esse per se, intellectu faciliora, ac manifestiora; vt sunt illa loca de dogmatis fidei & morum ad salutem intellectu necessaria, quæ tam manifeste sunt propósita, tam sæpè repetita, atque etiam multis in locis expósita, vt paucioribus interpretationis & cognitionis regulis contenta sint. Indigent autem hæc ipsa Spiritu Dei sancto, sine quo spiritualia quæque, etiam maximè perspicua, ab homine verè intelligi non possunt. Quamobrem qui hæc ignorat quæ in se tam manifesta sunt, planè cæcus est, & de ipsius salute actum esse videtur. Quòd si tectum fit Evangelium nostrum tectum est ijs qui pereunt. 2. Cor. 4.
units.tr: Although it is true that Scripture and all its passages are simply and in themselves most manifest and easy to understand, yet on account of us and our blindness they are obscure and difficult. Nevertheless it cannot be denied that some passages of Scripture are by themselves clearer than others, easier to understand and more manifest. Such are the passages on the doctrines of faith and of morals that are necessary to know for salvation. These are set forth so plainly, repeated so often, and explained in so many places, that they need only a few rules of interpretation and knowledge. Yet even these need the Holy Spirit of God, without whom no spiritual matters, even the most perspicuous, can truly be understood by man. Therefore whoever does not know these things, which are so manifest in themselves, is plainly blind, and his salvation seems to be at stake. "But if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who perish" (2 Cor. 4).

units.la: Quod ad alia Scripturæ loca quæ in se magis obscura sunt, quum non sint de necessarijs fidei & morum dogmatis, ignorari possunt citra jactura fidei ac salutis: etsi quidem eorum cognitio luce aliquâ afferre possit ad illa ipsa fidei & morû dogmata intellectu necessaria magis cognoscenda. Eorum etiam tolerabilis aliqua & fidei analoga interpretatio haberi potest, si ferventur cognitionis & interpretationis illę regulę, quę vulgò à viris doctis tradi solent: quarum principium repetimus à Spiritu sancto intus nos illuminante & docente; Alię quę deinceps numerātur regulę Spiritus sancti organa sunt & media, & sumuntur partim ex ipsa Scriptura, ut ex collatione locorum Scripturę, vel eorundem, vel sensu vel phrasi similium; partim aliunde, ut ex locis communibus theologicis, ex testimonio Ecclesię, ex ipsa Grammatica, præsertim hebraica & græca, ex Rhetorica, ex Dialectica, quæ non tantum argumenta simplicia, sed etiam argumentorum dispositionem in axiomatibus, in syllogismo, in methodo considerat. Dialectica enim docet, id quod vocant cohærsione antecedentium & consequentium, quæ quidem non parum facit ad locorum obscuriorum cognitionem. Vt de aliis nunc taceam, utilis est etiam ad hanc rem saltem tolerabilis aliqua cognitio scientiarum aliarum particularium, ut Ethicæ, ut Physicæ, &c. Ad hæc omnia accedere debent assiduę ad Deum precęs & feriæ, vt velit oculos mentis nostræ Spiritu suo sancto aperire & illuminare. Hæc media si serveturin Scripturarum & locorum Scripturæ difficilium interpretatione, non facile quis aberrabit à vero.
units.tr: As for other passages of Scripture which are more obscure in themselves, since they do not concern the necessary doctrines of faith and morals, they can be left unknown without loss to faith and salvation. Yet their knowledge can certainly throw some light on those very doctrines of faith and morals which are necessary to know more fully. A tolerable and faith-consistent interpretation of them can also be had, if the rules of knowledge and interpretation that are commonly handed down by learned men are observed. The first of these rules we take from the Holy Spirit, who illuminates and teaches us within. The other rules that follow are the instruments and means of the Spirit. They are drawn partly from Scripture itself, such as from the comparison of passages of Scripture that are alike either in sense or in wording; partly from elsewhere: from theological commonplaces, from the testimony of the Church, from grammar itself, especially Hebrew and Greek, from rhetoric, and from dialectic. Dialectic considers not only simple arguments but also the arrangement of arguments in axioms, in syllogisms and in method. For dialectic teaches what they call the cohesion of antecedents and consequents, which contributes not a little to the knowledge of more obscure passages. To say nothing of others now, a useful and at least tolerable knowledge of other particular sciences, such as ethics and physics, is also helpful for this purpose. To all these must be added constant prayers to God and times of rest, that he would be pleased to open and illuminate the eyes of our minds by his Holy Spirit. If these means are observed in interpreting the Scriptures and the more difficult passages of Scripture, one will not easily go astray from the truth.

units.la: Hic insurgunt adversarij, contenduntque pluribus argumentis Scripturas etiam per se & in se, etiam in ijs quę ad salutem pertinent, obscuras esse: scilicet vt homines vulgò abstinentes à Scripturarum lectione, pendeant ab ipsorum somnijs, & vt interpretationes suas obtrudant Ecclesiæ, nempe, eas quas ipsi volunt, & quas fere pluris faciunt quam ipsum Scripturę textum; detorquetes potius Scripturæ textum ad glossam suam, quàm ex Scripturæ textu interpretatione deducentes. Partim igitur testimonio ipsarum Scripturarum agunt, partim testimonio Doctorum & Patrum, partim denique rationibus, quæ omnia facile dissolvi possunt ex ijs quæ supra à nobis jacta sunt fundamentis. Satis sit nunc si ad vnam aut alteram eorum objectionē responde amus.
units.tr: Here the adversaries rise up and contend, with many arguments, that the Scriptures are obscure even in themselves and by themselves, even in those matters that pertain to salvation. Their purpose, of course, is that common people, who abstain from reading the Scriptures, should depend on their dreams, and that they should thrust their own interpretations upon the Church, namely those which they themselves wish, and which they value almost more than the text of Scripture itself, twisting the text of Scripture to their own gloss rather than deducing their interpretation from the text. So they argue partly from the testimony of Scripture itself, partly from the testimony of teachers and Fathers, and partly from reasons. All of these can easily be dissolved from the foundations we have laid down above. It is enough now if we answer one or another of their objections.

units.la: Quærunt, An non hæ Scripturæ quæ extant veteris & novi Testamenti egeant commentarijs, qui etiam quam plurimi à quam-
units.tr: They ask: do not these Scriptures of the Old and New Testament that exist need commentaries, of which very many have been written by very many people?

units.la: plurimis sunt conscripti? Respondeo per se quidem Scripturas sacras non indigere hominum commentationibus & scriptis interpretationibus, Scripturas enim habemus pro viva voce Dei ipsius: & quid est quaeso quod potest vocem illa in se clariorem & apertiorē efficere? An potest vel homo vel Angelus clarius eloqui aliquid, quàm ipse Deus? & an Deus de industria affectat obscuritatē? quorum vtrumque dictu blasphemum est. Commentarios tamen hominum doctorum & piorum qui in Scripturis Dei aliquanto plus temporis triverunt, vulgo hominum ac rudioribus non parum prodesse haud diffitemur; neque parum adjumenti afferre ad dispellendas istas naturae tenebras.
units.tr: I answer: in themselves the holy Scriptures do not need the commentaries and written interpretations of men, for we hold the Scriptures to be the living voice of God himself. And what, I ask, can make that voice clearer and plainer in itself? Can man or angel speak anything more clearly than God himself? Does God deliberately seek obscurity? Either of these is blasphemous to say. Yet we do not deny that the commentaries of learned and godly men, who have spent a good deal more time in the Scriptures of God, are of no small benefit to the common people and to the less learned, and bring no small help in dispelling those darknesses of nature.

units.la: Sed major quaestio est & gravior de praedicatione verbi Dei, & de Scripturarum explicatione quae in publicis fidelium congressibus & coetibus a pastoribus haberi solet: an non haec explicatio & praedicatio verbi necessaria est, haec, inquam, quae fit viva voce Pastorum & Doctorum? Respondeo Scripturas Dei quas nos habemus pro viva voce ipsius Dei ne hac quidem explicatione per se indigere, neque ministerio hoc, quod est in praedicando & explicando Scripturas sacras, De-um um aut verbum ipsius per se opus habere; verùm necessitatem hanc esse κάλα τι tantùm, & respectu nostri, cæcitatis & ignorantiæ nostræ, qui pueri sumus, imò infantes, tantisper dum hic vivimus. Vide Ephef.4.1.Cor.13. Postquam autem in viros evaserimus, quod futurum est in altero demùm sæculo, tum nullo nobis opus erit istiusmodi ministerio, sed contenti erimus & impleti sola illa luce Dei & Christi, sine doctrina aliqua vel hominum vel Angelorum. Atq; hæc hactenus de secunda Scripturæ proprietate, deque controversia quarta.
units.tr: But a greater and weightier question concerns the preaching of the Word of God, and the explanation of the Scriptures which is customarily given by the ministers in the public assemblies and gatherings of the faithful. Is not this explanation and preaching of the Word necessary, I mean this which is done by the living voice of ministers and teachers? I answer that the Scriptures of God, which we hold to be the living voice of God himself, do not in themselves need even this explanation, and that the Word of God does not need the ministry of preaching and explaining the holy Scriptures. Rather, this necessity is only in some measure [κατά τι], and with respect to our blindness and ignorance, since we are children, indeed infants, for as long as we live here. See Ephesians 4 and 1 Corinthians 13. But once we have grown into men, which will happen only in the other age, then we shall have no need of such a ministry, but shall be content and filled with that light of God and Christ alone, without any teaching of men or angels. And so far on the second property of Scripture, and on the fourth controversy.

units.la: De tertia Scripturæ sacræ proprietate, de qua Controversia quinta. CAP. II.
units.tr: On the third property of Holy Scripture, which is the fifth controversy. CHAPTER 2.

units.la: TErtia proprietas Scripturæ sacræ est, quòd simplicissima sit, quòd ad verba & loquutionem attinet, neque vllam habeat in se ambiguitatem & amphibologiam. Differt autem hæc proprietas à superiori, quòd cum perspicuitas latiùs pateat & ad verba & ad res, simplicitas sit verborum tantùm. Dicimus itaque Scripturam esse in se simplicissimam, neque in se vllam habere ambiguitatem & amphibologiam, saltem non alicubi explicatam, si aliquid habeat obscuritatis. Sermo enim Domini,& Spiritus ipsius simplicissimus est, neque loquitur vnquam Deus, vt homines dubio & ambiguo sermone capiat, quod faciunt Diabolus & Sophistæ: sed vt homines veritatem doceat. Spiritus enim veritatis deducit nos in omnem veritatem. Ioh.16.13. Scriptura autem est θεόπνευστος, & verbum Dei, vt jam ostensum est: Ergo, nisi Deo velimus insignem facere injuriam, necesse est fateamur Scripturā in se simplicissimam sensu & significatione. Dico in se sensu simplicissimā esse, quia si sit in Scripturæ sermone ambiguitas aliqua, ea ambiguitas & multiplicitas nō jam imputanda est Scripturæ, sed cæcitati & ignorantiæ hóminum, etiam eorum qui non ex malitia Scripturas detorquent. Nam non desunt qui Scripturas malitiosè pervertunt, torquent & retorquent, quum sciant tamen simplicè esse earum sensum. Cum sit hæc Scripturæ simplicitas, primùm ipse filius Dei ex Scriptura sacra adversus Satanæ insultus & quosvis adversarios disputans tela deprompsit, & ad Scripturam sacram omnes remisit. Deinde Apostoli, eorumque successores,& patres ipsi,ex Scriptura sacra contra hæreticos argumenta confirmandi sanam doctrinam & confutandi hæreses desumpserunt.
units.tr: The third property of Holy Scripture is that it is most simple, so far as words and speech are concerned, and that it has in itself no ambiguity or amphibology. This property differs from the previous one in that clarity extends more widely, to both words and things, whereas simplicity concerns words only. We say, therefore, that Scripture is in itself most simple, and has in itself no ambiguity or amphibology, at least not anywhere left unexplained, if it contains any obscurity. For the speech of the Lord and of his Spirit is most simple; God never speaks so as to leave men to grasp his meaning through doubtful and ambiguous speech, as the devil and the Sophists do, but so as to teach men the truth. For the Spirit of truth leads us into all truth (John 16:13). Scripture, however, is θεόπνευστος [God-breathed], and the Word of God, as has already been shown. Therefore, unless we wish to do a great injury to God, we must confess that Scripture is most simple in sense and meaning. I say that it is most simple in sense in itself, because if there is any ambiguity in the language of Scripture, that ambiguity and multiplicity is not to be imputed to Scripture but to the blindness and ignorance of men, including those who distort the Scriptures not out of malice. For there are not lacking those who maliciously pervert, twist and turn the Scriptures, although they know that their sense is plain. Given this simplicity of Scripture, first the Son of God himself, disputing from Holy Scripture against the assaults of Satan and any adversaries, drew his weapons from it and referred all men to Holy Scripture. Then the Apostles, their successors, and the Fathers themselves, drew from Holy Scripture the arguments by which they confirmed sound doctrine against heretics and refuted heresies.

units.la: Sed adversus hanc quoque Scripturæ sacræ proprietate adversarij insurgunt, & Scripturam sacram dubiam esse, ambiguâ, flexiloquam, alutæ instar, cereum habere nasum, flećti hinc inde posse blasphemant: quò fieri dicunt ut liber hæreticorum sit, ex quo hæreses oriuntur, & omnes suis erroribus patrocinium quærere conantur. Sed responsio ex ijs quæ jam diximus facilis est. Nam ambiguitas illa & flexibilitas non est imputanda Scripturæ, quæ est Θεοπνευστος, & nobis vice ipsius viuæ vocis Dei: sed vel ignorantiæ, vel malitiæ, & petulantiæ hominum, qui vel non possunt deprehendere Scripturæ simplicem & verum sensum, vel Scripturam in alium sensum ex malitia animi detorquent.
units.tr: But the adversaries also rise up against this property of Holy Scripture, and they blaspheme that Scripture is doubtful, ambiguous, pliable in speech, like a lump of clay, has a nose of wax, and can be bent this way and that. From this, they say, it follows that it is a book of heretics, from which heresies arise, and by which all men try to find patronage for their errors. But the answer is easy from what we have already said. For that ambiguity and pliability is not to be imputed to Scripture, which is θεόπνευστος [God-breathed] and to us in place of the living voice of God itself; it is to be imputed to the ignorance, malice and wantonness of men, who either cannot grasp the simple and true sense of Scripture, or out of malice of mind twist Scripture into another sense.

units.la: At, inquiunt, in Scriptura passim reperiuntur tropi, allegoriæ, parabolæ, voces homonymæ, & loquutiones amphibologicæ, visiones; quæ omnia habent ambiguitatem. Respondeo, quo tota res hæc manifestior evadat paulò altius nonnihil est repetendum. Cum ambiguitas quæ simplicitati contraria est, sit in verbis non in rebus: verba enim ambigua sunt, non autem res ambiguæ: ambiguitatem quæ est in verbis omnem ad quinque capita reducemus; primùm enim sunt verba voce simplicia, quæ homonyma vocant. 2. sunt verba tropica siue modificata. 3. sunt orationes totæ & loquutiones quas vocant amphibologicas. 4. sunt orationes allegoricæ constantes tropis continuatis. 5. sunt verba & orationes typicæ, quæ sunt de typis & figuris.
units.tr: But, they say, tropes, allegories, parables, homonymous words, amphibological expressions and visions are found everywhere in Scripture, and all of these have ambiguity. I answer: so that this whole matter may become clearer, we must go back a little further. Since the ambiguity that is opposed to simplicity lies in words and not in things (for words are ambiguous, but things are not ambiguous), we shall reduce all the ambiguity that is in words to five heads. First, there are words that are simple in form but which they call homonyms. Second, there are tropical or modified words. Third, there are whole sentences and expressions which they call amphibological. Fourth, there are allegorical sentences consisting of continued tropes. Fifth, there are typical words and sentences, which concern types and figures.

units.la: De his omnibus in genere dico, vnum tantùm & simplex significari à Spiritu sancto per hæc omnia. Nam quod ad voces homonymas attinet, quæ plures res significant, si quæ voces huiusmodi in Scripturis reperiantur, & in primis illis linguis, hebraica & græca (vt necesse quidem est eas reperiri in Scripturis, & in originalibus illis linguis) Primùm dico eas accipi à Spiritu sancto in vno aliquo & simplici significato, idque ex propósito & de industria. Spiritus enim sanctus non quærit fallere & decipere more Sophistarum. Deinde dico illud vnum & simplex significatum deprehendi posse, vel ex proposito Spiritus, quod est in eo loco & textu in quo reperitur vox homonyma, vel ex collatione aliorum locorum Scripturæ, in quibus eadem illa vox homonyma reperitur, vel ex locis Scripturæ eundem sensum aliis verbis exprimentibus, vel denique ex Grammaticis accidentibus, accentibus, punctis, & reliquis. Si verba tropi-
units.tr: Of all these in general I say that one thing only, and that simple, is signified by the Holy Spirit through all of them. For as regards homonymous words, which signify several things, if words of this kind are found in the Scriptures, and especially in those languages, Hebrew and Greek (as they must indeed be found in the Scriptures and in those original languages), first I say that they are taken by the Holy Spirit in one single and simple meaning, and that deliberately and with purpose. For the Holy Spirit does not seek to deceive and mislead in the manner of the Sophists. Second, I say that this one simple meaning can be discerned either from the purpose of the Spirit in that place and text in which the homonymous word is found, or from the comparison of other passages of Scripture in which that same homonymous word is found, or from passages of Scripture expressing the same sense in other words, or finally from grammatical features, accents, points and the rest. If tropical words...

units.la: ca, ea, & in alium sensum a proprio suo & genuino sensu traducta reperiantur in textu Scripturæ, dico primùm ea vsurpari a Spiritu de industria ad significantius & efficacius exprimendum Spiritus sancti mentem & sensum duntaxat unum ac simplicem. Vt cum dicitur (Hoc est corpus meum) per metonymiam hanc, quæ est in verbo Corporis, significantius loquitur Spiritus, quam si dixisset, hoc est signum corporis mei: nam loquutione illa metonymica plane innuit Spiritus, sacramentalem illam vnionem signi & rei significatæ: deinde dico si tropus fit paulò obscurior, haberi ex eadem Scriptura, vel eodem in loco vbi tropus invenitur, vel in alio Scripturæ loco, ejus tropi significationem per verbum proprium expressum.
units.tr: ...are found in the text of Scripture, and are transferred into another sense from their proper and genuine sense, I say, first, that the Spirit uses them deliberately in order to express more forcefully and effectively the mind and sense of the Holy Spirit, which is one and simple. Thus when it is said, "This is my body," the Spirit speaks more significantly through this metonymy, which lies in the word "body," than if he had said, "this is the sign of my body"; for by that metonymical expression the Spirit clearly points to that sacramental union of the sign and the thing signified. Second, I say that if the trope is somewhat obscure, its meaning is to be had from the same Scripture, either in the same place where the trope is found, or in another passage of Scripture, where its meaning is expressed by a proper word.

units.la: Si occurrat in Scriptura oratio quæ videtur amphibologica, primùm sciendum, non de industria ambiguè loqui Spiritum ad fallendum more Sophistarum, verùm simplicem esse Spiritus sancti mentem: homines verò vel ex ignorantia, vel ex malitia, verba contextus male construere & accipere. Deinde dico alia Scripturæ loca idipsum clariùs & apertiùs proponere. Si deniq; reperiantur in Scripturis allegoriæ, de ijs dico, primũ quod
units.tr: If a sentence occurs in Scripture which seems amphibological, we must first know that the Spirit does not speak ambiguously on purpose, to deceive in the manner of the Sophists, but that the mind of the Holy Spirit is simple; men, however, through ignorance or malice, construe and take the words of the context wrongly. Second, I say that other passages of Scripture set forth the same thing more clearly and openly. Finally, if allegories are found in the Scriptures, I say of them, first, that

units.la: ad illustriorem significationem adhibeantur, deinde dico quòd simplicem habeat sensum: & is sensus vel manifestus est,& nulla eget explicatione,vel non manifestus est, & explicatur clariùs in Scriptura alicubi.
units.tr: they are employed for a clearer signification; second, I say that they have a simple sense; and that sense is either manifest and needs no explanation, or is not manifest, and is explained more clearly somewhere in Scripture.

units.la: Quod ad orationes de typis,dico primùm illas habere vnum sensum,& significare typos duntaxat,non etiam res typis rursus significatas: deinde ille vnus sensus,qui est typorum, accommodatur ad aliud significandum, hoc est,ad corpus ipsum: nam ipsi typi significant res significatas, & adumbratas typis, non autem verba ipsa, quæ typis significandis imponuntur. In illa enim ad Gal.4. historia,nomen Saræ significat vxorem Abrahami,hoc est,typum duntaxat: deinde typus significat pastionem, hoc est, rem adumbratam, figuratam, et significatam. Atque hæc hactenus de tertia proprietate & controversia quinta.
units.tr: As to sentences concerning types, I say, first, that they have one sense, and signify only the types, not also the things again signified by the types; second, that this one sense, which belongs to the types, is adapted to signify something else, that is, the body itself; for the types themselves signify the things signified and foreshadowed by the types, not the words themselves, which are imposed to signify the types. For in that history in Galatians 4, the name Sarah signifies the wife of Abraham, that is, only the type; then the type signifies the covenant, that is, the thing foreshadowed, figured and signified. And so far, thus far, on the third property and the fifth controversy.

units.la: De Proprietate quarta, Controversia autem sexta. CAP. 12.
units.tr: On the Fourth Property and the Sixth Controversy. CHAP. 12.

units.la: Dicimus itaque Scripturam sacram per se maximè vivam, efficacem, & vocalem, respondentem quærentibus de omnibus ad salutem necessarijs. Vitam hic intelligo non crassam istam,qualis est hominum ; sed spiritualem illam, qualis est Dei: & vocem vivam intelligo, spiritualem, quæ loquitur, non tam auribus, quàm animis. Primùm enim si substantiam revelationis respicias, hoc quod dicimus est extra controversiam. Continet enim Scriptura sermonem Dei, qui vivus est et efficax, &c. Heb.4. Deinde si revelationis modum, hoc est, ipsam scriptionem respicias, verum quoq; erit. Nam 1. ea est Θεόπνευστος: Quod autem divinitus inspiratum est, illud vivum in se oportet esse, ac spirituale. Deinde Scriptura hæc est nobis, si non ipsa viva Dei vox, certè pro viva Dei voce. Non enim habemus nos aliam vivam Dei vocem quâ hanc: Nam quod ad vocem Ecclesiæ, Pastorum & Doctorum in Ecclesia, ea est errori obnoxia, neq; Dei vox proprie dici potest. Dei autem vocem oportet viva dicere: Ergo. Tertiò, ipsa Scriptura de se loquitur, ac si vivam voce haberet: ut legere est Rom.9. Dicit Scriptura &c. Scriptura Esaiæ dicitur clamare super Israel. Rom.9. 27. Quartò ad eam remittuntur quærentes de re aliqua ad salutem necessaria. Esaiæ.8. Numquid non populus à Deo suo requiret? pro vivis ne ad mortuos? ad legem magis & ad testimonium; quòd si non dixerint juxta verbum hoc, non erit ijs matutina lux. Item filius dei ad quæstiones de lege, de divortiö, de Sabbatho, de Messia, de regeneratione, de refurrectione, deque ratione consequendi salutem semper ex Scriptura sacra respondit, & scitantes ad Scripturam remisit. Quomodò legis, inquiens; An non legistis; Nunquam legistis; Quomodò scriptum est. Apostoli etiam Christi sua omnia ex veteri Scriptura probant atque confirmant. Apollo vir potens in Scripturis vehementer Iudæos convincebat publicè, ostendens ex Scripturis quòd Iesus esset Christus. Act. 18. Beroeenses recepto sermone cum omni animi promptitudine quotidie scrutabantur Scripturas, an hæc ita se haberent. Act. 17. Sic primitiva Ecclesia; sic patres ex Scriptura sacra hæreses impugnarunt ac refutarunt. Denique imprimis æterna memoria dignum est factum Imperatoris Constantini Magni, qui in concilio Niceno patribus Biblia proposuit, dicens. In medio sunt Evangelici libri & Apostolici, antiquorumque Prophetarum sanctiones, quæ nos erudiunt quid de sacra lege sapiamus: expellentes itaque hostile certamen, ex verbis divinitus inspiratis solutione quæstionum mente percipiamus. Dixi per se esse vivam & vocalem, quia ratione hominum mortuorum, furdorum, hoc est, ψυχικῶν, non ϑεοδιδακτῶν, mortua est & muta.
units.tr: We say, therefore, that Holy Scripture is above all living, effective and vocal in itself, answering those who ask about everything necessary to salvation. By life I mean not that crude life which belongs to men, but that spiritual life which belongs to God; and by a living voice I mean a spiritual voice, which speaks not so much to the ears as to the minds. First, if you look at the substance of the revelation, what we say is beyond dispute. For Scripture contains the word of God, which is living and effective, etc. Heb. 4. Next, if you look at the mode of revelation, that is, the writing itself, this too will be true. For, first, it is God-breathed [θεόπνευστος]; what has been breathed into by God must itself be living and spiritual. Second, this Scripture is to us, if not the living voice of God itself, certainly in place of the living voice of God. For we have no other living voice of God than this one. As for the voice of the Church, of the ministers and of the teachers in the Church, it is liable to error and cannot properly be called the voice of God. But the voice of God must be called living; therefore, etc. Third, Scripture itself speaks of itself as if it had a living voice, as can be read in Rom. 9. "Scripture says," etc. The Scripture of Isaiah is said to cry out over Israel, Rom. 9. 27. Fourth, those who ask about some matter necessary to salvation are referred to it. Isa. 8. "Shall not a people seek its God? Shall the living seek to the dead? To the law and to the testimony! If they do not speak according to this word, there will be no morning light for them." Likewise the Son of God, to questions about the law, about divorce, about the Sabbath, about the Messiah, about regeneration, about the resurrection, and about the way of obtaining salvation, always answered from Holy Scripture, and sent those who asked back to Scripture. "How is it written in the law?" he says; "Have you not read?"; "Have you never read?"; "As it is written." The apostles of Christ, too, prove and confirm all their teaching from the old Scripture. Apollos, a man mighty in the Scriptures, vehemently refuted the Jews in public, showing from the Scriptures that Jesus was the Christ. Act. 18. The Bereans received the word with all readiness of mind and examined the Scriptures daily, to see whether these things were so. Act. 17. So did the primitive Church; so did the Fathers, who from Holy Scripture attacked and refuted heresies. Finally, the deed of the Emperor Constantine the Great deserves eternal remembrance above all, for at the Council of Nicaea he set the Bibles before the Fathers, saying: "In the midst are the Gospel and Apostolic books and the decrees of the ancient prophets, which teach us what to think about the sacred law. Therefore, casting out hostile strife, let us grasp, by resolving our questions from words divinely inspired, what is true." I said that it is living and vocal in itself, because for men who are dead, deaf, that is, psychic [ψυχικῶν] and not taught by God [ϑεοδιδακτῶν], it is dead and mute.

units.la: Hic adversarij insurgunt blasphemantes Scripturam sacram tanquā mortuam literam, mutam, non respondentem, ex qua certamina & controversię de religione dirimi nequeunt: ex adverso vero Ecclesiæ vocem, quæ proficiscitur ex Scriptura illa quæ vivis cordibus est insculpta à Spiritu Dei vivo, jactitat vivam esse, vocalem esse, respondentem quærentibus de omnibus ad salutem necessariis, non patientem se truncari, & torqueri, sed sui per omnia similem perse verantem. Responsio, qua occurritur huic calumnię & blasphemię, jam patet ex ijs quæ dicta sunt; probavimus enim Scripturam sacram per se vivam esse & vocalem maximè. Quòd autem non statim ex Scripturis deprehendantur controversiarum decisiones in causa sunt homines, qui vel adeò ignari sunt & stupidi natura, ut loquentem & respondentem, imò clamantem, Scripturā intelligere & audire nequeant; vel adeò malitiosi sunt & obstinati, ut audire & intelligere nolint, imò velint sæpenumero vocem Scripturæ contra conscientiam in alium sensum detorquere, idque suo exitio. Quare illud manet Scripturam vivam esse & vocalem maxi-
units.tr: Here the adversaries rise up, blaspheming Holy Scripture as a dead and mute letter, which does not answer, and by which controversies and disputes about religion cannot be settled. On the other hand, they boast that the voice of the Church, which proceeds from that Scripture engraved on living hearts by the living Spirit of God, is living and vocal, answers those who ask about all things necessary to salvation, and does not allow itself to be mutilated and twisted, but remains entirely like itself. The answer to this calumny and blasphemy is now plain from what has been said, for we have proved that Holy Scripture is in itself most of all living and vocal. That the decisions of controversies are not immediately found in Scripture is due to men who are either so ignorant and dull by nature that they cannot understand or hear Scripture speaking, answering, indeed crying out; or so malicious and obstinate that they are unwilling to hear and understand, and indeed often want, against their own conscience, to twist the voice of Scripture into another sense, and to their own ruin. Hence it remains that Scripture is living and vocal most of all

units.la: ψυχικῶν ... ϑεοδιδακτῶν: Greek terms, as printed. maximè per se,&in se.
units.tr: [ψυχικῶν ... ϑεοδιδακτῶν] through itself and in itself.

units.la: Vt autem nobis sit viva & vocalis, & nos eam loquentem et respondentem ad omnia quæ de Religione possunt controverti intelligamus,illa media, de quibus jam diximus, & inter quæ numeratur etiam ipsa grammatica, sunt adhibenda. Eorum enim mediorum beneficio oculi nostri & aures nostræ aperiuntur ad videndum Scripturæ mentem, & audiendum Scripturæ vocem, si modò visum sit Spiritui sancto efficaciter per ipsa operari in mentibus & cordibus nostris. Quòd si Spiritus velit esse efficax per ea, tum quidé Scriptura clariori voce, & magis viva, distincta, & articulata, ut sic dicam, respondebit ad omnes controversias de Fide & Religione, quàm respondebunt omnes quotquot sunt in Ecclesia homines, qui nihil sani, veri, certi respondere possunt, nisi priùs ipsi idipsum excipiant ex ore Scripturæ, & ex Scripturæ verbis respondeant. Nam quod dicunt isti Ecclesiæ vocem vivam esse, vocalem, quæ audiatur ab omnibus, neq; patiatur se truncari & torqueri: ad id respondeo, primùm Ecclesiæ vocem, ut dixi, pendere à Scripturæ voce; deinde Ecclesiæ vocem erroribus obnoxiam esse, et mutationibus: adeò ut aliud hodie respondeat, aliud
units.tr: So that it may be living and vocal for us, and so that we understand it speaking and answering on everything that can be disputed about religion, those means of which we have already spoken, among which grammar itself is counted, must be employed. For by the benefit of these means our eyes and ears are opened to see the mind of Scripture and to hear the voice of Scripture, provided it has pleased the Holy Spirit to work effectively through them in our minds and hearts. But if the Spirit wills to be effective through them, then Scripture will answer, with a clearer and more living voice, distinct and articulate, so to speak, to all controversies about faith and religion, more than all the men in the Church, who can answer nothing sound, true or certain unless they first receive the same thing from the mouth of Scripture and answer from the words of Scripture. As for what those men say, that the voice of the Church is living and vocal, heard by all, and does not allow itself to be mutilated and twisted, to that I answer: first, that the voice of the Church, as I have said, depends on the voice of Scripture; second, that the voice of the Church is liable to errors and changes, so that it answers one thing today and another

units.la: [illegible, ~5 letters] aliud verò cras respondere possit, & Iesbia sit quodammodò norma ac regula controversiarum de Fide & Religione. Quod ad Ecclesiam Romanam, ita jam pridem ab ea responsum est de Fide & Religione, vt mundus abductus sit à veritate ad mendacia, errores, et hæreses infinitas; vt non sit quod isti vendite nobis, vel vocem, vel vocalitatem Ecclesiæ suæ corruptæ & adulteræ.
units.tr: [illegible, about five letters] but may answer otherwise tomorrow, and is in some sense the Lesbian rule and standard of controversies about faith and religion. As for the Roman Church, it has for some time now answered about faith and religion in such a way that the world has been led away from the truth into lies, errors and countless heresies. So these men have nothing to sell us, neither the voice nor the vocality of their corrupted and adulterated Church.

units.la: De Proprietate Scripturæ sacræ quinta, Contro- versia autem septima.
units.tr: On the Property of Holy Scripture, the fifth; the controversy, however, the seventh.

units.la: CAP. 13.
units.tr: CHAPTER 13.

units.la: NVnc demonstrandum est Scripturam esse summè & simpliciter necessariam. Si Scripturæ nomine intelligas substantiam & rem ipsam quæ literis est consignata, negari non potest adeò necessariam esse, vt sine ea non possit esse in terris Ecclesia: nam ex verbo Dei, tanquâ ex femine incorruptibili, nata est Ecclesia. 1. Pet. 1. Sin verò intelligas Scripturæ nomine ipsam quoque scriptionem, & revelationis formam; dico & hac quoque ratione necessariam adeò, vt sine ea non possit esse Ecclesia. Nam viva vox Dei est necessaria simpliciter, Scriptura quodammodò est viva vox Dei: Ergo necessaria simpliciter.
units.tr: It must now be shown that Scripture is supremely and absolutely necessary. If by the name of Scripture you understand the substance and the thing itself which has been recorded in writing, it cannot be denied that it is so necessary that the Church could not exist on earth without it, for the Church was born from the word of God as from an incorruptible seed. 1. Pet. 1. But if by the name of Scripture you understand also the writing itself and the form of revelation, I say that on this ground too it is so necessary that the Church could not exist without it. For the living voice of God is necessary absolutely, and Scripture is in a certain sense the living voice of God; therefore it is absolutely necessary.

units.la: H
units.tr: H

units.la: Fateor equidem cum ipsa viva Dei vox sonabat in Ecclesia, non fuisse tum necessariam hanc scriptionem & revelationis hanc formam: at postquam cessavit loqui Deus, data pro ipsius viva voce scriptione, jam scriptio non minus diceda est necessaria nunc, quàm tunc fuit ipsius viva vox. Vocem enim Dei ad hoc ut Ecclesia fit & perfistat semper necesse est esse in Ecclesia, & audiri ab Ecclesia, vel per se, vel per id quod vivae ipsius vocis vicem gerat. Ante Mosen per se audiebatur: Post Mosen sonuit in voce & scripto Mosis & Prophetarum: In adventu Christi viva vox ipsius Christi audiebatur: Post Christi ascensionem, pro viva voce ipsius Dei & Christi, audiebatur aliquandiu vox Apostolorum simulque vox Scripturae veteris: Hinc coepit Scriptura Apostolorum, quae post Apostolos manet in Ecclesia una cum veteri Scriptura pro viva voce, non tantum Apostolorum, sed etiam ipsius Dei & Christi. Ex his apparet in Ecclesia Dei necessariam esse simpliciter omni tempore Dei vocem vivam, vel ipsam per se, vel ipsius vicariam aliquam, quam nos dicimus nunc solam esse Scripturam veterem & novam, proindeque Scripturam hac summe necessariam.
units.tr: I grant that while the living voice of God was sounding in the Church, this writing and this form of revelation were not then necessary. But after God ceased to speak, and writing was given in place of his living voice, writing is now no less necessary than the living voice was then. For it is always necessary that the voice of God be present in the Church, so that the Church comes into being and persists, and that it be heard by the Church, either directly or through something that takes the place of that living voice. Before Moses it was heard directly. After Moses it sounded in the voice and writings of Moses and the Prophets. At the coming of Christ, the living voice of Christ himself was heard. After the ascension of Christ, in place of the living voice of God and Christ, the voice of the Apostles was heard for a while, together with the voice of the Old Scripture.
