From this point the Scripture of the Apostles began, and it remains in the Church after the Apostles together with the Old Scripture, in place of the living voice not only of the Apostles but also of God and Christ himself. From these things it is clear that in the Church of God the voice of God, living, is absolutely necessary at all times, either in itself or through some substitute for it, which we now say is the Old and New Scripture alone; and therefore Scripture is supremely necessary.

units.la: Huic assertioni, vt & aliis superioribus, opponunt Adversarij, negantque Scripturam esse simpliciter necessariam; necessariam quidem esse ad bene esse Ecclesiæ fatentur, hoc est, vtilem esse Ecclesiæ: negant autem necessariam ad ipsum Ecclesiæ esse: Atque hanc Scripturæ necessitatem ideo negant, vt locus sit testimonio & traditionibus Ecclesiæ, hoc est, somnijs suis, quas dicunt simpliciter esse necessarias, & Scripturæ præferunt. Ex his quæ diximus facile responderi potest ad eorum sententiam. Si enim Scripturæ nomine ipsam Scripturæ substantiam intelligant, negari non potest Scripturam esse simpliciter necessariam: Sin vero intelligant non substantiam tantum, sed etiam scriptionem, & hoc quoque modo accepto Scripturæ nomine, jam demonstravimus Scripturam esse necessariam simpliciter, cum sit nobis vice ipsius viva vocis Dei. Quare falsum est quod afferunt, sive hoc sive illo modo accipiatur Scriptura.
units.tr: Our opponents, as with the other points above, oppose this assertion and deny that Scripture is absolutely necessary. They admit that it is necessary for the well-being of the Church, that is, that it is useful to the Church; but they deny that it is necessary for the Church's very existence. They deny this necessity of Scripture so that room may be made for the testimony and traditions of the Church, that is, for their own fancies, which they say are absolutely necessary and prefer to Scripture. From what we have said, an answer to their view can easily be given. For if they understand by Scripture the very substance of Scripture, it cannot be denied that Scripture is absolutely necessary. But if they understand not only the substance but also the writing, and taking the name of Scripture in this sense, we have already shown that Scripture is absolutely necessary, since for us it stands in place of the living voice of God. Therefore what they assert is false, whichever way Scripture is taken.

units.la: At, inquiunt, Ecclesia sine Scriptura fuit annos circiter bis mille, quibus conservata est Religio sola traditione: Ergo Scriptura non est necessaria simpliciter. Respondeo. Si Scripturæ nomine intelligas ipsam substantiam, non sequitur: Nam substantia Scripturæ fuit in
units.tr: But, they say, the Church was without Scripture for about two thousand years, during which religion was preserved by tradition alone; therefore Scripture is not absolutely necessary. I reply: if by Scripture you understand its substance, the conclusion does not follow, for the substance of Scripture was in

units.la: [Remaining text of this page: none further.] in ijs ipsis traditionibus quibus conservata est Ecclesia: Sin hoc nomine intelligas etiam ipsam scriptionem, tum quidem concedo Scripturam ipsam non extitisse illis tot annis, & ne necessariam quidé tum fuisse, quia tum audiebatur viva ipsius Dei vox. Si concludat ex eo quod non fuerit scriptio tunc necessaria, ideo non esse necessariam etiam nunc; aut etiam non fuisse necessariam postquam Deus eam imperavit, & postquam coepit esse; prosecto sequela est pessima: nam alio tempore, alia atque alia mundi ætate, alia atque alia revelationis forma necessaria est.
units.tr: [Remaining text of this page: none further.] in those very traditions by which the Church was preserved. But if by this name you also understand the writing itself, then I grant that Scripture itself did not exist in those many years, and was not even necessary then, because the living voice of God was heard at that time. If they conclude from the fact that writing was not necessary then that it is not necessary now, or that it was not necessary even after God commanded it and it began to exist, the inference is surely very bad, for at different times, in different ages of the world, different forms of revelation are necessary.

units.la: Eadem Controversia de Scripturæ neces- sitate brevius.
units.tr: The same controversy on the necessity of Scripture, more briefly.

units.la: SCriptura est necessaria non tantum ad benè esse; sed etiam ad esse Ecclesiæ; & hactenus est simplex necessitas. Ratione autem temporis necessitas est κατα τι: nam non omni tempore necessitas fuit Scripturarum. Scripturæ nomine intelligo non modò substantiam, sed etiam revelationis modum: sed simplex hæc necessitas prædicatur de substantia & revelationis modo alia atque alia ratione: Nam Scriptura quoad substantiam necessaria est Ecclesiæ omni tempore, quoad verò revelationis uelationis modum necessaria est certo tempore, nempè quo visum est Deo docere Ecclefiam suam per Scripturam. Argumentum 1. Non enim dedisset Deus Ecclesiæ Scripturam nisi necessariam duxisset eam, etiam ad esse Ecclesię. Argumentum 2. Viva vox Dei fuit suo tempore necessaria; ergo etiam Scriptura suo tempore: nam eadem est vtriusque ratio. Argumentum 3. Necesse est aliquo modo reveletur Ecclesiæ voluntas Dei, vel viva voce, vel scriptione, vel vtroque: at nunc cessavit viva vox, ergo nunc scriptio est necessaria.
units.tr: Scripture is necessary not only for the well-being of the Church but also for its existence; and so far the necessity is simple. But with respect to time the necessity is in a certain respect (kata ti), for the necessity of the Scriptures did not hold at all times. By Scripture I mean not only the substance but also the mode of revelation. But this simple necessity is predicated of the substance and of the mode of revelation in different ways. For Scripture as to its substance is necessary to the Church at all times; as to the mode of revelation, however, it is necessary at a certain time, namely when it pleased God to teach his Church through Scripture. Argument 1: God would not have given Scripture to the Church unless he had judged it necessary, even for the Church's existence. Argument 2: the living voice of God was necessary in its time; therefore Scripture is necessary in its time too, for the reason for both is the same. Argument 3: the will of God must be revealed to the Church in some way, either by living voice, or by writing, or by both; but now the living voice has ceased; therefore writing is now necessary.

units.la: Adversarij hanc simplicem necessitatem negant, his argumentis. 1. Ab Adamo ad Mosen nulla fuit Scriptura: Ergo. Respondeo toto illo tempore non visa est Deo necessaria; At postquam cœpit Deus ipse scribere, & inspiravit Scriptură sanctis viris, primùm Prophetis, deinde Apostolis, tum cœpit scriptura esse necessaria, & simpliciter quidem necessaria. Argumentum 2. A Mose ad Christum Iob, & amici ejus sine Scriptura & crediderunt & servati sunt. Respondeo hos quoque legisse Scripturas verisimile est ex historia Eunuchi. Act. 8. Deinde cum ijs qui erant extra Ecclesiam visibilem extra ordinē egisse videtur
units.tr: The opponents deny this simple necessity, with these arguments. (1) From Adam to Moses there was no Scripture: therefore... I answer: during all that time it did not seem necessary to God; but after God himself began to write, and breathed Scripture into holy men, first the Prophets, then the Apostles, then Scripture began to be necessary, and indeed simply necessary. Argument 2: From Moses to Christ, Job and his friends both believed and were saved without Scripture. I answer: it is likely that these also had read the Scriptures, from the history of the Eunuch (Acts 8). Then, it seems, he acted outside the ordinary way with those who were outside the visible Church.

units.la: {*} tem-pore videtur Deus. Argumentum 3. Vsi sunt magis traditionibus quam scripto in secunda aetate. Respondeo, falsum est. Argumentum 4. In tertia aetate multo post Christum tempore non fuit Scriptura novi Testamenti: Ergo. Respondeo non longo post Christum tempore coepit Scriptura Apostolica: deinde toto illo tempore, fateor, non fuit necessaria, at decedentibus e vita Apostolis, ac cessante viva voce, coepit jam esse necessaria.
units.tr: {*} at that time God seems to have done so. Argument 3: They used traditions rather than writing in the second age. I answer: this is false. Argument 4: In the third age, a long time after Christ, there was no Scripture of the New Testament: therefore... I answer: not long after Christ the apostolic Scripture began; and then, I admit, throughout that whole time it was not necessary, but once the Apostles had departed this life and the living voice had ceased, it began at once to be necessary.

units.la: De Proprietate sexta, Controversia octava.
units.tr: On the sixth Property, eighth Controversy.

units.la: CAP. 14.
units.tr: CHAP. 14.

units.la: SCriptura est perfecta, & omnia continet quae ad fidem & mores sunt necessaria, non tantum sufficienter, sed & abundanter; haec est enim illa perfectio de qua loquimur. Sensus itaque propositionis hic est: Revelationis iste modus continet omnia quae ad &c. probatur. Argumentum 1. Viva vox continebat omnia dogmata fidei & morum: Ergo & Scriptura: Ratio est, quia nihil viva voce quoad substantiam est dictum, quod non scripto quoque commissum fit. Argumentum 2. Si non perfecte omnia comprehederet tum mala esset nostrae Ecclesiae conditio, quae non audit vivam vocem hominis θεοπνευστους, vel Prophetæ, vel Apostoli. Argumentum 3. Experiuntur pij & Sɛcᵾʃ, sufficientiam in Scripturis sacris, imo abundantiam esse. Testimonia sequuntur. Deut.4. Non addetis ad verbum quod ego loquor, &c. Apocal. 22. Si quis adjecerit ad hæc imponet ei Deus plagas scriptas in libro isto. Hæc etsi de particularibus libris accipienda sunt proprie, tamen eadem est ratio omnium librorum et Scripturæ totius; atque adeo major est ratio: Nam si particularibus libris non licet addere, quanto magis non licet addere toti Canoni. Prov.30. Ne adjicias quicquam verbis illius: hoc de tota Scriptura accipiendum videtur. Mat.28. Docetes eos servare omnia quæ mandavi vobis. Gal.1. Etiamsi nos aut Angelus e cælo evangelizet vobis præter id quod evangelizauimus, anathema esto. Iohan.20. Hæc scripta sunt ut credatis, &c.
units.tr: Scripture is perfect, and contains everything that is necessary for faith and morals, not merely sufficiently but abundantly as well; for this is the perfection of which we speak. The meaning of the proposition is therefore this: this mode of revelation contains all the things that are necessary for faith and morals. This is proved as follows. Argument 1: The living voice contained all the doctrines of faith and morals; therefore so does Scripture. The reason is that nothing has been said by the living voice, as to its substance, that has not also been committed to writing. Argument 2: If Scripture did not comprehend everything perfectly, the condition of our Church would be wretched, since it does not hear the living voice of a man who is God-breathed [θεοπνευστους], or of a prophet, or of an apostle. Argument 3: The godly and the saints experience that there is sufficiency, indeed abundance, in the holy Scriptures. Testimonies follow. Deut.4. You shall not add to the word that I speak, etc. Apocal. 22. If anyone adds to these things, God will lay upon him the plagues written in this book. Although these words are properly to be taken of the particular books, the reason is the same for all books and for all of Scripture, and so the reason is even stronger: for if it is not lawful to add to particular books, how much less is it lawful to add to the whole canon. Prov.30. Add nothing to his words: this seems to be said of the whole of Scripture. Mat.28. Teaching them to observe all things that I have commanded you. Gal.1. Even if we, or an angel from heaven, preach to you anything besides what we have preached to you, let him be anathema. Iohan.20. These things are written that you may believe, etc.

units.la: De sententia adversariorum, qui dicunt Scripturam mutilam, & mancam, vide imprimis Bellarminum, ejusque in hanc sententiam argumenta. Hanc Scripturæ imperfectionem docent, ut locus fit traditionibus & figmentis ipsorum: ideò de traditione dicemus pauca. De Traditionibus.
units.tr: On the opinion of our opponents, who say that Scripture is maimed and defective, see above all Bellarmine and his arguments for this view. They teach this imperfection of Scripture so that room may be made for their traditions and fictions; therefore we shall say a few things about tradition. On Traditions.

units.la: Traditionis nomen generale est, significatque catque doctrinam vel scriptam, vel non scriptam: & ita quidem accipitur nomen hoc traditionis tam in sacris literis, quàm in scriptis Patrum: licet Papistæ dicant apud Patres accommodari hoc nomé tantùm ad significandum doctrinā non scriptā. Testimonia Scripturę quibus ostenditur generalis acceptio vocis. Act.6.14. Et mutaturum ritus quos tradidit nobis Moses. 2.Thess.2.15. Tenete traditam doctrinam, quam edocti estis, siue per sermonem, siue per Epistolam nostram.
units.tr: The name tradition is general, and signifies doctrine either written or unwritten; and this is how the name tradition is taken both in the sacred letters and in the writings of the Fathers, although the Papists say that among the Fathers this name is applied only to signify unwritten doctrine. Testimonies of Scripture showing the general use of the word: Acts 6.14. And the customs which Moses delivered to us will change. 2 Thess.2.15. Hold to the doctrine that was delivered to you, whether by word or by our letter.

units.la: Traditionis partitio sequitur: Traditionis nomen in Scripturis attribuitur nonnunquâ rebus necessarijs, & perpetuis; nonnunquam non necessarijs & temporarijs. De doctrina necessaria testimonium est. 2. Thess. 2. 15. de ceremonijs intelligitur locus qui est. Act.16.4 loquitur enim de decreto concilij Hierosolymitani, quod erat de sanguine, suffocato, & Idolothytis, de quibus. Act. 15. 28. Quod ad traditiones attinet quæ sunt de necessarijs dogmatis vel fidei, vel morum, ea primùm viua voce tradiderunt: eorum deinde summam scriptis comprehenderunt, vt liquet de Cœna.
units.tr: The division of tradition follows: the name tradition in Scripture is sometimes given to things necessary and perpetual, sometimes to things unnecessary and temporary. A testimony concerning necessary doctrine is 2 Thess. 2. 15. The passage about ceremonies is Acts 16.4, for it speaks of the decree of the council of Jerusalem, which concerned blood, what was strangled, and idol-sacrifices; see Acts 15.28. As for traditions which concern the necessary doctrines of faith or morals, these they first delivered by the living voice, and afterwards they comprehended the sum of them in writings, as is clear about the Supper.

units.la: 1. Cor.11.23. item 1. Thess.4.2. vbi de præceptis honestæ vitæ agitur. Item 2. Thess. 2. 15. Quod ad traditiones de non necessarijs & ceremoniremonialibus, ea vel scripto commiserunt, ut de Ecclesiasticis ordinibus, de quibus. 1.Cor. 11.14. vel non commiserunt scripto. 1.Cor.11. 34. Cetera cum venero disponam: Ordinaturu se pollicetur ceremonialia, nominatum autem quae ad Coenam dominicam spectant. De ceremonialibus hoc tantum dicam: neque erant immodica, neque inutilia, neque cum opinione necessitatis tradita ad obligandum hominum conscientias, neque his quae scripta erant contraria: Imo affirmo nihil ab Apostolis fuisse traditum quod non haberet fundamentum in verbo Dei, hoc est, in literis Propheticis, & in doctrina Christi, quae postmodum ab Evangelistis & Apostolis comprehensa fuit libris. Traditiones autem Papisticae, immodicae sunt, & inutiles, utpote aniles nugae, necessitatis opinione fere omnes traditae, pleraque Apostolicae doctrinae qua maxime adversatur. Sic nos partimur traditiones.
units.tr: 1 Cor.11.23. Likewise 1 Thess.4.2, where the precepts of an honest life are treated. Likewise 2 Thess. 2. 15. As for traditions about things not necessary, and about ceremonies, they either committed these to writing, as about ecclesiastical orders (see 1 Cor. 11.14.), or they did not commit them to writing: 1 Cor.11.34. "The rest I will set in order when I come." He promises to arrange the ceremonies, but names those that pertain to the Lord's Supper. About ceremonies I will say only this: they were neither excessive nor useless, nor handed down with an opinion of necessity so as to bind men's consciences, nor contrary to what was written. Indeed I affirm that nothing was handed down by the Apostles that did not have its foundation in the word of God, that is, in the prophetic writings and in the doctrine of Christ, which was afterwards comprehended in books by the Evangelists and Apostles. But the Papistical traditions are excessive and useless, like old wives' trifles, handed down almost all with an opinion of necessity, and most of them strongly opposed to apostolic doctrine. This is how we divide traditions.

units.la: Adversarij traditionis nomine intelligunt doctrinam non scriptam; non eam quidem quae nusquam est scripta, sed quae non est scripta a primo suo authore, hoc est, ab eo qui ipsam tradidit viva voce. Haec est igitur ipsorum Papistarum confessio, non posse se suas traditiones in Scripturis invenire, nec per Scripturas probare.
units.tr: Our opponents understand by the name tradition doctrine that is not written; not indeed doctrine that has been written nowhere, but doctrine that was not written down by its first author, that is, by the one who delivered it by the living voice. This, then, is the confession of the Papists themselves: they cannot find their traditions in Scripture, nor prove them by Scripture.

units.la: De Proprietate septima, Controversia nona. CAP. 15.
units.tr: On the seventh Property, ninth Controversy. CHAP. 15.

units.la: SCriptura sancta est judex omnium controversiarum: Controversias intelligo, quæ sunt de Religione: Duæ autem sunt de religione controversiæ maximè insignes; prima est, de ipsa Scriptura, quo nimirum judice constabit Scripturam esse verbum Dei; secunda est de sensu ac interpretatione Scripturæ, quo nimirum judice constabit hunc vel illum sensum esse Scripturæ genuinum. Iudicium voco sententiam definitivam cum authoritate pronunciatam, in qua omnes acquiescere oportet. Scripturæ nomine intelligo non tantum substantiam, sed & modum revelationis, qui & ipse est Θεόπνευστος. Loquutio autem ista impropria est qua prædicatur de Scriptura quòd sit judex controversiarum. Nam proprie loquendo Spiritus sanctus est judex, cum judicem oporteat esse personam, Spiritus autem sanctus persona in Trinitate tertia est. Dicitur ergo Scriptura judex improprie, quia est vox & sententia judicis pronunciata, primarium organon quo judicat Spiritus, sententiam suam pronunciat, nos docet, ac fidem cordibus nostris ingignit. Spiritus autem hic judicat liberè in quocunque vult, non in certo to aliquo hominum genere, vt in Pastoribus, & Doctoribus Ecclesiæ, sed in quibus cunq; ipsi visum est.
units.tr: Holy Scripture is the judge of all controversies. By controversies I mean those which concern religion. There are two notable controversies about religion: the first is about Scripture itself, by whose judgment it will be established that Scripture is the word of God; the second is about the sense and interpretation of Scripture, by whose judgment it will be established that this or that sense is the genuine sense of Scripture. I call a judgment a definitive sentence pronounced with authority, to which all must assent. By the name Scripture I understand not only the substance but also the mode of revelation, which is itself God-breathed [Θεόπνευστος]. But this way of speaking is improper, by which it is said of Scripture that it is the judge of controversies. For properly speaking the Holy Spirit is the judge, since a judge must be a person, and the Holy Spirit is the third person in the Trinity. Scripture is therefore called judge improperly, because it is the voice and pronounced sentence of the judge, the primary instrument by which the Spirit judges, pronounces his sentence, teaches us, and engenders faith in our hearts. This Spirit judges freely in whomever he wills, not in a certain class of men, such as the pastors and teachers of the Church, but in whomever it has pleased him.

units.la: Tria igitur hic occurrunt de quibus est hoc loco quærendum. 1. An Spiritus sanctus sit judex. 2. An Scriptura sit princeps ejus vox, qua pronunciat sententiam suam. 3. An judicet in quibuscunque sine discrimine, an verò alligatus sit certo cuidam hominum generi.
units.tr: Three questions therefore arise here, which must be examined in this place. 1. Whether the Holy Spirit is the judge. 2. Whether Scripture is the primary voice by which he pronounces his sentence. 3. Whether he judges in anyone at all without distinction, or whether he is bound to a certain class of men.

units.la: Quod ad primum, respondeo Spiritum sanctū esse judicē. 1. Quia promissus est à Christo jam discedente Ecclesiæ suæ, & est datus tanquam Christi vicarius ad docendum, & judicandum, &c. 2. Quia inter cetera ejus officia hoc vnum est, judicare. Verùm quia de Spiritu non valdè contendunt Adversarij, quòd nimirùm per Spiritum sanctum omnia sunt judicāda, & per eum intelligēdę Scripturæ; ideò de Spiritu judice nos pauca dicimus.
units.tr: As to the first, I answer that the Holy Spirit is the judge. 1. Because he was promised by Christ when Christ was about to depart from his Church, and was given as Christ's vicar to teach and to judge, etc. 2. Because among his other offices this one is to judge. But since our opponents do not contend much about the Spirit, namely that all things are to be judged by the Spirit and that Scripture is to be understood through him, we say only a few things here about the Spirit as judge.

units.la: Quod ad secundum: Quòd Scriptura sit vox judicis primaria, judiciaria, ac propria, qua fidem ipse ingignit cordibus nostris, patet his rationibus. 1. Scriptura est verbum Dei. 2. Est antiquissima. 3. Est apertissima, & ita deinceps. His addo testimonium ipsius Scripturæ. Suggeret vobis omnia quæ dixi vobis.Ioh.14.26.Addo quoque experientiam communem. Sunt & alia Spiritus sancti media, sed hæc posteriora minúsque principalia, in quibus quoque est Ecclesiæ testimonium. Adversarij impugnant hanc nostrā de Scriptura, quòd sit vox judicis propria, sententiam, his argumentis. 1. Non est Scriptura inscripta cordibus digitis Dei, neq; vox Dei primaria. 2. recens est. 3. obscura. 4. ambigua, & ita deinceps. His addit Bellarminus quædam alia, de quibus lege apud ipsum. Statuunt autem vocem Spiritus judicis primariā et propriam, Ecclesiæ vocem. Prob. Est Scriptura in corde Scripturæ exarata Dei digito, & vox Dei primaria: & reliqua quæ nos Scripturæ sacræ tribuimus ad Ecclesiā suam transferunt.
units.tr: As to the second: that Scripture is the primary, judicial and proper voice of the judge, by which he himself engenders faith in our hearts, is clear from these reasons. 1. Scripture is the word of God. 2. It is the most ancient. 3. It is the most clear, and so on. To these I add the testimony of Scripture itself: He will bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you (John 14.26). I add also common experience. There are other means of the Holy Spirit, but these are later and less principal, and in them too there is the testimony of the Church. Our opponents attack this view of ours, that Scripture is the proper voice of the judge pronouncing sentence, with these arguments: 1. Scripture is not written on hearts by the finger of God, nor is it the primary voice of God. 2. It is recent. 3. It is obscure. 4. It is ambiguous, and so on. Bellarmine adds certain other points to these, which you may read in him. But they hold that the primary and proper voice of the Spirit as judge is the voice of the Church. Their proof: Scripture is written in the heart by the finger of God and is the primary voice of God, and they transfer to his Church the rest of what we attribute to holy Scripture.

units.la: Quòd autem Spiritus hic judex sit non alligatus certo hominum generi, vt Ecclesiastici hominibus, Papæ, & concilijs, vt ipsi loquuntur: sed sine discrimine judicium exerceat in quocunque ipsi visum est, apparet. 1. Quia nisi Spiritus sanctus judicans, sive de ipso Scripturæ contextu, an sit verbum Dei, sive de interpretatione Scripturæ; nisi, inquā, sit in homine ipso, profectò nulla vnquam sutura est fides. Spiritus enim solus est, qui fidē ingignit cordi. 2. Spiritus sanctus alias functiones suas liberè exercet in quocunq; Ergo go & hanc functionem quæ est in judicando. Nam quid quæso aliud est judicare quàm illuminare, & docere hanc Scripturam esse Αὐτόπιστον, hunc esse Scripturæ hujus sensum genuinum. 3. Id ipsum experientia docet: nam experimur liberè eum judicare in quibus ipsi visum est. Hanc rem confirmant etiam testimonia ex Scriptura. 1. Cor. 12.1. Sed omnia hæc efficit unus Spiritus distribuens privatim ea cui vult: & Esaiæ.54.Erunt omnes Θεοδίδακτοι. Ieremiæ.31.Inscribam legem meam cordibus eorum,&c. Adversarij hoc oppugnant certis quibusdam argumetis, de quibus lege apud Bellarminum. Alligant autem Spiritum sanctum Papæ, & Concilijs per ipsum confirmatis, id quod nostri homines oppugnant argumentis pluribus; inter quæ hoc vnum est. Sic enim sequeretur Papam, & Concilia per eum confirmata esse supra Scripturam: Quod absurdum est. Reliqua pete ex eorum disputationibus.
units.tr: That this Spirit who judges is not bound to a certain class of men, such as churchmen, the Pope and councils, as they themselves put it, but exercises judgment without distinction in whomever he pleases, is clear. (1) Unless the Holy Spirit judges, whether concerning the very content of Scripture, whether it is the Word of God, or concerning the interpretation of Scripture, unless, I say, he is in the man himself, no faith will ever follow. For the Spirit alone is the one who engenders faith in the heart. (2) The Holy Spirit freely exercises his other functions in whomever he will; therefore also this function, that of judging. For what, I ask, is judging other than illuminating and teaching that this Scripture is self-authenticating [αὐτόπιστον], and that this is the genuine sense of this Scripture? (3) Experience itself teaches this, for we experience him judging freely in whomever he pleases. Passages of Scripture also confirm this. 1 Cor. 12.1. "But all these things one and the same Spirit works, distributing to each one individually as he wills." Isa. 54. "All shall be taught by God" [θεοδίδακτοι]. Jer. 31. "I will write my law on their hearts," etc. Our opponents attack this with certain arguments, about which read in Bellarmine. But they bind the Holy Spirit to the Pope and to councils confirmed by him, which our people attack with many arguments, among which is this one. For thus it would follow that the Pope and the councils confirmed by him are above Scripture, which is absurd. Seek the rest in their disputations.

units.la: De Proprietate octava, Controversia autem decima.
units.tr: De Proprietate octava, Controversia autem decima.

units.la: CAP. 16.
units.tr: CAP. 16.

units.la: POstremò dicimus Scripturam sacram esse summæ authoritatis, præstantiæ, & dignitatis tatis. Scripturæ nomine intelligimus & substantiam & scriptionem. Dignitatem eam intelligimus, qua ipsa est fide dignissima, & fidem procurat Ecclesiæ: Unde ipsa columna & stabilimentum veritatis vocatur. 1. Timoth. 3. 15. & accipit alia elogia, quæ ipsi in Scripturis sacris passim tribuuntur. Probatur ex theorematis jam ante demonstratis: Est verbum Dei, est apertissima, est simplicissima, & ita deinceps. Ergo.
units.tr: Lastly, we say that Holy Scripture is of the highest authority, excellence and dignity. By the name of Scripture we understand both the substance and the writing. By dignity we understand that by which it is most worthy of belief and produces faith in the Church; hence it is called the pillar and foundation of the truth, 1 Tim. 3:15, and it receives the other praises which are attributed to it throughout the holy Scriptures. This is proved from the theses already demonstrated: it is the Word of God, it is most clear, most simple, and so on. Therefore.

units.la: Adversarij de hac authoritate Scripturæ, diverse sentiunt: alij enim summæ ipsius authoritati detrahunt, dicuntq; eam per se quidem authenticam non esse, sed accipere authoritatem suam ab Ecclesia. Eckius in Enchiridio. Pighius lib. 1. de Hierarchia; Hermannus quidam impudentissimus Papista, dicit Scripturam nihilo plus momenti habere, quia fabulas Æsopi sine testimonio Ecclesiæ, &c. Alij vero, & ij quidem recentiores & cautiores, dicunt per se & in se authoritatem habere Scripturam, & authenticam esse: quoad nos vero non esse, ante sententiam Ecclesiæ. In hac sententia sunt Bellarminus, Coclæus, Canus, Stapletonus, Canisius, &c. Eorum sententia, qui dicunt quoad nos non esse ante sententiam Ecclesiæ authenticam hæc est, quod non tenemur nos Scripturis credere quod authenticae sint, antequam Ecclesia id dicat; quodque nihil peccemus, ideo quod non credamus ante definitivam Ecclesiae sententiam. Sed nos dicimus hoc quoque salsum esse, Scripturam quoad nos non esse authenticam sine Ecclesiae authoritate. Spiritus enim sanctus est qui docet quemq; Scripturam esse authenticam, & in se authoritatem habere, eamque summam. Docet autem hoc non per externum aliquod medium primum, sed per ipsam Scripturam sacram, per quam solam fidem hujus rei proprie ingignit cordibus nostris. Nos freti hoc Spiritu sancto docente nos ex ipsa Scriptura hanc Scripturae authoritatem, eam esse jam credimus, etsi totus mundus contradicat. Hactenus de quaestionibus de Scriptura magis essentialibus.
units.tr: Our opponents differ in their views about this authority of Scripture. Some detract from its supreme authority and say that it is not authentic in itself, but receives its authority from the Church: Eck in the Enchiridion, Pighius book 1 of De hierarchia, and a certain most shameless Papist, Hermann, who says that Scripture has no more weight than the fables of Aesop without the testimony of the Church, etc. Others, and these more recent and more cautious, say that Scripture has authority in itself and is authentic in itself, but that for us it is not authentic before the sentence of the Church. Bellarmine, Cochlaeus, Canus, Stapleton, Canisius, etc. hold this view. The argument of those who say that Scripture is not authentic for us before the sentence of the Church is this: we are not bound to believe that the Scriptures are authentic before the Church says so, and we sin in no way by not believing before the Church's definitive sentence. But we say that this too is false, that Scripture is not authentic for us without the authority of the Church. For it is the Holy Spirit who teaches each person that Scripture is authentic, that it has authority in itself, and that this authority is supreme. He teaches this not through any external first means, but through Holy Scripture itself, through which alone he properly engenders the faith of this matter in our hearts. Relying on this Holy Spirit teaching us from Scripture itself, we now believe this authority of Scripture, that it is so, even if the whole world contradicts it. Thus far on the questions about Scripture that are more essential.

units.la: De quaestionibus de Scriptura sacra magis accident- alibus, ac primum de libris quibus conti- netur Scriptura.
units.tr: On the questions about Holy Scripture that are more incidental, and first on the books in which Scripture is contained.

units.la: CAP 17.
units.tr: CAP 17.

units.la: Prima quaestio est de libris in quibus continetur Scriptura, ita a nobis jam explicata & elogijs suis exornata. Libri igitur vocantur vulgo βιβλια και εξοχως. Biblia autem ista quae vulgo vulgò habemus in manibus librorum duo genera continent. Primùm libros Canonicos, deinde Apocryphos. Canonici siue regulares sunt hi qui continèt regulam fidei et morum.
units.tr: The first question concerns the books in which Scripture is contained, which we have now explained and adorned with its praises. Books are therefore commonly called [τὰ βιβλία] and, by preeminence, [ἐξοχήν]. The Bibles we commonly have in our hands contain two kinds of books: first the canonical books, then the Apocrypha. The canonical, or regular, books are those which contain the rule of faith and of morals.

units.la: Canon primus, sunt libri Mosis, qui nullo alio externo Canone, quasi mensurantur: Nam nihil scriptum extitit ante libros Mosis. Authoritas autem personae tam sanctae, et ipsorum librorum spiritualitas, vt sic dicam, & sanctitas conciliavit ijs authoritatem, vt de aliis taceam. Canonem secundum constituunt libri Prophetarum, qui Canonici sunt judicati ex externo illo Canone librorum Mosis, ad quem ipsi sunt examinati. Deinde etiam ex sua spiritualitate, & rerū, & verborum, quā qui θεόπνευστοι, id est, interiùs per Spiritum erant docti, facilè deprehenderunt. Canonem tertium constituunt libri Apostolici novi Testamenti, qui Canonici judicati sunt partim ex libris Mosis canonicis, partim ex libris Prophetarum, partim ex suâ ipsorum spiritualitate, quam qui θεόπνευστοι sunt facilè deprehendunt.
units.tr: The first canon consists of the books of Moses, which are measured by no other external canon, for nothing was written before the books of Moses. The authority of so holy a person, and the spirituality of the books themselves, and, so to speak, their holiness, has won them authority, to say nothing of the others. The second canon consists of the books of the Prophets, which were judged canonical by that external canon of the books of Moses, against which they were examined, and then also by their own spirituality, and by their matters and words, which those who are God-breathed [θεόπνευστοι], that is, inwardly taught by the Spirit, easily perceived. The third canon consists of the apostolic books of the New Testament, which were judged canonical partly from the canonical books of Moses, partly from the books of the Prophets, and partly from their own spirituality, which those who are God-breathed easily perceive.

units.la: Canonici libri Bibliorum partim sunt veteris, partim novi Testamenti. Veteris Testamenti Canonici sunt. Mosis libri quinque. Iehosuæ lib. vnus. Iudicum lib. vnus. Ruthæ lib. vnus. Samuelis lib. duo. Regum lib. duo. Chronicorum lib. duo. Esdræ lib. vnus. Nehemiæ lib. vnus. Esteræ lib. vnus. Iob lib. vnus. Psalmi. Proverbia. Ecclesiastes. Liber Canticorum. Iesaias. Ieremias. Ieremiæ Lament. Ezechiel. Daniel. Minores Prophetæ duodecim.
units.tr: The canonical books of the Bible are partly of the Old Testament and partly of the New. The canonical books of the Old Testament are: the five books of Moses; Joshua, one book; Judges, one book; Ruth, one book; Samuel, two books; Kings, two books; Chronicles, two books; Ezra, one book; Nehemiah, one book; Esther, one book; Job, one book; the Psalms; Proverbs; Ecclesiastes; the Song of Songs; Isaiah; Jeremiah; the Lamentations of Jeremiah; Ezekiel; Daniel; and the twelve Minor Prophets.

units.la: Novi Testamenti Canonici sunt omnes illi libri qui vulgò habentur.
units.tr: The canonical books of the New Testament are all those books that are commonly held to be such.

units.la: Evangelium secundum Matthæum. Evangelium secundum Marcum. Evangelium secundum Lucam. Evangelium secundum Iohannem. Acta Apostolorum. Pauli Epist. ad Rom. Ad Corinthios duæ. Ad Galatas. Ad Ephesios. Ad Philippenses. Ad Colossenses. Ad Thessal. duæ. Ad Timotheum duæ. Ad Titum. Ad Philemonem. Ad Hebræos. Iacobi Epistola. Petri Epist. duæ. Iohannis Epist. tres. Iudæ Epistola. Apocalypsis.
units.tr: The Gospel according to Matthew. The Gospel according to Mark. The Gospel according to Luke. The Gospel according to John. The Acts of the Apostles. Paul's Epistles: to the Romans; two to the Corinthians; to the Galatians; to the Ephesians; to the Philippians; to the Colossians; two to the Thessalonians; two to Timothy; to Titus; to Philemon; to the Hebrews. The Epistle of James. Two Epistles of Peter. Three Epistles of John. The Epistle of Jude. The Apocalypse.

units.la: Etsi quidé de aliquibus est dubitatum, idq; non ab omnibus, aliquandiu, vtpote de Epistola ad Hebræos, Iacobi Epistola, posteriore Petri, secunda & tertia Iohannis, Epistola Iudæ, Apocalypsi: tamen non sunt plané rejecti illi vllo tempore, sed dubitatum est an essent recipiendi. Canonici hi veteris & novi Testamenti scripti sunt à viris Dei sanctis, actis Spiritu sancto. 2. Pet.1.21. & hi partim Prophetæ sunt dicti à Spiritu Prophetico, qui scripserunt libros Canonicos veteris Testamenti; partim Apostoli à munere suo, qui scripserút libros novi Testamenti. Libri Canonici veteris & novi Testameti partim habent Scriptores suos vel nominibus expressis, vel notis quibusdam indicatos, partim vero minimè, ea re significante nobis Spiritu sancto scriptores illos tantum instrumenta fuisse, non authores horum librorum: Itaque non tanti faciendum eorum nomen, neque ita sedulò in id inquirendum, si quado non sit expressum. De Canonicis hactenus.
units.tr: Although some of these books, not by all, have been doubted for a time, namely the Epistle to the Hebrews, the Epistle of James, the later Peter, the second and third of John, the Epistle of Jude, and the Apocalypse, yet these were never entirely rejected at any time; the question was only whether they ought to be received. These canonical books of the Old and New Testament were written by holy men of God, moved by the Holy Spirit (2 Pet. 1.21.). Some of them are called prophets, from the prophetic Spirit, who wrote the canonical books of the Old Testament; others are called apostles, from their office, who wrote the books of the New Testament. Some of the canonical books of the Old and New Testament name their writers, either expressly or by certain marks, while others do not. By this the Holy Spirit signifies to us that those writers were only instruments, not the authors of these books. Therefore the name of the writer is not to be valued so highly, nor is it to be searched for so diligently, if it is not stated. So much for the canonical books.

units.la: De Apocryphis.
units.tr: On the Apocrypha

units.la: Nunc de Apocryphis. Ideò autem dicti sunt Apocryphi quia Ecclesia voluit eos abscondi, non autem publicè legi, vel doceri in Ecclesia, sed permisit privatam duntaxat eorum librorum lectione. Apocryphi libri tantum sunt veteris Testamenti, & numerantur vndecim vulgo. Iudith. | Adiectiones ad Danielem. Tobit. | Oratio Manassis. Esdrae tertius et quartus. | Libri Machabaeorum. Sapientia Salomonis. | Esdrae reliquum a vers. 3. Cap. 10. Ecclesiasticus. | Baruch. | Epistola Ieremiae.
units.tr: Now concerning the Apocrypha. They are so called because the Church wished them to be hidden away, not publicly read or taught in the Church, but permitted only for private reading. The Apocryphal books are only of the Old Testament, and commonly they are numbered as eleven: Judith; additions to Daniel; Tobit; the Prayer of Manasseh; 3 and 4 Ezra; the books of the Maccabees; the Wisdom of Solomon; the rest of Ezra from chapter 10, verse 3; Ecclesiasticus; Baruch; the Epistle of Jeremiah.

units.la: Ex his sunt quos ipsi adversarij Apocryphos judicant. 1. Est oratio Manassis. 2. Esdrae liber tertius & quartus. 3. Machabæorum tertius, item quartus, cujus Athanasius meminit in Synopsi. Sed nobis demonstrandum est omnes pariter esse Apocryphos. Argumentum primum est à scriptoribus. Omnes Canonici Libri veteris Testamenti sunt scripti à Prophetis: At hi non sunt scripti à Prophetis: Ergo non sunt Canonici, sed Apocryphi. Probo propositionem. Luc.16. Habent Mosen & Prophetas, hoc est, scriptum Mosis & Prophetarum. Luc.24. de Christo dicitur quod exorsus à Mose & Prophetis interpretatus est in omnibus, &c. Ergo Moses et Prophetæ scriptores erant veteris Testamenti.
units.tr: Among these are some which even the adversaries themselves judge to be Apocryphal: (1) the Prayer of Manasseh; (2) the third and fourth books of Ezra; (3) the third book of the Maccabees, and likewise the fourth, which Athanasius mentions in his Synopsis. But we must show that all of them alike are Apocryphal. The first argument is from the writers. All the canonical books of the Old Testament were written by prophets; but these were not written by prophets; therefore they are not canonical but Apocryphal. I prove the premise. In Luke 16 it is said, "They have Moses and the Prophets," that is, the writing of Moses and the Prophets. In Luke 24 it is said of Christ that, beginning from Moses and the Prophets, he interpreted in all things, etc. Therefore Moses and the Prophets were the writers of the Old Testament.

units.la: Scripturas vocat Propheticas: & 2. Pet. 1. λογον vocat προφητικον, nempe, Scripturam veteris Testamenti. Ad assumptionem, At hi non sunt scripti à Prophetis: probatur, Prophetarum vltimus fuit Malachias; Inter Malachiam autem & Iohannem Baptistam nullus surrexit Propheta. At hi Libri sunt scripti post Malachiam, idque de quibusdam negari non potest, vt de Ecclesiastico, & lib. Machabæorum: Ergo. Argumentum. 2. est à lingua qua scripti sunt omnes Libri Canonici. Sunt ij scripti lingua Canaan, lingua Hebræa, lingua Prophetarum: vtpote à Prophetis conscripti. At hi libri non sunt scripti lingua Hebræa, sed plerique omnes Græca: Ergo. Propositio manifesta est: Assumptio patet, & comprobatur reipsa, vt nihil de Patrum testimonio dicam, nihil etiam de adversariorum confessione. Argumentum 3. à testimonio veteris Ecclesiæ Iudaicæ. Si essent Canonici, veteres Hebræi de iis aliquid audivissent. At nihil audiverunt: Ergo. Propositio patet: Assumptio probatur: Nam ætate Esdræ omnes Canonici sunt in vnum collecti, & ea fuit Iudæorum cura de iis, vt etiam literas quotquot in Prophetis reperiebantur numerarint, & in vnam summam redegerint: quanto magis gis curæ fuissent ijs toti libri isti, si modò de ijs aliquid audivissent. Argumentum 4. à testimonio recentioris Ecclesiæ Iudaicæ quæ fuit Christi ætate. Si Canonici essent eos recepissent recentiores Iudæi: at non receperunt, imò rejecerũt. Ergo Canonici non sunt. Propositio probatur: Nám si Canonicos non recepissent, proculdubiò eo nomine à Christo reprehensi fuissent, cum ab eo reprehensi sint propter sinistras & perversas interpretationes Scripturarum Canonicarum. Assumptionem confitentur ipsi adversarij. Argumentum 5. à testimonio Christi & Apostolorum. Si Canonici essent, Christus & Apostoli doctrinam suam alicubi ex ijs fuissent testati: at id nunquam reperitur: Ergo. Propositio manifesta est, assumptionem res ipsa docet. Argumentum 6. Hi continent quædam diversa ab ijs quæ in Canonicis habentur, imò quædam cum ijs pugnantia, quædam falsa, quædam fabulosa, quædam impia. Ergo non sunt Canonici. Prob. antecedens. Tobit. 3.8. & 3. 25. & 5.15. & 11.12. Iudith. 8.6. & 9.2. & 9.13. & 16.8. Baruch. 6.2. Adjectiones ad Danielem. 13.1. & 14.32. Adjectiones ad Hester. 15.1. 2. Machab. 2.1. & 7.8.27. & 12.43. & 14.37. & 15.39. Argumentum. 7. Hi continent tinent ἀσυμφωνα & pugnantia inter se : Ergo. Probatur antecedens. Confer. 1.Machab.6.8. & 2. Machab. 1. 16. & 2.Machab.9.5. Confer. 1.Machab. 9.3. & 2. Machab. 10. 1. Confer 1. Machab.4. 36. & 2. Machab. 10.1. Confer 1. Machab.6.17. & 2.Machab. 10. 11. Argumentum 8. est à testimonio humano petitum. 1. Conciliorum. 2. Patrum, primum veterum, deinde recentiorum. Concilia quæ Canones habent de Canonicis Libris & Apocryphis hæc fere sunt; Laodicenum, quod celebratum est post natum Dominum anno 300. Carthaginense tertium, post natum Dominum anno 400. Trullanum, celebratum anno 600, Florentinum, anno 1150. Tridentinum nostra ętate. His positis argumentamur: Concilium Laodicenum, quod ex his à nobis enumeratis est antiquissimum, hos excludit tanquam Apocryphos. Vide ejus concilij Canonem 59. Ergo. At objiciunt adversarij: Nondum constitutus fuit Canon ante concilium Carthaginense tertium: Respondeo. 1. Concilium illud non nisi post natum Christum annos 400. celebratum fuisse: at absurdum est tam diu non fuisse in Ecclesia aliquem Canonem: Ergo. 2. Concilium illud non generale, sed provinciale fuit: At non licet provinciali statuere de Canone totius Ecclesiæ: Ergo. At, inquiunt, confirmatum est per concilium Trullanum? Respondeo, At per Trullanum confirmatum est concilium Laodicenum. Illud deinde Trullanum est improbatum ab ipsis Papistis in multis.
units.tr: He calls them "prophetic Scriptures," and in 2 Peter 1 he calls the word "prophetic" [προφητικόν], namely the Scripture of the Old Testament. As to the minor premise, that these were not written by prophets: it is proved thus. The last of the prophets was Malachi; but between Malachi and John the Baptist no prophet arose. These books, however, were written after Malachi, and this cannot be denied of some of them, such as Ecclesiasticus and the books of the Maccabees. Therefore... The second argument is from the language in which all the canonical books were written. They were written in the language of Canaan, the Hebrew language, the language of the Prophets, since they were written by prophets. But these books were not written in Hebrew, but almost all of them in Greek. Therefore... The major premise is plain; the minor is evident and is confirmed by the thing itself, not to mention the testimony of the Fathers or the confession of the adversaries. The third argument is from the testimony of the ancient Jewish Church. If they had been canonical, the ancient Hebrews would have heard something of them. But they heard nothing; therefore... The major premise is plain. The minor is proved: for in the time of Ezra all the canonical books were gathered into one, and the Jews took such care of them that they even counted every letter that was found in the Prophets and reduced it to a single total. How much more would they have cared for these whole books, if they had at least heard something of them? The fourth argument is from the testimony of the later Jewish Church, which existed in Christ's time. If they had been canonical, the later Jews would have received them; but they did not receive them, indeed they rejected them. Therefore they are not canonical. The premise is proved: for if they had not received them as canonical, they would undoubtedly have been rebuked by Christ on that account, since he rebuked them for their perverse and wrong interpretations of the canonical Scriptures. The adversaries themselves confess the minor premise. The fifth argument is from the testimony of Christ and the Apostles. If they were canonical, Christ and the Apostles would somewhere have borne witness to their teaching from them; but this is never found. Therefore... The major premise is plain; the minor the thing itself teaches. The sixth argument: these books contain some things different from those held in the canonical books, indeed some contrary to them, some false, some fabulous, some impious. Therefore they are not canonical. The antecedent is proved: Tobit 3.8; 3.25; 5.15; 11.12; Judith 8.6; 9.2; 9.13; 16.8; Baruch 6.2; the additions to Daniel 13.1 and 14.32; the additions to Esther 15.1–2; 2 Maccabees 2.1; 7.8, 27; 12.43; 14.37; 15.39. The seventh argument: these books contain things inconsistent [ἀσύμφωνα] and contradictory among themselves. Therefore... The antecedent is proved: compare 1 Maccabees 6.8 with 2 Maccabees 1.16 and 2 Maccabees 9.5; compare 1 Maccabees 9.3 with 2 Maccabees 10.1; compare 1 Maccabees 4.36 with 2 Maccabees 10.1; compare 1 Maccabees 6.17 with 2 Maccabees 10.11. The eighth argument is drawn from human testimony: (1) of councils, (2) of the Fathers, the earliest first and then the later. The councils which have canons concerning the canonical and Apocryphal books are roughly these: the Council of Laodicea, held in the year 300 after the birth of the Lord; the Third Council of Carthage, in the year 400 after the birth of the Lord; the Council in Trullo, held in the year 600; the Council of Florence, in the year 1150; the Council of Trent in our own age. Having laid these down, we argue thus: the Council of Laodicea, which is the oldest of those we have listed, excludes these books as Apocryphal; see canon 59 of that council. Therefore... But the adversaries object: the canon was not yet established before the Third Council of Carthage. I answer: first, that council was held no earlier than four hundred years after Christ, but it is absurd that there was no canon in the Church for so long; therefore... Second, that council was not a general but a provincial one; but it is not lawful for a provincial council to decide on the canon of the whole Church; therefore... But, they say, it was confirmed by the Council in Trullo? I answer: the Council in Trullo confirmed the Council of Laodicea, not the reverse; and besides, that Council in Trullo has been rejected by the Papists themselves in many points.

units.la: Hactenus de Concilijs, nunc ad Patres. Patres veteres hos rejecerunt tanquā Apocryphos: Ergo. Probatur inductione. 1. Athanasius in Synopsi. 2. Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus. 3. Hilarius Episcopus Pictaviensis. 4. Melito Sardensis. 5. Nazianzenus in carmine suo. 6. Hieronymus in Prologo Galeato qui prefigitur lib. Regum. 7. Gregorius magnus. 8. Iosephus contra Appionem. 9. Russinus in expositione Symboli Apostolici. 10. Augustinus. Excipiunt contra hos adversarij. At hi loquuti sunt de Canone veteris Testamenti Hebræorum non Christianorum? Respondeo, 1. quasi vero alium oportet esse Canonem Hebræorum, quàm Christianorum. 2. Eundem illum Canonem Hebræorum ipsi approbarunt. At nondum, inquiunt, forte illorum temporibus constitutus fuit Canon? Resp. Quando igitur constitutus fuit, aut in quo Concilio? an in concilio Tridentino? at nimis recens est, ætate utpote nostra.
units.tr: So much for the councils; now to the Fathers. The ancient Fathers rejected these as Apocryphal; therefore... This is proved by enumeration: (1) Athanasius in his Synopsis; (2) Cyril of Jerusalem; (3) Hilary, bishop of Poitiers; (4) Melito of Sardis; (5) Nazianzen in his poem; (6) Jerome in the Galeatus Prologue prefixed to the books of Kings; (7) Gregory the Great; (8) Josephus against Apion; (9) Rufinus in his exposition of the Apostles' Creed; (10) Augustine. The adversaries object against these: but did they speak of the canon of the Hebrews of the Old Testament, not of the Christians? I answer: (1) as if the canon of the Hebrews ought to be different from that of the Christians; (2) they themselves approved that same canon of the Hebrews. But, they say, perhaps the canon had not yet been established in their times? I reply: when then was it established, and in which council? In the Council of Trent? But that is far too recent, being of our own age. In the Council of Florence? That too is far too recent. In the Third Council of Carthage? But that council (1) was provincial, and (2) is rejected in some points by the Papists themselves, as in that canon about the high priest, which is number 26.

units.la: An in concilio Florentino? nimis etiam recens. An in concilio Carthaginensi tertio? At illud concilium. 1. provinciale fuit. 2. improbatur in quibusdam ab ipsis Papistis, vt in illo Canone de summo Sacerdote qui numero est 26. At, inquiunt, confirmatum est per Trullanum? Resp. 1. sic & Laodicenum. 2. sic seriùs constitutus est Canon, nempè anno Christi 400. 3. Trullanum improbatur in multis ab ipsis Papistis. 4. Post Trullanum exiterunt patres qui Apocryphos non receperunt. Atq; ita peruenimus ad Patrum secundam classem, nempè, recentiorum.
units.tr: Or at the Council of Florence? That too is far too recent. Or at the Third Council of Carthage? But that council (1) was only provincial, and (2) is rejected in some points by the Papists themselves, such as the canon about the high priest, which is numbered 26. But, they say, it was confirmed by the Trullan council? Reply: (1) so was the Laodicean council too; (2) the canon was settled later, namely in the year of Christ 400; (3) the Trullan council is rejected in many points by the Papists themselves; (4) after the Trullan council there arose Fathers who did not receive the Apocrypha. And so we come to the second class of Fathers, namely the more recent ones.

units.la: Sic itaque argumentor. Recentiores non numerant hos inter Canonicos: Ergo. Probatur inductione. Isidorus in lib. de officijs, Iohannes Damascenus, Nicephorus, Leontius, Rabanus Maurus, Radulphus, Lyranus, Carthusianus, Abulensis, Antoninus, Hugo Cardinalis, Erasmus alicubi, Cajetanus Cardinalis. At hi omnes fuerunt post Trullanum concilium, nonnulli etiam ex ijs post Florentinum ab Ecclesia Romana pro filijs sunt habiti. Ex his testimonijs primùm Conciliorum, deinde Patrum, patet nullum judicio legitimo constitutū fuisse Canonicum inter istos: sienim fuisset hoc factum, isti tot patres veteres & recentiores agnovissent. Quare Apocryphi sunt.
units.tr: I argue as follows. The more recent writers do not count these among the canonical books; therefore they are not canonical. This is proved by induction: Isidore in his book On Offices, John of Damascus, Nicephorus, Leontius, Rabanus Maurus, Radulf, Lyra, the Carthusian, Abulensis, Antoninus, Cardinal Hugo, Erasmus in places, Cardinal Cajetan. But all of these lived after the Trullan council, and some of them, after Florence, were even counted as sons by the Roman Church. From these testimonies, first of the councils and then of the Fathers, it is plain that none of these books was established as canonical among them by a lawful judgment. For if this had been done, those many ancient and recent Fathers would have acknowledged it. Therefore they are Apocryphal.

units.la: Adversarij pro sua sententia afferunt quoq; testimonium humanum, quod illis fere unicum est, utpote Concilia illa de quibus diximus, ut Carthaginense tertium, Trullanum, Florentinum, Tridentinum. At nos duo posteriora tanquam tyrannica & congregata aduersus veritatem rejicimus. De Trullano etiam & Carthaginensi tertio sententiam nostram adduximus. Patres vero pro se afferunt potissimum Pontifices, ut Innocentium, ut Gelasium, etiam Augustinum alicubi. At respondeo. 1. Neq; tot neq; tam vetustos afferre pro se possunt. 2. Patres illi cum vocant hos quos nos rejicimus Canonicos, Canonicorum nomen latius accipiunt, pro libris aliquam sanctitatem præter & supra scripta prophana habentibus; non autem paris authoritatis cum ijs qui revera sunt Canonici. Et nos quoq; non negamus in plerisq; ex his ea inveniri sanctitate quæ non invenitur in alijs scriptis prophanis. De Apocryphis hæc hactenus.
units.tr: The adversaries also bring forward human testimony for their opinion, which is almost their only support, namely those councils we have mentioned: the Third Council of Carthage, the Trullan, Florence, and Trent. But we reject the last two as tyrannical and gathered against the truth. We have also set out our own view about the Trullan council and the Third Council of Carthage. The Fathers they bring forward for themselves are chiefly popes, such as Innocent and Gelasius, and even Augustine in places. But I reply: (1) they cannot bring forward so many, or such ancient, witnesses for themselves; (2) those Fathers, when they call the books we reject canonical, take the name of canonical more broadly, for books having some sanctity beyond and above profane writings, and not of the same authority as those which are truly canonical. We too do not deny that in many of these books there is found a sanctity that is not found in other profane writings. So much on the Apocrypha.

units.la: De authentica Bibliorum editione.
units.tr: On the authentic edition of the Bible.

units.la: CAP. 18.
units.tr: CHAPTER 18.

units.la: CVM multæ extent Bibliorum editiones in multis & varijs linguis, ut Hebraica, Græca, Latina, & linguis alijs vernaculis, quæritur quæ ex his omnibus authentica habenda sit? Respondeo Hebraica editio veteris Testamenti, & Græca editio novi pro authenticis habendæ sunt; adeò vt ex his omnia sint definienda, & omnes aliæ editiones ita comprobandæ, si cum his conveniant. Dicemus itaque primùm de editione Hebraica Testamenti veteris. Affirmamus igitur editionem veteris Testamenti Hebraicam authenticam esse. Hanc propositionem demonstrabimus, postquàm pauca quædam præfati fuerimus de lingua Hebraica, de scriptione veteris Testamenti in lingua Hebraica, de conservatione librorum veteris Testamenti in lingua hebraica conscriptorū in hodiernum vsq; diem.
units.tr: CVM there are many editions of the Bible in many and various languages, such as Hebrew, Greek, Latin, and other vernacular tongues, the question arises which of all these is to be held authentic? I answer that the Hebrew edition of the Old Testament and the Greek edition of the New are to be held authentic, so that all things are to be decided by these, and all other editions are to be tested by them, insofar as they agree with them. We shall therefore speak first of the Hebrew edition of the Old Testament. We affirm, then, that the Hebrew edition of the Old Testament is authentic. We will demonstrate this proposition after we have said a few things beforehand about the Hebrew language, about the writing of the Old Testament in Hebrew, and about the preservation of the books of the Old Testament written in Hebrew down to the present day.

units.la: Lingua Hebraica omnium prima fuit, adeòque vnica ad diluvium vsque & exstructionem arcis Babylonicæ.Gen.11. Erat vniversa terra sermonis ejusdem, & erant verba eadem. In extructione arcis Babylonicæ cœpit linguarum confusio, & ex prima Hebraica quasi matre multæ aliæ sunt enatæ: nam aliæ omnes nihil fere sunt aliud quàm dialecti, & dialecti linguæ Hebraicæ, quarum aliæ matri similiores sunt, aliæ ab ea magis deflexerunt. In confusione illa linguarum conservata est Hebraica
units.tr: Hebrew was the first of all languages, and so the only one until the flood and the building of the Babylonian tower (Gen.11.). The whole earth had one speech and the same words. With the building of the Babylonian tower the confusion of tongues began, and from the first Hebrew, as from a mother, many others have sprung. For all the others are almost nothing but dialects, and dialects of the Hebrew language: some of them are more like their mother, others have strayed further from her. In that confusion of tongues Hebrew was preserved.

units.la: {y} Hebraica lingua matrix, vt Hieronymus vocat, in familia Heber, qui quartus fuit à Noacho, & vixit eo ipso tempore quo extructa est arx Babylonica, coepitq; confusio linguarum. Ab Hebere est Hebraica primum appellata, & ab eo propagata ad posteros, non quidé omnes, sed eos ex quibus ortus est Abrahamus: hinc ad vltimos vsque Prophetas transfinissé est. Nam Chaggai, Zacharias, Malachias Prophetæ hac lingua scripserunt. Hactenus de lingua dictum.
units.tr: The Hebrew language, the mother, as Jerome calls it, was preserved in the family of Heber, who was the fourth from Noah and lived at the very time when the Babylonian tower was built and the confusion of tongues began. It was first called Hebrew after Heber, and was handed down by him to posterity, not indeed to all his descendants, but to those from whom Abraham sprang; from there it continued down to the last of the Prophets. For the prophets Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi wrote in this language. So much on the language.

units.la: Lingua hac Hebraica & sancta scriptum est primum vetus Testamentum. Scriptor primus fuit Moses; hunc sequuti sunt Prophetæ; quorum alij ante captivitatem, alij in captivitate, alij post eam scripserunt: Et scripserunt quidem omnes hebraicè, si Danielem excipias, & Esdram, qui quædam Chaldaicè scripserunt: Sed hoc nihil impedit quo minùs vetus Testamentum totū hebraicè scriptum esse dicatur, cùm Chaldaica Hebraicæ sit vicina.
units.tr: The Old Testament was first written in this Hebrew, the holy language. The first writer was Moses; the prophets followed him, some writing before the captivity, some during it, and some after it. And indeed all of them wrote in Hebrew, except Daniel and Ezra, who wrote some parts in Chaldee. But this does not prevent the whole Old Testament from being said to be written in Hebrew, since Chaldee is close to Hebrew.

units.la: Nunc de conservatione horum librorum veteris Testamenti dicendum est. Libri Moses & Prophetarum, hoc est, vetus Testamentum hebraicè scriptum, admirabili Dei providentia conservati sunt ad hodiernum vsq; diem: conservati, inquam, in temporibus difficillimis & periculosissimis, ut in incendio urbis, & templi Hierosolymitani, in captivitate & persequutione illa Antiochi Epiphanis longe gravissima: nam is & in ipsos libros saevijt; in persequutionibus post Christum sub Imperatoribus Romanis.
units.tr: Now we must speak of the preservation of these books of the Old Testament. The books of Moses and the Prophets, that is, the Old Testament written in Hebrew, have been preserved by the admirable providence of God down to the present day: preserved, I say, in the most difficult and dangerous times, such as the burning of the city and temple of Jerusalem, the captivity, and that most grievous persecution under Antiochus Epiphanes, for he raged even against the books themselves; and in the persecutions after Christ under the Roman emperors.

units.la: Sed hic quaestum, an ijdem libri qui à Mose & Prophetis ante captivitatem scripti sunt, pervenerint in manus nostras? Respondeo de hac re fuerunt variae hominum sententiae: non enim defuerunt qui putarunt illos Mosis & Prophetarum libros consumptos fuisse in incendio illo urbis & templi, hos autem quos nos habemus reparatos fuisse & rescriptos denuo ab Esdra jurisperito, extra ordinem à Deo inspirato, & vocato ad id muneris. In hac sententia fuerunt Basilius in Epistola ad Chilonem, Irenæus, Tertullianus, Clemens Alexandrinus, Isidorus de officijs, Rabanus Maurus, Leontius. Adducti sunt fortassis ad hanc sententiam propter historiam illam, vel fabulam potius, de qua legimus Esdræ 4. 14. Sed liber ille Apocryphus est, & rejectus, non tantum à nostra Ecclesia, sed etiam pontificia. Sententia autem sic refutari potest. 1. Si ab Esdra fuissent de integro rescripti, profectò scripti fuissent, ut verisimile est, non Hebraicè sed Chaldaicè, vel certè lingua mixta ex Hebraica & Chaldaica. Nam Esdras sic ipse scripsit lingua illa mixta duos libros Esdræ. 2. Nehemiæ. 8. dicitur Esdras attulisse & legisse non libros suos, aut à se scriptos, sed libros legis Mosis. 3. Non est verisimile nullum extitisse pium, vel Prophetā, vel alium, qui tempore incendij, vel non eripuerit sacros libros ex incenso templo, vel certè apud se nullū horum exemplar habuerit; præsertim cum eo tempore vixerint Ezechiel et Daniel extra omnem controversiā. 4. Vel ipsum nomen quod à Daniele Monarchiæ illi chaldaicæ tributum est, cum aureain eam appellat, arguit non ab ea sævitiū esse in libros sacros: Quod si enim delevissēt libros sacros, puto tā præclaro nomine à Spiritu sancto nunquam fuisset infignita: Ergo falsa est illa sententia; vera autem est quod reservati sint libri Mosis & veterum Prophetarum in vrbis & templi incêdio, & in captivitate, venerint; tandem in manus nostras. Neque tamen inficiamur, quod à pijs viris scriptum legimus, Esdrani post reditum populi libros illos Mosis & Prophetarum repurgasse, in vnum corpus digessisse, & certo ordine eos distribuisse. De hac quæstione hactenus.
units.tr: But here it is asked whether the very same books that were written by Moses and the Prophets before the captivity have come into our hands. I answer that on this matter there have been various opinions among men. For there were not wanting those who thought that the books of Moses and the Prophets were consumed in that burning of the city and temple, and that the ones we have were restored and rewritten afresh by Ezra, a jurist, raised up beyond the ordinary course by God and called to that office. In this opinion were Basil in his Epistle to Chilon, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, Isidore in On Offices, Rabanus Maurus and Leontius. They were perhaps led to this view by that story, or rather fable, which we read in Ezra 4. 14. But that book is Apocryphal and rejected, not only by our Church but also by the Papists. The opinion can be refuted as follows. (1) If they had been rewritten from scratch by Ezra, they would surely, as is likely, have been written not in Hebrew but in Chaldee, or at least in a mixed language of Hebrew and Chaldee. For Ezra himself wrote in that mixed language, as do the two books Ezra. 2. Nehem. 8. (2) In Nehem. 8. it is said that Ezra brought and read not his own books, or books written by himself, but the books of the law of Moses. (3) It is not likely that there was no pious man, prophet or other, who either rescued the sacred books from the burning temple or at least had no copy of them at hand, especially since Ezekiel and Daniel lived at that time, beyond all controversy. (4) The very name that Daniel gave to that Chaldean monarchy, when he calls it golden, shows that there was no cruelty against the sacred books from it. For if they had destroyed the sacred books, I think it would never have been honoured with so noble a name by the Holy Spirit. Therefore that opinion is false; but it is true that the books of Moses and the old Prophets were preserved through the burning of the city and temple and through the captivity, and at last came into our hands. Nor do we deny what we read written by pious men, that Ezra, after the people's return, purged those books of Moses and the Prophets, gathered them into one body, and arranged them in a fixed order. So much on this question.

units.la: Nunc his præmissis probabimus editio‑ nem hebraicam veteris Testamenti authenti‑ cam esse solam. Ea editio quæ scripta est lin‑ gua omnium prima, & primùm lingua omni‑ um prima, & in hac lingua purè & integrè conservata est ad nostra vsque tempora, ea, in‑ quam, editio authentica est veteris Testamen‑ ti: At talis est hebraica editio: Ergo.
units.tr: With these things premised, we shall prove that the Hebrew edition of the Old Testament alone is authentic. That edition which was written in the first of all languages, and first in that language which is the first of all, and which has been kept pure and entire in this language down to our own times: that edition, I say, is the authentic edition of the Old Testament. But such is the Hebrew edition. Therefore it is the authentic edition.

units.la: Adversarij non possunt negare scriptam esse linguam omnium prima ac matre aliarum, neq; etiam primùm scriptam esse hac lingua, neq; etiam conservatam esse in puritate cer‑ tè aliqua ad hodiernum vsq; diem: Sed sum‑ mam hanc, quam nos dicimus, puritatem ei denegant. Bellarminus ex toto veteri Testa‑ mento quinq; duntaxat loca protulit quibus conatus est probare perturbatũ esse, aliqua cer‑ tè ex parte, fontem hebraicum. Primus locus est Esaiæ 9.6. vbi legitur hebraicè [Vajikra schemo pele] Et vocabit nomen eius (nem‑pè Iehova) admirabilem. At vulgata Latina editio legit, Et vocabitur, quam lectionem approbat Calvinus: Ergo vel confessione Calvini hic fons Hebraicus turbatus est. Resp. 1. Sensus idé est siue legatur, vocabit, siue legatur, vocabitur. 2. Eædem literæ sunt vtriusque vocis hebraicæ, Vocabit, vocabitur, punćta puncta autem diversa, quæ corpus vocis ipsius non faciunt aliud & diversum. 3. Hebræi Doctores, vt Vatablus, tradunt sæpe apud Hebræos verbum personale tertiæ personæ pro impersonali accipi, vt hic Vocabit pro Vocabitur. 4. Tremellius & Iunius retinent lectionem hebraicam, & reddunt, & vocat nomen eius, &c.
units.tr: The opponents cannot deny that the language which is first of all languages and the mother of the rest was written down, nor that it was first written in this language, nor that it has been kept in some measure of purity down to the present day. But they deny it that highest purity which we claim for it. Bellarmine brought forward from the whole Old Testament only five passages by which he tried to prove that the Hebrew source has been disturbed, at least in some part. The first is Isaiah 9.6., where the Hebrew reads [Vajikra schemo pele] And he will call his name (namely Jehovah) Wonderful. But the Vulgate Latin edition reads And he will be called, a reading which Calvin approves. Therefore, even by Calvin's own confession, this Hebrew source is disturbed here. Reply: 1. The sense is the same whether one reads he will call or he will be called. 2. The letters of the two Hebrew forms, will call and will be called, are the same; the points are different, but these do not make the body of the word another and different thing. 3. Hebrew teachers, such as Vatablus, hand down that among the Hebrews a verb of the personal third person is often taken impersonally, as here he will call for it will be called. 4. Tremellius and Junius keep the Hebrew reading and render it calls his name, etc.

units.la: Secundus locus. [VEZEH SCHEMO ASCHER JIKREO, IEHOVAH TSIDKENV] Ier. 23.6. Et hoc nomen eius, quo vocabit eum, Iehova Iustitia nostra. At vulgata Latina editio legit, Quod vocabunt eum, Dominus iustitia nostra: quam lectionem etiam approbat Calvinus. Ergo hic hebraicus fons, vel teste ipso Calvino, perturbatus est. Resp. 1. Sensus non est incommodus si legatur, Quo vocabit eum, nempe, Iehova iustitia nostra: nomen autem quod præcessit nomen est populi securitatis, populi qui securè habitat, vt Tremellius & Iunius intelligunt & vertunt. 2. Sexaginta vertunt καλεῖ, vocabit. 3. Hieronymus liberum facit. 4. Hebræi Doctores Vatablus, Paginus, Arias Montanus legunt vocabit, & vertunt vocabunt.
units.tr: The second passage is [VEZEH SCHEMO ASCHER JIKREO, IEHOVAH TSIDKENV] Jer. 23.6. And this is his name by which he will call him, Jehovah our righteousness. But the Vulgate Latin edition reads By which they will call him, The Lord our righteousness, a reading which Calvin also approves. Therefore this Hebrew source is disturbed here too, by Calvin's own testimony. Reply: 1. The sense is not awkward if one reads By which he will call him, namely Jehovah our righteousness; the name that precedes is the name of the people of safety, the people who dwell securely, as Tremellius and Junius understand and translate it. 2. The Seventy render [καλεῖ] will call. 3. Jerome takes a free rendering. 4. The Hebrew teachers Vatablus, Pagninus and Arias Montanus read he will call and translate they will call.

units.la: Tertius locus est Psal. 22. 17. [GAARI JAUDAI VERAGLAI.] Foderunt manus meas & pedes pedes meos. In Latina editione legitur Foderunt: ita legunt omnes Christiani, cum in hebraica legatur, sicut Leo: quare hoc loco corruptus est fons hebraicus. Resp. Masoritæ testantur in nonnullis exemplaribus hebraicis lectum fuisse, [CARV] hoc est, Foderunt: ijdem testatur in quibus libris legitur [CAARI] verbum hoc non accipi in trita significatione. Chaldæus paraphrastes vtrunque conjungit, Sicut Leo pertundit dentibus, sic isti foderunt, &c. At hi fuerunt ante Hieronymum, Masoritæ, inquam, & Chaldæus paraphrastes: Ergo salsum est hunc locum corruptu fuisse à Iudeis post Hieronymum. Hieronymus in Psalterio suo retinet hanc lectionem [CAARI] & tamen vertit Foderunt. Quidam homo Pontificius Augustinus Iustinianus qui edidit lib. Psal. coilectum ex varijs linguis, aperte admonet hunc locum non esse corruptum, sed defectum esse verbi, quem supplevit Chaldæus paraphrastes.
units.tr: The third passage is Ps. 22.17. [GAARI JAUDAI VERAGLAI.] They pierced my hands and my feet. In the Latin edition it reads They pierced, and all Christians so read it, whereas in the Hebrew it reads like a lion. Therefore the Hebrew source is corrupted at this place. Reply: The Masoretes attest that in some Hebrew copies it was read [CARV], that is, they pierced; the same Masoretes attest that in the books where [CAARI] is read, the word is not taken in its common meaning. The Chaldee paraphrast combines both: As a lion tears with its teeth, so those men pierced, etc. But these men, the Masoretes I mean and the Chaldee paraphrast, were before Jerome. Therefore it is false that this passage was corrupted by the Jews after Jerome. Jerome in his Psalter retains this reading [CAARI] and yet translates they pierced. A certain Papist, Augustinus Justinianus, who published the Psalter collected from various languages, clearly warns that this passage is not corrupted but that a word is missing, which the Chaldee paraphrast supplied.

units.la: Quartus locus est Psal. 19. 5. [BECOL HAARETS JATSA CAVVAM.] In omnem terram exiuit linea vel delineatio eorum. At non modò vulgata versio, sed etiā Septuaginta, quossequitur Apostolus Rom. 12. legunt, sonus eorum, φθογγος: Ergo hic locus est corruptus. Ad hoc respondeat vel solus Genebrardus in scholijs suis in psalmos, qui dicit Septuaginta & Paulum sensum potius verbi quam significatum genuinum ac proprium expressisse, nam delineatio quodammodo vocem suam edit.
units.tr: The fourth passage is Ps. 19.5. [BECOL HAARETS JATSA CAVVAM.] Their line or delineation went out into all the earth. But not only the Vulgate version, but also the Septuagint, whom the Apostle follows in Rom. 10, read their sound [φθογγος]. Therefore this passage is corrupted. To this Genebrardus alone replies in his scholia on the Psalms, saying that the Septuagint and Paul expressed the sense of the word rather than its genuine and proper meaning, for a delineation in a way gives out its own voice.

units.la: Quintus locus est Exod.2. post versum 22. in latina vulgata editione totus hic locus legitur de altero Mosis filio: Alterum vero peperit quem vocavit Eliezer, dicens, Deus enim Patris mei adiutor meus, & eripuit me de manu Pharaonis. At hic totus locus desideratur in hebraica editione: Ergo. Respondeo, obeliscus est inustus huic loco etiam in editionibus Lovanienfibus, qui admonet hunc locum irrepsisse: Et puriores ex Papistis eum putant non esse genuinum, vt Cajetanus, qui sic in hunc locum scribit: Tota ista particula de secundo filio superflua est. Ex his igitur non concludit Bellarminus hebraicam editionem corruptam esse, ac proinde non esse authenticam.
units.tr: The fifth passage is Exod. 2., after verse 22. In the Latin Vulgate edition the whole of this passage about the second son of Moses is read: But she bore another, whom she called Eliezer, saying, For the God of my father was my helper, and delivered me from the hand of Pharaoh. But this whole passage is missing from the Hebrew edition. Therefore, etc. I answer: an obelisk is marked against this passage even in the Louvain editions, which warns that the passage has crept in. And the more careful among the Papists think it is not genuine, such as Cajetan, who writes on this place: That whole clause about the second son is superfluous. Therefore Bellarmine does not conclude from these that the Hebrew edition is corrupted, and so is not authentic.

units.la: Ergo vicissim vno hoc argumento concludo non esse corruptam hebraicam editionem. Si corrupta est a Iudæis, id factum est vel ante Christi ætatem, vel post: Non ante: id quod, omissis Patrum testimonijs, vel hoc solo argumento ostendi potest: Si a Iudæis suisset corrupta editio hebraica id flagitium non dissimulasset Christus in adventu suo: Atnusquam legimus Christum Iudaeos insimulasse hoc nomine, quod ab ijs editio hebraica fuerit corrupta, imo vero legimus eum ipsos remisisse ad hanc ipsa editionem, quam in manibus habebant. Scrutamini, inquit, Scripturas. Iohan.5.39. Non potest Christi aetatem corrupta est, id quod praetermissis patrum testimonijs hac sola ratione offendi potest; Iudaei non potuerunt omnia exemplaria hebraica corrumpere, etiamsi id quam maxime voluissent, cum pleraque in manibus Christianorum fuerint. Hinc sequitur, quod si neque ante, neq; post aetatem Christi corrupta fuerit editio hebraica, non fuisse corruptam omnino. At forte dicent post Augustini & Hieronymi tempora a Iudeis corruptam fuisse? Respondeo, Quibus quaeso in locis? an in illis quinque quę Bellarminus in medium attulit? At iam ostendimus tempore Hieronymi & ante Hieronymum ea sic lecta fuisse, ut leguntur hodierno die. Ergo maneat hebraica editio omni ex parte pura, ac proinde sola veteris Testamenti editio authentica.
units.tr: Conversely, then, I conclude by this one argument that the Hebrew edition is not corrupted. If it was corrupted by the Jews, that happened either before the age of Christ or after it. Not before: and this can be shown, leaving aside the testimonies of the Fathers, by this argument alone. If the Hebrew edition had been corrupted by the Jews, Christ would not have passed over that crime in his coming. But nowhere do we read that Christ charged the Jews with this, that the Hebrew edition had been corrupted by them; rather we read that he sent them back to this very edition which they had in their hands. Search the Scriptures, he says. John 5.39. Nor can it have been corrupted after the age of Christ, which can be shown by this argument alone, apart from the testimonies of the Fathers: the Jews could not have corrupted all the Hebrew copies, even if they had most wished to, since most of them were in the hands of Christians. From this it follows that if the Hebrew edition was corrupted neither before nor after the age of Christ, it was not corrupted at all. But perhaps they will say that it was corrupted by the Jews after the times of Augustine and Jerome? I reply: in what places, I ask? In those five which Bellarmine brought forward? But we have already shown that in the time of Jerome, and before Jerome, they were read as they are read today. Therefore the Hebrew edition remains pure in every respect, and so is the only authentic edition of the Old Testament.

units.la: De editione graeca Novi Testamenti.
units.tr: On the Greek edition of the New Testament.

units.la: CAP. 19.
units.tr: CHAPTER 19.

units.la: CVM plures sint novi Testamenti editiones, nos ex omnibus dicimus authenticam esse graecam, id quod hoc initio sumpto demonstrabimus. 1. In adventu Christi & tempore Apostolorum inter linguas Gentium graeca fuit praestantissima. 2. Ut praestantissima, ita celeberrima & vulgatissima: nam etsi tum longissime patuerit Romanum imperium, non tamen longissime patuit lingua Romana, hoc est, Latina, teste Cicerone in oratione pro Archia Poeta. 3. Graeca lingua conscripta est Idololatria Gentium, & tota philosophia Graecorum. His rationibus aliisque praerogativis adductus Dominus, quo tempore visum est ei Evangelium suum ex angustiis Iudeae in campum latiorem educere; his, inquam, rationibus ac praerogativis adductus, voluit Evangelium suum graece scribi potissimum.
units.tr: Since there are several editions of the New Testament, we say that the Greek is the authentic one of them all, and we will demonstrate this from the following starting points. (1) At the coming of Christ and in the time of the Apostles, Greek was the most excellent of the languages of the Gentiles. (2) As it was the most excellent, so it was also the most widely known and used. For although the Roman empire then extended very far, the Roman language, that is Latin, did not extend nearly as far, as Cicero testifies in his speech for the poet Archias. (3) The idolatry of the Gentiles and the whole philosophy of the Greeks were written in Greek.
