Moved by these reasons and other advantages, the Lord, at the time when he saw fit to lead his Gospel out of the narrow confines of Judea into a wider field, chose, I say, moved by these reasons and advantages, that his Gospel should be written chiefly in Greek.

units.la: Scriptores autem erant partim Apostoli, partim Evangelistae, qui omnes graece primum scripserunt, si forte Matthaeum excipias, & Scriptorem Epistolae ad Hebraeos: nam de Matthaeo, ut dicam primum, Athanasius in Synopsi sua testatur eum primum hebraice scripsisse. fisse: idem dicit Irenæus lib. 3. idem Nazian‐ zenus in carmine: idem Hieronymus in præ‐satione in 4. Evangelistas ad Damafum. Hie‐ronymus in Catalogo in Matthæo scripsit suâ ætate editionem hebraicam asservari in bib‐ liotheca Cæsariensi, quam Pamphilus Mar‐ tyr exstruxerat. Athanasius dicit hebraicam Matthæi editionem græce redditam à Iacobo Apostolo, alij Iohanni Apostolo, alij ipsi Mat‐ thæo versionem tribuunt. Hæc sententia est Patrum, quæ non satis firmis præsidijs muni‐ ta est: Nam quo tempore vixit Christus cum Apostolis suis Iudæi omnes loquuti sunt Sy‐ riacè, hoc est, lingua confusa, & mixta ex He‐ braica & Chaldaica. Ergo si voluisset Matthæ‐ us alia lingua quàm Græca scribere, scripsisset Syriacè potissimùm: in qua sententia sunt e‐ tiam Papistæ quidam nostri temporis. Quam‐ obrem incertum est an Hebraicè, an Syriacè, an Græcè primùm scripserit Matthæus: Pro‐ babile tamen magis est eum græce primùm scripsisse, cum ea lingua & Iudæis non fuerit incognita, & alij Apostoli ea primùm scrip‐ serint, non solùm omnibus promiscuè Iudæis & Gentibus, sed etiam Iudæis peculiariter. Vtut est, græca Matthæi editio, quam habe‐ mus in manibus, authentica est, vtpote vi‐ ventibus adhuc Apostolis & scripta & comprobata: Nam quod ad editionem hebraicam, si quæ fuit ea, nunc nusquam est. Et hoc exemplar hebraicum quod vulgo habetur, genuinum non est.
units.tr: The writers were partly Apostles and partly Evangelists, and all of them first wrote in Greek, except perhaps Matthew and the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews. As for Matthew, to take him first: Athanasius, in his Synopsis, testifies that he first wrote in Hebrew. Irenaeus says the same in book 3, Gregory Nazianzen in a poem, and Jerome in his preface to the four Evangelists addressed to Damasus. Jerome, in the Catalogue, under Matthew, wrote that in his own day a Hebrew edition was kept in the library at Caesarea, which Pamphilus the Martyr had built up. Athanasius says that the Hebrew edition of Matthew was translated into Greek by the Apostle James; others attribute the translation to the Apostle John, others to Matthew himself. This is the opinion of the Fathers, but it is not supported by very firm proofs. For at the time when Christ lived with his Apostles, all the Jews spoke Syriac, that is, a confused language mixed from Hebrew and Chaldean. Therefore, if Matthew had wished to write in some language other than Greek, he would have written chiefly in Syriac; some Papists of our own time also hold this view. Hence it is uncertain whether Matthew first wrote in Hebrew, in Syriac, or in Greek. It is nevertheless more probable that he first wrote in Greek, since that language was not unknown to the Jews, and the other Apostles first wrote in it, not only for Jews and Gentiles alike but also for the Jews in particular. However that may be, the Greek edition of Matthew which we have in hand is authentic, since it was written and approved while the Apostles were still living. As for a Hebrew edition, if there ever was one, it is now nowhere to be found. And the Hebrew copy that is commonly held is not genuine.

units.la: De Epistola ad Hebrꝛos Hieronymus in Catalogo, in Paulo, testatur primùm hebraicè scriptam, deinde versam græcè vel à Barnaba, vel à Luca, vel à Clemente: sed incerta est res, & magis probabile est eam Epistolam jam primùm græcè scriptam esse. Vt ut est hæc græca quam habemus editio hujus Epistolæ authentica est.
units.tr: Concerning the Epistle to the Hebrews, Jerome in the Catalogue, under Paul, testifies that it was first written in Hebrew and then translated into Greek, either by Barnabas, or by Luke, or by Clement. But the matter is uncertain, and it is more probable that this Epistle was first written in Greek. However that may be, the Greek edition of this Epistle which we have is authentic.

units.la: Iam Novum Testamentum græcè scriptum ab Apostolis & Evangelistis, admirabili Dei providentia conservatum est, etiam in medijs persequutionibus & hæresibus ad nostra usque tempora, & omni ætate à viris piis & orthodoxis, à depravatione hæreticorum vindicata; adeò vt purissima venerit in manus nostras. His positis sic paucis argumentor. Ea editio Novi Testamenti quæ scripta est lingua omnium præstantissima, & primùm ac originaliter scripta ea lingua, vtpote græca, & omnium ætate in puritate est conservata, ea, inquam, pro authentica haberi debet ab omnibus. At talis est ista græca Novi Testamenti editio : Ergo.
units.tr: Now the New Testament, written in Greek by the Apostles and Evangelists, has been preserved by the wonderful providence of God, even amid persecutions and heresies, down to our own times. In every age it has been vindicated by pious and orthodox men against the corruption of heretics, so that it has come into our hands in the most pure state. Having set this down, I argue briefly as follows. That edition of the New Testament which was written in the most excellent of languages, and first and originally written in that language, namely Greek, and has been preserved in purity in every age, that edition, I say, ought to be held authentic by everyone. But this Greek edition of the New Testament is such. Therefore it is authentic.

units.la: Adversarij excipiunt tantùm adversus puritatem: Nam etsi ex ijs recentiores & doctiores, vt Bellarminus, non dicant omninò corruptam esse editionem Novi Testamenti græcam, vt alij sunt calumniati, tamen sic puram fatentur, vt authentica esse non possit, cum aliquot in locis sit corrupta. Bellarminus nominatim septem in medium affert loca, quibus conatur offendere corrupta esse, ac proinde non authenticam, hanc editionem græcam.
units.tr: Our opponents object only to its purity. For although the more recent and learned among them, such as Bellarmine, do not say that the Greek edition of the New Testament is wholly corrupt, as others have slanderously alleged, yet they admit it to be so far pure that it cannot be authentic, since it is corrupt in some places. Bellarmine names seven passages, by which he tries to show that this Greek edition is corrupt and therefore not authentic.

units.la: Primus est. 1. Cor. 15. 47. ὁ πρῶτος ἄνθρωπος ἐκ γῆς χοϊκός, ὁ δεύτερος ἄνθρωπος ὁ κύριος ἐξ οὐρανοῦ. Primus homo ex terra terrenus, secundus homo Dominus e cælo. At in Latina vulgata legitur, secundus e cælo cælestis, quæ lectio est approbata: Ergo græca editio corrupta est & non authentica. Respondeo. 1. Etsi sic legatur vt in græca editione legitur, sensus tamen bonus & orthodoxus, & idem cum eo qui est ex altera lectione, tantùm verbo, non re ipsa differens.
units.tr: The first is 1 Cor. 15:47: ὁ πρῶτος ἄνθρωπος ἐκ γῆς χοϊκός, ὁ δεύτερος ἄνθρωπος ὁ κύριος ἐξ οὐρανοῦ. The first man is of the earth, earthy; the second man is the Lord from heaven. But in the Latin Vulgate it is read, the second man from heaven is heavenly, and this reading is approved. Therefore the Greek edition is corrupt and not authentic. I answer: (1) even if it is read as it is in the Greek edition, the sense is good and orthodox, and the same as that of the other reading, differing only in wording and not in the thing itself. (2) The Arabic and Syriac versions read it in this way. (3) The Fathers Chrysostom and Theophylact read it in this way. (4) Epiphanius, Haeresis 22, section 2, where he lists all the passages Marcion corrupted, does not mention this passage there. But, it is said, Tertullian in book 5 against Marcion testifies that Marcion corrupted and falsified this passage? I answer that in that book and place Tertullian reads this passage exactly as we do, the Lord from heaven, and points out a preceding passage as corrupted.

units.la: 2. Arabica & Syra versio sic legunt. 3. Patres, Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, sic legunt. 4. Epiphanius Hæresion 22. 2. vbi recenset omnia loca quæ corrupit Marcion, non ibi meminit huius loci. At, inquit, testatur Tertullianus lib. 5. contra Marcionem hunc locum à Marcione corruptum ac vitiatum esse? Respondeo eo libro ac loco plane similiter atque nos legit Tertullianus hunc locum: Dominus e caelo, praecedentem quendam vt corruptum obseruat.
units.tr: The second passage is 1 Cor. 7:33: ὁ δὲ γαμήσας μεριμνᾷ τὰ τοῦ κόσμου, πῶς ἀρέσει τῇ γυναικί, καὶ μεμέρισται [?] καὶ ἡ γυνὴ ἡ ἄγαμος καὶ ἡ παρθένος μεριμνᾷ τὰ τοῦ κυρίου &c. He who has married is anxious about the things of the world, how he may please his wife; and the wife and the virgin are divided. The unmarried woman is anxious about the things of the Lord, &c. This is the Greek reading. But in the Vulgate it is read thus: "He who is with a wife is anxious about the things of the world, how he may please his wife, and he is divided. But the unmarried woman and the virgin thinks about the things of the Lord, both in body and in spirit."

units.la: Secundus locus est, 1.Cor. 7. 33. ὁ δὲ γαμήσας μεριμνᾷ τὰ τοῦ κόσμου, πῶς ἀρέσει τῇ γυναικί, καὶ μεμέρισται [?] καὶ ἡ γυνὴ ἡ ἄγαμος καὶ ἡ παρθένος μεριμνᾷ τὰ τοῦ κυρίου &c. Qui uxore duxit curat quae sunt huius mundi, quomodo placeat uxori. Discreta sunt uxor & virgo: Innupta curat: &c. Haec lectio est graeca. Verum in vulgata sic legitur: Qui autem cum uxore est, solicitus est quae sunt mundi, quomodo placeat uxori & diuisus est: At mulier innupta & virgo cogitat quae Domini sunt & corpore & spiritu.
units.tr: Therefore the Greek edition here is corrupt, and so not authentic? I reply: first, the sense that comes from the Greek reading is not only orthodox but more elegant than the sense that comes from the reading approved by the Vulgate. Second, the Syriac version reads it in this way. Third, Theophylact, the Greek scholia, and Basil read it in this way. But, it is said, Jerome in book 1 against Jovinian writes that this reading is not the truth of the Apostles. Yet the same Jerome, against Helvidius and Eusebius, reads this passage as we do. Therefore, since he varies in his opinion, he is not a sufficiently reliable witness.

units.la: Ergo hic editio graeca est corrupta: Quare non authentica. Resp. Primo sensum qui est ex graeca lectione, non modo orthodoxum, sed illo qui est ex lectione quam approbat vulgata editio concinniorem esse. 2. Syra versio sic legit. 3. Theophylactus, Graeca Scholia, Basilius, sic legunt. At, inquit, Hieronymus lib. 1. contra Iovinianum scribit hanc lectionem non esse Apostolicae veritatis. At idem Hieronymus contra Helvidium & Eusebium sic legit hunc locu vt nos legimus. Quare cum variet sententiam non est testis satis idoneus.
units.tr: The third passage is Rom. 12:11: τῷ καιρῷ δουλεύοντες, serving the time; but the Old Latin reads τῷ Κυρίῳ, serving the Lord. Therefore... I answer: (1) even if it is read thus, the sense is true and orthodox. (2) The reading varies in different Greek codices: the interpreter of Origen, who reads Κυρίῳ, testifies to this, and he notes that in some books καιρῷ was read. Ambrose also testifies to this, since he reads καιρῷ, serving the times, and he attests that in some books Κυρίῳ was read. (3) The Syriac version, Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Basil read Κυρίῳ, which reading we also prefer more. Therefore our Beza translates it to the Lord.

units.la: Tertius locus est, Rom. 12. 11. τῳ καιρῳ δουλευοντες: at Vetus Latina legit τῳ Κυριῳ. Ergo. Resp. 1. Etsi sic legatur, sensum esse verum & orthodoxum. 2. Varia est lectio in variis codicibus graecis, teste interprete Origenis, qui legit Κυριῳ: Admonet interea in nonnullis libris lectum fuisse καιρῳ; teste etiam Ambrosio, qui legit καιρῳ, Tempori servientes: Testatur interea in aliquibus libris lectum fuisse Κυριῳ. 3. Syra versio, Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, Basilius, legunt Κυριῳ, quam etiam lectionem nos magis approbamus: Ideo Beza noster vertit Domino.
units.tr: The third passage is Rom. 12. 11., where the Greek reads [τῷ καιρῷ δουλεύοντες], but the Old Latin version reads [τῷ Κυρίῳ], "serving the Lord." Therefore: Answer: (1) Even if it is read that way, the sense is true and orthodox. (2) The reading varies among the Greek manuscripts. The interpreter of Origen, who reads [τῷ Κυρίῳ], testifies to this, and he also notes that in some books [τῷ καιρῷ] was read. Ambrose also testifies to it: he reads [τῷ καιρῷ], rendering it serving the times, and he attests that in some books [τῷ Κυρίῳ] was read. (3) The Syriac version, Chrysostom, Theophylact and Basil all read [τῷ Κυρίῳ]. We also prefer this reading, and so our Beza translates it the Lord.

units.la: Quartus locus est Iohan. 8. vbi capitis principio in multis graecis libris desideratur tota illa historia Adulterae, quam vulgata editio habet, & Ecclesia approbat vt Canonicam. Resp. 1. Graecos nostros codices, quos nos pro authenticis habemus, habere hanc historiam, & Ecclesiam nostram eandem recipere.
units.tr: The fourth passage is Iohan. 8., where at the beginning of the chapter many Greek books lack the whole story of the adulteress, which the Vulgate edition contains and the Church accepts as canonical. Answer: (1) Our Greek manuscripts, which we hold to be authentic, contain this story, and our Church receives it in the same way.

units.la: 2. Non tamen dissimulandum est huic fuisse contradictum, & Syra versio non habet eam.
units.tr: 2. Yet it must not be concealed that this has been contradicted, and the Syriac version does not contain it.

units.la: Quintus locus est, Marc. 16. vbi in multis graecis codicibus totum illud caput desideratur, quod in vulgata editione habetur: Ergo. Resp. 1. Et omnes Graecos nostros libros quos nos authenticos ducimus, hoc caput habere, & Ecclesias nostras ipsum recipere tanquam Canonicum. 2. Hieronymus alicubi movit suspitionem de eo, sed frustrà.
units.tr: The fifth passage is Mark 16, where in many Greek manuscripts the whole chapter is missing, though it is found in the Vulgate edition. Therefore: (1) All our Greek books, which we regard as authentic, contain this chapter, and our churches receive it as canonical. (2) Jerome somewhere raised suspicion about it, but in vain.

units.la: Sextus locus est, 1.Ioan.7. vbi versus septimus, qui praeclarum de Trinitate continet testimonium, desideratur in multis graecis codicibus, cum habeatur ille versus in vulgata editione: Ergo. Resp. 1. nostri libri graeci, quos nos pro authenticis habemus, hunc versum continent, & nostra Ecclesia recipit. 2. non est dissimulandum tamè huic fuisse contradictum.
units.tr: The sixth passage is 1 John 7, where the seventh verse, which contains the notable testimony concerning the Trinity, is missing from many Greek manuscripts, though that verse is found in the Vulgate edition. Therefore: (1) our Greek books, which we regard as authentic, contain this verse, and our Church receives it. (2) It must nevertheless not be concealed that this has been contradicted.

units.la: Septimus locus est, Math.6.13. ὅτι σοῦ ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία, &c. Quia tuum est regnum, potentia, & gloria in secula, Amen. At hic locus non habetur in vulgata editione: Ergo. Respondet Valla hunc locum non adiectum graeco, sed detractum latino: et quid quaeso vel haereticum, vel non orthodoxum habet hic locus? Ex his sequitur non probare ex his locis Aduersarios graecam Novi Testamenti editionem corruptam esse, ac proinde non authenticam. Maneat ergo, ut hebraica Veteris, ita graeca Novi Testamenti editio, sola authentica.
units.tr: The seventh passage is Matthew 6:13, "for yours is the kingdom [ὅτι σοῦ ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία], the power and the glory for ever, Amen." But this passage is not found in the Vulgate edition. Valla replies that the passage was not added to the Greek but removed from the Latin. And what, I ask, does this passage contain that is heretical or unorthodox? From these examples it follows that the Adversaries do not prove from these passages that the Greek edition of the New Testament is corrupt and therefore not authentic. Let the Greek edition of the New Testament, then, remain the sole authentic one, just as the Hebrew is for the Old Testament.

units.la: De versionibus Veteris Testamenti.
units.tr: On the Versions of the Old Testament.

units.la: CAP. 20.
units.tr: CHAP. 20.

units.la: NUnc de versionibus Veteris & Novi Testamenti dicendum: ac primùm de verfionibus Veteris Testamenti. Vetus Testamentum primùm hebraicè scriptum, postea verlum est in varias linguas, imprimis Chaldaicam & Græcam. De Chaldaica versione dicemus primùm: deinde de Græca: Ac de Chaldaica dicemus 1. qualis fit versio Chaldaica. 2. à quibus facta. 3. cujus fit authoritatis. Quod ad primum. Chaldaica versio paraphraftica est, non ad verbum facta. Paraphrafin ipsi Targum vocant. Quod ad fecundum, Pentatenchon vertit R. Aquila, qui Onkelos dictus est ab ijs: Reliquos libros veteris Testamenti verterunt, partim R. Jonathan, partim R. Iofeph cæcus. Hi paulò ante Christum vel circa Christi tempora vixerunt. Quod ad tertium Chaldaica paraphrafis apud veteres magnæ fuit & celebritatis & authoritatis: imprimis verò illa Pentatenchi: nam quod ad reliquam paraphrafin Cardinalis quidam Ximenius in præfatione in Biblia Complutenfia, testis est eam Iudaicis fabulis,et Thalmudiftarum nugis conspersa esse. Atque hæc paucis de paraphrasi Chaldaica.
units.tr: Now we must speak of the versions of the Old and New Testaments, and first of the versions of the Old Testament. The Old Testament was first written in Hebrew and afterwards translated into various languages, above all Chaldee and Greek. We shall deal first with the Chaldee version, and then with the Greek. About the Chaldee version we shall consider three things: (1) what kind of version the Chaldee is; (2) by whom it was made; (3) what authority it has. As to the first: the Chaldee version is a paraphrase, not a word-for-word translation. The Jews themselves call the paraphrase the Targum. As to the second: Rabbi Aquila translated the Pentateuch, and he was called Onkelos by them. The remaining books of the Old Testament were translated partly by Rabbi Jonathan and partly by Rabbi Joseph the blind. These men lived shortly before Christ or around the time of Christ. As to the third: the Chaldee paraphrase was held in great esteem and authority among the ancients, especially that of the Pentateuch. As for the rest of the paraphrase, the Cardinal Ximenes, in his preface to the Complutensian Bible, bears witness that it is full of Jewish fables and the trifles of the Talmudists. So much, briefly, about the Chaldee paraphrase.

units.la: Nunc de græca versione Veteris Testamenti agendum. Græca versio veteris Testamenti varia fuit. Quidam versiones græcas novem numerant. Inter eas & prima & celeberrima fuit ea quam septuaginta duo seniores iussu Ptolemei Philadelphi fecerunt: nam quod Clemens Alexandrinus libro primo Stromatum scribat, multo ante Scripturam græcè versam, & à Platone lectam fuisse, non est probabile. Neque enim vel Plato, vel Pythagorici sacras literas vnquam viderunt. De versione itaque ista Septuaginta interpretum dicemus: quæ autem dicemus revocabimus doctrinæ gratia ad certas aliquot quæstiones, nempè, sex numero: Prima est, An fuerit verfio græca facta à Septuaginta duobus interpretibus. 2. Si fuerit, quando facta. 3. Quorum librorum fuerit. 4. Quomodò facta. 5. Quanta eius authoritas. 6. An hæc fit germana versio Septuaginta duorum interpretum quam nos habemus in manibus.
units.tr: Now we must deal with the Greek version of the Old Testament. The Greek version of the Old Testament was of various kinds. Some count nine Greek versions. Among them, the first and most celebrated was that which the seventy-two elders made at the command of Ptolemy Philadelphus. For it is not probable, as Clement of Alexandria writes in the first book of the Stromata, that the Scripture had been translated into Greek long before and read by Plato. Neither Plato nor the Pythagoreans ever saw the holy writings. We shall therefore speak of that version of the Seventy interpreters. But, for the sake of teaching, we shall bring what we say back to certain questions, namely six in number: (1) Was there a Greek version made by the seventy-two interpreters? (2) If so, when was it made? (3) Of which books was it made? (4) How was it made? (5) How great is its authority? (6) Is this the genuine version of the seventy-two interpreters which we have in our hands?

units.la: Quod ad quæstionem primam, facilis est responsio: Non enim dubium est quin versio græca facta fuerit à Septuaginta duobus interpretibus, cum id tota antiquitas testetur. Testes sunt Epiphanius in libro de mensuris & ponderibus, Eusebius de Præparatione Evangelica, uangelica, Iuftinus Martyr in dialogo cum Tryphone,alijque multi.
units.tr: As to the first question, the answer is easy. There is no doubt that the Greek version was made by the seventy-two interpreters, since all antiquity bears witness to it. Witnesses are Epiphanius in his book on weights and measures, Eusebius in his Preparation for the Gospel, Justin Martyr in his dialogue with Trypho, and many others.

units.la: Quod ad quæstionem secundam, facilis quoque ad eam est responsio: Nam regnante Ptolemæo Philadelpho,eoq; jubente,factam esse versionem illam græcam testatur omnes: Iofephus, Philo, Athanasius in Synopsi,Epiphanius, Tertullianus, Aristæus in historia sua de hac ipsa re,alijque multi.
units.tr: As to the second question, the answer is equally easy. For all bear witness that this Greek version was made in the reign of Ptolemy Philadelphus, at his command: Josephus, Philo, Athanasius in his Synopsis, Epiphanius, Tertullian, Aristeas in his account of this very matter, and many others.

units.la: Quod ad tertiam quæstionē de libris versis, responsio non tam facilis est: quidam enim ab ijs versam esse legem duntaxat arbitrantur; Legem autem intelligunt Pentateuchon.In hac sententia fuit Iofephus in proœmio Antiquitatū, Hieronymus videtur quoque eò propendere. Alij vniversam Scripturam ab ijs versam esse testantur: atque hæc sententia verior est: primùm enim Ptolemæus Rex non fuisset contentus sola versione Pentateuchi 2. Apostoli Christi vsi sunt versione græca in citandis testimonijs ex Prophetis: At temporibus Apostolorum non suit alia versio quàm Septuaginta. 3. Nullum fuisset miraculum in celeritate hujus versionis, si tantū Pentateuchon fuisset versum, quæ nemo suit septuaginta duorum dierum spatio absoluta: Tradunt enim versionem hanc miraculosam fuisse. 4. Testes hujus rei sunt ex Patribus, ut Chrysostomus, Theodoretus. Quare verior est haec sententia, totius veteris Scripturae versionem ab ijs factam esse.
units.tr: The third question, about which books were translated, does not have so easy an answer. For some think that only the Law was translated by them, and by the Law they mean the Pentateuch. Josephus held this view in the preface to his Antiquities, and Jerome also seems to lean that way. Others testify that the whole of Scripture was translated by them, and this view is more true. For: (1) King Ptolemy would not have been content with a version of the Pentateuch alone. (2) The apostles of Christ used the Greek version when citing testimonies from the Prophets, and in the time of the apostles there was no other version than the Septuagint. (3) There would have been no miracle in the speed of this version if only the Pentateuch had been translated, since no one could finish that in the space of seventy-two days; for they report that this translation was miraculous. (4) Witnesses to this fact among the Fathers are Chrysostom and Theodoret. Therefore this view is the more true, that the version of the whole of the Old Testament Scripture was made by them.

units.la: Quod ad quaestionem de modo versionis, hunc fuisse modum narrat; Septuaginta duo senes ex tribubus Israel utriusque linguae hebraicae & graecae peritissimi, jussu Ptolemaei Philadelphi, miraculosa celeritate, nempe 72. dierum spatio, admirabili consensione, ad Phanum Ægypti, versionem hanc absolverunt: Alij singulos seorsim sedibus disclusos, alij binos; alij omnes confertim confidentes uno loco, & operas conferentes; versionem hanc confecisse tradunt. Miraculosam igitur fuisse versionem narrant, sed miracula haec quae dicunt fuisse ad amplificandam hujus versionis authoritatem, fidem non habent.
units.tr: As to the question about the manner of the translation, they relate that it was done in this way: the seventy-two elders from the tribes of Israel, most skilled in both the Hebrew and the Greek languages, at the command of Ptolemy Philadelphus, completed this version with miraculous speed, namely in the space of seventy-two days, with admirable agreement, at Pharos in Egypt. Some report that they were each shut up separately in their own rooms, others two by two, others all sitting together in one place and comparing their work, that they made this version. They therefore relate that the translation was miraculous, but they are not to be believed in the miracles they tell, which, they say, were there to magnify the authority of this version.

units.la: Quod ad quaestionem quintam, de authoritate hujus versionis, ad eam varie respondet: Nam quidam plus aequo huic tribuunt. Epiphanius in libro de mensuris & ponderibus, non interpretes tantum dicit fuisse, sed prope Prophetas. Augustinus nimius est in laude hujus interpretationis, divina dispensatione factam dicit, θεόπνευστον putat. Alij non tantum ei tribuunt: Hieronymus in praefatione in Pentatenchon interpretes eos non vates fuisse dicit contra Epiphanium. Idem in commentarijs saepe eam reprehendit non tantum vt corruptam, sed in se vitiosam, quod profecto non fecisset si Σεπτουαγινταinterpretes putasset. Quantacunque sit ejus authoritas, profecto non est alia quam interpretationis: neque Σεπτουαγινταaut Scripturae parem eam fatemur.
units.tr: As to the fifth question, about the authority of this version, answers vary. For some ascribe to it more than is fair. Epiphanius, in his book on weights and measures, says that the translators were not only interpreters but almost prophets. Augustine is excessive in praising this translation: he says it was made by divine arrangement and thinks it [θεόπνευστον] divinely inspired. Others do not grant it even this much. Jerome, in the preface to the Pentateuch, says that those translators were not prophets, contrary to Epiphanius. The same Jerome often finds fault with it in his commentaries, not only as corrupt but as faulty in itself, which he certainly would not have done if he had thought it the work of the Seventy. However great its authority may be, it is certainly no more than that of a translation; we do not admit that it is equal to the Septuagint or to Scripture.

units.la: Quod ad quaestionem sextam, quidam putant superesse adhuc veterem illam versionem Septuaginta; sed corruptam adeo & vitiatam, vt non sit tutum codices vel hebraicos vel latinos ex ea emendare. Bellarminus ita sentit. Alij interijsse putant veterem illam versionem 72. interpretum: hanc autem quam nos habemus mixtam esse, corruptam ac vitiatam. Corruptam esse ac vitiatam inductione quadam facta locorum corruptorum ostendunt. Primo, liber Graecus annos a mundo condito ad diluvium numerat 2242. vt apud Augustinum, Eusebium, & Nicephorum in Chronologia legitur: Hebraica autem veritas non plures numerat quam 1656. Ergo numerum Hebraicum Graecus superat annis 586. Secundo, a diluvio ad Abrahamum juxta 72. interpretes anni sunt 1032. Sin veritatem hebraicam consulas, non sunt plures quam
units.tr: As to the sixth question, some think that the old version of the Seventy still survives, but so corrupted and vitiated that it is not safe to correct either Hebrew or Latin codices from it. Bellarmine thinks so. Others think that the old version of the seventy-two interpreters has perished, and that the one we have is mixed and corrupt and vitiated. They show by a certain induction of corrupt passages that it is corrupt and vitiated. First, the Greek book counts 2242 years from the creation of the world to the flood, as is read in Augustine, Eusebius, and Nicephorus in their Chronology; but the Hebrew truth counts no more than 1656. So the Greek exceeds the Hebrew number by 586 years. Second, according to the seventy-two interpreters, the years from the flood to Abraham are 1032; but if you consult the Hebrew truth, they are no more than

units.la: 292. Ita sunt in Græco codice 790. anni plures quam in Hebraico. Tertiò in Græco codice Adam dicitur vixisse annos 230. in nonnullis exemplaribus. 330. cum Sethum genuisset: Hebræus vero codex testatur Sethum esse genitum cum Adamus 130. annos vixisset. Quartò in græco codice Methusalem vixit annos 14. post diluvium, quod ridiculum est: nam ubi vixit? & ubi conservatus est ab aquis? An in arca? At octo tantum animæ ingressæ sunt arcam, in quibus non numeratur Methusalem. Hebræus liber longè verius de annis ac ætate Methusalem scripsit. Unde illum esse eodem anno mortuum quo tota terra diluvio oppressa est colligimus, anno nempe mundi 1656. Quintò in Iona græcus codex post tertium diem exitium Ninivitis denunciat: Adhuc tres dies & Ninive destruetur. At in Hebræo libro exitium Ninivitis non nisi post 40. dies denunciatur. Adhuc quadraginta dies & Ninive destruetur. Ex his videmus magnum esse discrimen inter numeros græcos & hebræos: Omnes autem fatentur numeros hebraicos veros esse. Augustinus libro de civitate Dei 18. in hac numerorum mutatione nescio quid mysterij confinxit, ut authoritatem interpretationis 72. tueretur, quam tamen in loco de Methufalem defendere non potuit. Hieronymus autem magis candide & aperte à Septuaginta in numeris erratum esse scripsit. Ex his aliisque infinitis locis vitiosis, concludimus non esse hanc, quam habemus versionem græcam, illam quam fecerunt 72. senes Iudæi; vel si fit, ita foedatam esse ut nunc perexiguæ sit authoritatis.
units.tr: 292. Thus the Greek codex has 790 years more than the Hebrew. Third, in the Greek codex Adam is said to have lived 230 years, and in some copies 330, when he had begotten Seth; but the Hebrew codex testifies that Seth was born when Adam had lived 130 years. Fourth, in the Greek codex Methuselah lived 14 years after the flood, which is ridiculous: for where did he live, and where was he preserved from the waters? In the ark? But only eight souls entered the ark, and Methuselah is not counted among them. The Hebrew book has written far more truly about the years and age of Methuselah. Hence we gather that he died in the same year that the whole earth was overwhelmed by the flood, namely in the year of the world 1656. Fifth, in Jonah the Greek codex announces the destruction of the Ninevites after the third day: Yet three days, and Nineveh shall be destroyed. But in the Hebrew book the destruction of the Ninevites is announced only after forty days: Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be destroyed. From these we see that there is a great difference between the Greek and Hebrew numbers, yet all admit that the Hebrew numbers are true. Augustine, in book eighteen of the City of God, invented I know not what mystery in this change of numbers, so that he might defend the authority of the translation of the Seventy; yet he could not defend it in the passage about Methuselah. Jerome, however, more candidly and openly wrote that the Septuagint erred in the numbers. From these and countless other faulty passages we conclude that the Greek version we have is not that which the seventy-two Jewish elders made; or, if it is, it has been so disfigured that it now has very little authority.

units.la: Hactenus de editione græca 72. interpretum, nunc de alijs versionibus græcis, quæ factæ fuerunt postquam jam Evangelium longe latèq; per orbem terrarum esset diffusum. Octo autem numerantur. Prima fuit Aquilæ cujusdam Synopensis, imperante Adriano facta, ut testis est Epiphanius. Hic Aquila primum gentilis fuit; deinde ad Christianos transfivit, & baptizatus est: Postremo cum propter nimium Iudiciariæ Astrologiæ studium reprehensus esset, tandemque ejectus ex Ecclesia, ad Iudæos descivit; apud Iudæos dum ageret linguam literasque hebrææs didicit, & Scripturam veteris Testamenti ex hebræo in græcum transtulit: sed animo pravo perversoque, ut testis est Theodoretus, quò nimirum testimonia quæ doctrinam Christi confirmant obscuraret, & apostasiæ suæ sucum faceret.
units.tr: So much for the Greek edition of the Seventy translators. Now for the other Greek versions, which were made after the Gospel had already spread widely through the world. Eight are counted. The first was made by a certain Aquila of Sinope under the emperor Hadrian, as Epiphanius attests. Aquila was at first a Gentile; then he went over to the Christians and was baptized. Finally, he was rebuked for his excessive devotion to judicial astrology and at last expelled from the Church, and he then defected to the Jews. Among the Jews he learned the Hebrew language and letters, and he translated the Scripture of the Old Testament from the Hebrew into Greek. But he did so with a wicked and perverse mind, as Theodoret attests, plainly in order to obscure the testimonies that confirm the doctrine of Christ and to make a sauce of his apostasy.

units.la: Post hanc Aquilæ versionem, fuit versio Theodotionis cujusdam, imperante Commodo; vt idem Epiphanius testis est. Hic homo Ponticus fuit, ex secta Marcionis hæretici, postmodùm secta sua improbata, omnique Religione Christiana abjurata, ad Iudæos defecit, linguam Hebraicam didicit, Scripturam veteris Testamenti ex hebræo in græcum transtulit; sed perverso animo & fide mala, teste eodem Theodoreto, ad consutationem sectæ suæ.
units.tr: After Aquila's version came the version of a certain Theodotion, under the emperor Commodus, as the same Epiphanius attests. This man was a native of Pontus, of the sect of the heretic Marcion. Later, when his sect had been condemned and he had renounced every Christian religion, he deserted to the Jews, learned the Hebrew language, and translated the Scripture of the Old Testament from Hebrew into Greek. But, as the same Theodoret testifies, he did so with a perverse mind and bad faith, to refute his own sect.

units.la: Post versionem Theodotionis fuit versio græca Symmachi cujusdam, imperante Severo Augusto, vt testis est Epiphanius: hic Samaritanus fuit genere, & cum principatum apud suos non obtineret, Iudæis se adjunxit, & secundò circumcisus est; quo autem modo id fieri potuerit idem Epiphanius docet ex 1. Cor. 7. nempè, attracto præputio post primam Circumcisionem, vt esset secundæ Circumcisionis materia. Hic Scripturam veteris Testamenti ex hebræo in græcum transtulit, sed mala fide, teste Theodoreto, in confutationem nimirum Samaritanorum Gentilium suorum.
units.tr: After Theodotion's version came the Greek version of a certain Symmachus, under the emperor Severus Augustus, as Epiphanius attests. This man was a Samaritan by birth, and when he did not gain standing among his own people, he joined the Jews, and he was circumcised a second time. Epiphanius explains how this could have happened from 1 Cor. 7: namely, by drawing back the foreskin after the first circumcision, so that there would be material for a second circumcision. He translated the Scripture of the Old Testament from Hebrew into Greek, but with bad faith, as Theodoret attests, plainly to refute the Samaritans, his own Gentiles.

units.la: Post hanc versionem Symmachi fuerunt aliæ duæ <bl>ἑρμηνείαι</bl>, quarum authores non nominantur: prior fuit inventa apud Hiericho in dolijs sub Imperatore Caracalla. Posterior reperta est apud Nicopolin Aquilonarem sub Imperatore Alexandro Mammæç filioj Testes Epiphanius, Theodoretus, &alij.
units.tr: After Symmachus's version there were two other interpretations [ἑρμηνείαι], whose authors are not named. The first was found at Jericho in jars under the emperor Caracalla. The second was discovered at Nicopolis in the north under the emperor Alexander, son of Mammaea. Epiphanius, Theodoret and others attest this.

units.la: Post hos fuit Origenes, qui vixit an. 261. sub Valeriano & Galieno princip. Origenes in aliorum qui ante ipsum fuerunt versionibus conferendis comparandisq; incredibiliter elaboravit. Nam versiones quatuor, nempe 1. Aquilæ. 2. Symmachi. 3. Septuaginta. 4. Theodotionis, in vnum volumen compegit, & quatuor columnis distinxit; & hæc erant Origenis τετραπλα. Deinde ad has quatuor columnas adjecit feriem hebraici textus duplicem, vnam hebraicis, altera græcis characteribus exaratam, & hæc erant Origenis ἑξαπλα. Postremo ad has columnas sex adjunxit ἀνωνυμως illas quas diximus editiones, & hæc erant Origenis ὀκταπλα, opus laboriosum, divivum, & maximo Ecclesiæ malo amissum. Origenes in libris suis notavit ἀστερισκους, ὀβελους, λημνισκους, & υπολημνισκους, prout editionum varia ac multiplex ratio postulabat. Amissionem hujus operis quidam vir pius & doctus deflevit in hæc verba. Cujus, inquit, operis jactura deplorare possumus, compenfare non possumus.
units.tr: After these came Origen, who lived in the year 261, under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus. Origen laboured incredibly hard in collating and comparing the versions made before his time. For he gathered four versions into one volume, namely (1) Aquila's, (2) Symmachus's, (3) the Septuagint's, and (4) Theodotion's, and set them out in four columns; and these were Origen's Tetrapla [τετραπλα]. Then to these four columns he added a double series of the Hebrew text, one written in Hebrew characters and the other in Greek characters; and these were Origen's Hexapla [ἑξαπλα]. Finally, to these columns he added six anonymous editions, which we have mentioned, and these were Origen's Octapla [ὀκταπλα], a laborious and divine work, lost to the great harm of the Church. In his books Origen marked asterisks, obeli, lemniscoi and hypolemniscoi [ἀστερισκους, ὀβελους, λημνισκους, υπολημνισκους], as the varied and manifold character of the editions required. A certain godly and learned man lamented the loss of this work in these words: "We can deplore the loss of this work, but we cannot make it good."

units.la: Post Origenem fuit Luciani cujusdâ versio circa tempora Diocletiani. Hic fuit Ecclesiæ Antiochenæ Presbyter & Martyr: hujus editionis, vt scriptum legimus, exemplar ipsius Martyris manu exaratum inventum suit Nicomediæ in arce quadam marmorea. Hieronymus in Catalogo scribit ipsius ætate fuisse exemplaria græca quæ Lucianea sunt appellata.
units.tr: After Origen there was a version of a certain Lucian, around the time of Diocletian. He was a presbyter and martyr of the Church of Antioch. As we read, a copy of this edition, written out by the martyr's own hand, was found at Nicomedia in a marble citadel. Jerome writes in his Catalogue that in his own time there were Greek copies that were called Lucianic.

units.la: Denique post hanc Luciani versionem fuit editio Hesychij cujusdam qui interpretationem 72. interpretum emendavit,& Ecclesijs Ægypti tradidit. Atq; hæc hactenus de octo versionibus græcis quæ post Christum exiterunt, quæ omnes perierunt; nisi quod Papistæ Theodotionis quædam retineant. Dan. 13.& 14. cap. et fragmentum impij Theodotionis, hæretici primùm, deinde apostatæ, pro Canonica Scriptura hodierno die vendunt. Nam quod ad græcam hanc quæ extat editionem Veteris Testamenti, ea ex illis veteribus nulla pura est, sed mixta & corrupta, vt suprà observavimus. Atque hæc de versionibus veteris Testamenti, primùm Chaldæa paraphrastica: deinde græcis varijs.
units.tr: Finally, after this version of Lucian there was the edition of a certain Hesychius, who emended the translation of the Seventy and handed it on to the churches of Egypt. So much for the eight Greek versions that appeared after Christ, all of which have perished, except that the Papists still retain some of Theodotion's work. They sell Dan. 13 and 14, and a fragment of the impious Theodotion, a heretic first and then an apostate, as canonical Scripture to this day. As for the Greek edition of the Old Testament that now exists, none of it is pure from those ancient versions, but it is mixed and corrupted, as we observed above. So much for the versions of the Old Testament: first the Chaldee paraphrase, then the various Greek ones.

units.la: De versione Noui Testamenti Syra.
units.tr: On the Syriac version of the New Testament.

units.la: CAP. 21.
units.tr: CHAP. 21.

units.la: NVnc veniendum ad versionem novi Teftamenti. Novum Testamentum primùm græcè conscriptum, versum est in Syram linguam, quæ ætate Christi & Apostolorum Iudeis popularis & vernacula fuit, tum propter diuturnam captivitatem Babylonicam, tum propter Assyriorum in Iudæam translationem. Syræ versionis quis author fuerit incertum est, quo etiam tempore facta non cognitum: Tremellius veritati prorsus consetaneum putat hanc versionem factam circa initia Ecclesiæ Christianæ, idque ab Apostolis vel Apostolorum discipulis. Venerandam ejus antiquitatem idem probat. 1. ex linguæ elegantia. 2. ex defectu certorum librorum & locorum novi Testamenti, qui reperitur in Syra versione, ut 2. Petri, Iohannis 2. & 3. Iacobi Epistolæ, Iudæ Epistolæ, Apocalypsis, historiæ adulteræ, quæ reperitur in initio capitis 8. Evangelij Iohannis. Ex hoc defectu colligit, quòd cum Syra versio fuerit ante hos libros receptos ab Ecclesia pro Canonicis, Syra verfio antiqua admodum fuerit. Fidelitatem Syræ versionis summam dicit sese conferendo linguam Syram cum lingua græca & originali. nali expertum esse, quam quidem experientiam alijs quibuscunq; visum erit has linguas inter se conferre permittit. Ex his sequitur Syram versionem & fuisse olim, & nunc esse, magnæ in Ecclesia authoritatis. Hactenus de veteris Testamenti Chaldaica & græcis versionibus varijs, & de novi Testamenti Syra.
units.tr: Now we must come to the version of the New Testament. The New Testament, first written in Greek, was translated into the Syriac language, which in the time of Christ and the Apostles was the native and vernacular tongue of the Jews, both because of the long Babylonian captivity and because of the transplanting of the Assyrians into Judea. The author of the Syriac version is uncertain, and the time when it was made is not known. Tremellius thinks that this version, made wholly in accord with the truth, was produced near the beginnings of the Christian Church, and by the Apostles or their disciples. The same writer argues for its venerable antiquity: (1) from the elegance of its language; (2) from the absence of certain books and passages of the New Testament that is found in the Syriac version, such as 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, James, Jude, Revelation, and the story of the adulteress found at the beginning of John chapter 8. From this absence he concludes that, since the Syriac version came before these books were received by the Church as canonical, the old Syriac version must be very ancient. He says that he has found the Syriac version to be of the highest fidelity by comparing the Syriac language with the Greek and the original, and he allows anyone else who wishes to test these languages against one another to do the same. It follows that the Syriac version both was of old and now is of great authority in the Church. So much for the Chaldee and various Greek versions of the Old Testament, and for the Syriac version of the New.

units.la: De Latinis versionibus utriusque Testamenti. CAP. II.
units.tr: On the Latin versions of both Testaments. CHAP. II.

units.la: NVnc de Latinis versionibus utriusque & veteris & novi Testamenti dicemus. Latinæ versiones Bibliorum valde multæ fuerunt. Testis Augustinus de doctrina Christiana, lib. 2. cap. 11. Hieronymus in proœmio in lib. Iosuæ, de tam varia ac multiplici versione latina conqueritur. Ex versionibus Latinis prima fuit Itala quædam: hanc Augustinus omnibus aliis anteponit, ut & verbis adstrictiorem, & sententijs magis perspicuam, lib. 2. de doctrina Christiana cap 15. Hæc non fuit illa Hieronymi versio: nam hanc illa Hieronymi versione multò antiquiorem suisse constat. Quo autem authore sit facta non est cognitum.
units.tr: Now we shall speak of the Latin versions of both the Old and the New Testament. The Latin versions of the Bible were very many. Augustine bears witness in De doctrina Christiana, book 2, chapter 11, and Jerome, in the preface to his book on Joshua, complains of the so varied and manifold Latin version. Of the Latin versions the first was a certain Italic one: Augustine places it above all the others, both as more closely bound to the words and as clearer in meaning (De doctrina Christiana, book 2, chapter 15). This was not that version of Jerome, for it is evident that it was much older than Jerome's version. By whom it was made, however, has not been known.

units.la: Post hanc Italam fuit versio Hieronymi: eam duplicem fuisse scribunt veteris Testamenti, priorem ex græca editione 72. interpretum in latinum, posteriorem ex hebræa veritate in latinum facta. Nam, quod ad novum Testamentum, Hieronymus dicitur non ipsum vertisse in latinum, sed veterem latinam emendasse: Testis est ipse Hieronymus pluribus in locis. Hæc Hieronymi editio cum primum prodijt, mox cœpit recipi in Ecclesia, & publice lectitari (Augustinus Epistola 10. ad Hieronymum scripta) Ita tamen ut non contemneretur vetus illa Itala: Nam teste Gregorio duæ hæ versiones, vetus illa Itala, & hæc Hieronymi nova, in Ecclesijs Latinis celeberrimæ fuerunt, & maximè usitatæ. Tandem omnes illæ versiones latinæ obscuriores ex manibus hominum effluxerunt, etiam illa Itala intercidit; reliqua fuit sola Hieronymi versio, si modò hæc sit merito dicenda Hieronymi versio, quam nos in manibus habemus, & quæ hodierno die circumfertur ipsius nomine: nam docti de eo magnopere ambigunt. Nunc itaque de hac, quæ vulgo dicitur, Hieronymi versione nobis est dicendum. Duo autem in universum de ea quæremus. Primum, quo authore sit facta: Secundum, quanta sit ejus authoritas.
units.tr: After this Italic version came the version of Jerome. They write that it was twofold in the Old Testament: the former made from the Greek edition of the seventy-two interpreters into Latin, the latter made into Latin from the Hebrew truth. As for the New Testament, Jerome is said not to have translated it himself into Latin, but to have emended the old Latin; Jerome himself is witness to this in many places. When this edition of Jerome first appeared, it soon began to be received in the Church and to be read publicly (Augustine, in his tenth letter, written to Jerome). Yet the old Italic was not despised; for, according to Gregory, these two versions, the old Italic and this new one of Jerome, were most famous and most in use in the Latin churches. At last all those Latin versions, being more obscure, slipped out of men's hands; even the Italic perished. The only one left was the version of Jerome, if indeed this is rightly to be called the version of Jerome which we have in our hands and which today goes about under his name; for learned men greatly doubt it. Now, therefore, we must speak of this version which is commonly called Jerome's. We shall ask two things about it in general: first, by whom it was made; second, what its authority is.

units.la: De authore hujus versionis latinæ variæ sunt hominum sententiæ: quidam tenent eam Hieronymi esse, et eam quidem puram & non mixtam: Ita sentiunt fere qui nunc sunt Papistæ, præsertim Iesuitæ. Alij non esse Hieronymi scribunt, vt Sanctes Pagninus in præfatione in interpretationem suam Bibliorum ad Clementem. 7. Pontificem, Paulus Fororsempronianus Episcopus, vt de Erasmo, Munstero, & alijs etiam pontificijs hominibus taceam. Alij Hieronymi quidem esse putarunt, sed non puram: In hac sententia fuit Ioan. Driedo, Sixtus Senensis; Bellarminus non valde videtur ab ea recedere, vt ex ipsius propositionibus & rationibus de hac re facile potest colligi. Nos non esse Hieronymi, neque puram, neque mixtam affirmamus, idq; hoc argumento demonstrabimus.
units.tr: Concerning the author of this Latin version opinions of men vary. Some hold that it is Jerome's, and indeed pure and unmixed; this is roughly the view of those who are now Papists, especially the Jesuits. Others write that it is not Jerome's, as Sanctes Pagninus does in the preface to his own translation of the Bible addressed to Pope Clement VII, and Paul, bishop of Fossombrone, not to mention Erasmus, Münster and other papal men. Others have thought it is indeed Jerome's, but not pure: John Driedo and Sixtus of Siena held this view; Bellarmine does not seem to depart much from it, as can easily be gathered from his propositions and arguments on this matter. We affirm that it is neither Jerome's, nor pure, nor mixed, and we shall demonstrate this by the following argument.

units.la: Hieronymus accurate translulit vetus Testamentum ex hebræo in latinum: At hæc vulgata editio non est accurata: Ergo non est Hieronymi. Propositio probatur. Hieronymus ipse multis in locis testatur versionem suam accuratam fuisse, vt præfatione in Pentateuchon, præfatione in libros Regum, præsatione in Psalterium ad Sophronium, quibus in locis testatur se nihil de hebræa veritate mutasse, & ad hebræos provocat qui testentur
units.tr: Jerome translated the Old Testament from Hebrew into Latin accurately. But this Vulgate edition is not accurate. Therefore it is not Jerome's. The proposition is proved as follows. Jerome himself testifies in many places that his version was accurate, as in the preface to the Pentateuch, the preface to the books of Kings, and the preface to the Psalter addressed to Sophronius, where he testifies that he had changed nothing from the Hebrew truth, and he appeals to the Hebrews to bear witness

units.la: 4 tur de fidelitate versionis suæ. Augustinus de Civitate Dei. lib. 18. cap 43. scribit Hebrœos ipsos fateri Hieronymi versionem veracem esse. Hispalensis Isidorus lib. 6. Etymol. cap. 5. versionem Hieronymi omnibus aliis præfert, vtpote & verborum tenaciorem, & sententiæ perspicuitate clariorem. Ergo, si istis credimus, Hieronymi versio accurata fuit. De propositione igitur hactenus, nunc ad as-sumptionem veniamus. At vulgata editio latina non est accurata, neque consentit cum hebraeo fonte, imò adeò dissentit ab eo, vt necesse sit alterutrum esse, vel hanc versionem latinam corruptissimam esse, vel hebræum fontem perturbatissimum; quod posterius non affirmat ipse Bellarminus, imò eos reprehendit qui id asseverant: & merito. Restat itaque vt summam istam dissensionem ostendamus. Id autem alia ratione fieri non potest nisi collatione facta vulgatæ huius versionis cum hebraeo fonte. Comparatio facienda est initio sumpto à libro Geneseos. Comparatio autem erit non omnium locorum dissentientium, cum infinita sunt, sed certorum aliquot selectorum, ex quibus facile erit conjecturam facere de reliquis. Vitia autem quæ conspicientur ex hac comparatione, non erunt vnius generis, sed partim erunt propter immutationem, partim propter defectum, partim denique propter redundantiam. His enim modis omnibus vitiata est editio vulgata latina. Meo judicio nō aliunde melius discetur hęc comparatio, quàm ex vulgata editione Latina emendata per Iohannem Benedictum theologum Parisiensem, ad quam nos, brevitatis studiosi, lectorem remittimus. Ex comparatione ista facta, videbis una eademque opera, & non esse Hieronymi, & non esse authenticam vulgatam hanc versionem latinam, ut non sit opus laborare in altera illa quæstione tractanda.
units.tr: to the faithfulness of his version. Augustine, in De civitate Dei, book 18, chapter 43, writes that the Hebrews themselves acknowledge that Jerome's version is true. Isidore of Seville, Etymologies, book 6, chapter 5, prefers Jerome's version to all others, as both more tenacious of the words and clearer in the perspicuity of its sense. Therefore, if we believe these men, Jerome's version was accurate. So much for the proposition; now let us come to the assumption. But the Vulgate Latin edition is not accurate, nor does it agree with the Hebrew source; indeed it so differs from it that one of two things must be true: either this Latin version is most corrupt, or the Hebrew source is most disordered. Bellarmine himself does not affirm the latter, indeed he rebukes those who assert it, and rightly so. It remains, therefore, that we show this great disagreement. This cannot be done in any other way than by collating this Vulgate version with the Hebrew source. The comparison is to be made beginning with the book of Genesis. The comparison will not be of all the disagreeing passages, since they are infinite, but of certain selected ones, from which it will be easy to form a conjecture about the rest. The faults which appear from this comparison will not be of one kind, but partly will arise from alteration, partly from omission, and partly finally from redundancy; for the Latin Vulgate edition is corrupted in all these ways. In my judgment this comparison can be learned nowhere better than from the Latin Vulgate edition emended by John Benedict, Parisian theologian, to which we refer the reader, being mindful of brevity. From the comparison made in this way you will see at one and the same time that this is neither Jerome's nor the authentic Latin version, so that there is no need to labour in that other question as well.

units.la: De versionibus vernaculis.
units.tr: On vernacular versions.

units.la: CAP. 23.
units.tr: CHAPTER 23.

units.la: NVnc restat ut dicamus de editionibus, sive versionibus vernaculis. Vernaculas voco eas, quæ factæ sunt in linguas vulgares & plebeias, ut sunt Germanica, Italica, Gallica, Anglica, Scotica, Hispanica, &c. De vernaculis versionibus tria quæremus. 1. An liceat Scripturas sacras vertere in linguas vernaculas. 2. An in linguis vernaculis sacra publica sint peragenda. 3. An populo fit permittenda lectio Scripturarum jam versarum in linguas vernaculas.
units.tr: Now it remains to speak of editions, or vernacular versions. I call vernacular those versions made into the common and popular tongues, such as German, Italian, French, English, Scottish, Spanish, and so on. Concerning vernacular versions we shall ask three things. 1. Whether it is lawful to translate the holy Scriptures into the vernacular tongues. 2. Whether public sacred services may be conducted in the vernacular tongues. 3. Whether the people may be allowed to read the Scriptures already translated into the vernacular tongues.

units.la: Ad primam quæstionem respondemus nos, licere quidem atque etiam expediens esse. Id aliquot argumentis demonstrabimus. Argumentum 1. Sacræ Scripturæ coram toto populo legendæ sunt: Ergo vertendæ in linguas vernaculas: secus enim sine fructu legerentur in Ecclesia. Probatur antecedens. Deut. 31. præcipit Dominus ut legantur libri Mosis omnibus promiscuè, viris, fæminis, parvulis, peregrinis. Ierem. 36. mandat Propheta Baruch o Scribæ ut librum ex ipsius ore exceptum legat coram toto populo. At dicet aliquis, præceptum hoc non fuit perpetuum, verùm temporarium? R. Imò perpetuum esse indicat finis, qui subjectus est præcepto. Deut. 31. Ut populus audiat, discat, timeatq; Iehovam. Finis hic perpetuus: quare lex perpetua: præsertim cum lectio Scripturarum sit ordinarium & necessarium medium, quo assequimur propositum hunc finem. Sic probato antecedente sequitur Scripturas esse vertendas in linguas vernaculas.
units.tr: To the first question we answer that it is not only lawful but even expedient. We shall demonstrate this by several arguments. Argument 1. The holy Scriptures are to be read before the whole people; therefore they are to be translated into the vernacular tongues, for otherwise they would be read in the Church to no profit. The antecedent is proved. Deut. 31. commands the Lord that the books of Moses be read to all without distinction, men, women, little ones, and strangers. In Ierem. 36. the prophet orders Baruch the scribe to read the book taken from his mouth before the whole people. But someone will say that this command was not perpetual but temporary? I reply that the purpose attached to the command shows that it is perpetual: Deut. 31. that the people may hear, learn, and fear Jehovah. This purpose is perpetual, so the law is perpetual, especially since the reading of the Scriptures is the ordinary and necessary means by which we attain this purpose. So, the antecedent being proved, it follows that the Scriptures are to be translated into the vernacular tongues.

units.la: Argumentum 2. Lectio Scripturarum populo est permittenda: Ergo Scripturæ vertendæ in linguas vernaculas; secus enim non possent legi à populo. Probatur antecedens. Scripturæ sacræ suppeditant arma quibus muniendus est populus adversus Satanam exemplo Christi Mat.4. qui non alijs armis quàm Scripturæ testimonijs Satanam repulit.Iehan.5. Christus turbæ præcipit vt scrutétur Scripturas. Act. 17. laudantur Beroenses, quòd scrutati sint Scripturas vt viderent an ita fe haberent, quæ dixerunt Apostoli. Sed fufiorem de hoc antecedente disputationem remittimus ad explicationem quæstionis tertiæ.
units.tr: Argument 2. The reading of the Scriptures is to be permitted to the people; therefore the Scriptures are to be translated into the vernacular tongues, for otherwise the people could not read them. The antecedent is proved. The holy Scriptures supply the weapons with which the people must be armed against Satan, following the example of Christ, Matt. 4, who repelled Satan with no other weapons than the testimonies of Scripture. John 5: Christ bids the crowd search the Scriptures. Acts 17: the Bereans are praised because they searched the Scriptures to see whether what the apostles said was so. But we refer a fuller discussion of this antecedent to the explanation of the third question.

units.la: Argumentum 3. Papistæ quidem concedunt legendas Scripturas coram populo, sed contendunt id oportere fieri ignota lingua. Sic igitur argumentor, fi ignota & peregrina lingua legantur Scripturæ coram populo id fiet fine fructu & ædificatione: Ergo vertendæ Scripturæ in linguas vernaculas. Antecedens probatur. 1. Cor.14. Si veniam ad vos linguis loquens, quid vobis prodero, quasi dixisset, nihil. Et pòst eodem capite. Malo quinque verba loqui ex intelligentia mea, vt alios instituam, quam decem millia verborum ἐν γλώσσῃ, in lingua, scilicet, ignota. Sed de hac re etiam pòst pluribus erit agendum.
units.tr: Argument 3. The Papists indeed concede that the Scriptures are to be read before the people, but they contend this must be done in an unknown language. I argue thus: if the Scriptures are read before the people in an unknown and foreign tongue, this will be without fruit or edification; therefore the Scriptures are to be translated into the vernacular tongues. The antecedent is proved. 1. Cor. 14. If I come to you speaking in tongues, what shall I profit you? as if to say, nothing. And later in the same chapter: I would rather speak five words with my understanding, so as to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue [ἐν γλώσσῃ], that is, in an unknown language. But this matter too will be treated at greater length later.

units.la: Argumentum 4. In populo Dei requiritur sapientia, scientia, eruditio: Ergo legendæ Scripturæ: Ergo vertendæ in linguas vernaculas. Probatur antecedens Deut.4. vult Dominus
units.tr: Argument 4. Wisdom, knowledge, and learning are required in the people of God; therefore the Scriptures are to be read, and therefore translated into the vernacular tongues. The antecedent is proved: Deut. 4. The Lord wills

units.la: ἐν γλώσσῃ
units.tr: in a tongue [ἐν γλώσσῃ]

units.la: Dominus populum suum intelligentem & eruditum, adeo vt exteræ gentes de eo audientes admirentur, & dicant: Ecce populus sciens & intelligens, gens magna. Apostolus ad Coloss. 3. vult sermonem Christi inhabitare in ijs πλουσίως, copiose & opulenter. In Epistolis suis Paulus passim vult eos ad quos scribit impleri omni cognitione. Multa disputant adversarij adversus hanc popularem intelligentiam.
units.tr: the Lord to want his people to be understanding and learned, so much so that the foreign nations, hearing of them, marvel and say: Behold, a wise and understanding people, a great nation. The Apostle in Col. 3 wills the word of Christ to dwell in them richly [πλουσίως], abundantly and copiously. Throughout his Epistles Paul wants those to whom he writes to be filled with all knowledge. Our opponents dispute much against this popular understanding.

units.la: Argumentum 5. Christus, cum ageret inter Iudæos, lingua vernacula loquutus est & prædicavit: Apostoli Christi etiam lingua vernacula annunciarunt Evangelium, vt in die Pentecostes & post: & ob eam ipsam causam, quo possent loqui singulis nationibus & populis in linguis vernaculis & popularibus, datum est ijs illud donum linguarum. Hoc posito sic argumentor. Si annunciare Evangelium linguis vernaculis non fuit ipsum profanare, aut contaminare, pari ratione scribere Evangelium linguis vernaculis non est Evangelium contaminare aut profanare: nam par ratio est.
units.tr: Argument 5. Christ, when he dealt among the Jews, spoke and preached in the vernacular tongue; the apostles of Christ also proclaimed the Gospel in the vernacular tongue, as on the day of Pentecost and afterwards; and for this very reason, so that they could speak to each nation and people in their own vernacular and common tongues, the gift of tongues was given to them. Granting this, I argue thus. If to proclaim the Gospel in the vernacular tongues was not to profane or defile it, then by the same reasoning to write the Gospel in the vernacular tongues is not to profane or defile it, for the reason is the same.

units.la: Argumentum 6. est ex visu perpetuo & proxi totius Ecclesiæ veteris. Nam tempore Ecclesiæ veteris Scriptura sacra in linguas pene nè omnes est transfusa, verbi gratia Chaldaicam,Syram,Arabicam, Armenicam, Ægyptiacam,Æthiopicam,Indicam,Persicam,Scythicam,Sauromaticam. Testes hujus rei multi sunt: Chrysostomus homilia 1. in Iohannem. Theodoretus de corrigendis Græcorum affectibus. lib. 5. Augustinus de doctrina Christiana. lib.2. cap.5. Extant etiamnum hodierno die Chaldaica, Syra, Arabica, Ægyptiaca, Æthiopica,versiones,quas omnes docti affirmant factas esse Apostolorum temporibus. Chrysostomus vertit Scripturam sacram in linguam Armenicam, teste Sixto Seneufe. Hieronymus vertit eam in linguam Dalmaticam, teste Alphonso à Castro, item Eccio,Hosio,Erasmo. Methodius vertit eam in linguam Sclavonicam,teste Aventino in annalib. suis. Vlphilas Gotthorū Episcopus vertit eam in linguā Gotthicam, teste Socrate in Tripartita historia sua. Augustinus de civitate Dei, lib. 15. scribit vetus Testamentum versum fuisse in linguam Syram. Hardingus adversus Iovellum,& Eccius scribunt Russos & Moscovitas legisse Scripturā sacrā in linguas suas vernaculas versam. Anglicana historia habet versionem Scripturarum factam in linguam Anglicam ante Bedam. Be
units.tr: Argument 6 is drawn from the constant and near practice of the whole ancient Church. For in the time of the ancient Church the holy Scripture was translated into almost all tongues, for example the Chaldean, Syriac, Arabic, Armenian, Egyptian, Ethiopian, Indian, Persian, Scythian, and Sauromatian. There are many witnesses to this: Chrysostom, Homily 1 on John; Theodoret, On Correcting the Affections of the Greeks, book 5; Augustine, On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chapter 5. Chaldean, Syriac, Arabic, Egyptian, and Ethiopian versions still exist today, and all learned men affirm that they were made in the times of the apostles. Chrysostom translated Scripture into the Armenian tongue, according to Sixtus Senensis. Jerome translated it into the Dalmatian tongue, according to Alphonsus à Castro, and likewise Eck, Hosius, and Erasmus. Methodius translated it into the Slavonic tongue, according to Aventinus in his Annals. Ulfilas, bishop of the Goths, translated it into the Gothic tongue, according to Socrates in his Tripartite History. Augustine, in The City of God, book 15, writes that the Old Testament had been translated into the Syriac tongue. Harding against Jewel, and Eck, write that the Russians and Muscovites read the holy Scripture translated into their vernacular tongues. The English history records a version of the Scriptures made into English before Bede.

units.la: de da ipse scribit aliquam novi Testamenti partem à se versam fuisse. Hactenus de praxi veteris Ecclesiæ, ex qua, vt ex alijs superioribus argumentis, sequitur Scripturam sacram vertendam esse in linguas vernaculas.
units.tr: Bede himself writes that he had translated some part of the New Testament. Thus far on the practice of the ancient Church, from which, as from the other arguments above, it follows that the holy Scripture is to be translated into the vernacular tongues.

units.la: Nunc quid ad propositam quæstionem respondeant Papistæ videbimus. Ante annos aliquot negarunt simpliciter Scripturam sacram vertendam in linguas vernaculas, Petrus Asoto de horis Canonicis, Censura Coloniensis, Hardingus, cuius paulò ante meminimus scribit aliquos esse qui judicant Scripturam sacram non esse vertendam in linguas vernaculas & plebeias. Hinc factum vt qui verterunt à Papa sint proscripti & condemnati: ipsi libri versi prohibiti & exusti: cum autem viderent hoc omnibus odiosum esse, mutarunt sententiam, ac nunc dicunt licere quidem vertere Scripturam sacrā in linguas vernaculas, ita tamen si hoc à Papa fit permissum. Atq; hoc, etsi verbis aliud videatur esse, tamen reipsa idem est. Papa enim nemini hoc permittet, nisi ei qui volet omnes mendas quotquot reperiuntur in vulgata versione latina transfundere in versiones vernaculas, & ad posteros transmittere. Hæc sententia est Bellarmini, hæc Rhemensium est sententia. Nos autem contrà affirmamus licere cuique pio, docto, linguarum perito, translationem facere, etiamsi non permittat Papa, etiamsi Papa contradicat, & licere Ecclesiae Christi eam translationem post examinationem recipere, etiamsi non intercedat Papa sua authoritate. Nam tempore veteris Ecclesiæ, quo non invalüit Papæ authoritas vel tyrannis potius, sine Papa translationes illæ & factæ sunt, & receptæ ab Ecclesijs. Atque hæc de prima hac quæstione hactenus.
units.tr: Now let us see what the Papists answer to the question proposed. Some years ago Peter Soto, in his book on the canonical hours, the Censure of Cologne, and Harding flatly denied that the holy Scripture was to be translated into the vernacular tongues. Harding, whom we mentioned a little earlier, writes that there are some who judge the holy Scripture is not to be translated into the vernacular and common tongues. Hence it came about that those who translated it were outlawed and condemned by the Pope, and the translated books themselves were forbidden and burned. But when they saw this was hateful to everyone, they changed their opinion, and now say it is indeed lawful to translate the holy Scripture into the vernacular tongues, provided the Pope permits it. And this, though in words it seems something different, is in fact the same thing. For the Pope will permit it to no one except one who undertakes to carry over into the vernacular versions every error found in the Vulgate Latin version, and to hand them on to posterity. This is the opinion of Bellarmine; this is the opinion of the Rhemists. We, on the contrary, affirm that it is lawful for any pious, learned person skilled in languages to make a translation, even if the Pope does not permit it, even if the Pope contradicts it, and that it is lawful for the Church of Christ to receive that translation after examination, even if the Pope does not interpose his authority. For in the time of the ancient Church, when the authority of the Pope, or rather his tyranny, had not yet grown strong, those translations were made without the Pope and received by the churches. Thus far on this first question.

units.la: Nunc secundo loco quaeritur an sacra publica celebranda sint linguis vernaculis & popularibus? Sacra publica appello ea sacra quæ publicè peraguntur in coetibus Ecclesiasticis. Ejusmodi sunt preces publicæ, lectio Scripturarum, administratio Sacramentorum, cantiones Psalmorum, &c. haec vocantur divina officia, λειτουργίαι. Nunc ad quæstionem respondemus, nos quidem affirmate; peragenda esse sacra publica linguis vernaculis. Argumentum primum ex 1.Cor.14. vbi a versu 6. ad versum 23, Apostolus docet nihil esse agendum in Ecclesia linguis ignotis & peregrinis.
units.tr: Now, in the second place, it is asked whether public sacred services are to be celebrated in the vernacular and popular tongues. By public sacred services I mean those sacred rites which are publicly performed in ecclesiastical assemblies. Such are public prayers, the reading of the Scriptures, the administration of the sacraments, the singing of psalms, and so on. These are called divine offices, liturgies [λειτουργίαι]. Now we answer this question affirmatively: public sacred services are to be conducted in the vernacular tongues. The first argument is from 1 Cor. 14, where, from verse 6 to verse 23, the Apostle teaches that nothing is to be done in the Church in unknown and foreign tongues.

units.la: At Bellarminus excipit illo capite agi de collatione & exhortatione potissimum, quæ in veteri Ecclesia sequebatur administrationem sacrorum publicorum, ad eamque citat ex Iustino Martyre Apolog. 2. morem veteris Ecclesiae. Conueniebant Christiani diebus Dominicis, & primùm legebantur Scripturæ: deinde fiebat concio ab Antistite: tum celebrabantur mysteria: postremò, inter se de rebus diuinis sermones miscebant. Respondeo, hîc agi ab Apostolo in genere de omnibus officijs Ecclesiasticis, idque hoc ordine; primùm est generalis doctrina à versu 6. ad versum 14: deinde est specialis de precib. concipiendis, cantionibus canendis, lingua non ignota, sed nota & vernacula, ad versum 19: posteà redit ad generalem doctrinam.
units.tr: But Bellarmine objects that in that chapter Paul deals chiefly with the exhortation and instruction which in the ancient Church followed the administration of the public sacred rites, and to this he cites Justin Martyr, Apolog. 2., for the custom of the ancient Church. Christians used to assemble on the Lord's days, and first the Scriptures were read; then a sermon was given by the president; then the mysteries were celebrated; and finally they exchanged discourses among themselves about divine matters. I reply: here the Apostle deals in general with all the ecclesiastical offices, and does so in this order. First comes the general teaching, from verse 6 to verse 14; then the specific teaching about composing prayers and singing hymns, in a language not unknown but known and vernacular, to verse 19; afterwards he returns to general teaching.

units.la: Bellarminus rursus excipit Paulum agere de cantionibus quas in collatione ij canebant qui extra ordinem dono Spiritus sancti erant imbuti. Respondeo: Apostolus distinctè nominat preces & cantiones; deinde de ijs precibus & gratiarum actionibus loquitur, quibus respondebat populus amen; non autem respondebat populus amen, nisi precibus publicis: de publicis ergo precibus hîc agit, quæ concipiebantur in celebrandis sacris publicis.
units.tr: Bellarmine again objects that Paul is speaking of the songs which those who had been endowed with the gift of the Holy Spirit outside the ordinary ministry sang in the assembly. I reply: the Apostle distinctly names prayers and songs; then he speaks of those prayers and thanksgivings to which the people answered "Amen"; but the people answered "Amen" only to public prayers. Therefore he is here speaking of public prayers, which were composed for the celebration of the public services.

units.la: Excipit Bellarminus: At Corinthi celebrabantur sacra publica lingua græca & nota populo,id que sciebat Apostolus: Quare non erat opus aliquid præscriberet de sacris publicis. Respondeo,ut detur illud, Corinthi celébrari solita sacra publica lingua nota & vernacula, tamen non sequitur Apostoli doctrinam non esse generalem de quibusvis Ecclesiasticis officijs. Deinde verisimile est fuisse inter Corinthios dono linguarum præditos qui eo dono abusi sunt ad ostentationem,etiam in celebrandis sacris publicis, idque eo capite reprehendit Apostolus. Atque hæc de primo Argumento.
units.tr: Bellarmine objects: but at Corinth public services were celebrated in Greek, a language known to the people, and the Apostle knew this; so there was no need for him to prescribe anything about public services. I reply: granting that public services at Corinth were customarily celebrated in a language known and vernacular, it does not follow that the Apostle's teaching is not general concerning all church offices. Moreover, it is likely that among the Corinthians there were some endowed with the gift of tongues who abused that gift for display, even in the celebration of public services; and this is what the Apostle rebukes in that chapter. So much for the first argument.

units.la: Secundum est ejusdem Apostoli eodem cap. versu. 6. Si veniam ad vos linguis loquens, scilicet,ignotis, quid vobis prodero? Hinc concludo,sacra publica celebranda lingua non ignota, sed nota. Respondet Bellarminus,imò proderit aliis, qui peragit sacra publica lingua ignota : satis enim est si Deus intelligat: idque à simili declarat; Vt, inquit, si quis latinè pro aliquo rustico & linguæ latinæ imperito agat cum Rege, hic satis est si Rex intelligat,ad hoc vt beneficium perveniat ad rusticum. Resp. Quid aliud est hoc, quâ dicere, virtute operis operati sacra publica & ministerium publicum prodesse populo, etiam cum ipse sit absque fide, absque notitia. Sed de hoc alias.
units.tr: The second argument is from the same Apostle, in the same chapter, verse 6: "If I come to you speaking in tongues," that is, unknown tongues, "what will I profit you?" From this I conclude that public services are to be celebrated in a language not unknown but known. Bellarmine replies: on the contrary, it will profit others, for he who performs public services in an unknown language does good; it is enough if God understands. He illustrates this by a comparison: "as if," he says, "someone were to speak Latin on behalf of some rustic who has no skill in the Latin language before a king; it is enough if the king understands, so that the benefit reaches the rustic." I reply: what else is this than to say that by the virtue of the work done (ex opere operato) public services and the public ministry profit the people, even when the people themselves are without faith and without knowledge? But of this elsewhere.

units.la: Tertium Argumentum est ejusdem Apostoli eodem cap. versu 11. Qui loquitur lingua, scilicet ignota, apud me barbarus fuerit: Ergo sacra publica peragenda sunt lingua nota & vernacula. Respondet Bellarminus, imo qui hebraice, græce & latine loquutus fuerit, etsi non intelligatur, tamen non erit barbarus; quia linguae illae barbarae non sunt: Verum si alia quavis lingua loquatur barbarus erit. Respondeo, si loquens his ipsis linguis non intelligatur, erit ei qui non intelligit barbarus. Ovidius enim cum in Ponto exularet questus est se latine loquentem barbarum suisse apud exteros: Barbarus hic ego sum, quia non intelligor ulli. Anacharsis cum Athenis ei esset objectum quod barbarus esset: Imo inquit, Athenienses mihi sunt barbari.
units.tr: The third argument is from the same Apostle, in the same chapter, verse 11: "If I know not the meaning of the voice, I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian," that is, when the speaker uses an unknown language; therefore public services are to be performed in a known and vernacular language. Bellarmine replies: on the contrary, one who speaks in Hebrew, Greek and Latin will not be a barbarian, even if he is not understood, because those languages are not barbarous; but if he speaks in any other language, he will be a barbarian. I reply: if the speaker, using these very languages, is not understood, he will be a barbarian to one who does not understand. For Ovid, when he was in exile in Pontus, complained that, speaking Latin, he was a barbarian among foreigners: "I am a barbarian here, because I am understood by no one." When Anacharsis was charged at Athens with being a barbarian, he said: "On the contrary, the Athenians are barbarians to me."

units.la: Quartum Argumentum est ejusdem Apostoli eodem cap. versu 16. Si benedixeris spiritu, ignota scilicet lingua loquens, is qui implet locum idiotæ quomodo respondebit amen ad gratiarum actionem tuam? Ex quo sequitur precandum, omninoque omnia sacra publica peragenda lingua nota & vernacula. Respondet Bellarminus satis esse si aliqui ex populo intelligant, & respondeant amen: Imò satis est,inquit, si Clericus,quem vocant, pro populo respondeat amen. At, inquam,non fuit hic mos veteris illius Ecclesiæ,quæ de Clerico nihil vnquam audivit.
units.tr: The fourth argument is from the same Apostle, in the same chapter, verse 16: "If you bless with the spirit, speaking in an unknown tongue, how will he who fills the place of the layman say Amen to your thanksgiving?" From this it follows that prayer, and indeed all public services, must be performed in a known and vernacular language. Bellarmine replies that it is enough if some of the people understand and answer Amen; indeed, he says, it is enough if the so-called Clerk answers Amen on behalf of the people. But I say this was not the custom of that ancient Church, which never heard anything of a Clerk.

units.la: Quintum Argumentum est ejusdem Apostoli eodem cap. versu 40. Omnia decenter fiant & ordine in Ecclesia. At si precetur Minister lingua ignota,populus privatas concipiet preces alias à precibus ministri, atque ita minister suas concipiet;quisque ex populo suas & alias. Quæ autem est ista ἐυταξία,cum sic divellitur populus inter precandum, qui inter precandum publicè unas & eafdè preces vno animo vnoq; ore Deo offerre debet?
units.tr: The fifth argument is from the same Apostle, in the same chapter, verse 40: "Let all things be done decently and in order in the Church." But if the minister prays in an unknown language, the people will compose private prayers different from the minister's prayers, and thus the minister will compose his own and each one of the people his own and others. What kind of good order (εὐταξία) is this, when the people are so divided during prayer, when in public prayer they ought to offer to God one and the same prayers with one mind and one mouth?

units.la: Sextum Argumentū est ex concessis Bellarmini. Fatetur Corinthi celebrari solita sacra publica lingua græca & nota, cur non igitur eadem ratione in omnibus Ecclesijs celebrarentur sacra publica lingua nota & vernacula? Quid hic respondebit,nisi hoc fortasse quòd celebrata sunt Corinthi sacra publica lingua vernacula;non quia vernacula erat,sed quia græca; ea enim est græcæ linguæ Papistis prærogativa.
units.tr: The sixth argument is drawn from Bellarmine's own concessions. He admits that public services were customarily celebrated at Corinth in Greek, a language known. Why, then, by the same reasoning, should public services not be celebrated in all churches in a known and vernacular language? What will he answer here, except perhaps that public services were celebrated at Corinth in a vernacular language, not because it was vernacular but because it was Greek? For that is the prerogative the Papists grant to the Greek language.

units.la: Septimum Argumentum est ex concessis quoque Bellarmini.
