Collationes,vt ipse fate-tur, tur, & exhortationes debent fieri lingua vernacula: cur non pari ratione sacra publica peragenda sunt lingua vernacula & populo nota? Respondet non esse eandem rationem collationum & sacrorum publicorum. Nam, inquit, collationes ad instructionem & confolationem populi pertinent; sacra publica praecipue ad Dei cultum. Respondeo: an non in sacris publicis totus populus colit Deum, an non igitur oportet Deum colat lingua sibi nota & cognita, si modo fide colat Deum suum.
units.tr: The seventh argument is also drawn from Bellarmine's concessions. He himself admits that gatherings and exhortations must be conducted in the vernacular language; why, by the same reasoning, should public services not be performed in the vernacular and known to the people? He replies that the reason for gatherings and for public services is not the same: gatherings, he says, pertain to the instruction and comfort of the people, while public services pertain chiefly to the worship of God. I reply: in public services does not the whole people worship God? Must it not therefore worship God in a language known and understood by it, if indeed it worships its God in faith?

units.la: Octavum Argumentum est a praxi vete- ris & purioris Ecclesiae:
units.tr: The eighth argument is from the practice of the old and purer Church:

units.la: Tempore veteris Ecclesiae versiones tot sunt factae sacrarum literarum non in alium finem, nisi ut celebrarentur sacra publica, Scripturae legerentur coram populo lingua vernacula & nota. Aeneas Sylvius libro de origine Bohemorum scribit Cyrillo & Methodio concessum fuisse, ut Moravi lingua vernacula celebrarent sacra publica. Hodierno die Armeni, Aethiopes, Aegyptii, Moscovitae celebrant sacra publica lingua nota. Respondet Bellarminus haereticos istos esse. At, inquam, non magis haeretici quam sunt Papistae. Equidem quod ad celebrationem sacrorum publicorum attinet, malim in haec haeresi esse cum iis, quam cum Papistis, ut ipsi putant, recte sentire. Atque de sententia nostra haec hactenus.
units.tr: In the time of the old Church so many versions of the sacred letters were made for no other purpose than that public worship be celebrated and Scripture read before the people in the vernacular and familiar tongue. Aeneas Sylvius, in his book on the origin of the Bohemians, writes that Cyril and Methodius were granted permission for the Moravians to celebrate public worship in their own vernacular. Today the Armenians, Ethiopians, Egyptians and Muscovites celebrate public worship in a language the people know. Bellarmine replies that these are heretics. But, I say, they are no more heretics than the Papists are. Indeed, as far as the celebration of public worship is concerned, I would rather be in this heresy with them than with the Papists, who think they judge rightly. And so much for our view.

units.la: Sententia Adversariorum est, quod sacra publica non sint peragenda linguis vernaculis & notis, sed lingua vel hebraica, vel graeca, ut in Orientalibus & Graecis Ecclesijs, vel lingua latina, ut in Latinis & Occidetalibus Ecclesijs. Argumenta ad hoc ostendendum afferunt: primum ex linguarum praerogativis: Argumentum eorum primum est: Christus titulo crucis suae honoravit has tres linguas: Ergo sacra publica his linguis peragenda. R. ut valeat antecedens, non sequitur consequens: imo vero contrarium rectius infertur, in hunc modum: Dominus voluit causam mortis Christi toti populo innotescere ijs linguis, quae tum maxime notae erant, & omnibus cognitae, quod de graeca & latina negari non potest: Ergo sacra publica peragenda sunt linguis vulgatis, & populo non ignotis.
units.tr: The opponents' view is that public worship must not be conducted in vernacular and familiar languages, but in Hebrew or Greek, as in the Eastern and Greek Churches, or in Latin, as in the Latin and Western Churches. They bring arguments to show this. The first is from the prerogatives of the languages: Christ honoured these three languages with the title of his cross; therefore public worship is to be conducted in these languages. Answer: even if the antecedent is granted, the consequent does not follow. The contrary is rather more correctly inferred, in this way: the Lord willed the cause of Christ's death to be known to the whole people in those languages which were then most widely known and familiar to all, which cannot be denied of Greek and Latin. Therefore public worship is to be conducted in commonly used languages, not unknown to the people.

units.la: Argumentum secundum. Hae tres linguae Hebraea, Graeca, & Latina sunt linguae omnium amplissimae, antiquissimae, gravissimae: Ergo his linguis solis celebranda sacra publica. R. ut jubeam valere antecedens, non sequitur consequens, quia vel donum illud linguarum quod datum est Apostolis die Pentecostes fatis arguit quamcunque linguam, etiam viliffimam quamquc, sanctificatam ad sacros vr sus,& officia publica atque Ecclesiastica.
units.tr: Second argument: these three languages, Hebrew, Greek and Latin, are the most extensive, most ancient and most dignified of all languages; therefore sacred public worship should be celebrated in these languages alone. Answer: even if the antecedent is granted, the consequent does not follow. The gift of tongues given to the Apostles on the day of Pentecost sufficiently proves that any language, even the humblest, is sanctified for sacred uses and public and ecclesiastical duties.

units.la: Argumentum tertium.Scriptura est originaliter scripta his tribus linguis: Ergo sacra publica peragenda his solis. R. ad antecedens, falsum est Scripturam,vel aliquam Scripturæ partem, originaliter scriptam lingua Latina; Nam quod de Marci Evangelio dicunt,quòd Latinè scriptum fit originaliter, falsum est. Sed de hac re alias. Deinde respondeo, non sequi ex illo antecedente sacra publica celebranda linguis ignotis: Quin potiùs contrarium sequitur: Cum scripta fit tum primùm illis linguis duabus,Hebraica & Græca,tota sacra Scriptura, ideò quòd hæ linguæ tunc temporis erant vulgatiffimæ & populo notiffimæ:sequitur,inquâ,sacra publica celebranda linguis quibufq; notissimis et vulgatiffimis
units.tr: Third argument: Scripture was originally written in these three languages; therefore public worship is to be conducted in these alone. Answer: as to the antecedent, it is false that Scripture, or any part of Scripture, was originally written in Latin; for what they say of Mark's Gospel, that it was written originally in Latin, is false. But of this matter elsewhere. Next I reply that it does not follow from that antecedent that worship is to be celebrated in unknown languages. Rather the contrary follows. Since the whole of holy Scripture was first written in those two languages, Hebrew and Greek, because these languages were then most widespread and best known to the people, it follows, I say, that public worship is to be celebrated in the languages most widely known and common to all.

units.la: Hactenus fuerunt argumenta à linguarum trium prærogativa: sequuntur argumeta quç sunt ab Ecclesiarum praxi & vsu ; ex his primum est. Ab Efdra ad Christum in Ecclesia Iudaica legi folebat sacra Scriptura lingua hebraica.i. ignota: Ergo celebranda sacra publica linguis ignotis. R. Hebraica, fateor,folebat legi; sed ignota,nego. Nam Nehemiæ s, plane nè apparet sacram Scripturam, hebraicè lectam ab Esdra, à populo præsente & audiente intellectam fuisse. Ex quo sequitur consequens contrarium: Legebatur Scriptura olim in Ecclesia Iudaica lingua nota populo: Ergo hodierno die legenda linguis popularibus & notis.
units.tr: So far the arguments from the prerogative of the three languages. There follow arguments from the practice and custom of the Churches. The first of these is: from Ezra to Christ, holy Scripture was customarily read in the Jewish Church in Hebrew, that is, in an unknown language; therefore public worship is to be celebrated in unknown languages. Answer: I grant that it was customarily read in Hebrew; but that it was unknown, I deny. For Nehemiah 8 plainly shows that the Scripture read in Hebrew by Ezra was understood by the people present and listening. From this the contrary consequence follows: Scripture was once read in the Jewish Church in a language known to the people; therefore today it is to be read in popular and familiar languages.

units.la: Argumentum 2. est à praxi Synagogæ Iudaicæ, quæ est hodierno die. Etiamnum, inquit, hodierno die legitur Scriptura lingua hebraica in Synagoga Iudæorum: Ergo celebranda sacra publica lingua ignota. Respondeo non sequi à malo exemplo Synagogæ Iudæorum, cùm id quòd legatur in Synagoga eorum lingua ignota vetus Testamentum faciat quò minus ex vulgo Iudæorum hodierni temporis plures convertantur ad fidem Christi.
units.tr: The second argument is from the practice of the Jewish synagogue, which continues today. Even now, it says, Scripture is read in Hebrew in the Jewish synagogue; therefore public worship is to be celebrated in an unknown language. I reply that it does not follow from the bad example of the Jewish synagogue. The fact that the Old Testament is read in their synagogue in an unknown language is itself what keeps more of the Jewish common people of our time from being converted to faith in Christ.

units.la: Argumentum 3. est ex praxi primitivæ Ecclesiæ. In primitiva Ecclesia celebrabantur sacra publica harum linguarum aliqua: Ergo. Respondeo: antecedens falsum esse ex eo apparet, quòd, ut antea docuimus, tempore veteris Ecclesiæ, imò Apostolorum Ecclesiæ, sacra Scriptura transfusa fit in omnes fere linguas.
units.tr: The third argument is from the practice of the primitive Church. In the primitive Church public worship was celebrated in one of these languages; therefore, and so on. Answer: the antecedent is false, as appears from the fact that, as we taught above, in the time of the old Church, indeed in the Church of the Apostles, holy Scripture was translated into almost all languages.

units.la: Argumentum 4. est à praxi perpetua Catholicæ Ecclesiæ, in qua celebrata sunt sacra publica, vel græca vel latina lingua. R. si Catholicam intelligant Romanam, tum nihili fecero ejus Ecclesiæ exemplum & praxin: Sin hoc nomine veram Catholicam intelligant, tum ex ijs quæ jam tradidimus constat antecedens esse falsum. Atque hæc Argumenta hactenus ab vsu & praxi Ecclesiarum sumpta.
units.tr: The fourth argument is from the perpetual practice of the Catholic Church, in which public worship has been celebrated either in Greek or in Latin. Answer: if they understand by Catholic the Roman Church, then I count that Church's example and practice as nothing. But if by this name they understand the true Catholic Church, then from what we have already set out it is clear that the antecedent is false. So far these arguments taken from the use and practice of the Churches.

units.la: His argumentis alia adjiciunt, ut argumentum ab vsu & fine vtili: Sacra publica celebrata ab omnibus vel a multis Ecclesijs lingua vna, vt latina, plurimum faciunt ad vnitatem fidei confervandæ. Cui respondeo, imò contra ad vnitatem infidelitatis & ignorantiæ. Præterea experientia docet, etiam in summa varietate linguarum vernacularum, Deo sit gratia, conservari in reformatis Ecclesijs fidei vnitatem.
units.tr: To these arguments they add others, such as the argument from use and useful end: public worship celebrated by all, or by many Churches, in one language, such as Latin, greatly serves to preserve the unity of faith. To this I reply: on the contrary, it serves rather the unity of unbelief and ignorance. Moreover, experience teaches that, even with the greatest variety of vernacular languages, by God's grace the unity of faith is preserved in the reformed Churches.

units.la: Argumentantur deinde ab inutili. Nihil prodest populo quod legantur Scripturæ linguis vernaculis, nam non intelligit sententias Scripturarum, etsi verba nota sint? Respondeo, imò idiota quivis, si cum timore Dei & reverentia accedat ad audiendam lectionem Scripturæ sacræ, aliquam vtilitatem ex ea capiet.
units.tr: Then they argue from uselessness: does it do the people no good that the Scriptures are read in vernacular languages, since they do not understand the meaning of the Scriptures, even if the words are familiar? I reply: on the contrary, any ordinary person, if he comes with the fear of God and reverence to hear the reading of holy Scripture, will gain some benefit from it.

units.la: Rursus ab inutili argumentantur. Imò lectio vernacula Scripturarum magis obest & nocet populo; nam diminuta magis quàm aucta est pietas postquam coeperunt sacra publica linguis vernaculis celebrari. R. Non valet sequela: sacra Scriptura vernacula lingua lecta multis obest: Ergo non legenda lingua vernacula: quia per accidens & vitio ipsius populi obest & nocet. Sic Evangelium prædicatum est odor mortis ad morte non paucis: Ergo non prædicandum Evangelium. Præterea non est ista religio & vera pietas, quæ est cum ignorantia, quo tempore sacra Scriptura legitur, & sacra publica peraguntur lingua peregrina & ignota; sed stupenda superstitio, quæ etiam, fateor, licentiam peccandi refrenat. Hactenus à finibus & effectis argumenta fuerunt tria.
units.tr: Again they argue from uselessness. On the contrary, the vernacular reading of the Scriptures rather harms and injures the people, for piety has diminished rather than increased since public worship began to be celebrated in vernacular languages. Answer: the consequence does not hold. Holy Scripture read in the vernacular harms many; therefore it is not to be read in the vernacular, because it harms and injures only incidentally and through the people's own fault. So too the Gospel preached is a smell of death to death for not a few; therefore the Gospel is not to be preached. Moreover, that is not religion or true piety which goes with ignorance at the time Scripture is read and sacred public worship is conducted in a foreign and unknown language; it is rather a stupid superstition, which, I admit, does restrain licence to sin. So far there have been three arguments from ends and effects.

units.la: Argumentantur præterea ab absurdo, primum hoc modo. Si legendæ Scripturæ linguis vernaculis, tum versiones sunt renovandæ singulis ætatibus: Nam verborum vetus interit ætas; quod quidem est incommodum. R. Quid hic incommodi etsi versiones dicas renovandas singulis ætatibus? Sed non tam totæ verriones quàm vocabula aliqua absoleta & inusitata renovantur.
units.tr: They further argue from absurdity, first in this way: if Scripture is to be read in the vernacular languages, then the versions must be renewed in every age, for the age of words wears out; and this is indeed an inconvenience. Answer: what inconvenience is there here, even if you say the versions must be renewed in every age? In fact not so much whole versions are renewed as some obsolete and unusual words.

units.la: Rursus ab incommodo argumentantur. Papa nô intelligit omnes linguas vernaculas: Sacra autem publica celebranda sunt lingua Papæ nota. Ergo. R. Nego celebranda neces-sario lingua Papæ nota. Hoc probant, quia universalis est Episcopus: Et hoc quoq; nego. Quare nihil incommodi est etsi Papa non intelligat linguas illas vernaculas quibus celebrantur sacra publica. Hactenus de secunda quæstione.
units.tr: Again they argue from inconvenience: the Pope does not understand all vernacular languages, but public worship must be celebrated in a language known to the Pope; therefore, and so on. Answer: I deny that it must necessarily be celebrated in a language known to the Pope. They prove this because he is universal bishop, and this too I deny. Hence there is no inconvenience even if the Pope does not understand the vernacular languages in which public worship is celebrated. So far on the second question.

units.la: Sequitur tertia. An vulgo & laicis, ut vocant, permittenda sit Scripturarum lectio. In hac quæstione tractanda ero brevior. Nos igitur respondemus licere cuivis etiam ex fæce populi legere Scripturas sacras. De hac re vide Deut. 6. & 11. & 17. Iosue 1. Iob. 5. Scrutamini Scripturas ait Dominus. Act. 17. Beroenses scrutati sunt Scripturas, & ideo laudati a Spiritu sancto. Matth. 4. exemplum illud Christi qui Satanā non alijs quam Scripturæ armis oppugnavit docet Scripturam ejusque lectionem suppeditare arma, quibus muniendus est quivis ex populo adversus Satanam. Postremò idem probat praxis Ecclesiæ: Nam quorsum versæ sunt Scripturæ tempore veteris Ecclesiæ in linguas populares, nisi ut a populo legi & intelligi possent. Atq; hæc paucis est sententia nostra.
units.tr: Next comes the third question: whether the reading of Scripture should be permitted to the common people and the laity, as they call them. I shall be briefer in treating this question. We therefore answer that it is lawful for anyone, even from the dregs of the people, to read the holy Scriptures. On this matter see Deut. 6. & 11. & 17. Iosue 1. Iob. 5. "Search the Scriptures," says the Lord. Act. 17. The Bereans searched the Scriptures, and for this were praised by the Holy Spirit. Matth. 4. That example of Christ, who fought Satan with no weapons other than Scripture, teaches that Scripture and its reading supply the arms with which anyone from the people must be fortified against Satan. Lastly, the practice of the Church proves the same thing: for to what end were the Scriptures translated into popular languages in the time of the old Church, unless that the people might read and understand them? This, in brief, is our view.

units.la: Quæ vero adversariorum? Ante aliquot annos responderunt non licere omninò vul-go go & Laicis, quos vocât, legere sacram Scriptu-ram: Vide Censuram Coloniensem. Postea, cum videret hoc odiosum esse, mutarunt sententiam, ac nunc quidem dicunt licere, sed addita conditione, si permittatur: permittatur, inquam, à quibus? Respondent post Papam, ab Episcopis aut Inquisitoribus. An ab his, inquam, solis? Respondent, non solis, sed adhibito in consilium Parocho aut Confessario. Accipio qui permittant lectionē Scripturae: nunc quæro quibus permittatur? Respondent, non quibusvis promiscuè, sed ijs duntaxat quos Parochus, quem Curatum vocant, tum ex confessione, tum ex tota vitæ ratione hominem verè Catholicum esse cognovit, hoc est, pertinacem Papistam. Accipio quibus permittatur lectio Scripturarū: Quarum autem vernacularum versionum lectio permittitur? Non quidem quarumcunque sine discrimine, sed earum quas Catholici aliqui authores ediderunt, vt est hodierno die versio Anglica Rhemensium novi Testamenti. Hæc paucis de illa permissione quæ licentiæ huius conditionem constituit. Atque hęc sententia est juxta decretum Pij quarti Papæ, quod quidem decretum confirmatum est à Synodo Tridentina, & laudatum à Rhemensibus in præfatione editionis suæ vernaculæ. Hæc quoque Bellarmini est sententia, quæ verbis quidem differt à priori illa Papistarum sententia, sed res eadem recidit: nam quid interest siue non permittatur omninò. siue hoc modo, & hac conditione permittatur.
units.tr: What, then, of our opponents? Some years ago they replied that the common people and the laity, as they call them, were not allowed to read Holy Scripture at all; see the Censure of Cologne. Later, when they saw that this was unpopular, they changed their view. Now they say it is permitted, but with an added condition: if it is granted. Granted, I say, by whom? They reply: by the Pope, and after him by the bishops or inquisitors. By these alone, I ask? They reply: not by these alone, but with the parish priest or confessor called in as adviser. I accept who grants the reading of Scripture. Now I ask, to whom is it granted? They reply: not to just anyone indiscriminately, but only to those whom the parish priest, whom they call the curate, has come to know, both from confession and from the whole manner of the person's life, as truly Catholic, that is, as stubborn Papists. I accept to whom the reading of Scripture is granted. But which vernacular versions may be read? Not any whatsoever without distinction, but those published by certain Catholic authors, as at present the English version of the New Testament by the Rhemists. These few words on that permission, which sets the condition of this licence. And this view accords with the decree of Pope Pius IV, which was indeed confirmed by the Council of Trent and praised by the Rhemists in the preface to their vernacular edition. This is also the opinion of Bellarmine, which differs in words from that earlier view of the Papists, but the matter comes to the same thing. For what difference does it make whether it is not permitted at all, or is permitted in this way and on this condition?

units.la: Atque hæc hactenus de tertia quæstione, et omninò de controversiis quæ hodierno die agitantur de sacra Scriptura. Quod sciam equidem nulla est ex omnibus quam intactam prorsus reliquimus. Dictum igitur sit de verbo Dei, quod est verbum utriusque fœderis: Item de Scriptura sacra, quæ modus est quidam, quo Deo visum est verbum suum hominibus revelare. Sequitur nunc ut dicamus de Peccato & miseria hominis.
units.tr: So much for the third question so far, and in general for the controversies about Holy Scripture that are debated in our day. As far as I know, there is no one among all of them that we have left entirely untouched. Let us therefore say what needs to be said about the Word of God, which is the Word of both covenants, and likewise about Holy Scripture, which is a certain mode by which God has been pleased to reveal his word to human beings. It now follows that we speak of sin and the misery of man.

units.la: De Peccato in genere.
units.tr: De Peccato in genere.

units.la: CAP. 24.
units.tr: CAP. 24.

units.la: IOcus de Peccato, vt & superiores, subalternus est loco de vocatione. Est enim vocatio translatio hominis ex statu peccati et miseriæ, in statum justitiæ & beatitudinis. De peccato igitur primùm in genere est dicendum, tum veniedum ad ejus species, siue partes. Peccati nomen significat quiddam compositum ex materia quadam sua & forma.
units.tr: The locus on sin, like the preceding ones, is subordinate to the locus on vocation. For calling is the transfer of a man from the state of sin and misery into the state of righteousness and blessedness. Therefore we must first speak of sin in general, and then come to its kinds, or parts. The name sin signifies something compounded of a certain matter and a form.

units.la: Materia peccati, vt de ea dicam priori loco, est ens quoddam: Ens autem illud non est substantia, sed accidens; atque illud quidem vel qualitas, vel actio: Qualitas autem haec et actio non sunt cujusvis creaturae; sed rationalis duntaxat creaturae, Angeli vel Hominis: Nam his solis lex a Deo data est. Entis hujus, quod materiam peccati esse dicimus, Deus ipse author est & principalis efficiens; nam is solus est qui vocat ea quae non sunt tanquam sint, & qui res omnes creat, tam substantias, quam accidentia: Creatura autem nullius omnino entis principalis efficiens vel est, vel dicitur. Ens igitur illud quod est peccati materia, cum ejus efficiens principalis sit Deus, necessario in se & per se bonum est: Quicquid enim creat vel efficit Deus, illud insitam habet bonitatis formam. Gen. 1. 31. Cum inspiceret (inquit) Deus quidquid fecerat, ecce bonum erat valde. Bonitatis ista forma adeo insita est & essentialis enti quod facit Deus, sive qualitati, sive actioni, ut ab eo nunquam separetur. Induit fateor hoc ipsum ens formam aliam, nempe ἀτοπίαν, cujus causa est malum instrumentum, ut postea dicemus: verum ἀτοπία haec tantum adventitia est, neque destruit essentialem illam entis ipsius bonitatis formam, quae a Deo à Deo creatore & effectore proficiscitur. Nil enti quod Deus facit nihil potest addi vel detrahi, quo vel melius vel deterius in se fiat. De materia peccati hactenus.
units.tr: The matter of sin, of which I shall speak first, is a certain being. But that being is not a substance, but an accident, and this is either a quality or an action. These quality and action, however, belong not to every creature but only to a rational creature, an angel or a man, for to these alone has the law been given by God. God himself is the author and principal efficient cause of this being, which we say is the matter of sin; for he alone is the one who calls those things which are not as though they were, and who creates all things, both substances and accidents. A creature, however, either is, or is said to be, the principal efficient cause of no being whatever. Therefore that being which is the matter of sin, since its principal efficient cause is God, is necessarily good in itself and through itself. For whatever God creates or effects bears within it the form of goodness. Gen. 1. 31. When God (it says) saw all that he had made, behold, it was very good. This form of goodness is so inborn and essential to the being that God makes, whether a quality or an action, that it is never separated from it. I admit that this very being takes on another form, namely ἀτοπία [atopia, wrongness], whose cause is a bad instrument, as we shall say later. But this atopia is merely adventitious, and it does not destroy that essential form of goodness of the being itself, which proceeds from God the creator and maker. Nothing can be added to or taken from what God makes, so that it becomes in itself either better or worse. So much on the matter of sin.

units.la: Nunc de forma dicendum est. Forma peccati ἀνομία dicitur, hoc est, ut sic loquar, carentia conformitatis cum voluntate & lege divina. 1 Ioan. 3. ἁμαρτία peccatum ex forma sua sic definitur, ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐστιν ἡ ἀνομία: Anomia haec, quam peccati formam & rationem esse dicimus, non est ens aut aliquid positivum, sed mere privativum quid, nempe privatio, &, ut sic dicam, carentia conformitatis quae est cum lege Dei. Anomia haec fit causa & culpa mali instrumenti, quo utitur Deus in ente vel operesuo faciendo; atque eo quidem vel Diabolo, vel homine malo & infideli. Diabolus enim vel homo malus, dum concurrit cum Deo ad opus ipsius producendum, ipsius entis sive operis causa non est principaliter efficiens, sed instrumentaria duntaxat & ministra; Anomia vero Diabolus vel homo causa est principaliter efficiens.
units.tr: Now we must speak of the form. The form of sin is called ἀνομία [anomia, lawlessness], that is, if I may so speak, the lack of conformity with the will and law of God. 1 John 3. Sin is defined by its form thus: ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐστιν ἡ ἀνομία [hē hamartia estin hē anomia, sin is lawlessness]. This anomia, which we say is the form and character of sin, is not a being or anything positive, but something purely privative: a privation and, if I may so speak, a lack of conformity with the law of God. This anomia becomes the cause and fault of the bad instrument which God uses in making his being or work; and that instrument is either the Devil or a wicked and unfaithful man. For the Devil or wicked man, when he concurs with God to produce God's work, is not the principal efficient cause of the being or work itself, but only its instrumental and serving cause. But anomia is caused principally and efficiently by the Devil or the man.

units.la: Anomia autem haec, cujus efficiens est malum instrumentum, existit vel ex eo quod ipsa actio vel opus pugnet cum lege Dei, ut cum quis perpetrat homicidium: homicidij enim actio pugnat cum expressa lege illa. Ne committe homicidium: vel ex eo est quòd fons & principiū actionis aut operis pugnet cum lege Dei, etiamsi ipsa actio in se le legi conformis sit: Lex enim Dei, quemadmodum actionem sive opus ipsum praecipit, ita fontis & principij actionis rationem habet; mandatq; vt omne illud opus quod praecipitur lege, procedat ex corde puro, sancto, & fideli, illius nimirum instrumenti, quo vtitur Deus in opere suo faciendo. Exemplum huius generis αὐθαίρετος est, vt cum quis eleemosynam erogat, quod opus quidè est à Deo mandatum, non tamen ex charitate id facit. Vide 1. Corinth. 13. Vel denique ἀναγκαῖα ex eo existit, quòd finis quem malum instrumentum sibi habet in agendo sive cooperando cum Deo propositum, cum lege Dei pugnet. Lex enim Dei, vt opus ipsum, vt operis fontem & principium, sic quoque finem praecipit, nempe, summum illum, Dei ipsius gloriam: Sive editis, sive bibitis, sive quid facitis, omnia facite in Dei gloriam. 1. Cor. 10. Hoc modo ἀναγκαῖα est, quando quis facit quicquam non propter Deum, non propter ipsius gloriam: sed propter se, propter suum commodum, propter suā gloriam duntaxat.
units.tr: This anomia, whose efficient cause is a bad instrument, arises either because the action or work itself conflicts with the law of God, as when someone commits murder; for the act of murder conflicts with that express law: Do not commit murder. Or it arises because the source and principle of the action or work conflicts with the law of God, even though the action itself in its own nature conforms to the law. For the law of God, just as it prescribes the action or work itself, so also has regard to the source and principle of the action. It commands that every work which the law prescribes should proceed from a pure, holy and faithful heart, namely that of the instrument which God uses in carrying out his work. An example of this kind is αὐθαίρετος [authairetos, self-chosen, wilful], as when someone gives alms, which is indeed a work commanded by God, yet does not do it out of love. See 1 Cor. 13. Or finally, ἀναγκαῖα [anankaia, compelled, forced] arises when the end which the bad instrument proposes to itself in acting or cooperating with God conflicts with the law of God. For the law of God prescribes not only the work itself and the source and principle of the work, but also its end, namely that supreme end, the glory of God himself. 1 Cor. 10. Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God. In this way the anomia is compelled whenever someone does anything not for God, not for his glory, but for himself, for his own advantage, for his own glory alone.

units.la: Notandum quòd qui peccat in fonte actionis, is continuò peccet in fine, & è contrà. Quare hi duo modi ἀνομίας posteriores perpetuò conjuncti sunt. Notandum rursus quòd qui peccat in fonte & in fine, non continuò peccet in ipsa actione. Actio enim vel opus instrumenti, etiam pessimi in se, bonum legiq; conforme esse potest. Quare modus ἀνομίας primus, & duo posteriores, non sunt necessariò conjuncti: Iam verò ἀνομία hæc, quam rationem & formam peccati esse diximus, accedens ad ens illud, cujus author est Deus, & quòd in se bonum est, sive illud qualitas sit, sive actio, conficit hoc quod peccatum dicimus, quodque sic vocatur à forma sua, non autem à materia, cùm res omnes appellationes suas à formis suis sortiantur.
units.tr: It should be noted that whoever sins in the source of an action will continually sin in its end, and conversely. Hence these two later modes of anomia are always joined together. It should be noted again that whoever sins in the source and in the end does not necessarily sin continually in the action itself. For the action or work of an instrument, even a very wicked one, can in itself be good and conformed to the law. Hence the first mode of anomia and the two later ones are not necessarily joined. Now this anomia, which we have said is the character and form of sin, when it attaches to that being whose author is God and which is good in itself, whether it be a quality or an action, produces what we call sin. It is named sin from its form, not from its matter, since all things receive their names from their forms.

units.la: His expositis, facile erit definitionem peccati aliquam colligere, ut sit peccatum, qualitas vel actio creaturæ rationalis ἀνομίας sive pugnans cum lege Dei. Proprietas peccati in genere, sive ejus consequens est reatus: Reatus autem est meritum pœnæ. Ut igitur peccatum consequitur reatus, ita reatus consequens est pœna temporaria & æterna.
units.tr: With these things set out, it will be easy to draw up a definition of sin: sin is a quality or action of a rational creature that is lawlessness (ἀνομία), or that conflicts with the law of God. The property of sin in general, or its consequence, is guilt, and guilt is the desert of punishment. As guilt follows sin, so punishment, temporal and eternal, follows guilt.

units.la: Hæc de peccato in genere; quibus cognitis facilè est respondere ad ea quæ de peccato quæri queri solent; & ad hoc nominatim quod quærunt: An peccatum fit à Deo? vel an Deus sit author peccati? Resp. In peccato duo sunt; ens, & ἀνομία. Deus entis illius author est, & principalis efficiens; ἀνομίας vero non est author Deus, verùm malum instrumentum.
units.tr: So much for sin in general. Once these points are known, it is easy to answer the questions that are usually asked about sin, and especially the one they ask: Is sin made by God, or is God the author of sin? Answer: in sin there are two things, being (ens) and lawlessness (ἀνομία). God is the author of that being and its principal efficient cause, but God is not the author of lawlessness; an evil instrument is.

units.la: Rursus quæritur, an nullo modo hæc ἀνομία est à Deo? R. A Deo est, non quidem efficiente, sed permittente: permittit enim eam fieri à malo instrumento. Tertiò quæritur an permittat Deus illam ἀνομιαν quâ ἀνομία est? Resp. Minimè. Quod vel hac sola ratione ostendi potest. Permittit eam ad gloriâ suam: omnia autem media gloriæ divinæ, quâ talia, boni rationem habent, & ipsæ tenebræ, vt à Deo permittuntur ad gloriam nominis sui, in lucem evadunt.
units.tr: Again it is asked whether this lawlessness is in no way from God. Answer: it is from God, not indeed as efficient cause but as permitting, for he permits it to be done by an evil instrument. Thirdly, it is asked whether God permits that lawlessness by which it is lawlessness. Answer: by no means. This can be shown by this reason alone: he permits it for his glory. But all means to the divine glory, as such, have the character of good, and even darkness, when permitted by God for the glory of his name, emerges into light.

units.la: Hîc deinde si quæratur: Annon igitur si ἀνομία quâ ἀνομία est, non permittatur à Deo, annon necesse est ἀνομιαν quâ ἀνομία est Deo invito fieri? R. Non sequitur: nam quod invito Deo fit, id proprie dicitur fieri contra Dei decretum, non autem contra revelatam ipsius voluntatem, sive expressam legem: ἀνομία autem quâ ἀνομία est, non fit contra decretum aliquod: Ergo ἀνομία quâ ἀνομία est, non fit invito Deo. Assumptio ostenditur, quia Deus non decrevit ab æterno ne fieret à malo instrumento ἀιτίας quâ ἀιτία est. Ergo, inquis, decrevit ut fieret? Resp. Non sequitur; nam utrumque hoc verum est de Deo: Deus neque decrevit ne fieret ἀιτία quâ ἀιτία est, neque decrevit ut fieret ἀιτίας quâ ἀιτία est. Nullum enim de ἀιτία quâ ἀιτία est extat Dei decretum, sive in hâc, sive in illâ parte.
units.tr: If it is then asked here: does it not follow that, if lawlessness as lawlessness is not permitted by God, lawlessness as lawlessness must necessarily happen against God's will? Answer: it does not follow. For what happens against God's will is properly said to happen against God's decree, not against his revealed will or expressed law, and lawlessness as lawlessness does not happen against any decree. Therefore lawlessness as lawlessness does not happen against God's will. The assumption is shown because God did not decree from eternity that it should not be done by an evil instrument as sin [ἁμαρτίας] as sin. "Therefore," you say, "he decreed that it should happen?" Answer: it does not follow, for both of these are true of God: God neither decreed that it should not happen as sin, nor decreed that it should happen as sin. For there is no decree of God concerning sin as sin, in this part or in that.

units.la: Sed quæras, annon aliquo modo à Deo permittente fiat ἀιτία quâ ἀιτία est? R. Deo permittente dicitur aliquid fieri duobus modis; per se, vel per accidens. Quod Deo permittente per se fit, id necesse est habeat rationem, & induat aliquo modo naturam boni; cum illud ipsum Deus & proponat, & dirigat ad bonum finem: Quod autem fit per accidens Deo permittente, sive deserente creaturam, nihil vetat quo minus illud fit malum quâ tale: Nam Deo permittente sibi ipsi creaturam & malum instrumentum, creatura quidem agit quod malum est, quâ malum est: neque fieri potest quin id faciat, quippe deserta ab eo qui boni omnis est author: Sed jam illud malum, quâ malum, Dei permittentis & deserentis respectu, per accidens fit, non per se; cum Deus in deserendo, malum quâ malum est non propositum, sed contrâ quâ boni rationem habet, & medium est gloriæ suæ, præsertim per misericordiam, consequendæ: Nam omnia media, sive ea faciat ipse Deus, sive ea permittat à malis instrumentis fieri, primo loco & destinantur à Deo, & diriguntur ad gloriam misericordiæ, quæ est ex salute creaturæ: Conclusit Deus omnes in contumacia, ut omnium misereretur. Secundo autem loco propter duritiem hominis, & cor quod resipiscere nescit, peccata & mala quæ fiunt à malo instrumento inserviunt gloriæ quam sibi ex justitia sua & justis pœnis acquirit.
units.tr: But you may ask: is sin as sin not done in some way with God's permission? Answer: something is said to be done with God's permission in two ways, per se or per accidens. What is done per se with God's permission must have the character of good and in some way take on the nature of good, since God himself both proposes it and directs it to a good end. But what happens per accidens with God's permission, that is, with God forsaking the creature, nothing prevents its being evil as such. For when God permits the creature and the evil instrument to act of their own accord, the creature indeed does what is evil as evil, and it cannot be that it does not do so, being forsaken by him who is the author of all good. But now that evil as evil, with respect to God permitting and forsaking, happens per accidens and not per se, since in forsaking, God does not propose evil as evil, but on the contrary as having the character of good, and as a means to his glory, to be attained especially through mercy. For all means, whether God himself does them or permits them to be done by evil instruments, are in the first place both ordained by God and directed to the glory of mercy, which arises from the salvation of the creature: "God has shut up all in disobedience, that he might have mercy on all." In the second place, on account of man's hardness and a heart that cannot repent, the sins and evils done by an evil instrument serve the glory which he gains for himself from his justice and just punishments.

units.la: Quòd si contra hæc objicias: Deus permittit peccatum ut ipsum puniat: punit autem peccatum, quà peccatum est, ἁμαρτίαν ut ἁμαρτία est: Ergo permittit peccatum quà peccatum est, ἁμαρτίαν quà ἁμαρτία est? Resp. ad assump. Peccatum, ut ex eo consequitur pœna, quæ ipsa bona est, & cedit in gloriam Dei, peccatum, inquam, illud, non jam habere rationem peccati, sed rationem boni producentis bonum effectum: Mala enim causa, ut mala est, boni effectus esse non potest: Sed si statuatur etiam ea causa quæ in se mala est, boni essectus causa, necesse est aliquo modo ipsa naturam boni induat. Concedo equidem peccatum quà peccatum est causam esse pœnæ, sed
units.tr: But if you object to these things: God permits sin in order to punish it; he punishes sin as sin, as sin is sin; therefore he permits sin as sin, sin as sin? Answer to the assumption: sin, insofar as punishment follows from it, which punishment is itself good and redounds to God's glory, that sin, I say, no longer has the character of sin but the character of good producing a good effect. For an evil cause, as evil, cannot be the cause of a good effect; but if that cause which is evil in itself is also posited as the cause of a good effect, it must in some way take on the nature of good. I grant indeed that sin as sin is the cause of punishment, but

units.la: ἁμαρτίαν, ἁμαρτία: Greek words as printed in the text above. jam profecto vt poena est effectum malæ causæ necesse est ipsa sit mala: Et revera poena quæ infligitur, duobus modis consideratur; primùm vt quiddam in se malum: Nam evenit est aliqua in omni poena, & omnis poena aliquo modo etiā peccatum est. Deinde consideratur vt quiddam bonum, vtpote medium divinæ gloriæ. In summa dicam: Omnia media etiam quæ in se & per se sunt mala, respectu Dei proponentis, & respectu finis, gloriæ divinæ, aliquo modo bona fiunt: Atque omnino tota series illa mediorū, quæ est inter Deum proponentem tanquam caput & principium, & Dei gloriam tanquam vltimum finem, series est rerum, quæ vel per se bonæ sunt, vel certè naturam boni aliquo modo induunt. Nam duo illa extrema tenebras omnes in lucem quodam modo commutant.
units.tr: sin as sin [ἁμαρτίαν, ἁμαρτία]. Now, as punishment is the effect of an evil cause, it must itself be evil; and indeed the punishment that is inflicted is considered in two ways. First, as something evil in itself, for there is some evil in every punishment, and every punishment is in some way even sin. Then it is considered as something good, namely as a means of divine glory. In sum, I say: all means, even those which are evil in themselves and per se, with respect to God who proposes them and with respect to the end, the glory of God, become in some way good. And altogether that whole series of means, which lies between God proposing them as head and principle and the glory of God as ultimate end, is a series of things that are either good in themselves or in some way take on the nature of good. For those two extremes in a way change all darkness into light.

units.la: De Peccato Originali. CAP. 25.
units.tr: On Original Sin. CHAP. 25.

units.la: HActenus de peccato in genere dictum sit: Peccati prima divisio est in originale, & actuale. De originali, vt dicamus primo loco, primùm occurrit consideranda nominis huius ratio & notatio. Peccatum originale ideo dicitur quòd sit ab origine, conceptione, et nativitate nostra: fit enim per propagatio‑ nem, & derivatur ex parentibus in liberos, vt hæreditarius quidam morbus, veluti scabies, lepra, calculus.
units.tr: So far I have spoken of sin in general. The first division of sin is into original and actual. Concerning original sin, and to take it first, we must begin by considering the meaning and derivation of the name. Original sin is so called because it comes from our origin, our conception and our birth. It is transmitted by propagation and passes from parents to children, like a hereditary disease such as scabies, leprosy or the stone.

units.la: Quòd autem fit hoc peccati genus, id manifeftius est quàm vt de eo quæri debeat: Nemo enim est omnium tam stupidus & omnis sensus expers, qui non ipse sentiat in se hæreditarium istum morbum, & naturæ suæ vitium, ac corruptelam. Verùm Spiritus sanctus, qui probè novit quid fit in homine, multis Scripturæ sacrę testimonijs docet esse malum hoc originis. Gen.5.3. Cum gigneret, inquit, Adam filium in imagine sua, secundum similitudinem suam. Vide hîc propagatione corruptæ illius imaginis, quæ in Adamo fuit, in ipsius filium Sethum. Iob. 14. 5. Quis edat mundum ex immundo? ne vnus quidem. Vide propagationem immunditiei. Pfal. 51.7. En in iniquitate formatus sum, & in peccato fovit me mater mea. Vide peccatum quod haurimus ex ipso vtero. Iohan.3.6. Quod genitum est ex carne, caro est: Vide propagationem carnis, hoc est, corruptæ naturæ. Rom.5. 12. Sicut per vnum hominem peccatum in mundum introiit, ac per peccatum mors, &c. Vide peccati propagationem. Ephes.2.3. Eramus mus natura filij iræ. Vide natura corruptam, ideoque iræ Dei obnoxiam. Atque hactenus docuimus peccatum originis esse.
units.tr: That this kind of sin exists is too plain to need any inquiry. No one is so dull and so devoid of feeling that he does not sense in himself this hereditary disease and the defect and corruption of his nature. But the Holy Spirit, who knows well what is in man, teaches by many testimonies of Holy Scripture that this evil is from our origin. Gen.5.3. When Adam begot a son, it says, in his own image, according to his likeness. Here see the propagation of that corrupted image which was in Adam into his son Seth. Job 14.5 Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? Not one. See the propagation of uncleanness. Ps. 51.7 Behold, I was formed in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me. See the sin we draw in from the very womb. John 3.6 That which is born of the flesh is flesh. See the propagation of the flesh, that is, of corrupted nature. Rom. 5.12 As by one man sin entered the world, and death by sin, and so on. See the propagation of sin. Eph. 2.3 We were by nature children of wrath. See nature corrupted, and therefore liable to the wrath of God. So far I have shown that original sin exists.

units.la: Nunc videndum quod sit ejus subjectum in quo inhæret. Subjectum originalis peccati, est totus homo quatus quatus est, & quoad animam, & quoad corpus: Id quod docet vel sola illa appellatio veteris hominis, Rom. 6.6. et alibi, qua significatur nihil aliud quàm totus homo corruptus, vel corruptela in toto homine. Quod animus sit vitiatus hoc malo, id docet, primùm ipse sensus, deinde multa Scripturæ testimonia. Gen. 6.5. Cum videret Iehova omne figmentum, id est, cogitationes cordis ejus tantum ad mala esse omni tempore. Gen. 8.21. Quamvis figmentum cordis hominis malum sit ab adolescentia ejus. Eph. 2. 5. Faciendo quæ carni & cogitationibus libebant: Quod corpus sit infectum hac peste. vide Rom. 6. 12. Ne regnet peccatum in mortali vestro corpore. Quod etiam membra corporis singula infecta sint ac vitiata, vide eodem cap. verf. 13. Neque sistite membra vestra arma iniustitiæ peccato. Subjectum huius mali quodnam sit, etiam indicant ipsius appellationes, vt cùm caro vocatur, cùm concupiscentia, cùm lex membrorum, cùm corpus peccati, cùm corpus denique mortis: De subjecto peccati originis hactenus:
units.tr: Now we must see what its subject is, that is, the thing in which it inheres. The subject of original sin is the whole man, in whatever state he is, both as to soul and as to body. This is taught by the very name "the old man", Rom. 6.6 and elsewhere, which means nothing other than the whole man corrupted, or corruption in the whole man. That the soul is vitiated by this evil is taught first by our own experience, and then by many testimonies of Scripture. Gen. 6.5 When the LORD saw that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil at all times. Gen. 8.21 Although the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth. Eph. 2.5 Doing the desires of the flesh and of the thoughts. That the body is infected with this plague, see Rom. 6.12 Let not sin reign in your mortal body. That the individual limbs of the body are also infected and vitiated, see the same chapter, verse 13: Neither yield your members as instruments of unrighteousness to sin. The names given to this evil also indicate what its subject is, as when it is called the flesh, the concupiscence, the law of the members, the body of sin, and finally the body of death. So much for the subject of original sin.

units.la: Nunc ad partes ipsius veniendum, & cùm sit quiddā compositum videndum primùm quæ ejus materia, deinde quæ forma. Materia originalis peccati triplex est, ac prima quidem materię ipsius pars est apostasia illa & defectio, quā in Adamo omnes defecimus: Hanc haurimus ex ipso utero, & omnes nascimur apostatæ & defectores. Quòd autem desectio illa prima, nō tam solius Adami fuerit, quàm nostrūm omnium, primùm illud ratio ipsa docet: fuimus enim tum omnes in lumbis ipsius, & quasi particulæ substantiæ & naturæ primi hominis, quas omnes oportuit simul cum ipso labi ac deficere. Hac ipsa de causa Heb. 7. dicitur Levi, cum nondum natus esset, decimas Melchisedeco persoluisse; quia nimirum in lumbis Abrahami fuit, qui tum decimas illas persoluit Melchisedeco. Factum igitur Abrahami, factum fuit pariter Levi & posterorum ipsius, qui tum in ipsius lumbis fuerunt. Deinde idipsum docet Scriptura, nominatim ille locus qui est. Rom. 5. 12. In quo (subaudi Adamo) omnes peccavimus.
units.tr: Now we must come to its parts. Since it is a kind of compound, we must consider first its matter and then its form. The matter of original sin is threefold. The first part of this matter is that apostasy and defection by which we all fell in Adam. We draw this from the very womb, and all of us are born apostates and defectors. That this first defection belongs not so much to Adam alone as to all of us, reason itself teaches first: for we were all then in his loins, and were as it were parts of the substance and nature of the first man, and all of us had to fall and fail together with him. For this very reason it is said in Heb. 7 that Levi, though not yet born, paid tithes to Melchizedek, because, of course, he was in the loins of Abraham, who then paid those tithes to Melchizedek. What was done by Abraham was therefore done equally by Levi and his descendants, who were then in his loins. Second, Scripture itself teaches the same, especially the passage Rom. 5.12 In whom (understand, in Adam) all have sinned.

units.la: Transijt fateor ac evanuit illa prima apostasia, ut & omnis actio transit; sed tamen aliquo
units.tr: I admit that this first apostasy passed away and vanished, as every action passes away; but nevertheless

units.la: 4 quo modo manere dicitur, quia licet ipsa per se transierit, tamen in reatu suo manet: Omnis enim homo natura reus nascitur primæ illius defectionis. Idem judicium faciendum est de quocunq; peccato, homicidio, adulterio, furto, &c. Quodcunq; enim fit, illud omne manere dicitur quantisper ejus reatus manet. Manet igitur in singulis lapsus & defectio illa prima, tantisper dum reatus ipsius auferatur & abluatur per sanguinem mediatoris. Apostasiam hanc, sive mavis reatum, quocum omnes nascimur, testimonia Scripturæ ostendunt. Rom. 5.15: Vnius offensa multi mortui sunt: Quamobrem etiam reos esse multos oportet ejusdem illius offensæ. Rom. 5.16. Reatus ex vna offensa introijt ad condemnationem. Atq; hæc de prima parte materiæ peccati originalis, defectione nimirum illa & apostasia, quam ex ipso utero nobiscum auferimus & exportamus.
units.tr: it is said to remain in some way, because although it has itself passed away, it remains in its guilt. For every man is born guilty of that first defection by nature. The same judgment must be made of every sin, whether murder, adultery, theft, and so on. For whatever is done, it is said to remain for as long as its guilt remains. So that first fall and defection remains in each of us until its guilt is removed and washed away through the blood of the Mediator. The testimonies of Scripture show this apostasy, or if you prefer, the guilt with which we are all born. Rom. 5.15 Through the offence of one, many have died. Therefore it is necessary that many also be guilty of that same offence. Rom. 5.16 The guilt arising from one offence came to condemnation. So much for the first part of the matter of original sin, namely that defection and apostasy which we carry away and bring with us from the womb.

units.la: Sequitur originalis peccati materiæ pars secunda, quæ est defectus quidam, & vt sic dicam carentia justitiæ originalis, hoc est, rectitudinis illius, in qua fuit creatus homo, efformatæ ad Archetypum & exemplar justitiæ illius & rectitudinis quæ est in ipso Deo creatore. Hominem enim creavit ad imaginem suam sapientem, justum, sanctum. In his enim Apostolus ad Ephes. & ad Coloss. collocat similitudinem illam, quam cum Deo habuit homo in creatione. Carentia haec quam dico justitiae originalis effectum primum est defectionis illius, quam diximus. Defectio enim illa, cujus rei omnes nascimur, privat nos in ipso statim ortu, imo in ipsa conceptione, justitia illa originali & Dei imagine. Hanc partem materiae originalis peccati probat ipse sensus, probant multa Scripturae testimonia; ea intelligo, quae de peccato loquuntur negativè vel privativè: Ea enim omnia satis indicant defectum in nobis esse, & carentiam originalis justitiae. Rom. 3.23. Omnes deficiuntur gloria Dei. Rom. 7.18. Novi non habitare in me, id est, in carne mea bonum: & ibidem paulo post; Perficere quod bonum est non invenio. Rom. 8.7. Intelligentia carnis legi Dei non subjicitur, nam nec potest quidem. 1. Cor. 14. Animalis homo non est capax eorum quae sunt Spiritus Dei, nec potest ea cognoscere. 2. Cor. 3.5. Non sumus ex nobis ipsis idonei ad cogitandum quidquam boni. Ephes. 4.18. Cogitationem habentes obtenebratam, & alienatam à vita Dei. Atque haec de secunda parte materiae peccati originalis, nempe, carentia Originalis justitiæ.
units.tr: Next comes the second part of the matter of original sin, which is a certain defect, and, if I may so call it, the lack of original righteousness, that is, of that rectitude in which man was created, formed after the archetype and pattern of that righteousness and rectitude which is in God the Creator himself. For he created man in his own image, wise, just and holy. For in these things the Apostle, in Ephesians and in Colossians, places that likeness which man had with God in creation. This lack of original righteousness, as I call it, is the first effect of that defection which we have described. For that defection, of which we are all born guilty, deprives us from the very moment of birth, indeed from the very moment of conception, of that original righteousness and the image of God. This part of the matter of original sin is proved by our own experience and by many testimonies of Scripture. I mean those which speak of sin negatively or privatively. For all these sufficiently show that there is a defect in us and a lack of original righteousness. Rom. 3.23 All have fallen short of the glory of God. Rom. 7.18 I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, nothing good dwells. And a little later in the same chapter: How to perform what is good I do not find. Rom. 8.7 The mind of the flesh is not subject to the law of God, for indeed it cannot be. 1 Cor. 2.14 The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, nor can he know them. 2 Cor. 3.5 We are not of ourselves sufficient to think anything good. Eph. 4.18 Having their understanding darkened, and alienated from the life of God. So much for the second part of the matter of original sin, namely the lack of original righteousness.

units.la: Sequitur tertia, quam dicimus esse inclinationem, & qualitatem, originali justitiæ & rectitudini illi, de qua diximus, contrariam, in ejus locum succedentem: Hæc est illa, quā vocant, nativa corruptio; et effectum est secundum apostasiæ illius & defectionis, de qua supra dictum est. Apostasia enim illa primum privat nos originali justitia, sive Dei imagine: Deinde in ejus locum justo Dei judicio introducit qualitatem justitiæ illi contrariam, qua fit, ut natura simus propensi ad omne malum. Qualitatem hanc, & inclinationem contrariam probat ipse sensus, probant etiam testimonia illa Scripturæ, quæcunque de peccato loquuntur affirmatè, vel ut sic dicam, positivè. Rom. 7.7. Concupiscentiam non noscem, nisi lex dixisset, Non concupisces. Rom. 7.23. Video aliam legem in membris meis repugnantem legi mentis meæ. Ephes. 2.3. Facientes quæ carni & cogitationibus libebant. Huc pertinet illud quod supra citavimus ex Gen. 1. & 3. Atque hæc de tertia parte materiæ peccati originalis.
units.tr: Next comes the third part, which we say is the inclination and quality contrary to that original righteousness and rectitude of which we have spoken, and which takes its place. This is what they call native corruption, and it is the effect of that apostasy and defection of which we spoke above. For that apostasy first deprives us of original righteousness, or the image of God. Then, by the just judgment of God, it introduces in its place a quality contrary to that righteousness, by which we are naturally inclined to every evil. This contrary quality and inclination is proved by our own experience, and also by those testimonies of Scripture which speak of sin affirmatively, or, if I may so put it, positively. Rom. 7.7 I would not have known lust, unless the law had said, You shall not covet. Rom. 7.23 I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind. Eph. 2.3 Doing the desires of the flesh and of the thoughts. To this belongs what we cited above from Genesis 1 and 3. So much for the third part of the matter of original sin.

units.la: De defectu & inclinatione, quæ duæ partes sunt materiæ peccati originalis, hoc admonendum est: nullam esse animi nostri facultatem cultatem quæ non laboret vtroque simul isto morbo. Facultates animi nostri præcipuas sacimus, mentem, voluntatem, & affectiones. Duas has posteriores facultates vocabulo cordis intelligit Scriptura: quia nimirum in corde sedem habent voluntas, & affectiones. In mente igitur primum est defectus, siue carentia lucis & cognitionis; est etiam carentia sanctitatis, hoc est, qualitatis, qua ipsa cognitio siue lux affici debet, & reipsa affecta fuit in prima creatione. Lux siue cognitio mentis duplex est, naturalis, & spiritualis: In mente carentia est lucis sive cognitionis naturalis, non quidem in universum, sed ex parte: Manent enim etiam post lapsum, in homine non renato notiones quædam generales, de rebus bonis & malis, quæ jubentur & vetantur in lege Dei: sed illæ quidem hujusmodi, ut homines tantum inexcusabiles reddant, cum & manc\u0303 sint, & corruptæ. Rom. 1, 19. In mente carentia est lucis spiritualis, non ex parte, sed in universum: Nam quod ad ea quæ ad regnum Dei pertinent, ita obcæcatur intelligentia, ut ea non modò non capiat, sed ne capere quidem possit. 1.Cor.2.14. Denique in mente est carentia sanctitatis, quia neque ea quæ intelligit, bene sancteq; intelligit, sed male & impure purè omnia, etiam ea quæ in se & per se bona sunt: Facultas enim intelligendi, etsi non sit plané amissa, tamen sanctitas illa facultatis, in qua creata fuit ad imaginem Dei in lapsu hominis prorsus deperdita est. Carentiam naturalis lucis probat Apost. Rom.1.21. Propterea quod cum Deum cognoverint, tamen ut Deum non glorificaverunt. Posteriora hæc verba innuunt notitiam naturalem mancam esse, statimque evanescere. Carentiam spiritualem docet Apost. 1.Cor.2.14. Animalis homo non est capax eorum quæ sunt Spiritus Dei. Carentiam sanctitatis docet Apost. Rom.8.7. Intelligentia carnis inimicitia est adversus Deum; etiam tum cum intelligit ea, quæ alioqui in se bona sunt & vera. 2.Cor.3.5. Non quod idonei simus ex nobis ipsis ad cogitandum quidquam, subaudi, bene sancteque. Eph.4.18. Cogitationem habentes obtenebratam, & abalienatam à vita Dei: & ibidem versu 23. Renovari verò Spiritu mentis vestræ. Atque hæc de carentia quæ est in mente.
units.tr: On the defect and the inclination, which are the two parts of the matter of original sin, this must be noted: there is no faculty of our soul that does not labour under both of this disease at once. We take the chief faculties of our soul to be the mind, the will, and the affections. Scripture understands the last two by the word "heart", because the will and the affections have their seat in the heart. In the mind, then, there is first a defect, that is, a lack of light and knowledge; there is also a lack of holiness, that is, of the quality with which knowledge or light ought to be endowed, and with which it was in fact endowed at the first creation. The light or knowledge of the mind is twofold, natural and spiritual. In the mind there is a lack of natural light or knowledge, not indeed altogether, but in part: for even after the fall there remain in the unregenerate man certain general notions about good and evil things, which are commanded and forbidden in the law of God; but these are of such a kind that they make men only inexcusable, since they are both diminished and corrupted. Rom. 1.19. In the mind there is a lack of spiritual light, not in part but altogether: for as regards those things that pertain to the kingdom of God, the understanding is so blinded that it not only does not grasp them but cannot even grasp them. 1 Cor. 2.14. Finally, in the mind there is a lack of holiness, because the things it understands it does not understand well and holily, but badly and impurely, all things, even those that are good in themselves and in their own nature: for the faculty of understanding, though not altogether lost, has utterly lost that holiness of the faculty in which it was created in the image of God through the fall of man. The Apostle proves the lack of natural light at Rom. 1.21: "because, when they knew God, they did not glorify him as God." These last words imply that the natural knowledge is imperfect and straightway vanishes. The Apostle teaches the lack of spiritual light at 1 Cor. 2.14: "The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God." He teaches the lack of holiness at Rom. 8.7: "The mind of the flesh is enmity against God", even when it understands those things which otherwise are good and true in themselves. 2 Cor. 3.5: "Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything", supply: well and holily. Eph. 4.18: "having the understanding darkened, and alienated from the life of God"; and in the same place, verse 23: "be renewed in the spirit of your mind." So much for the lack that is in the mind.

units.la: Est deinde qualitas in mente, quæ successit luci & sanctitati, qua in lapsu privata est mens hominis. Luci successerunt tenebræ: Eratis olim tenebræ, nunc autem lux in Domino. Eph.5.8. Sanctitati & rectitudini successit ecfsit impuritas & perverfitas quædam, quæ fatis appa ret, dum dicitur Rom.8.5. Qui secundum carnē sunt quæ carnis sunt sapiunt. Hęc sapientia est ex aliqua qualitate mala 1.Cor.1.18. Sermo crucis ijs qui pereunt stultitia est, & 1.Cor.2.14. Sunt enim ei stultitia. Hoc verbum stultitię arguit perversum mētis judiciū.
units.tr: Next there is a quality in the mind, which has taken the place of the light and the holiness of which the mind of man was deprived in the fall. Darkness has succeeded to light: "You were once darkness, but now are you light in the Lord." Eph. 5.8. Impurity and a certain perversity have succeeded to holiness and rectitude, which is sufficiently evident where it is said: "Those who are according to the flesh mind the things of the flesh." Rom. 8.5. This wisdom comes from some evil quality. 1 Cor. 1.18: "The word of the cross is foolishness to those who perish", and 1 Cor. 2.14: "For it is foolishness to him." This word "foolishness" argues a perverse judgment of the mind.

units.la: Hactenus de carentia & qualitate contraria quæ est in mente. Vtrumque hoc similiter est in voluntate & affectionibus singulis. Carentiam rectitudinis in voluntate innuit Apostolus dum dicit, Perficere bonum non invenio. Rom.7.18. Ad Phil.2.13. Is est qui efficit in vobis, & ut velitis, & ut efficiatis: Præsentiam pravitatis, sive perversitatis voluntatis & effectuum multa docent Scripturæ testimonia: ut illud, Figmentum cordis humani tantummodò malum. Gen.6. Facientes quę carni ac cogitationibus libebant. Ephes.2.3.
units.tr: So far concerning the lack and the contrary quality that is in the mind. Both of these are likewise in the will and in each of the affections. The Apostle hints at the lack of rectitude in the will when he says: "To perform the good I do not find." Rom. 7.18. Compare Phil. 2.13: "It is God who works in you both to will and to do." The presence of depravity, or perversity, of the will and of its acts is taught by many testimonies of Scripture: such as, "The imagination of the thoughts of the human heart is only evil." Gen. 6. "Doing the desires of the flesh and of the thoughts." Eph. 2.3.

units.la: Hoc addo postremò, originis hoc malo magis esse vitiatam & corruptam voluntatem hominis, quàm mentem: Unde illud: Video meliora proboque, (mentis nimirùm beneficio) Deteriora sequor (voluntatis nimirùm maleficio.) Hoc ipsum innuit Apost. Ephes.4.18. dum dicit ignorantiam quæ mentis est ex obduratione cordis existere. Item Rom.1.28. Non visum, inquit, est ijs Deum in notitia retinere: Vide vt obstinata voluntas lucè mentis oppugnet, & tenebras menti inducat.
units.tr: I add this last point: the will of man is more injured and corrupted by this original evil than the mind. Hence the saying: "I see the better things and approve them" (by the benefit of the mind, of course), "but I follow the worse" (by the wickedness of the will, of course). The Apostle himself hints at this at Eph. 4.18, when he says that the ignorance which belongs to the mind arises from the hardening of the heart. Likewise Rom. 1.28: "They did not think it fit," he says, "to retain God in knowledge." See how an obstinate will assails the light of the mind and induces darkness upon the mind.

units.la: Atque hæc haetenus de peccati Originalis materia triplici. Hæ partes materiæ peccati originalis, cum totidem entia sint, & ab authore Deo sint, insitam sibi qualitatem bonitatis habent singulæ: Nam apostasia siue defectio in se ac per se bona est; item carentia originalis justitiæ, cum entis cujusdam rationem habeat, & res quædam sit facta motu illo defectionis; carentia, inquam, à Deo est, & in se bona est; denique qualitas illa positiva, quæ succedit in locum sanctitatis & imaginis Dei, à Deo est tanquam principali efficiente, & per se bona est. Prout igitur triplex est entitas, ita triplex est bonitas.
units.tr: So much, then, concerning the threefold matter of original sin. These parts of the matter of original sin, since they are as many beings and come from God as author, each has an inborn quality of goodness: for apostasy, or defection, is good in itself and by its own nature; likewise the lack of original righteousness, since it has the character of a certain being and is a thing made by that movement of defection, this lack, I say, is from God and is good in itself; finally, that positive quality which succeeds in the place of holiness and the image of God is from God as the principal efficient cause and is good in itself. Therefore, as the being is threefold, so the goodness is threefold.

units.la: Forma originalis peccati sequitur. Est autem ea ἁμαρτία siue pugnantia cum lege Dei, eaque speciali s, vtpote quæ certam peccati speciem constituit: Quemadmodum autem peccati originalis materia triplex est, ita triplex est ἁμαρτία: Vnaquaeque enim materiæ pars suam habet ἀνομίαν, & adventitiam formam, in qua posita est peccati ratio: Apostasia suam habet ἀνομίαν carentia suam, positiva denique qualitas suam. Hæc triplex ἁμαρτία non est à Deo efficiente, verùm à malis instrumentis Diabolo primùm, Adamo deinde, eo denique homine, quisquis is est, qui ex Ada‑ mo nascitur: Nam & nos quoque qui labo‑ ramus hoc morbo hæreditario, ipsi causæ su‑mus morbi nostri. Atque hæc de forma pec‑ cati originis.
units.tr: The form of original sin follows. This is ἁμαρτία, or contrariety to the law of God, and it is specific, inasmuch as it constitutes a certain specific kind of sin. Just as the matter of original sin is threefold, so the ἁμαρτία is threefold: for each part of the matter has its own ἀνομία, and an adventitious form in which the nature of sin is set: apostasy has its own ἀνομία, the lack has its own, and the positive quality has its own. This threefold ἁμαρτία is not from God as efficient, but from evil instruments: first the Devil, then Adam, and lastly that man, whoever he is, who is born of Adam; for we also who labour under this hereditary disease are ourselves the causes of our own disease. So much concerning the form of original sin.

units.la: Nunc ex materia & forma sua definien‑dum est hoc originis peccatum: vt sit pecca‑ tum originis, apostasia siue defectio, carentia justitiæ originalis, & positiua qualitas, ἀντιμάχα siue pugnantes cum lege Dei. Pro genere est triplex materia, pro forma triplex ἀντιμάχα. Vt peccati in genere consequens est reatus in ge‑ nere, sic originalis peccati consequens est re‑ atus specialis: Is autem triplex est prout tri‑ plex est materia, triplex item forma: Nam & apostasia suum quendam reatum habet, & ca‑ rentia suum, & qualitas positiua suum. Rea‑ tus autem vnusquisque meritum est mortis, & pœnæ etiam æternæ.
units.tr: Now from its matter and form this original sin must be defined: original sin is apostasy or defection, the lack of original righteousness, and a positive quality, being contrary to and warring against the law of God. In respect of its genus there is a threefold matter; in respect of its form there is a threefold contrariety. Just as a consequent guilt in general belongs to sin in general, so a specific guilt belongs to original sin: and this guilt is threefold, according as the matter is threefold and likewise the form: for apostasy has a certain guilt of its own, and the lack has its own, and the positive quality has its own. Each guilt, however, is the desert of death, and of eternal punishment also.

units.la: Superest nunc vt, cum constet propagari hoc peccatum originis ex parentibus in libe‑ ros, inquiramus in propagationis modum, quem sic explicabimus. Omninò propagatio peccati aliquo trium modorum fit: propaga‑ tur enim vel per animam, vel per corpus pa‑ rentis, vel denique per ipsius culpam. Per animam parétis propagari peccatum dici non potest, quia ipsa anima parentis non propagatur in liberos, vel secundum se totam, vel secundam partem sui, vt constat: Quare per animam parentis propagatio hujus peccati esse non potest.
units.tr: It remains now that, since it is agreed that this original sin is propagated from parents to children, we inquire into the manner of propagation, which we shall explain thus. Certainly the propagation of sin takes place in one of three ways: for it is propagated either through the soul, or through the body of the parent, or finally through the parent's own fault. That sin can be propagated through the soul of the parent cannot be said, because the soul of the parent is not propagated into the children, either wholly in itself or in any part of itself, as is evident. Therefore propagation of this sin cannot take place through the parent's soul.

units.la: Per corpus parentis propagationem peccati aliquam esse non inepte dicitur, et eam quidem propagationem & in corpus geniti, & in ipsius animam. Propagatio peccati per corpus gignentis in corpus geniti facilè cognoscitur: Nam semen gignentis, quod transmittitur in genitum corruptum est, atque vitiatum peccato: Ex quo sequitur oportere corpus geniti, quod nascitur ex hoc semine corrupto & immundo, corruptum & immundum pariter esse.
units.tr: It is not unfitting to say that there is some propagation of sin through the parent's body, and this propagation both into the body of the begotten and into its soul. Propagation of sin through the body of the begetter into the body of the begotten is easily recognised: for the seed of the begetter, which is transmitted into the begotten, is corrupted and vitiated by sin; from which it follows that the body of the begotten, which is born from this corrupt and unclean seed, must likewise be corrupt and unclean.

units.la: Propagatio peccati per corpus gignentis in animam geniti paulò difficiliorem habet explicationem: Nos tamen eam quæ nobis videtur probabilis trademus. Postquàm per corpus gignentis propagatum est peccatum in corpus geniti, jam corpus genitum cum corruptum fit ac vitiatum. animam jam primùm creatam à Deo, & ipsi momento creationis infusam, contagione quasi sua inficit, eamque eamq; corrumpit. Quæres an quo primùm tempore creatur anima, & infunditur in corpus, pura sit atque integra; postea autem corporis quasi attactu inquinetur? R. id non esse verisimile, cum uno eodemq; temporis puncto, & creetur anima, & infundatur, & corrumpatur. Corruptio autem hæc existit partim ex Dei desertione; partim ex corporis in quod infunditur contagione: Nam Deus eodem momento quo animā creat & infundit, justo suo judicio eam deserit, permittitq; corpori corrumpendam: Ergo eodé momento & temporis puncto anima creatur, infunditur, deseritur à Deo, corrumpitur à corpore.
units.tr: The propagation of sin through the body of the begetter into the soul of the begotten has a somewhat more difficult explanation; nevertheless we will set out the one that seems to us probable. Once sin has been propagated through the body of the begetter into the body of the begotten, the begotten body is then corrupted and defiled. It infects with its contagion, as it were, the soul, which was first created by God and infused into the body at the moment of creation, and so corrupts it. You may ask whether the soul, at the first moment it is created and infused into the body, is pure and whole, and is only afterwards defiled by a kind of touch of the body. I answer: this is not likely, since the soul is both created and infused and corrupted at one and the same point of time. This corruption arises partly from God's desertion and partly from the contagion of the body into which the soul is infused. For God, at the same moment that He creates and infuses the soul, in His just judgment forsakes it and permits the body to corrupt it. Therefore at one and the same moment and point of time the soul is created, infused, forsaken by God, and corrupted by the body.

units.la: Sequitur modus propagationis qui dicitur esse per culpā parentis, quem sic explico. Adamus per culpam illam & offensam suam primam, tanquam per portam quandā, transmisit in omnes posteros suos quidquid fuit in ipso mali: Unde Apost. Rom.5. Per unum hominem (nempe peccantem) introijt peccatum in mundum.
units.tr: There follows the mode of propagation which is said to be through the fault of the parent, which I explain thus. Adam, through that first offence and sin of his, passed on to all his posterity, as through a certain gate, whatever evil there was in himself. Hence the Apostle in Rom. 5: "Through one man (namely, the one who sinned) sin entered into the world."

units.la: Quæres unde fit ista efficacia primi illius peccati, ad propagandum peccatum in omnes & singulos Adami posteros? R. efficaciam illius peccati ex verbo & fœdere quodam Dei esse, quod in prima creatione pepigit cum Adamo, his quasi conceptis verbis. Quòd si steterit homo in ea innocentia in qua creatus est, habebit sibi & suis: sin minùs steterit sed lapsus fuerit, labetur sibi & suis: & quodcunque malum in ipso est, id omne transmittet in posteros suos. Atque hic modus postremus propagationis peccati originalis, cum nitatur authoritate & verbis Apostoli, nobis magis arridet, & moderatis ingeniis omnibus debet satisfacere. Atque hactenus fuit nostra de peccato originali sententia.
units.tr: You may ask: whence comes this efficacy of that first sin, to propagate sin into all and each of Adam's posterity? I answer: the efficacy of that sin rests on the word and a certain covenant of God, which He made with Adam at the first creation, in words as it were set down as follows: "If man stands in that innocence in which he was created, he will have it for himself and his own; but if he does not stand, but falls, he will fall for himself and his own; and whatever evil is in him, he will transmit all of it to his posterity." And this last mode of the propagation of original sin, since it rests on the authority and words of the Apostle, pleases us more, and ought to satisfy all moderate minds. So far our view on original sin.

units.la: Hæreticorum autem & adversariorum, tam veterum, quàm recentiorum, de peccato originali sententiam paucis duntaxat attingemus. Primùm occurrit hæresis Pelagij Monachi, & Cælestij ejus discipuli, qui dixerunt peccatum originis nullum esse; Adamum lapsu suo sibi soli nocuisse, non etiam posteris suis, nisi dicas exemplo. Peccatum quidem posterorum contenderunt esse, non quidè ex propagatione, sed per imitationem prævaricationis Adami.
units.tr: Of the heresies and opposing views, both ancient and recent, concerning original sin, we will touch on only a few. First there arises the heresy of Pelagius the monk and of his disciple Caelestius, who said that there is no original sin: that Adam by his fall harmed himself alone and not also his posterity, unless by way of example. They contended indeed that the sin of the posterity exists, not by propagation, but through the imitation of Adam's transgression.

units.la: Quum objectum fuit iis, infantes modò natos mori, quodquidem non contingeret, nisi in iis esset peccatum originis. Responderunt Adamum moriturum fuisse etsi non peccasset, lege & conditione naturæ. Argumentum Pelagij contra originale peccatum. hoc præcipuum fuit. Quòd si propagetur peccatum necesse est id fieri, vel per animā, vel per corpus, vel per vtrumq;. At non per animam, quia non est tradux animæ: Non per corpus, quia brutum est, neq; in eo sedem habet peccatum proprië & primùm: Non denique per vtrumque, quia non per partes: Ergo non est omninò originale peccatum. Responsio facilis est ex ijs quæ dicta sunt suprà de propagationis modo. Primùm enim propositio non continet plenam modorum propagationis enumerationem: Est enim præter illos modos propagatio quæ dicitur per culpam parentis. Deinde etiam falsitas est in assumptione: nam licet propagatio non fit per animam, tamen per corpus non inepte dicitur propagari peccatum, vt suprà docuimus. Hactenus de Pelagij & Cælestij hæresi.
units.tr: When it was objected to them that infants who have just been born die, which would not happen unless original sin were in them, they replied that Adam would have died even if he had not sinned, by the law and condition of nature. This was the chief argument of Pelagius against original sin: "If sin is propagated, it must be propagated either through the soul, or through the body, or through both. But not through the soul, because there is no traducing of souls; not through the body, because the body is brutish, and sin does not properly and primarily have its seat in it; and finally not through both, because not through parts. Therefore original sin does not exist at all." The answer is easy from what has been said above about the mode of propagation. For first, the major premise does not contain a full enumeration of the modes of propagation: besides those modes there is propagation which is said to be through the fault of the parent. Next, the minor premise is also false: for although propagation does not occur through the soul, nevertheless sin is not inappropriately said to be propagated through the body, as we have taught above. So much for the heresy of Pelagius and Caelestius.

units.la: Scholasticorum deinde de originis peccato variæ fuerunt sententiæ: Quidam originis peccatum in reatu tantùm peccati Adami posuerunt: alij verò tantùm in carentia originalis justitiæ. Petrus Lombardus his confutatis posuit ipsum etiam in positiva qualitate mala. Albertus Pighius, & Ambrosius Catharinus peccatum originale dixerunt nihil aliud esse, quàm primam illam Adami inobedientiam. Ex hac sententia tres alias deduxerunt: quarum prima fuit, Peccatum originis vnum est tantùm & idem in omnibus hominibus. Secunda, Hoc peccatum in Adamo fuit re ipsa, in posteris autem ipsius est per imputationem: Tertia fuit, Nihil est in infantibus, quod revera peccati rationem habeat: Nam reatum, privationem justitiæ, maculam, & similia, poenæ non culpæ rationem habere affirmarunt, nisi forte improprie, quo modo nomen causæ accommodatur effectui.
units.tr: Then among the Schoolmen there were various opinions on original sin. Some placed original sin only in the guilt of Adam's sin; others only in the lack of original righteousness. Peter Lombard, having refuted these, held that it lies also in a positive evil quality.
