Albert Pighius and Ambrosius Catharinus said that original sin is nothing other than that first disobedience of Adam. From this opinion they drew three others. The first was: original sin is one and the same in all men. The second: this sin was in Adam in reality, but in his posterity it is by imputation. The third: there is nothing in infants that truly has the nature of sin; for they affirmed that guilt, privation of righteousness, stain, and the like have the nature of punishment, not of fault, unless perhaps improperly, in the way that the name of a cause is applied to its effect.

units.la: Bellarminus his omnibus succedens reprehendit primùm Lombardi sententiam de positiva qualitate, deinde Pighij tanquâ hæ-reticam damnat. Ex argumentis ijs quibus Lombardi sententiam refutat hoc vnum est & præcipuum. Positivæ illius qualitatis vel Deus author est, vel non: Si est, igitur est author peccati: Si non est, igitur Deus non est author omnium rerum. Ergo non est omninò positiva qualitas. Ad assump. respondemus. In positiva illa qualitate mala duo sunt; primū, qualitas ipsa, quod ens est; secundum, malitia sive ἀτοµία, quæ privatio est. Qualitatis ipsius & entis Deus est author & efficiens principalis: Malitiæ verò & ἀτοµίας non Deus, sed malum instrumentum efficiens est,
units.tr: Bellarmine, following all these, first criticises Lombard's opinion concerning a positive quality, and then condemns Pighius as a heretic. Among the arguments by which he refutes Lombard's view, this one is the chief: "Either God is the author of that positive quality or He is not. If He is, then He is the author of sin; if He is not, then God is not the author of all things. Therefore there is absolutely no positive quality." To the minor premise we reply: in that positive evil quality there are two things: first, the quality itself, which is a being; second, the malice or ἀτοµία, which is a privation. God is the author and principal efficient cause of the quality itself and of the being; but of the malice and ἀτοµία God is not the author: the evil instrument is the efficient cause.

units.la: Tandem Iesuita suam sententiam affert, & in duobus ponit peccatum originis: Primùm, in prima illa Adami inobedientia ab ipso Adamo commissa, non quidem vt erat persona aliqua privata, sed vt personam totius generis humani gerebat: deinde ponit ipsum in carentia doni iustitiæ originalis: Recte quidem duas has statuit originalis peccati partes; sed malè tertiam illam, quæ est positiva qualitas mala, omisit. Atque hæc de adversariorum sententijs, omninòque de peccato originali, sequitur actuale.
units.tr: Finally the Jesuit sets out his own opinion, and places original sin in two things: first, in that first disobedience of Adam committed by Adam himself, not indeed as a private person, but as bearing the person of the whole human race; then he places it in the lack of the gift of original righteousness. He rightly establishes these two parts of original sin, but wrongly omits that third, which is a positive evil quality. So much for the opinions of the opponents, and altogether for original sin; there follows actual sin.

units.la: De Concupiscentia.
units.tr: On Concupiscence.

units.la: CAP. 26.
units.tr: CHAP. 26.

units.la: QVia autem de concupiscentia, quæ tertia pars est peccati originalis, controversia est, ideò de ea nonnihil seorsim erit dicendum. Concupiscētiæ nomē proprie ac primò significat facultatem concupiscendi, quæ est in inferiori anima; nempe sensibili, & naturali: Per tropum autem significat nativam corruptionem, & positivam qualitatem malam, quæ non tantùm est in facultate animæ concupiscibili, sed in omnibus animi humani facultatibus, etiam in ipsa ratione: Nam tam late patet in Scriptura concupiscentiæ nomen quàm veteris hominis, vel carnis: hæc enim nomina à Paulo pro eodem sumuntur, vetus homo, caro, concupiscetia, lex membrorum, nempè, pro tertia illa parte peccati originalis, quæ est positiva qualitas mala. Quòd autem concupiscentia proprie & vere peccatum sit, satis apparet ex Epistola ad Rom. cap. 7. Peccatum, ait, non novi nisi per legem: Concupiscentiam non cognovissem nisi dixisset lex, Non concupisces. Atque hæc in summa de concupiscentia est nostra sententia.
units.tr: Since the controversy concerns concupiscence, which is the third part of original sin, I shall say something about it separately. The name concupiscence properly and primarily signifies the faculty of desiring, which lies in the lower soul, namely the sensitive and natural soul. By a trope, however, it signifies the native corruption and the positive evil quality, which is found not only in the desiring faculty of the soul but in all the faculties of the human mind, even in reason itself. For the name concupiscence is used in Scripture as widely as the names old man or flesh. Paul uses these names for the same thing: old man, flesh, concupiscence, the law of the members. They all mean that third part of original sin which is a positive evil quality. That concupiscence is properly and truly sin is sufficiently clear from the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 7: "I did not know sin except through the law; I would not have known concupiscence unless the law had said, You shall not covet." This, in summary, is our view of concupiscence.

units.la: Pelagius concupiscentiam in naturæ bonis numerat: nam peccatum originis negat. Adversarij Papistæ Concupiscentiæ nomine nihil aliud intelligunt quàm illam ipsam vim, quæ est in anima inferiori; in se quidem rem bonam, vel certè indifferetem, malam autem per accidens & respectu aliquo: nempè, quia jam excussum quasi est frænum originalis justitiæ, quo concupiscentiam oportuit in ordinem cogi; & excusso jam fræno illo, inclinat ad peccandum. De concupiscentia hæc est Tridentini Concilij sententia, quòd verè & proprie peccatum non sit, peccatum autem appelletur, quia ex peccato est, & ad peccatum inclinat. Verùm concupiscentiam peccatum esse manifestius est ex doctrina Pauli, quàm ut probatione vlla indigeat: neque tantum peccatum esse in non renatis; verùm in ipsis quoque renatis. De Concupiscentia hactenus, omninòque de peccato originali.
units.tr: Pelagius counts concupiscence among the goods of nature, for he denies original sin. The Papist adversaries understand by concupiscence nothing other than that very power which lies in the lower soul. In itself it is a good or at least indifferent thing, but it is evil only by accident and in some respect: namely, because the bridle of original righteousness, by which concupiscence ought to have been kept in order, has been as it were cast off, and once that bridle is gone it inclines to sin. This is the sentence of the Council of Trent on concupiscence: that it is not truly and properly sin, but is called sin because it comes from sin and inclines to sin. Yet that concupiscence is sin is clearer from the teaching of Paul than to need any proof; and it is sin not only in the unregenerate but in the regenerate too. So much for concupiscence, and indeed for original sin.

units.la: De Actuali peccato.
units.tr: On Actual Sin.

units.la: CAP. 27.
units.tr: CHAP. 27.

units.la: ACtuale peccatum est fructus & effectus, atq; etiam poena originalis peccati. Actualis divisio prima & summa occurrit in actuale internum, & externum. Internum voco, peccatum animi & facultatum ipsius. Internum partim est omissionis, partim commissionis. Omissionis est priuatio sive carentia bonæ sanctæque motionis: Proficiscitur autem ex carentia originalis iustitiæ. Vt autem carentia illa est omnium animæ facultatum, sic peccatum hoc omissionis interni, est omnium animæ facultatum. De peccato omissionis loquitur Apostolus. 1. Cor. 2. 14. cum dicit, Animalis homo non capit ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei. Vide hic carentiam sanctæ motionis in humana carne: Cujus fundamentum paulò post subjicit, Nec potest ea percipere: Quibus verbis habes carentiam illius potentiæ & facultatis, ex qua est sancta motio.
units.tr: Actual sin is the fruit and effect, and also the punishment, of original sin. The first and chief division of actual sin is into internal and external. I call internal sin the sin of the mind and its faculties. Internal sin is partly of omission and partly of commission. Sin of omission is the privation or lack of good and holy motion, and it arises from the lack of original righteousness. As that lack extends to all the faculties of the soul, so this sin of internal omission extends to all the faculties of the soul. The Apostle speaks of sin of omission in 1 Cor. 2:14, when he says: "The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God." Here you see the lack of holy motion in the human flesh, and he adds its foundation shortly after: "nor can he know them." In these words you have the lack of that power and faculty from which holy motion comes.

units.la: Sequitur internum commissionis: Est autem motio animi mala pravaque: proficiscitur autem ex tertia parte peccati originis, nempe positiua qualitate mala, siue nativa corruptione. Quemadmodum autem positiua qualitas est omnium animi facultatum, sic internum commissionis peccatum est omnium animi facultatum. De peccato hoc passim loquitur Scriptura Rom.7.5. Cum essemus in carne, affectiones peccatorum per legem existentes vigebant in membris nostris, ad fructum ferendum morti. Vbi tria habentur, primum caro, quae est originale peccatum: Secundum, affectiones, quibus intelligitur internum commissionis peccatum. Tertio loco habes fructum καρπόν, quo quidem intelligitur peccatum actuale externum: Eadem illa tria habes Ephes.2.3. Facientes quae carni ac cogitationibus libebant. Primum est caro, peccatum originale: Secundum est cogitatio carnis, quod internum commissionis est peccatum: Tertium est facere, quod quidem est externum peccatum. Eadem illa habes Iacob. 1.15. Concupiscentia postquam concepit, parit peccatum. Concupiscentia est originale peccatum; Conceptio est actuale internum: Partus ejus est externum peccatum. De peccato actuali interno hactenus.
units.tr: Next comes internal sin of commission. This is an evil and perverse motion of the mind, and it arises from the third part of original sin, namely the positive evil quality or native corruption. As the positive quality extends to all the faculties of the mind, so internal sin of commission extends to all of them. Scripture speaks of this sin everywhere, Rom. 7:5: "When we were in the flesh, the passions of sins, which were through the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit [καρπόν] for death." Here are three things. First, the flesh, which is original sin. Second, the passions, by which internal sin of commission is understood. Third, you have the fruit [καρπόν], by which external actual sin is understood. You find these same three in Eph. 2:3: "doing the desires of the flesh and of the thoughts." The first is the flesh, original sin; the second is the thought of the flesh, which is internal sin of commission; the third is the doing, which is external sin. You find the same things in Jas. 1:15: "Concupiscence, when it has conceived, brings forth sin." Concupiscence is original sin; conception is internal actual sin; its birth is external sin. So much for internal actual sin.

units.la: Sequitur externum actuale, quod est peccatum corporis & membrorum ipsius: hoc quoque peccatum, partim est omissionis, partim commissionis. Omissionis externum est, cum non fiunt quae facienda sunt: Proficiscitur ex omissionis interno: Utque omissionis internum est omnium animi facultatum, sic & omissionis externum est omnium corporis membrorum. De hoc peccato testimonium est Rom. 7. 9. Non facio bonum quod volo. Sequitur commissionis externum: Est autem cum fiunt quae non sunt facienda, prosiciscitur autem ex interno commissionis peccato: estque omnium membrorum corporis, ut & internum commissionis est omnium animi facultatum. De hoc peccato testimonia Scripturae sunt, quae supra attulimus, & alia multa. Rom. 7. 19. Malum quod nolo, hoc ago.
units.tr: Next comes external actual sin, which is sin of the body and its members. This sin too is partly of omission and partly of commission. External omission is when the things that ought to be done are not done. It arises from internal omission, and as internal omission extends to all the faculties of the mind, so external omission extends to all the members of the body. Rom. 7:18 bears witness to this sin: "I do not do the good that I will." External commission is when the things that ought not to be done are done. It arises from internal sin of commission, and it extends to all the members of the body, just as internal sin of commission extends to all the faculties of the mind. The testimonies of Scripture to this sin are those we have already cited, and many others. Rom. 7:19: "The evil that I do not will, that I do."

units.la: Commissionis externum duplex est, partim ex errore & ignorantia est, partim ex cognitione. Ex ignorantia est, cum quis ignorans aliquid committit: Tale fuit peccatum Pauli 1. Tim. 1. 13. Nam ignorans id faciebam, fidei expers. Ignorantia haec vel juris est, vel facti. Ignorantia juris est ignoratia voluntatis Dei: De hoc peccato loquitur Christus. Luc.
units.tr: External commission is twofold: part of it comes from error and ignorance, part from knowledge. It comes from ignorance when someone commits something without knowing it. Such was Paul's sin, 1 Tim. 1:13: "For I did it in ignorance, in unbelief." This ignorance is either of law or of fact. Ignorance of law is ignorance of the will of God. Christ speaks of this sin in Luke: [Luc.]

units.la: Qui vero non novit voluntatem Domini suì, & fecit digna plagis, cædetur plagis paucis. Hæc quoque fuit Pauli ignorantia cum blasphemavit, & persequutus est Ecclesiam Christi. 1.Timoth.1. Ignorantia factì est, cum quis etiam quod facit ignorat: Ignorat autem quis factum suum, vel cum per negligentiam facit aliquid, vel cum per eum fit aliquid fortuna & casu, sive mavis, inevitabili Dei providentia: Exemplum peccati per negligentiam est, ut si gubernatoris negligetia amittatur navis: Exemplum peccati ex fortuna sive providentia Dei est, ut si quis jacto lapide praetereūtem aliquem, de quo ipse ne cogitavit quidem, interficiat. Hujus peccati causa constitutæ sunt in veteri populo civitates refugij. Num. 35.23. Hactenus de peccato commissionis externo, quod est ex errore sive ignorantia.
units.tr: "But he who did not know his lord's will, and did things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes." This was also Paul's ignorance when he blasphemed and persecuted the Church of Christ, 1 Tim. 1. Ignorance of fact is when someone does not know what he is doing, either because he does something through negligence, or because something is done through him by chance and accident, or, if you prefer, by the inevitable providence of God. An example of sin through negligence is the loss of a ship through the negligence of the pilot. An example of sin through chance or the providence of God is someone who, by throwing a stone, kills a passer-by whom he did not even think of. Cities of refuge were established among the ancient people for the sake of this sin, Num. 35:23. So far concerning external sin of commission that comes from error or ignorance.

units.la: Sequitur peccatum commissionis externum, quod ex cognitione committatur. Est autem cum quis sciens aliquid mali perpetrat. De hoc loquitur Christus. Luc. 12.47. Ille servus qui novit voluntatem Domini sui, nec facit, cædetur multis plagis. Hoc peccatum vel infirmitatis est, vel contumaciæ. Infirmitatis exemplum habemus in Petro, qui ter Dominum suum metu persequutionis & mortis abnegavit. Contumaciæ exemplum habemus in Iuda proditore. Peccatum contumaciæ rursus est vel hypocriticum, vt cum quis contumax est non aperte, sed sub larua hypocrisios. Hoc peccatum redarguitur ab Apostolo. Rom. 2. 5. Pro duritia tua, inquit, & corde quod resipiscere nescit, thesaurizas tibi iræ in diem iræ. Deinde contumacia est aperta, cum nimirum ad contumaciam accedit superbia in ipsum Deum: Vnde dicitur aliquid perpetrari elata manu Num. 15. 30. Aperta hæc contumacia & superbia, vel est aduersus secundam legis tabulam, vt est apertum homicidium, apertum adulterium: & tum quidem peccatum est minus grave. At intolerabilis est illa superbia, quæ est aduersus primam legis tabulam. Atque in hoc genere est hæresis primum, cum quis ex superba pertinacia contra veritatem, sententiam aliquam defendit.
units.tr: Next is external sin of commission that is committed with knowledge. This is when someone knowingly perpetrates some evil. Christ speaks of this in Luke 12:47: "That servant who knew his lord's will and did not do it shall be beaten with many stripes." This sin is either of weakness or of obstinacy. We have an example of weakness in Peter, who three times denied his Lord for fear of persecution and death. We have an example of obstinacy in Judas the traitor. Obstinate sin is again either hypocritical, when someone is obstinate not openly but under the mask of hypocrisy. The Apostle rebukes this sin, Rom. 2:5: "Because of your hardness, and your heart that does not know how to repent, you store up for yourself wrath for the day of wrath." Then obstinacy is open, when pride toward God himself is added to the obstinacy; hence something is said to be done with a high hand, Num. 15:30. This open obstinacy and pride is either against the second table of the law, as in open murder or open adultery, and then the sin is less grave; but that pride which is against the first table of the law is intolerable. In this class is heresy, first of all, when someone from proud stubbornness defends some opinion against the truth.

units.la: Omnium peccatorum, de quibus hactenus dictum, proprietas est, quòd eorum aliquem pœnitere possit. Vnde sequitur altera proprietas, quòd remissibilia sint omnia. At vero si ad cognitionem, superbi i, proterviam, accedat mera malitia in Spiritum sanctum, intus illuminantem & docentem, jam peccatum tum exurgit, quod vocant peccatum in Spiritum sanctum: cujus hæc est proprietas, quòd cum qui sic peccat peccati sui pœnitere non possit: Unde sequitur hoc peccatum irremissibile esse. Remitti autem non potest, non quòd ejus magnitudo superet magnitudinem gratiæ & misericordiæ Dei in Christo; sed quia hujus peccati pœna est finalis impœnitentia, quæ ipsi justo Dei judicio infligitur. De hoc vide. Matth. 12.31. Heb.6.4.5. & cap. 10.26. & 1.Iohan. 5.16. Atque hæc de peccato actuali hactenus.
units.tr: The property of all the sins so far discussed is that any of them can be repented of. From this follows the second property, that all of them are remissible. But if to knowledge there is added pride, obstinacy, and pure malice against the Holy Spirit, who inwardly illumines and teaches, then a sin arises which they call the sin against the Holy Spirit. Its property is that the one who sins in this way cannot repent of his sin, and from this it follows that this sin is irremissible. It cannot be forgiven not because its greatness exceeds the greatness of God's grace and mercy in Christ, but because the penalty of this sin is final impenitence, which is inflicted by God's just judgment. See Matt. 12:31, Heb. 6:4-5, chapter 10:26, and 1 John 5:16. So much for actual sin.

units.la: De peccato actuali sententia adversariorum sequitur. Controversia maximè est de divisione peccati actualis, in peccatum mortale, & veniale. Nos quidem affirmamus omne peccatum natura sua esse mortale, hoc est, habere consequentem reatum mortis æternæ: Si quod autem veniale fit, hoc est impetret veniam à Deo, id esse non quòd tale fit naturâ suâ, sed quòd veniale fit ex sola Dei misericordia in Christo Iesu. Hanc nostram sententiam confirmant multa Scripturæ loca. Rom.6. 23. Stipendia peccati mors. De peccato in genere loquitur & de morte æterna. Mat.5.19. Quisquis solverit unum ex mandatis hisce minimis, & ita docuerit homines, minimus vocabitur in regno coelorum, hoc est, nullus erit in coelis. Vide peccata etiam minima mereri exclusione ex regno coelorum. Deut.27.26. Execrabilis quisquis non manserit in omnibus quae sunt scripta in libro legis. Ergo nullum est peccatum, quod non meretur execrationem sive maledictionem. Nam cum denunciat execrationem omnibus, ne vnum quidem vel minimum aut levissimum excipit.Iacob.2.10. Quisquis totam legem seruaverit, offenderit autem in vno, omnibus tenetur. Ergo vnum aliquod peccatum contra legem ad missum, transgressorem facit totius legis, & reum peccatorum omnium, quae contra legem quovis modo committuntur: Vt non sit opus metiri reatum ex vno aliquo, coque minimo peccato. Nam etiam minimum peccatum habet consequentem reatum maximorum peccatorum, vt manifeste apparet ex hoc Iacobi loco. Matth.5.26. Nequaquam exibis illinc, quousque reddideris vltimum quadrantem. Ergo Deus in exigendis rationibus suis, rationem habet minutissimarum partium peccati,& peccatorum minimorum. Praecepto decimo prohibentur vel levissimi concupiscentiae motus. Mat.22.27. Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo,& ex tota anima tua, & ex tota cogitatione tua: Ergo lege præcipitur exactissima obedientia, in qua nihil desideretur: Quamobrem qui peccat etiam in minimo, legem transgreditur: Transgressionem autem legis sequitur maledictio æterna, nisi redemptio fiat per Christum Iesum. Matth. 5. 18. Vsquedum præterierit cœlum & terra, iota unum aut unus apex nequaquam præterierit ex lege, vsq; dum omnia facta fuerint. Ecce non præterit unum iota, vel unus apex, hoc est, vel minutissima pars legis violatæ, pro qua non fit satisfaciendum, vel per nosipsos, vel per mediatorem. Atque hæc de sententia nostra.
units.tr: Concerning actual sin, the view of our opponents follows. The controversy is chiefly over the division of actual sin into mortal and venial. We indeed affirm that every sin is by its nature mortal, that is, carries with it the liability to eternal death. If any sin is venial, that is, obtains pardon from God, this is not because it is such by its own nature, but because it is venial solely by the mercy of God in Christ Jesus. Many passages of Scripture confirm this our view. Rom. 6:23 The wages of sin is death. This speaks of sin in general and of eternal death. Matt. 5:19 Whoever breaks one of these least commandments, and so teaches men, will be called least in the kingdom of heaven, that is, will be in heaven at all. See that even the smallest sins deserve exclusion from the kingdom of heaven. Deut. 27:26 Cursed is whoever does not abide by all the things written in the book of the law. Therefore there is no sin which does not deserve execration or malediction, for when he pronounces the curse upon all, he excepts not even one sin, or the smallest or slightest. James 2:10 Whoever keeps the whole law but offends in one point is guilty of all. Therefore one sin committed against the law makes a man a transgressor of the whole law and guilty of all the sins that are committed against the law in any way, so that there is no need to measure guilt by one sin, and that the smallest. For even the smallest sin carries with it the guilt of the greatest sins, as is plainly evident from this passage of James. Matt. 5:26 You will by no means get out until you have paid the last penny. Therefore God, in exacting his accounts, takes into reckoning the smallest parts of sin and the least of sins. By the tenth commandment even the slightest motions of desire are forbidden. Matt. 22:37 You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. Therefore the law requires the most exact obedience, in which nothing is wanting. Wherefore whoever sins even in the smallest matter transgresses the law, and the transgression of the law is followed by eternal curse, unless redemption is made through Jesus Christ. Matt. 5:18 Till heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke of the law will pass away until all things have been fulfilled. Behold, not one iota or one stroke passes, that is, not even the smallest part of the violated law, for which satisfaction must be made either by ourselves or by the Mediator. So much for our view.

units.la: Adversarij, peccatum actuale ex gravitate sua, vel ex reatu pœnæ distribuentes, aliud faciunt mortale, aliud veniale. Mortale definiunt peccatum, quod extinguit charitatem sive iustitiam, nosque Deo inimicos reddit, ac proinde reos mortis æternæ. Veniale autem definiunt peccatu, quod non extinguit charitatem sive iustitiam, neque inimicos Deo reddit; sed iustitiam quam in charitate collocant, levi quodam modo afficit, & tanquam nævus quidam leviter ipsam deformat: quamobrem facili negotio veniam impetrat, & levi aliquo supplicio expiatur, cuiusmodi est in hac vita: Oratio Dominica repetita, Tunsio pectoris, Satisfactio, vel pœnitentia à Sacerdote imposita, vel etiam quam vltro homines ipsi sibi imponunt. Post hanc vitam est ignis purgatorius, quo expiantur peccata venialia, quæ non sunt expurgata in hac vita, illis, de quibus diximus, piaculis.
units.tr: Our opponents, dividing actual sin according to its gravity or the liability to punishment, make one sin mortal and another venial. They define mortal sin as that which extinguishes charity or righteousness and renders us enemies of God, and therefore liable to eternal death. Venial sin they define as that which does not extinguish charity or righteousness, nor make us enemies of God, but affects the righteousness which they place in charity in a slight way, and deforms it lightly, like a blemish; wherefore it obtains pardon with little difficulty and is expiated by some light punishment, such as in this life: the repeated Lord's Prayer, beating the breast, satisfaction, or penance imposed by the priest, or even what men impose on themselves of their own accord. After this life there is purgatorial fire, by which the venial sins are expiated which were not purged in this life by those expiations of which we have spoken.

units.la: Duplex faciunt peccatum veniale: Primum veniale esse dicunt, quia tale est ex natura & substantia sua, cujusmodi est: Verbum otiosum, Risus immodicus: Deinde veniale dicunt, quia tale est, non quidé ex natura sua, sed ex imperfectione, cum nimirùm peccatum natura sua mortale est; quia autē impersectum est quoad quantitatem mali, ideò veniale est. Imperfectionem hanc duplicem esse dicunt: vel enim imperfectio est ratione voluntatis, nempe cùm admotionem concupiscentiæ interiorem non accedit plenus voluntatis consensus. In hoc genere venialis peccati numerant motus quoscunque interiores malos, qui citiùs oriuntur in animo quàm mens de ijs deliberare potuit, quiq; non obtinent plenum voluntatis consensum, vt sunt motus cupiditatis, iræ, invidiæ, &c: deinde imperfectio est ratione materiæ circa quam versatur peccatum, nempe, cum materia ita parua est, ita exilis, vt peccatum ipsum veniale reddat, verbi gratia, cum quis fururatur vnū obolum, vel quid tale minutum, quo vel nihil, vel parum laeditur proximus, aut violatur charitas.
units.tr: They make venial sin twofold. First, they say it is venial because it is such by its nature and substance, such as an idle word or immoderate laughter. Second, they say it is venial because it is such not by its nature but by imperfection, since sin is by nature mortal; but because it is imperfect in respect of the quantity of evil, it is therefore venial. This imperfection they say is twofold. Either the imperfection lies in the will, namely when full consent of the will does not accede to the interior incitement of desire. In this class of venial sin they count any interior evil motions which arise in the mind more quickly than the mind could deliberate about them, and which do not obtain full consent of the will, such as motions of lust, anger, envy, and so on. Or the imperfection lies in the matter with which the sin is concerned, namely when the matter is so small and so slight that it makes the sin itself venial; for example, when someone steals a single obol, or some such trifle, by which the neighbour is harmed little or not at all, or charity is violated.

units.la: Peccatum veniale conantur confirmare variis argumentorum generibus. Primùm testimonijs tum Scripturæ, tum Ecclesiæ: deinde rationibus: In quibus omnibus refutandis nos non statuimus immorari. Pro peccato veniali citant Matth.12.32. Quisquis suerit loquutus adversus Spiritum sanctum non remittetur ei neque in hoc sæculo, neque in futuro. Ergo, inquiunt, est peccati aliquod genus, quod remittetur post hanc vitam: Illud autem est veniale, quod quidem expiatur igni purgatorio. Verùm phrases huius quæ est apud Matth. interpres est Marcus, cap. 3. 29. Quicunque, inquit, blasphemaverit in Spiritum sanctum, non habet remissionem in æternum; sed tenetur æterno judicio. Ergo cum dicit Matthæus, Neque in hoc sæculo, neque in futuro, idem est ac si dixisset, Non remittetur ei in æternum.
units.tr: They try to confirm venial sin by various kinds of arguments. First by testimonies, both of Scripture and of the Church; then by reasons. In refuting all of these we do not intend to linger. For venial sin they cite Matt. 12:32 Whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come. Therefore, they say, there is a kind of sin which will be forgiven after this life, and that sin is venial, which is expiated by purgatorial fire. But the phrase in Matthew is interpreted by Mark, chapter 3:29: Whoever, he says, blasphemes against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness for ever, but is liable to eternal judgment. Therefore when Matthew says, neither in this age nor in the age to come, it is the same as if he had said, will not be forgiven him for ever.

units.la: Adferunt deinde locum qui est Matth.5.22. Quicunque irascitur fratri suo temerè, tenebitur judicio: Quicunque verò dixerit fratri suo Racha, tenebitur consessu: Quisquis autem dixerit Fatue, tenebitur gehenna ignis. Tria, inquiunt, hic peccata sunt, quorum tertium duntaxat adjudicatur gehennæ sive inferis: Quamobrem duo præcedentia leviori aliquo supplicio expiantur, & venialia sunt. Respondeo hunc locum innuere inæqualitatem, primum peccatorum, deinde pœnarum, atque earum quidem spiritualium & infernalium, quas hic expressit Christus per allusionem ad pœnas politicas & civiles, easq; inæquales.
units.tr: They next adduce the passage at Matt. 5:22 Whoever is angry with his brother without cause shall be liable to judgment; whoever says to his brother Raca shall be liable to the council; but whoever says Fool shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna. There are three sins here, they say, of which only the third is adjudged to Gehenna or hell; therefore the two preceding are expiated by some lighter punishment and are venial. I answer that this passage points to the inequality, first of the sins, and then of the punishments, and indeed of the spiritual and infernal punishments, which Christ expressed here by an allusion to political and civil penalties, and those are unequal.

units.la: Tum rationibus agunt. Nemo, inquiunt, negat peccatum aliud alio levius esse sua natura: Ergo, annon quod levius est, veniale est sua natura? Respondeo, Non sequitur: quia vel levissimum quodque promeretur æternam damnationem suapte natura, licet fortasse non gravissimam: Nam pœnarum inæqualitatem non negamus.
units.tr: Then they argue by reasons. No one, they say, denies that one sin is by its nature lighter than another. Therefore, is not that which is lighter by its nature venial? I answer: it does not follow, because even the slightest sin deserves eternal damnation by its nature, although perhaps not the most grievous; for we do not deny the inequality of punishments.

units.la: Deinde annon peccatum aliud alio, quod ad quantitatem attinet imperfectius est? Annon igitur quod imperfectius est veniale est, vel propter ipsam imperfectionem? Respondeo, Non sequitur, quia vel imperfectissimum quodque meretur mortem æternam: Aut si veniale sit, tale est non propter imperfectionem nem, sed propter Christum ipsiusque satisfactionem.
units.tr: Next, is not one sin more imperfect than another as regards quantity? Is not, therefore, that which is more imperfect venial, or venial on account of the imperfection itself? I answer: it does not follow, because even the most imperfect sin deserves eternal death; or if it is venial, it is such not on account of imperfection but on account of Christ and his satisfaction.

units.la: Tertiò: Annon, inquiunt, illud peccatum quod non destruit justitiam, charitatem, & inhærentem gratiam, illud, inquam, annon veniale est? At sunt quædam peccata, quæ non destruunt vel extinguunt justitiam: Ergo sunt quædam venialia; Probatur assumptio. Septies in die cadit justus & iterum resurgit: Ecce peccat quis, etiam tum cum non cessat esse justus. Respondeo, Prop. falsa est: Nam etiam illud peccatum quod non extinguit gratiam Christi, & sanctitatem inhærentem, illud, inquam, suapte natura mortale est; Quòd autem veniale fit, atque etiam non extinguat sanctitatem, illud non ipsi peccato, sed Dei in Christo misericordiæ imputandum est.
units.tr: Thirdly: is not, they say, that sin which does not destroy righteousness, charity, and inherent grace, I say, is not that sin venial? But there are certain sins which do not destroy or extinguish righteousness; therefore there are some venial sins. The minor premise is proved: "A righteous man falls seven times a day and rises again." Behold, a man sins even when he does not cease to be righteous. I answer: the proposition is false. For even that sin which does not extinguish the grace of Christ and the inherent holiness is by its nature mortal; that it is venial, and does not even extinguish holiness, is to be imputed not to the sin itself but to the mercy of God in Christ.

units.la: De Peccato in Spiritum sanctum controversia.
units.tr: The controversy about the sin against the Holy Spirit.

units.la: CAP. 28.
units.tr: CHAP. 28.

units.la: ADversarij peccati hujus sex species numerant: Prima est præsumptio, qua quis nimis præsumit de gratia Dei & fide, dum interea operibus suis fidem abnegat: Hunc hominem reprehendit Iacobus in Epistola sua capite 2. ver. 14. & deinceps. Secunda est desperatio, præsumptioni contraria: Hoc peccatum fuit Caini & Iudæ. Tertia est ignitæ veritatis impugnatio. Huc spectat blasphemia in Spiritum sanctum, quod peccatum fuit Pharisæorum. Quarta est fraternæ gratiæ invidentia: Hoc peccatum fuit Iudæorum, qui gratiam Christi gentibus invidebant. Quinta est obstinatio, cum quis obstinato animo, scienter in peccato perseverit. Sic peccavit Pharao, sic obstinati Iudæi. Sexta finalis impœnitentia, quæ tum est cum quis cum contemptu Sacramenti pœnitentiæ & satisfactionis a ministerio Ecclesiastico impositæ, mortem obit. De hoc peccato intelligunt locum illum qui est. 1. Iohan. 5. 16. Est peccatum ad mortem, non pro illo dico ut roget. His omnibus modis peccari adversus Spiritum sanctum, tanquam fontem bonorum, peculiariter dicunt, atq; etiam peccari inexpiabiliter: & peccata hæc irremissibilia vocari, sed non eodem sensu omnia: Verum quinque priora ideo irremissibilia vocari dicunt, quia raro & difficulter remittuntur: quemadmodum raro & difficulter quis ducitur eorum pœnitentia. Postremum autem solum, quod est finalis impœnitentia, irremissibile proprie vocari censent; quod neque in hac vita, neque post hanc vitam, remittitur. Atque hæc est eorum sententia.
units.tr: The opponents of this sin list six kinds of it. The first is presumption, by which someone presumes too much upon the grace of God and faith, while meanwhile denying faith by his works. James rebukes this man in his Epistle, chapter 2, verse 14 and following. The second is despair, the opposite of presumption. This was the sin of Cain and of Judas. The third is the attack upon the truth once known. To this belongs blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, which was the sin of the Pharisees. The fourth is envy of the grace of one's brothers. This was the sin of the Jews, who begrudged the grace of Christ to the Gentiles. The fifth is obstinacy, when someone persists in sin knowingly, with an obstinate mind. So Pharaoh sinned, and so the obstinate Jews. The sixth is final impenitence, which occurs when someone dies with contempt for the sacrament of repentance and for the satisfaction imposed by ecclesiastical ministry. They refer the passage in 1 John 5:16 to this sin: "There is a sin unto death; I do not say that he should pray for it." They say that sinning against the Holy Spirit, as the fount of good things, is done in all these ways, and that these sins are called inexpiable, and that they are called unforgivable, though not all in the same sense. The first five, they say, are called unforgivable because they are seldom and with difficulty forgiven, just as it is rare and difficult to bring anyone to repentance for them. But the last alone, final impenitence, they judge to be properly called unforgivable, since it is not remitted either in this life or after it. This is their view.

units.la: Iohan. 5. 16. sententia de peccato in Spiritum sanctum.
units.tr: John 5:16: the opinion about the sin against the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Nos autem non didicimus ex Scripturis, nisi vnum peccatum esse, quod sic vocetur: quod Matth.12.31. Marc.3.29. Luca. 12.10. vocatur blasphemia in Spiritum sanctum. Ad Hebræos 6. describitio ejus habetur, tanquam apostasiæ cap. 6.4. & deinceps, item 10.26. 27. Sic etiam describitur. 2. Petri.2.20. & deinceps. 1. Iohan. 5. 16. vocatur peccatum ad mortem: Quod ad alias quas enumerant peccati hujus species, ex ijs quædam hujus peccati, quam blasphemiam dicimus, consequentia sunt, ad ipsumque pertinent: Nam desperatio est pœna hujus peccati, vt & impœnitentia finalis: Obstinatio est in natura hujus peccati; positum est enim in obstinata malitia. Quod ad reliquas quas numerant species, non video qua ratione vocentur peccata in Spiritum sanctum: Præsumptio enim, quid aliud est quàm hypocrisis? Fraterne vero gratiæ invidentia, peccatum est adversus proximum proprie & secundam legis tabulam. Ergo illud maneat vnum duntaxat esse peccatum, quod sic vocetur, nempe blasphemia in Spiritum sanctum, vel apostasiam à gratia Spiritus semel accepta: Idè enim reipsa sunt blasphemare adversus Spiritum sanctum & deficere cere à gratia accepta. Non nego tamen hoc peccatum quod substantia vnum est, augeri: Tum enim ad summum pervenit, cum fertur adversus totam veritatem, quæ est secundum pietatem. Deinde dicimus hoc peccatum quod vnum est, irremissibile esse, non quòd vel raro vel difficulter ipsi remittatur: sed quòd non remittatur ipsi omnino, cum non possit omnino cum pœnitere peccati sui, qui sic peccavit. Concrescit enim illi cor in eam duritiem, quæ in posterum resolvi vel emolliri nunquam poterit, idque justo Dei judicio. Quòd autem simpliciter sit irremissibile hoc peccatum, apparet ex verbis illis Domini in Evangelio suo, quæ supra citavimus: Nam cum apud Matthæum dicitur: Non remittetur ei neque in hoc sæculo, neque in futuro: Et apud Marcum, Non habet remissionem in æternum, sed tenetur æterno judicio: Annon hæc verba omnem remissionis spem adimunt, neque difficultatem tantùm significant, sed impossibilitatem omnimodam: vt mirum sit Rhemenses illos vim istam verborum Domini tam impudenter elevare. Ad Heb. 6. ἀδύνατον & impossibile esse dicit, vt, qui sic peccat, renovetur per resipiscentiam: Addit causam gravissimam & summè necessariam: Vt qui, inquiens, rursum crucifigat sibimet ipsi filium Dei, hoc est, quantum in se est id facit.
units.tr: We, however, have learned from the Scriptures that there is only one sin called by this name, which in Matthew 12:31, Mark 3:29 and Luke 12:10 is called blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. Its description is given in Hebrews 6 as apostasy, chapter 6:4 and following, and likewise in 10:26-27. It is also described in 2 Peter 2:20 and following. In 1 John 5:16 it is called a sin unto death. As for the other kinds of this sin which they enumerate, some of them follow from this sin, which we call blasphemy, and belong to it: for despair is the punishment of this sin, as is final impenitence. Obstinacy lies in the nature of this sin, for it consists in obstinate malice. As for the remaining kinds they list, I do not see on what ground they are called sins against the Holy Spirit. For what else is presumption but hypocrisy? Envy of a brother's grace is a sin against the neighbour, properly against the second table of the law. Therefore let it remain that there is only one sin rightly so called, namely blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, or apostasy from the grace of the Spirit once received; for these are in fact the same thing, to blaspheme against the Holy Spirit and to fall away from the grace received. I do not deny, however, that this sin, which is one in substance, can be increased; it reaches its height when it is directed against the whole truth which accords with godliness. Further, we say that this sin, being one, is unforgivable, not because it is seldom or only with difficulty forgiven, but because it is never forgiven at all, since the one who has sinned in this way cannot fully repent of his sin. For his heart hardens into such a stubbornness that it can never afterwards be softened or melted, and this by the just judgment of God. That this sin is absolutely unforgivable appears from the words of the Lord in his Gospel which we cited above. For when Matthew says, "It shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world nor in the world to come," and Mark, "He has no forgiveness for ever, but is liable to eternal judgment," do not these words take away all hope of forgiveness, signifying not merely difficulty but total impossibility? It is a marvel that the Rhemists so impudently lower the force of the Lord's words. In Hebrews 6 the author says it is impossible [ἀδύνατον] for one who sins in this way to be renewed through repentance, and he adds the most serious and most necessary reason: because such people crucify again for themselves the Son of God, that is, as far as they are concerned, they do it.

units.la: Quod quò melius intelligamus statuendum est discrimen inter alia quæcunque peccata, & peccatum hoc in Spiritum sanctum, quoad eorum remissionem & expiationem attinet. Alijs expiandis sufficit illud vnicum Christi sacrificium semel oblatum, & ipsius vis ad ea expianda & expurganda in perpetuum sese extendit: At verò vbi semel quis peccavit in Spiritum sanctum, & profanavit illum sanguinem, jam vis illius sanguinis & sacrificij sic ab ipso profanati, non extedit se ad expiationem illius peccati. Quare vt expietur illud peccatum opus est novo aliquo sacrificio, quod nullum vnquam dari potest: Quòd si enim daretur, vel daretur Christus rursum crucifigendus, vel daretur alia aliqua hostia: Sed non dari potest Christus rursum crucifigendus, vt neque dari potest alia quævis hostia, vt dicitur ad Heb. 10.26. Non adhuc pro peccatis reliqua est hostia. Ergo peccatum hoc expiari nunquâ potest, cum nulla possit dari nova hostia: Atque hæc est causa impossibilitatis summè necessaria.
units.tr: To understand this better, we must note the distinction between all other sins and this sin against the Holy Spirit, as far as their forgiveness and expiation are concerned. For other sins, the one sacrifice of Christ offered once is sufficient to expiate them, and its power extends to expiating and cleansing them for ever. But when someone has once sinned against the Holy Spirit and profaned that blood, the power of that blood and sacrifice, thus profaned by him, no longer extends to the expiation of that sin. Therefore, for this sin to be expiated, some new sacrifice would be needed, and none such can ever be given. For if one could be given, either Christ would have to be crucified again, or some other victim would have to be given. But Christ cannot be crucified again, and no other victim whatever can be given, as is said in Hebrews 10:26: "There remains no longer a sacrifice for sins." Therefore this sin can never be expiated, since no new victim can be given; and this is the most necessary cause of the impossibility.

units.la: Adversarij, nominatim Rhemesfes, in hunc Apost. locum annotantes, impossibilitatem
units.tr: The opponents, the Rhemists by name, commenting on this apostolic passage, interpret this impossibility

units.la: istam sic interpretantur: Pœnitentiam, siue renovationem, siue peccati expurgationem duplicem statuunt: Priorem, & eam quidem facilem ac non laboriosam, in Baptismo & per Baptismum: purgationem nimirùm peccatorum omnium quæ Baptismum antecesserunt per simplicem & facilem illam in Baptismo lotionem. Posteriorem dicunt pœnitentiam siue peccatorum purgationem eam, quæ fit in Sacramento, quod vocant, pœnitentiæ, & in hoc Sacramento hæc purgatio ijs est peccatorum eorum, quæ commissa sunt post Baptismum, & ea quidé difficilis ac laboriosa, vt quę opus habeat jejunijs, precibus, satisfactionibus, & afflictionibus corporalibus. Hac distinctione posita, impossibilem interpretantur renovationem respectu pœnitentiæ illius, renouationis, & purgationis peccati, quæ fit in Baptismo: Impossibile enim esse dicunt vt peccatū commissum post baptismum iterato aliquo baptismo expurgetur: Non enim sumus rebaptizandi. Quod ad posteriorem illam pœnitentiam & renouationem, possibilitatem in ea statuunt, dicuntque peccatum etiam gravissimum post baptismum commissum, posteriori hoc renouationis & pœnitentiæ modo expiari posse. Volunt itaque Apostolum tacitè peccantes post Baptismum ablegare ad Sacramentum, quod vocant, pœnitentiæ: ad hoc vt vi illius sacramenti ipsorum peccatum expietur, ipsique renoventur: Verùm hac sua interpretatione detorquent Scripturam sacram suo exitio: Nam illud certum est omnimodam impossibilitatem renovationis hoc loco significari ab Apostolo, id quod ratio addita facilè convincit.
units.tr: in this way. They posit a twofold repentance, or renewal, or cleansing of sin. The first, which is easy and not laborious, is in and through Baptism: namely the cleansing of all the sins that preceded Baptism, by that simple and easy washing in Baptism. The second they call repentance, or cleansing of sins, which takes place in what they call the sacrament of penance; in this sacrament this cleansing is of those sins committed after Baptism, and it is difficult and laborious, requiring fasts, prayers, satisfactions and bodily afflictions. With this distinction laid down, they interpret the impossible renewal as referring to that repentance, renewal and cleansing of sin which takes place in Baptism. For they say it is impossible that a sin committed after baptism should be cleansed by a second baptism; we are not to be rebaptized. As for that later repentance and renewal, they hold that there is possibility in it, and say that even the most grievous sin committed after baptism can be expiated by this second mode of renewal and repentance. They therefore want the Apostle to be understood as silently sending those who sin after Baptism to what they call the sacrament of penance, so that by the power of that sacrament their sin may be expiated and they themselves renewed. But by this interpretation they twist Holy Scripture to their own destruction. For it is certain that the Apostle here signifies a total impossibility of renewal, as the reason he adds easily proves.

units.la: Postremò ex illo Iohannis loco supra citato constat peccatum hoc irremissibile esse, idque proprië, neque vllo modo remissibile: Non enim orandum esse pro eo peccato dicit Iohannes. Quòd si non orandum nulla spes est vel resipiscentiæ vel remissionis. Non ignoro quid hic respondeant Rhemenses: nempè peccati, quod est ad mortem, nomine intelligi finalem impœnitentiam: Finalis impœnitentia non remittitur, quia non est pœnitentia, ac proinde pro ea non est orandum post mortem hominis qui sic peccavit, & mortuus est in impœnitentia cum contemptu nimirum sacramenti pœnitentiæ. Licere autem dicunt orare pro aliis peccatis etiā post mortem eorum qui peccarunt. Hæc quoque detortio est Scripturæ: neque enim orationem intelligit Apostolus vel concipiendâ vel non concipiendam post mortem ejus qui peccavit, sed non concipiendam pro homine vivo & vidente, postquam jam deprehensum est certis argumentis eum peccare ad mortem, ut pro Iuliano Apostata, pro quo viuo non orauit Ecclesia, imò contra vivum orauit, postquam jam certis argumentis deprehendit eum ad mortem peccare, id est, in Spiritum sanctum blasphemum esse. Praetereo hic locum Petri supra citatum, quo quidem non difficultas, sed mera impossibilitas renouationis, resipiscentiae, & remissionis significatur, cum dicitur, Facta est eorum conditio posterior, deteriior priore. Et posteà cum dicitur, sed accidit eis quod vero proverbio dici solet, Canis reuersus est ad suum ipsius vomitum, & sus lota ad volutabrum coeni. Atque haec de secunda hac controversia, omninoque de peccato dicta sunto.
units.tr: Lastly, from that passage of John cited above it is clear that this sin is unforgivable, and properly so, and cannot in any way be forgiven. For John says that one should not pray for that sin. If one should not pray for it, there is no hope either of repentance or of forgiveness. I am not unaware what the Rhemists reply here: namely that by the sin unto death is meant final impenitence; final impenitence is not forgiven, because it is not repentance, and therefore one should not pray for it after the death of the one who sinned and died impenitent, with contempt, that is, for the sacrament of penance. They say, however, that it is lawful to pray for other sins even after the death of those who have sinned. This also is a distortion of Scripture. For the Apostle does not mean that prayer is either to be offered or not to be offered after the death of the one who sinned, but that it is not to be offered for a living man who is in view, once it has been established by certain evidence that he sins unto death. So the Church did not pray for Julian the Apostate while he was alive; rather it prayed against him while he was living, once it had established by certain evidence that he sinned unto death, that is, that he was a blasphemer against the Holy Spirit. I pass over here the passage of Peter cited above, in which not difficulty but the sheer impossibility of renewal, repentance and forgiveness is signified, when it is said: "Their last state has become worse than the first." And afterwards, when it is said: "But it has happened to them according to the true proverb, The dog has returned to his own vomit, and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire." So much concerning this second controversy, and concerning sin in general.

units.la: De Fide iustificante
units.tr: Of Justifying Faith

units.la: CAP. 29.
units.tr: CHAP. 29.

units.la: VOcatio efficax fit per legem primùm, deinde Euangelium. Legis doctrina universa revocari potest ad hunc syllogismum. Maledictus quinon manserit in omnibus quae scripta sunt in libro legis huius vt faciat ea: At ego non mansi in ijs, Ergo ego maledictus. Propositio huius syllogismi est vox legis, & comminatio illa quæ adjecta est fœderi operû, quod sic cōcipitur: Hoc fac & viues; quòd si non feceris, morieris. Assumptio huius syllogismi, est conscientiæ cuiusque applicantis ad quemque legis transgressionem. Conclusio similiter conscientiæ est, applicantis ad quemque iustam pro peccato pœnam & maledictionem. Syllogismus hic non tam vocationis est, quàm præparationis nostri ad vocationem efficacem, quæ proprie fit per doctrinam Evangelij: Nam doctrinâ legis quæ comprehenditur hoc syllogismo consternimur & afficimur sensu miseriæ nostræ, qui sensus primus est ad salutem gradus.
units.tr: Efficacious calling comes first through the law and then through the Gospel. The whole teaching of the law can be reduced to this syllogism: Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things written in this book of the law to do them. But I have not continued in them. Therefore I am cursed. The major premise of this syllogism is the voice of the law, and the threat attached to the covenant of works, which is framed thus: Do this and you shall live; but if you do not, you shall die. The minor premise is the conscience of each person applying to himself the transgression of the law. The conclusion is likewise the conscience's application to himself of the just punishment and curse for sin. This syllogism belongs not so much to calling as to our preparation for efficacious calling, which properly comes through the doctrine of the Gospel. For by the teaching of the law, which is contained in this syllogism, we are struck down and seized with a sense of our misery, and this sense is the first step towards salvation.

units.la: Doctrina autem Euangelij comprehendi potest hoc syllogismo, Quisquis crediderit, justificabitur ac viuet: At ego credo: Ergo ego justificabor ac viuam. Propositio est vox Euangelij, vel ipsius Dei vocantis. Ea enim continetur prima vocationis efficacis pars, quæ nihil aliud est, quàm promulgatio quædam fœderis gratuiti, cuius formula habetur in hac propositione. Assumptio non est quidem naturalis conscientiæ, verùm supernaturalis fi-dei dei cuiusque applicantis ad quemque Iesum Christum foederis Mediatorem, & eum quidem crucifixum primum, deinde glorificatū. Conclusio similiter fidei est, applicantis ad quemq; beneficia Christi, iustitiam ipsius, salutem per ipsum. Hic syllogismus propriè vocationis est, cuiusque propositio prima pars vocationis est. Assumptio autem & conclusio secunda. Cum autem assumptio & conclusio sint fidei nostrae, qua nos quasi respondemus Deo vocati, profectò non immeritò dicemus secundam vocationis efficacis partem, nihil aliud esse, quàm fidem. Quamobrem locus de fide, generali loco de vocatione subalternus erit.
units.tr: The doctrine of the Gospel, however, can be comprehended in this syllogism: Whoever believes will be justified and will live. But I believe. Therefore I shall be justified and live. The major premise is the voice of the Gospel, or of God himself calling. For this contains the first part of efficacious calling, which is nothing other than a proclamation of the free covenant, whose formula is found in this proposition. The minor premise is not indeed the work of natural conscience, but of supernatural faith, by which each person applies to himself Jesus Christ, the Mediator of the covenant, first crucified and then glorified. The conclusion likewise belongs to faith, which applies to each person the benefits of Christ, his righteousness, and salvation through him. This syllogism properly belongs to calling, and its major premise is the first part of calling, while the minor and conclusion are the second. Since the minor premise and conclusion belong to our faith, by which we, as it were, answer God when called, we shall rightly say that the second part of efficacious calling is nothing other than faith. Therefore the locus on faith will be subordinate to the general locus on calling.

units.la: Sequitur ergo vt de fide dicamus, & ea quidem propriè & simpliciter sic dicta, hoc est, de fide quam iustificantem vocant. Nam quòd ad alias fidei species, quæ vulgò enumerantur, vt est fides mortua, &c. eæ sic vocantur non simpliciter, sed κατά τι, & cum adiectione, fides mortua, fides temporaria, &c. In fidei itaque explicatione primùm occurrit eius obiectum. Obiectum in genere est quicquid in verbo Dei continetur, hoc est, vniuersa veritas Dei. In specie verò, & propriè obiectum est Iesus Christus cum beneficijs suis.
units.tr: It follows, then, that we should speak of faith properly and simply so called, that is, of the faith which they call justifying. For the other kinds of faith that are commonly enumerated, such as dead faith, etc., are not so called simply, but κατά τι, with an addition: dead faith, temporary faith, etc. In explaining faith, then, its object comes first. The object in general is whatever is contained in the Word of God, that is, the whole truth of God. In particular, and properly, the object is Jesus Christ with his benefits.

units.la: Christi & beneficiorum ipsius duplex est consideratio: primùm enim Christus cum beneficijs suis consideratur vt offertur in verbo & sacramentis: hoc est, vt offertur in speculo nō tam Christus ipse, quàm imago quædam ipsius. De speculo hoc verbi & sacramenti habes 1. Cor. 13. 12. Cernimus enim nunc per speculum & per ænigma. Item 2. Cor. 3. 18. Nos autem omnes retecta facie gloriam Domini, vt in speculo intuentes, in eandem imaginem transformamur ex gloria in gloriam. Christus sic consideratus, nihil aliud est, quàm Christus prædicatus verbo, & in sacramento repræsentatus. Nos (ait) prædicamus Christum crucifixum 1. Cor. 1. 23. Euangelium enim prædicatum Christum quodammodo ob oculos ponit. Gal. 3. 1. Quibus ob oculos Iesus Christus prius fuerat depictus, inter vos crucifixus. Deinde consideratur Christus extra speculum hoc verbi & sacramenti, sicuti est in sese. De Christo sic considerato loquitur Apostolus 1. Cor. 13. 12. Tunc autem coram cernemus: Et 1. Ioh. 3. 2. Scimus autem fore, vt cùm ipse patefactus fuerit, similes ei simus, quoniam videbimus eum sicuti est.
units.tr: There is a twofold consideration of Christ and his benefits. For first Christ with his benefits is considered as he is offered in the Word and the sacraments, that is, as he is offered in a mirror, not so much Christ himself as a certain image of him. Concerning this mirror of Word and sacrament you have 1. Cor. 13. 12. For now we see through a mirror and in a riddle. Likewise 2. Cor. 3. 18. But we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory. Christ considered in this way is nothing other than Christ preached in the Word and represented in the sacrament. "We," he says, "preach Christ crucified" 1. Cor. 1. 23. For the Gospel, preached, sets Christ before our eyes in a certain way. Gal. 3. 1. Before whose eyes Jesus Christ had earlier been painted, crucified among you. Then Christ is considered outside this mirror of Word and sacrament, as he is in himself. The Apostle speaks of Christ thus considered in 1. Cor. 13. 12. But then we shall see face to face. And 1. Joh. 3. 2. We know that when he shall be revealed we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.

units.la: Vt duplex est Christi consideratio, ita ipsius cognitio & apprehensio duplex est. Prior fides vocatur, posterior <bl>s</bl>ive aspectus. De utroque hoc habes 2.Cor.5.7. Per fidem enim incedimus non per aspectum. Duo hi cognoscendi & apprehendendi modi conueniunt quidem inter se natura & essentia. Utrumque enim est cognitio & apprehensio Christi: differunt quantitate, &, vt loquuntur, secundū maius & minus: Nam fidei cognitio minor est, vt & apprehensio: Vnde 1.Cor.13.9. Ex parte cognoscimus. Aspectus vero cognitio & apprehensio major est, adeoque perfecta, vt quæ futura sit in altero sæculo. De hac persecta cognitione dicitur ibidem ver. 10. Postquam autem advenerit quod perfectum est. Et versu 12. Tunc vero cognoscam prout edoctus fuero.
units.tr: As Christ is considered in a twofold way, so the knowledge and apprehension of him is twofold. The former is called faith, the latter sight (or aspect). You have both in 2. Cor. 5. 7. For we walk by faith, not by sight. These two modes of knowing and apprehending agree with each other in nature and essence. For each is a knowledge and apprehension of Christ; they differ in quantity, or, as people say, in more and less. For the knowledge of faith is smaller, as is its apprehension. Hence 1. Cor. 13. 9. We know in part. But the knowledge and apprehension of sight is greater, and so perfect, as it will be in the other age. Of this perfect knowledge it is said in the same place, verse 10: When that which is perfect has come. And in verse 12: Then I shall know even as I have been known.

units.la: His positis & cognitis facile perspicitur, quod fit fidei speciale & primum objectum: nempe, Iesus Christus cum beneficijs suis, & is quidem vt sese offert in verbo & sacramentis. Vel objectum fidei est ipsum verbum, siue promissiones quæ de Christo fiunt, quod idéest. Ex hoc sequitur quo tempore cessabit hæc verbi prædicatio, & sacramentorum administratio, cessaturam pariter & fidem hanc per quam nunc incedimus: vide 1.Cor.13. Tum quod ex parte est abolebitur. Notandum denique de hoc objecto fidei, quòd speciale sit, specialiter & sigillatim oblatum mihi, tibi, & alijs singulis hominibus. Nam licet verba generaliter concipiantur, specialiter tamen sunt accipienda, quasi dicta mihi, tibi; vel de me, de te. De objecto fidei hactenus.
units.tr: With these points laid down and understood, it is easily seen what is the special and primary object of faith: namely, Jesus Christ with his benefits, and indeed as he offers himself in the Word and the sacraments. Or the object of faith is the Word itself, or the promises which are made concerning Christ, which is the same thing. From this it follows that at the time when this preaching of the Word and administration of the sacraments ceases, this faith also, through which we now walk, will cease likewise: see 1 Cor. 13, where it says: "that which is in part will be done away." Finally, it should be noted about this object of faith that it is special, offered specially and individually to me, to you, and to each other person. For although the words are expressed in general terms, they are nonetheless to be taken specially, as if said to me, to you, or about me, about you. So much for the object of faith.

units.la: Nunc de subjecto ejus dicendum est, nempe, in quo est, & à quo procedit. Subjectum fidei est animus humanus, & in animo humano rationales ac principales facultates: eas volo mentem primum, deinde voluntatem. Nam quòd ad alias & inferiores animi facultates & affectiones, fides non tam dicitur in ijs infidere, quâ eas sanctificare, & incitare ad bonum, & tanquam domina, regere. Unde dicitur, Fide purgatis cordibus eorum. Quòd autem fides sit mentis, apparet ex ijs appellationibus quæ fidei tribuuntur passim in Scriptura: vt cum vocatur cognitio, notitia, visio: vt cum dicitur, Cernimus nunc in speculo. Quòd autem fit in voluntate, apparet ex eo quod dicitur Rom. 10. 10. Corde enim creditur ad justitiam: Et Ephes. 3. 17. Vt inhabitet Christus per fidem in cordibus vestris: Sedes enim voluntatis cordi tribuitur. Porrò ipsa nomina, quibus fides insignitur in Scriptura, satis convincunt ejus sedem esse, non tantùm in mente, sed in voluntate & corde: vt cum apprehēsio dicitur, vt cū amplexus quidā vocatur, & alijs id genus nominibus, quæ functione cordis & voluntatis significat. De subjecto fidei hactenus.
units.tr: Now we must speak of its subject, namely, in whom it is and from whom it proceeds. The subject of faith is the human soul, and in the human soul its rational and principal faculties, which I call the mind first and then the will. For faith is not said to dwell in the other and lower faculties and affections of the soul so much as to sanctify them, to stir them to good, and to rule them as a mistress. Hence it is said, "by faith purifying their hearts." That faith belongs to the mind appears from the names given to faith throughout Scripture: when it is called knowledge, understanding, vision, as when it is said, "We now see in a mirror." That it is in the will appears from what is said in Rom. 10. 10: For with the heart one believes unto righteousness; and Eph. 3. 17: That Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith; for the seat of the will is attributed to the heart. Moreover, the very names by which faith is marked in Scripture sufficiently prove that its seat is not only in the mind but in the will and heart: as when it is called apprehension, as when it is called a certain embrace, and other names of this kind, which signify a function of the heart and will. So much for the subject of faith.

units.la: Nunc propius ad ipsius naturam, & naturæ partes accedamus. Prima pars fidei, est mentis cognitio siue intellectio, qua mens simpliciter sentit etiam, vel propositionem Euangelij aliquam, intelligit, nominatim autem propositione illā quæ est in Syllogismo illo Evangelico quem supra adduximus: Nam propositio illius syllogismi est quasi compēdium quoddam totius Evangelii. Ab hac parte, nempe, cognitione, tanquam primaria, nominatur fides passim in Scripturis.
units.tr: Now let us come closer to its nature and the parts of that nature. The first part of faith is the knowledge or understanding of the mind, by which the mind simply perceives and understands some proposition of the Gospel, and in particular that proposition which is in the evangelical syllogism we cited above; for the proposition of that syllogism is a kind of summary of the whole Gospel. It is from this part, namely knowledge, as the primary one, that faith is commonly named in the Scriptures.

units.la: Secunda fidei pars est ejusdem mentis judicium, sive, ut vocatur vulgò, assensio. De judicio hoc loquitur Scriptura passim, ut 1. Cor. 2.15. Spiritualis dijudicat quidem omnia. 1. Ioh. 4.1. Probate spiritus an ex Deo sint. Iudicium hoc duplex est, primum veritatis, deinde bonitatis. Veritatis judicium est, cum mēs assentitur propositioni Euangelicæ, quòd vera fit. De hoc judicio vide Ioh. 3.33. Qui recipit ejus testimonium, is obsignavit quòd Deus verax sit. 1. Tim. 1.15. Fidus est hic sermo, & modis omnibus dignus quem amplectamur, &c. Deniq; judicium hoc veritatis colligitur ex omnibus Scripturæ locis, in quibus fit mentio veritatis verbi diuini. Iudicium bonitatis est cum assentitur mens, rei, quæ est in propositione Euangelica, quòd bona sit, ac proinde sequenda. Nam sciendum est propositiones omnes Euangelicas practicas esse, vt vocantur, in quarum nuda speculatione & contemplatione non est inhærendū; sed quæ trahendæ sunt ad mores & vitam quotidianā. De judicio hoc bonitatis habes Rom. 7. 16. Consentio legi quod bona sit. 1. Cor. 1. 18. Sermo de cruce nobis qui servamur potentia Dei est: & ibidem postea versu 24. Prædicamus, inquit, Christum vocatis Dei potentiam ac Dei sapientiam. Atque hæc de judicio hoc duplici, quod diximus esse generalis illius propositionis syllogismi Evangelici. De quo utroque, hoc postremò tenendum est, quòd non tantum generale sit, verùmetiam speciale, quo ego judico vera esse de me, bona esse mihi, quæ dicuntur in Evangelio. Nam, vt supra diximus, de me, de te, specialiter dicta intelligenda sunt, quæ in Evangelio annunciatur: Estque hoc speciale judicium proprie illa quæ vocatur πληροφορία. Hanc sequitur πεποίθησις sive fiducia, quæ cordis est ac voluntatis, de qua proximè dicemus.
units.tr: The second part of faith is the judgment of that same mind, or, as it is commonly called, assent. Scripture speaks of this judgment throughout, as in 1 Cor. 2:15: The spiritual person indeed judges all things. 1 John 4:1: Test the spirits whether they are from God. This judgment is twofold: first of truth, then of goodness. The judgment of truth is when the mind assents to an evangelical proposition, that it is true. On this judgment see John 3:33: He who receives his testimony has set his seal to this, that God is true. 1 Tim. 1:15: This saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance, and so on. Finally, this judgment of truth is gathered from all the passages of Scripture in which mention is made of the truth of the divine Word. The judgment of goodness is when the mind assents that the thing in the evangelical proposition is good, and therefore to be followed. For it must be understood that all evangelical propositions are practical, as they are called, and are not to be rested in by mere speculation and contemplation, but are to be drawn into conduct and daily life. Of this judgment of goodness you have Rom. 7. 16. I consent to the law that it is good. 1. Cor. 1. 18. The word of the cross is to us who are being saved the power of God; and in the same place afterwards, verse 24. We preach, he says, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God to those who are called. And these are the points about this twofold judgment, which we have said belongs to that general proposition of the evangelical syllogism. Concerning both, this must finally be held: that it is not only general but also special, by which I judge that the things said in the Gospel are true of me and good for me. For, as we said above, what is announced in the Gospel must be understood as said of me, of you, specially. And this special judgment is properly that which is called [πληροφορία], full assurance. It is followed by [πεποίθησις], or confidence, which belongs to the heart and will, and of which we shall speak next.

units.la: Sequitur itaque tertio loco electio siue apprehensio voluntatis, quæ tum est, cum voluntate siue corde suo quisq; peculiariter ad se applicat id quod judicauit, primùm verû, deinde bonum, non tantùm in genere, sed etiam in specie. Apprehensio hæc siue applicatio, est in assumptione & conclusione syllogismi illius Euangelici suprà à nobis adducti. Nam postquàm mens vidit & judicavit generalem illam illius syllogismi propositionem, jam voluntas cujusque peculiariter applicat ad vnumquemque in assumptione & conclusione, bona illa de quibus fuit generalis illa propositio. De hac apprehensione habes 1. Tim. 6. 12. Apprehende vitam æternam. Phil. 3. Experiens an quoque apprehendam. 1. Tim. 1. Fidus est hic sermo, & modis omnibus dignus quem amplectamur: Denique appellationibus illis omnibus, quibus in Scripturis significatur voluntatis electio, tertia hæc fidei pars intelligenda venit. Ab hac parte fides, speciali fiducia, πεποίθησις nuncupatur: Natura enim fidei maximè in ea cernitur.
units.tr: Next, in third place, comes election, or the apprehension of the will. This happens when each person, with his will or heart, applies to himself in particular what he has judged to be true, first, and then good, not only in general but also in particular. This apprehension or application takes place in the minor premise and conclusion of that gospel syllogism which we adduced above. For once the mind has seen and judged the general proposition of that syllogism, the will then applies to each person, in the minor premise and conclusion, those good things of which the general proposition spoke. You have this apprehension in 1 Tim. 6.12: "Lay hold on eternal life." Phil. 3: "If I may by any means apprehend that for which I was also apprehended." 1 Tim. 1: "This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that we embrace." Finally, all those expressions by which the choice of the will is signified in the Scriptures belong to this third part of faith. From this part faith is called, by a special confidence, <bl>πεποίθησις</bl> [confidence]; for the nature of faith is seen chiefly in it.

units.la: His expositis facilè erit colligere definitionem fidei. Est enim fides Christi cum beneficijs suis, vt in verbo & sacramento offertur, primùm mentis cognitio; deinde voluntatis siue cordis apprehensio. In hac definitione habemus fidei objectum primùm, deinde subjectum, tertiò partes. Sub mentis cognitione intelligo quoque mentis judicium & assensionem, eamque duplicem, de qua suprà dictum est.
units.tr: Having set these things out, it will be easy to gather a definition of faith. Faith is the mind's knowledge of Christ with his benefits, as they are offered in the word and sacrament, first, and then the apprehension of the will or heart. In this definition we have first the object of faith, then the subject, and thirdly its parts. Under knowledge of the mind I understand also the judgment and assent of the mind, and this is twofold, as was said above.

units.la: Sciendum est fidem sic à nobis definitam improprie accipi pro functione & opere fidei cum fides propriè sit habitus (vt vocatur) infusus, siue qualitas sancta primùm mentis, deinde voluntatis siue cordis. Qualitas autem hæc in mente, quid aliud est quàm lux illa, de qua passim in Scriptura? Eratis olim tenebræ, nunc autem lux in Domino, Eph.5.8. Illuminatis oculis mentis vestræ, vt sciatis quæ sit spes illa vocationis ipsius. Eph.1.18. Deus qui dixit vt è tenebris lux splendesceret, is est qui splenduit in cordibus nostris ad præbendum lumen cognitionis gloriæ Dei in facie Iesu Christi.2.Cor.4.6. Nobis autem Deus ea reuelauit per Spiritum suum: Spiritus enim omnia scrutatur, etiam profunditates Dei.
units.tr: It must be noted that faith, as we have defined it here, is taken improperly, for the function and work of faith; for faith properly speaking is an infused habit (as it is called), or a holy quality, first of the mind and then of the will or heart. But what else is this quality in the mind than that light spoken of throughout Scripture? "You were once darkness, but now are you light in the Lord" (Eph. 5.8). "The eyes of your mind being enlightened, that you may know what is the hope of his calling" (Eph. 1.18). "God, who said that light should shine out of darkness, is he who has shone in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor. 4.6). "But God has revealed these things to us through his Spirit; for the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God."

units.la: Lux autem ista mentis, quæ prima fidei pars est, videtur non tantùm instauratio lucis naturalis, quæ in Adami lapsu labefactata est; sed etiam lux quędam supernaturalis per Spiritum Christi indita menti, ad hoc vt mens intueri possit ac videre ea quæ superant omnem cognitionem naturalem. Vnde Eph.3. 18.19. Vt in charitate radicati & fundati valeatis assequi cum omnibus sanctis, quæ sit illa longitudo, & latitudo, profunditas, & sublimitas, & cognoscere charitatem illam Christi omni cognitione superiorem. Hanc in Adamo, in prima creatione, ante lapsum ipsius, non fuisse exi-stimo. Adami enim ante lapsum omnis notitia mentis, vt sancta, ita naturalis videtur fuisse: ipsius Dei naturalis cognitio videtur fuisse: rerum creatarum omnium naturalis cognitio videtur fuisse. Neque Deũ in Christo Mediatore ante lapsum vidit, neq; opus fuit vt videret. Præterea hæc lux, quam dico, accenditur in mente nostra ex Christi mediatoris facie inspecta quasi in speculo Evangelii 2.Cor.3.18. Nos omnes retecta facie gloriam Domini, ut in speculo intuentes, in eandem imaginem transformamur ex gloria in gloriam: Item 4.6. Ad præbendum lumen cognitionis gloriæ Dei in facie Iesu Christi. Adamus autem ante lapsum suum, ut nihil audivit de Evangelio Christi, ita non vidit facie ipsius in illo Evangelii speculo. Adhęc 1.Cor. 15.45.
units.tr: This light of the mind, which is the first part of faith, seems to be not only a restoration of the natural light which was weakened in the fall of Adam, but also a certain supernatural light, placed in the mind through the Spirit of Christ, so that the mind may look upon and see those things which surpass all natural knowledge. Hence Eph. 3.18-19: "That you, being rooted and grounded in love, may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the length and breadth, depth and height, and to know the love of Christ which surpasses all knowledge." I do not think this light was in Adam in the first creation, before his fall. For before the fall all of Adam's knowledge, insofar as it was holy, seems also to have been natural: his natural knowledge of God himself seems to have been such, and his natural knowledge of all created things seems to have been such. Nor did he see God in Christ the Mediator before the fall, nor was there any need for him to see him. Moreover, this light, of which I speak, is kindled in our mind from beholding the face of Christ the Mediator, as in a mirror of the gospel (2 Cor. 3.18): "We all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are changed into the same image from glory to glory." Likewise 2 Cor. 4.6: "To give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ." But Adam before his fall, since he had heard nothing of the gospel of Christ, so did not see his face in that mirror of the gospel. Also 1 Cor. 15.45.

units.la: 1 Cor. 15.45. de Adamo dicitur: Factus est homo prior in animā viventem sive animal vivens: de Christo autem, Posterior Adam factus est Spiritus vivificus. Ex quibus verbis conspicitur discrimen inter Adamum & Christum: quòd Adamus factus sit ψυχικος duntaxat & naturalis, sanctus tamen; Christus vero factus sit spiritualis & supernaturalis: Nam spiritualia supernaturalia sunt. Ex hoc rursus discrimine colligimus spiritualem iltam lucem ac supernaturalem, quam solius Christi, hoc est, secundi Adami beneficio habemus, in Adamo ante lapsum non fuisse. Nam ibidem ver. 48. & 49. coelestis sive spiritualis nostra haec conditio ascribitur Christo. Sed de his hactenus & parce.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 15.45 says of Adam: "The first man Adam was made a living soul" (ψυχὴν ζῶσαν [psychēn zōsan]); but of Christ: "The last Adam was made a life-giving spirit" (πνεῦμα ζῳοποιοῦν [pneuma zōopoioun]). From these words we see the difference between Adam and Christ: Adam was made merely psychical [ψυχικός, psychikos] and natural, yet holy; but Christ was made spiritual and supernatural, for spiritual things are supernatural. From this difference again we gather that the spiritual and supernatural light which we have by the benefit of Christ alone, that is, of the second Adam, was not in Adam before the fall. For in the same place, verses 48 and 49, this heavenly or spiritual condition of ours is ascribed to Christ. But let this suffice for these matters, and be brief.

units.la: In voluntate sive corde deinde fides est ἐνέργεια sive efficacia supernaturalis ipsi indita per Spiritum Christi, de qua Coloss.2.12. Per fidem Dei efficaciter agentis. Hanc quoque ἐνέργειαν putamus non insitam fuisse in Adami corde ante lapsum, adducti ijsdem rationibus quas supra attulimus. Cum autem lux illa mentis & efficacia cordis supernaturales sint, sequitur pariter functiones lucis illius atque efficacię, nempe mentis cognitionem, & cordis apprehensionem supernaturales esse. Quā obrem ad definitionem illam fidei supra à nobis adductam, hanc particulam (supernaturalis) tanquam postremam adjicimus: ut sit fides justificans Christi cum beneficiis suis in verbo & sacramento oblati mentis cognitio & voluntatis apprehensio, non sancta modo, sed etiam supernaturalis. Ita quidem à nobis definita est fides, ut supra admonuimus, ut fidei nomen accipitur pro functione & opere fidei: sic enim vulgò Theologi eam definiunt, sic etiam in Scripturis sanctis nomen fidei fere solet accipi, nempe, pro functione & opere fidei τὸ ἔργον τῆς πίστεως vocatur 2.Thes.1.3. Quòd si autem cuiquam magis placeat descriptio fidei propriè, & pro habitu infuso acceptæ, sic eam quoque habeat: ut sit fides lux mentis & ἐνέργεια cordis supernaturaliter ipsis inditæ ad Christum cum beneficijs suis oblatum in verbo & sacramento, cognoscendum & apprehendendum.
units.tr: Next, in the will or heart, faith is an ἐνέργεια [energeia], that is, a supernatural efficacy, infused into it through the Spirit of Christ, as in Col. 2.12: "Through faith in the working of God." We think this energy was not implanted in Adam's heart before the fall, for the same reasons as those we brought forward above. Since, however, that light of the mind and that efficacy of the heart are supernatural, it follows that the functions of that light and efficacy, namely the knowledge of the mind and the apprehension of the heart, are likewise supernatural. Therefore, to the definition of faith which we gave above, we add this last clause, "supernatural," so that justifying faith is the knowledge of the mind and the apprehension of the will concerning Christ with his benefits as offered in the word and sacrament, not only holy but also supernatural.
