Faith has been defined by us in this way, as we noted above, taking the name of faith for the function and work of faith; for this is how the theologians commonly define it, and this is how the name of faith is usually taken in Holy Scripture, namely for the function and work of faith, which is called τὸ ἔργον τῆς πίστεως [to ergon tēs pisteōs], "the work of faith" (2 Thess. 1.3). But if anyone prefers a description of faith taken properly, as an infused habit, let him have it thus: faith is the light of the mind and the ἐνέργεια [energeia] of the heart, supernaturally infused into them, for knowing and apprehending Christ with his benefits as offered in the word and sacrament.

units.la: Reliquum nunc est, ut nonnihil dicamus de fidei effectis. Cognitio illa & apprehensio, quam diximus, Christi, quæ est principalium ac rationalium animi facultatum, mentis & voluntatis, otiosa esse non potest: neque sese continet intra limites superiorum facultatum animi, mentis & voluntatis: verùm in inferiori corde, hoc est, in affectionibus omnibus efficax est, neque ulla est omnium affectionū quæ non aliquo modo à cognitione hac & apprehensione afficitur, quę ab ea non sanctificatur modò, sed supra se ac natura ipsam rapitur. Nam quod de fide diximus, quòd sit supernaturalis cognitio & apprehensio, idipsum verum est de functionibus omnium assectuum: nam omnes non modò sanctæ, sed etiam supernaturales efficiuntur, supernaturali quadam facultate ipsis indita per Spiritum Christi.
units.tr: It remains now that we say something about the effects of faith. That knowledge and apprehension of Christ which we have described, belonging to the principal and rational faculties of the soul, the mind and the will, cannot be idle. Nor does it confine itself within the limits of the higher faculties of the soul, mind and will, but it is efficacious in the inferior heart, that is, in all the affections; and there is no affection which is not in some way affected by this knowledge and apprehension, and which is not not only sanctified by it, but is also lifted above itself and above nature. For what we have said of faith, that it is a supernatural knowledge and apprehension, is equally true of the functions of all the affections; for all of them are made not only holy but also supernatural, by a certain supernatural faculty infused into them through the Spirit of Christ.

units.la: Sed vt sigillatim de effectis fidei dicamus; Cognito jam & apprehenso Christo cum beneficijs ipsius, accenditur spes futuri boni, accéditur metus futuri mali, accenditur mirū in modū amor Christi, & desideriū ipsius, accéditur gaudiū atq; lętitia. Credētes ei exultatis gaudio ineffabili atq; glorioso. 1.Pet.1.8. Accenditur dolor qui secundū Deum est, cū suspiris inenarrabilibus. Rom.8.26. Deniq; totū cor in Deum exardescit. Per fidem quoq; excitantur affectiones erga proximum, idque propter Deum & Christum: vt charitas & dilectio proximi, & oblectatio in sanctis. Psal.16.3. Atque hi quidem sunt primi effectus fidei in inferiori corde sive affectionibus, & ij quidem interni.
units.tr: But to speak of the effects of faith one by one: when Christ with his benefits has now been known and apprehended, hope of future good is kindled, fear of future evil is kindled, love and desire for Christ are kindled in a wonderful way, joy and gladness are kindled. "Believing in him, you rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory" (1 Pet. 1.8). Sorrow which is according to God is kindled, with unutterable sighs (Rom. 8.26). Finally, the whole heart burns up toward God. Through faith also the affections toward our neighbour are stirred up, and that for God's sake and Christ's: such as love and charity toward the neighbour, and delight in the saints (Ps. 16.3). These are indeed the first effects of faith in the inferior heart, or in the affections, and they are internal.

units.la: Sunt etiam fidei externi effectus in corpore existentes, omnibusque membris corporis atque illi quidem sunt externæ actiones corporis, in quas erûpunt interni motus affectionum; Sunt autem eæ primùm, quæ Deum respiciunt, deinde quæ proximum propter Deum. Atque hæc hactenus de effectis fidei internis simul & externis: omninoque de fide proprie dicta, quam justificantem vulgò appellant.
units.tr: There are also external effects of faith, existing in the body and in all its members. These are the outward actions of the body, into which the inward motions of the affections break forth. They are, first, those that regard God, and then those that regard the neighbour for God's sake. So far, then, concerning the inward and outward effects of faith, and altogether concerning faith properly so called, which they commonly call justifying faith.

units.la: De improprijs Fidei acceptionibus.
units.tr: On the improper senses of faith.

units.la: CAP. 30.
units.tr: CHAPTER 30.

units.la: SEquitur vt dicamus de improprijs fidei acceptionibus. Fidei enim vocabulum ambiguum est, & plura significat. Proprie quidē significat fidem hanc quam justificantem vocant: Nam ea proprie ac simpliciter hoc nomine appellatur: deinde significat fidem illā quam historicam vocant, siue mortuam, quæ nihil aliud est, quàm quasi cadaver fidei justificantis: caret enim anima, hoc est, πληροφορία mentis, & πεποίθησις cordis, speciali assensu mentis, & fiducia sine apprehensione cordis. Tertiò significat fidem quam temporariam nuncupant, quæ fidei justificantis est quasi quædam Simia. Quartò denique fidem, quā vovocant, miraculosam. Tres hæ posteriores fidei acceptiones improprie sunt, & nomen fidei non nisi homonymos, & improprie his significandis imponitur. Neque enim ex his significatis aliquod vocatur fidei nomine, nisi καταλὶ dicas, secundum quid, & cum adjecto: verbi gratia; fides vocatur historiæ cognitio, sed cum hoc adjecto, historica, sive mortua, sic de cæteris. Communis autem vocabuli fidei notio est ea quæ habetur Heb. 11.1. Fides autem est notitia in genere, cum assensu & judicio omnium eorum quæ in verbo Dei habetur, eoque sive generali, sive particulari. Verbum particulare intelligo, cùm extra ordinem peculiariter aliquid alicui revelatur: qua quidé revelatione fiebat vt miracula per aliquem ederentur.
units.tr: It follows that we speak of the improper senses of faith. The word "faith" is ambiguous and has several meanings. Properly it signifies that faith which they call justifying, for it is properly and simply called by this name. Next it signifies that faith which they call historical or dead, which is nothing other than the corpse, as it were, of justifying faith: for it lacks the soul, that is, the full assurance [πληροφορία] of mind and the confidence [πεποίθησις] of heart, the special assent of the mind and the trust of the heart that grasps. Thirdly, it signifies the faith which they call temporary, which is, as it were, a kind of ape of justifying faith. Lastly, it signifies the faith which they call miraculous. These three latter senses of faith are improper, and the name "faith" is applied to signify them only as homonyms and improperly. For none of these things is called by the name of faith, unless you add kata [κατά], "according to what," with a qualifier: for example, the knowledge of history is called faith, but with this addition, historical or dead; and so with the rest. The common notion of the word "faith," however, is that which is given in Hebrews 11:1: Faith is the knowledge, in general, together with assent and judgement, of all those things which are contained in the word of God, whether general or particular. By particular word I mean when something is peculiarly revealed to someone outside the ordinary course; by which revelation it happened that miracles were performed through a person.

units.la: Dicendum itaque primo loco de fide historica sive mortua; ac primùm de ea Scripturæ testimonia sunt Iac. 2. 15. Fides si non habeat opera, mortua est per se. 1. Cor. 12. 9. Alijs vero fides per eundem Spiritum. Series contextus & collatio facta cum alijs quæ eo loco enumerantur Spiritus sancti donis, satis ostendunt de fide historica loqui Apostolum. Huc quoque pertinet locus qui est 1. Cor. 13. 2. Si habeam totam fidem, adeò vt montes transferam. Hic non tantùm fidem miraculosam intelligit,sed etiam historicam ; dicit enim totâ siue omnem fidem, deindè speciem subijcit: quasi dicat, nominatim, fidem miraculosam admontes transferendum . Ratio nominis hæc est: Vocatur historica, quia nuda duntaxat notitia est historiæ sacrç de Deo,de Christo,de voluntate Dei, de operibus ipsius, non etiam apprehensio rerum cognitarum . Cur mortua dicatur, rationem reddit Iacobus loco supra citato, nempè, quia non habet opera: Ratio est à consequenti siue signo. Nam privatio operum siue actionum arguit & ostē dit fidem quasi inanimem esse, & vitæ expertem: atqz, vt sic dicam, cadauer fidei:quemadmodum si nulli sint motus, nullæ actiones hominis, neque internæ, neque externæ, eo ipso indicatur hominem esse mortuū, & corpus esse inanime,siue cadauer hominis.
units.tr: So we must speak first of historical or dead faith, and first the testimonies of Scripture concerning it are Jas. 2:15: Faith, if it does not have works, is dead in itself. 1 Cor. 12:9: To another faith by the same Spirit. The sequence of the context, and the comparison made with the other gifts of the Holy Spirit listed in that place, sufficiently show that the Apostle is speaking of historical faith. To this also belongs the passage 1 Cor. 13:2: If I have all faith, so that I can move mountains. Here he understands not only miraculous faith but also historical faith; for he says "all," or every faith, and then adds a species, as if to say, by name, faith for moving mountains is miraculous. The reason for the name is this: it is called historical because it is merely a bare knowledge of the sacred history about God, about Christ, about the will of God and about his works, and not also the grasping of the things known. Why it is called dead, James gives the reason in the passage cited above, namely, because it has no works: the reason is from what follows or from a sign. For the lack of works or actions proves and shows that faith is, as it were, lifeless and without life; and so, to put it thus, is the corpse of faith, just as if there were no movements or actions of a man, neither inward nor outward, by that very fact it is shown that the man is dead and the body lifeless, or is a human corpse.

units.la: Adversarij, vt hoc obiter dicam, cum audiunt ex Iacobo 2.16. fidem ideò mortuam dei, quùd non habeat opera, statim concludūt charitatem & opera charitatis animam esse fidei : verùm hoc non sequitur, charitatem & opera charitatis animam esse fidei: sed hoc sequitur,charitatem & opera charitatis signa & indicia esse animæ;hoc est,nominatim apprehenfionis illius Christi, quæ cordis est: nam hæc re vera est anima & forma fidei. Exemplo similî rem declarabo. Homo, si nulla habeat opera, nullas actiones, neque internas, neque externas, id quidem arguit in eo non esse animam & formam, ex qua actiones sunt consequentes: non autem arguit opera vel actiones esse ipsammet animam & formam hominis.
units.tr: My opponents, to say this in passing, when they hear from James 2:16 that faith is therefore dead because it has no works, immediately conclude that charity and the works of charity are the soul of faith. But this does not follow: that charity and the works of charity are the soul of faith; what follows is that charity and the works of charity are signs and indications of the soul, that is, of that apprehension of Christ which belongs to the heart; for this is in truth the soul and form of faith. I will explain the matter by a similar example. If a man has no works, no actions, neither inward nor outward, this indeed proves that in him there is no soul and form from which the actions follow; but it does not prove that the works or actions are themselves the soul and form of the man.

units.la: Verum verba Iacobi quæ habentur cap. 2.26. pro sua sententia putant facere. Nam ex eo quod dicit Iacobus, Sicut corpus absque spiritu mortuum, ita & fides quæ est absque operibus mortua est: sic inferunt; Ergo quemadmodum spiritus est forma corporis, ita opera sunt forma fidei: Sed non valet sequela: Nam in eo non est comparatio & similitudo, sed in hoc, quòd quemadmodum corpus sine spiritu mortuum est, ita fides sine operibus mortua est. Corpus sine spiritu, tanquam anima & forma sua, mortuum est: fides sine operibus, tanquam signis & indicijs animi, mortua est. Quemadmodum igitur carentia spiritus sive animæ arguit mortem corporis; ita carentia signi & indicij animæ fidei arguit mortem fidei: Comparatio igitur est spiritus & operum in simili effecto, non autem in simili natura: Nam
units.tr: But the words of James found in chapter 2:26 they think favour their opinion. For from the fact that James says, As the body without the spirit is dead, so also faith without works is dead, they infer: therefore, just as the spirit is the form of the body, so works are the form of faith. But the inference does not hold: for the comparison and likeness lie not in this, but in this, that just as a body without spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead. The body without spirit is dead as without its soul and form; faith without works is dead as without the signs and indications of the mind. Therefore, just as the lack of spirit or soul proves the death of the body, so the lack of the sign and indication of the soul proves the death of faith. The comparison, then, is between the spirit and the works in a like effect, not in a like nature. For

units.la: [no footnotes] Nam effectum simile est utriusque, quod est mors, sed utrumque non est ejusdem naturæ. De ratione nominis hactenus.
units.tr: [no footnotes] For the effect of each is similar, namely death, but the two are not of the same nature. So much concerning the reason for the name.

units.la: Objectum fidei historicæ est tota historia sacra, hoc est, universa veritas, quæ est secundum pietatem, & omnino utriusque fœderis verbum, quo differt hæc fides à fide justificante, quæ pro objecto habet verbum Evangelij, siue fœderis gratuiti.
units.tr: The object of historical faith is the whole sacred history, that is, the entire truth which pertains to godliness, and in short the word of both covenants. By this it differs from justifying faith, which has as its object the word of the gospel, or of the free covenant.

units.la: Subjectum hujus fidei mens est, quæ cognoscit atque etiam judicat: Verum mentis judicium est veritatis, ut mihi videtur, historiæ tantum, non etiam bonitatis rerum ipsarum, quæ in historia continentur. Nam etsi hypocrita profiteatur vera esse omnia de quibus loquitur Evangelium, tamen non assentitur ijs intus animo, tanquam bonis, qui est primus gradus πρᾶξις & actionis. Iudicium enim bonitatis sequitur apprehensio quæ voluntatis est, ex qua deinde sunt motus affectuum: ex quibus denique existunt externæ corporis actiones. Ergo fides hæc mortua, non sincere saltem assentitur ijs quæ in verbo sunt tanquam bonis, quin potius reipsa ea auersatur & pro malis ducit. Sic Diabolus qui hanc fidem habet, dicitur contremiscere, Iacob. 2. 19. Ex quo apparet Diabolum auersari Christū, om-
units.tr: The subject of this faith is the mind, which knows and also judges. But the judgement of the mind, as it seems to me, concerns only the truth of the history, and not also the goodness of the things themselves which are contained in the history. For although a hypocrite professes that all the things about which the gospel speaks are true, nevertheless he does not assent to them inwardly in his mind as good, which is the first degree of praxis and action. For the judgement of goodness is followed by an apprehension which belongs to the will, from which then arise the motions of the affections, and from these finally the outward actions of the body. Therefore this dead faith does not sincerely assent even to those things which are in the word as good; rather, in reality it turns away from them and holds them to be evil. Thus the devil, who has this faith, is said to tremble, Jas. 2:19. From this it appears that the devil turns away from Christ and all his goods.

units.la: Iacob. 2. 19. omniaque ipsius bona. Horror enim iste ex auersatione est & odio: Ergo, vt verbo dicam, fides hæc historica tantùm mentis est, eamq; pro subjecto habet.
units.tr: Jas. 2:19. And, to say it in a word, this historical faith belongs only to the mind, and has the mind as its subject.

units.la: Sequitur vt de eius natura dicamus. Ex his quæ de subjecto dicta sunt, facilè disci potest quænam sit ipsius natura. Nam ea tota comprehensa est mentis notitia, & judicio veritatis, eoque generali: habet igitur vnum aut alterum gradum fidei justificatis. Ex his omnibus quę diximus de fide historica, facile est ejus definitionem aliquam colligere. Est enim fides historica vniversæ veritatis, tam legalis, quàm Evangelicæ, mentis cognitio, mentisque judicium, quod ad veritatem attinet. Hæc de fide historica sive mortua hactenus.
units.tr: Next we must speak of its nature. From what has been said about the subject, it can easily be learned what its nature is. For the whole of it is comprehended in knowledge of the mind and in judgement of the truth, and that in a general way; it therefore has one or another degree of justifying faith. From all that we have said about historical faith, it is easy to gather some definition of it. Historical faith is the knowledge of the mind, and the judgement of the mind as far as truth is concerned, of the whole truth, both of the law and of the gospel. So much for historical or dead faith.

units.la: Sequitur fides temporaria. De hac Fide testimonia sunt Mat. 13. 20. 21. Qui verò in petrosa semen excepit, is est qui sermonem audit, & eum statim cū gaudio excipit, non autè habet radicem in se, sed temporarius est, ortaque persequutione & oppressione propter sermonem, statim offenditur. In eandem sententiam lege Lucam 8. 13. De hac Fide vide quoque Heb. 6. 4. 5. Nam fieri non potest vt qui semel fuerint illuminati, gustauerintque bonum Dei verbum, ac virtutes futuri sæculi. De hac Fide lege denique Ioh.5.35. Ille (nempe Iohannes) erat lucerna ardens & lucens; vos autem voluistis ad tempus exultare in ejus luce. Ratio nominis hæc est: Temporaria vocatur, quòd non nisi ad tempus duret: Non nisi ad tempus durat, quia non habet radicem.
units.tr: Next comes temporary faith. Testimonies concerning this faith are Matt. 13:20, 21: But he who received the seed on stony ground is the one who hears the word and at once receives it with joy, but has no root in himself; he is temporary, and when tribulation or persecution comes on account of the word, he is at once offended. To the same effect read Luke 8:13. Concerning this faith see also Heb. 6:4, 5: For it is impossible that those who have once been enlightened, and have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come... Finally, read concerning this faith John 5:35: He (namely John) was a burning and shining lamp; but you were willing to rejoice for a time in his light. The reason for the name is this: it is called temporary because it lasts only for a time; it lasts only for a time because it has no root.

units.la: Objectum idem habet cum fide justificante & proprie dicta, nempe, Iesum Christum cum beneficijs suis in Evangelij verbo, & sacramento oblatum, quo differt à fide historica, quæ pro objecto habet universam veritatem. Subjectum idem habet cum fide justificante: Nam sedem suam habet & in mente, & in voluntate sive corde.
units.tr: Its object is the same as that of justifying and properly so-called faith, namely Jesus Christ with his benefits, offered in the word of the Gospel and in the sacrament. In this it differs from historical faith, which has for its object the whole of truth. Its subject is the same as that of justifying faith, for it has its seat both in the mind and in the will or heart.

units.la: Denique & naturæ partes habet totidem quot habet fides justificans: Nam ipsa, & mentis cognitio est, cum utroque mentis judicio: & voluntatis sive cordis apprehensio: Ex qua etiam sequitur commotio affectuum ut gaudij, ut delectationis, &c.
units.tr: Finally, it has as many parts of nature as justifying faith has. It is a knowledge of the mind, with both judgments of the mind, and an apprehension of the will or heart. From this there also follows a stirring of the affections, such as joy, delight, and so on.

units.la: Ut autem paulò fusius dicam de apprehensione ista, quæ est in Fide temporaria, deque gaudio isto. Primùm ex Scriptura constat ista esse in Fide temporaria: Nam Christus apud Matthæum dicit, Temporarium accipere sermonem, idq; cū gaudio. Et apud Iohannem dicuntur Iudæi exultasse ad tempus in luce Iohannis Baptistæ: Et ad Hebræos non tantum mentis illustratio huic Fidei tribuitur; sed etiam cordis gustatio, eaque facta non tantum per verbum, sed etiam per Spiritum: nam ait, Qui participes facti fuerint Spiritus sancti. Ergo in Fide temporaria est reipsa apprehensio quædam, est reipsa gaudium quoddam, quo differt fides temporaria à fide historica. Nam in Fide historica ista non sunt reipsa, sed qui eam habet simulat, fingit, mentitur, externa professione se ista habere: quare impudens est hypocrita: At vero qui Fidem habet temporariam, hęc reipsa habet, apprehensionem, inquam, & gaudium, suo quodam modo: neque sic fingit aut mentitur ut is qui Fidem habet historicam: hypocrita tamen est, quia apprehensio hęc, gaudium hoc, non sunt sincera, etsi suo quodam modo vera sint.
units.tr: But to speak a little more fully about this apprehension, which is in temporary faith, and about that joy. First, it is clear from Scripture that these things are in temporary faith. Christ in Matthew says that the one who receives the word temporarily does so with joy. In John the Jews are said to have rejoiced for a time in the light of John the Baptist. And in Hebrews this faith is credited not only with illumination of the mind but also with a tasting of the heart, and that tasting is done not only through the word but also through the Spirit, for it says, "who have been made partakers of the Holy Spirit." Therefore in temporary faith there is actually a certain apprehension and actually a certain joy, and this is how temporary faith differs from historical faith. For in historical faith these things are not actually present, but the one who has it pretends, feigns and lies, professing these things outwardly, and so he is a shameless hypocrite. But the one who has temporary faith actually has these things, apprehension, I mean, and joy, in a certain way. Nor does he pretend or lie as the one who has historical faith does. Yet he is a hypocrite, because this apprehension and this joy are not sincere, although in a certain way they are true.

units.la: Dico non esse sincera, quia non sunt propter eam causam propter quam esse debent, hoc est, non sunt propter ipsum Christum in verbo Evangelij oblatum, non sunt propter Deum, non sunt propter gloriam ipsius, non propter cœlestia illa Christi beneficia, justitiam ipsius, & vitam æternam: Verum sunt propter alias causas, vt propter novitatem Evangelij, quæ intelligenda est illo loco Ioh. 5. 35. Ille erat lucerna ardens & lucens, vos autem voluistis ad tépus exultare in luce ejus; nempè, propter rei novitatem: Deinde sunt propter licentiam peccandi, quam, audita justitia illa in Christo gratuita, & libertate Christiana, statim sibi arripiunt homines: Sunt denique propter divitias, honores, aliaque hujus vitæ compendia. Cum has sibi causas propositas habeat Temporarius in audiedo & accipiendo verbum atq; gaudendo, ista in eo non sint sincera oportet. Nihil enim sincerè agitur nisi idipsum respectu divinæ gloriæ agatur. Atque hac in re differt Fides temporaria à justificante: Nam justificans omnia facit propter Christum ipsum, Deum ipsum, cœlestia & spiritualia Christi beneficia, quantum per humanam infirmitatem potest fieri. Ex his itaq; sequitur Temporarium, etiam hypocritam esse, cùm non sit sincerus; & temporariam Fidem hypocriticam esse, cum non sit sincera.
units.tr: I say they are not sincere because they are not for the cause for which they ought to be, that is, they are not for Christ himself offered in the word of the Gospel, nor for God, nor for his glory, nor for those heavenly benefits of Christ, his righteousness and eternal life. Rather they are for other causes: for the novelty of the Gospel, which is to be understood in that passage Ioh. 5. 35. "He was a burning and shining lamp, but you were willing to rejoice for a time in his light," that is, on account of the newness of the thing. Then they are for licence to sin, which men at once seize upon when they hear of that free righteousness in Christ and Christian liberty. Finally they are for riches, honours and the other conveniences of this life. Since the temporary hearer, in hearing and receiving the word and rejoicing, has these causes set before him, these things in him must be unsound. For nothing is done sincerely unless it is done with respect to the divine glory. In this respect temporary faith differs from justifying faith, for justifying faith does everything for the sake of Christ himself, God himself, and the heavenly and spiritual benefits of Christ, as far as human weakness allows. From these things it follows that the temporary believer is also a hypocrite, since he is not sincere, and temporary faith is hypocritical, since it is not sincere.

units.la: Ex eo rursus quod non sit sincera aliud sequitur, nempè, non esse solidam eam ac firmam: Nihil enim quod non sincerum est, solidum esse potest. Causæ enim illæ quibus ea ninititur, solidæ non sunt, verbi gratia, res istæ mundanæ, vt diuitiæ, honores mundi, &c. qua in re differt Fides temporaria, à Fide justificante: Nam Fides justificans vt sincera est, ita solida est. De ea enim dicitur Coloff. 2. 5. Et soliditatem vestræ in Christo fidei. Est enim fides justificans solidum quasi corpus constans tribus dimensionibus, longitudine, latitudine & profunditate. Profundum enim atque imå cordis occupat: At fides temporaria non corpus est cum tribus quasi dimensionibus, sed superficies tantum hærens in convexitate cordis. Neque enim vel solida lux est, totū cor illustrans, vel solida apprehensio, ab imo cordis proficiscens: vel denique solidum gaudium, totum corpus occupans: sed ista omnia duntaxat superficiaria sunt in fide temporaria. Vnde Heb. 6. apprehensio illa quæ in ea est rerum cœlestium comparatur gustui, hoc est, levi attactui; cum cor quasi linguæ suæ extremitate & mucrone, cœlestia illa leuiter degustat, non autem penitus imbibit, atque in sese recipit.
units.tr: From the fact that it is not sincere there follows another thing, namely that it is not solid or firm, for nothing that is not sincere can be solid. The causes on which it rests are not solid, for example worldly things such as riches, worldly honours, and so on. In this respect temporary faith differs from justifying faith, for justifying faith, as it is sincere, so it is solid. Of it is said Col. 2. 5. "and the solidity of your faith in Christ." For justifying faith is like a solid body with three dimensions, length, breadth and depth, for it reaches the depths and innermost part of the heart. But temporary faith is not a body with three dimensions, but only a surface clinging to the convex outside of the heart. Its light is not solid, illuminating the whole heart; its apprehension is not solid, arising from the bottom of the heart; and its joy is not solid, filling the whole body. All these things in temporary faith are merely superficial. Hence in Heb. 6. the apprehension of heavenly things which is in it is compared to tasting, that is, a light touch. The heart, as it were with the tip and point of its tongue, lightly tastes those heavenly things but does not soak them up completely or receive them into itself.

units.la: Ex hoc rursus quòd fides temporaria non sit solida, sequitur & aliud, nempe, quòd non duret in perpetuum, sed duntaxat ad tempus. Quod enim non est solidum, durabile & perpetuum non est, sed temporarium tantum. Qua in re quoque differt à Fide justificante, quæ vt solida est, ita perpetua & constans. Ab hac proprietate Fides hæc nomen suum accepit, & temporaria vocata est: Præfupponitautem hæc proprietas præcedentes illas duas: nempè, primum quod non fit solida, deinde quod non fit sincera, etiamsi suo quodam modo vera.
units.tr: From this, again, that temporary faith is not solid, another thing follows, namely that it does not last forever but only for a time. For what is not solid is not durable and perpetual, but only temporary. In this respect too it differs from justifying faith, which, as it is solid, so is perpetual and constant. This faith received its name from this property and is called temporary. This property presupposes the two preceding ones: first, that it is not solid, and then that it is not sincere, even though in a certain way it is true.

units.la: Consideranti mihi diligentius trium istarum proprietatum causam, occurrit eam non tam imputandam esse externis illis rebus, propter quas fides hæc in verbo Christum apprehendit, eoque gaudet; quàm internæ ipsius cordis affectioni nialæ: Est enim cor hominis, vt Christus loquitur, terra petrosa, hoc est, neq; bonum, neque honestum est sua natura. Bonitatem hàc & honestatem metimur maximè simplicitate ac sinceritate, quę opponitur hypocrisi & simulationi. Cor igitur hominis occupat profunda, hypocrisis finceritati contraria. Sic autem affectum cor, credit, apprehendit, gaudet, non sincerè, propter veram causam, ob quam ista debet facere : sed propter alias causas, & mundanas. Sequitur ergo istorum malorum causam præcipuè in ipso corde delitescere. Quamobrem fi quis nolit esse Temporarius, ante omnia attendat ipse ad suum cor, ipsumque diligenter interdiu ac noctu excutiat, atque examinet, tantisper dum sentiat fidem Christi radices suas agere in imo cordis, totumque cor, quoad eius fieri poterit, penitus occupare.
units.tr: As I have considered more carefully the cause of these three properties, it seems to me that it is to be imputed not so much to those external things, on account of which this faith apprehends Christ in the word and rejoices in him, as to the inward disposition of the heart itself. For the heart of man, as Christ says, is stony ground, that is, it is neither good nor honest by its nature. We measure this goodness and honesty chiefly by simplicity and sincerity, which is opposed to hypocrisy and pretence. The heart of man is therefore occupied with depths, and hypocrisy is contrary to sincerity. Thus the heart believes, apprehends and rejoices in this way, not sincerely, for the true cause for which it ought to do these things, but for other, worldly causes. It follows, then, that the cause of these evils lies hidden chiefly in the heart itself. Therefore, if anyone does not wish to be temporary, let him first attend to his own heart, examine it diligently by day and by night, and test it, until he perceives faith in Christ taking root in the depths of the heart and occupying the whole heart as completely as it can.

units.la: Ex his quae diximus de proprietatibus huius fidei, deque earum causa; deprehenditur nota, qua quis internoscat veram fidem ac justificantem a temporaria. Est autem ea, ut verbo dicam, sinceritas in agendo, in credendo, apprehendendo, gaudendo, omnia denique in vita quotidiana faciendo: Sinceritas autem ex eo cognoscitur, si omnia fiant & gerantur a nobis propter Deum & propter Christum, sive ea parvi sint momenti, sive magni. Sive editis, sive bibitis, sive quid facitis, omnia facite ad Dei gloriam. 1. Cor. 10. 31.
units.tr: From what we have said about the properties of this faith and their cause, a mark is discovered by which one may distinguish true and justifying faith from temporary faith. To say it in a word, it is sincerity in acting, in believing, in apprehending, in rejoicing, in short in doing everything in daily life. Sincerity is known from this: if all things are done and carried out by us for God's sake and for Christ's, whether they are of little or of great importance. Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God. 1. Cor. 10. 31.

units.la: Ex his quae dicta sunt facile est definitionem aliquam huius fidei colligere: Est enim Fides temporaria Christi cum beneficiis ipsius, mentis cognitio, item voluntatis apprehensio, sed temporaria, vel ad tempus durans. Atque haec hactenus de Fide temporaria.
units.tr: From what has been said it is easy to gather some definition of this faith. Temporary faith is a knowledge of the mind of Christ with his benefits, likewise an apprehension of the will, but temporary, or lasting only for a time. So much for temporary faith.

units.la: Sequitur miraculosa, quae tertia est acceptio nominis Fidei impropria. De hac Fide testimonia sunt Matth. 17. Si habeatis fidem quantum est granum sinapis. 1 Cor. 13. Si omnem fidem habeam ita ut montes transferam. Ratio nominis hæc est: Vocatur miraculosa, ab effecto suo, quod efficax sit ad miracula edenda.
units.tr: Next comes miraculous faith, which is the third improper sense of the name of faith. Testimonies concerning this faith are Matth. 17. "If you have faith as a grain of mustard seed," and 1 Cor. 13. "If I have all faith so as to remove mountains." The name is derived thus: it is called miraculous from its effect, because it is effective in working miracles.

units.la: Objectum ejus non est nudum verbum generale, quin potius specialis promissio, aut revelatio alicui facta de edendo certo aliquo miraculo. Quod autem nudum verbum generale non sufficiat, ex eo apparet, quod multi sancti viri habuerint fidem in verbum generale, habuerint etiam justificantem Fidem in promissionem gratuitam, nec tamen miracula edere potuerint. Simon Magus Fide historica credidit in verbum generale, & tamen non potuit edere miracula: Ideo hanc facultatem voluit pecunia & pretio emere. Act. 8. 13. Nisi igitur ad verbum generale, accedat singularis promissio sive revelatio, non est Fides miraculosa, quæ donum quoddam est Spiritus speciale & extraordinarium. In quo vehementer errant adversarij, qui verbum generale sufficere putant ad hoc ut fit Fides miraculosa. Subjectum ejus est mens primum intelligens simul & judicans promissionem specialem: deinde voluntas sive cor, id quod promittitur apprehendens.
units.tr: Its object is not the bare general word, but rather a special promise, or a revelation made to someone, about the working of some particular miracle. That a bare general word is not sufficient is clear from this: many holy men have had faith in the general word, and indeed a justifying faith in the free promise, and yet they could not work miracles. Simon Magus believed the general word with historical faith, and yet he could not work miracles; that is why he wanted to buy this power with money and a price. Acts 8:13. Unless, therefore, a singular promise or revelation is added to the general word, there is no miraculous faith, which is a special and extraordinary gift of the Spirit. In this the adversaries greatly err, who think that the general word is enough to make faith miraculous. Its subject is the mind, which first understands and at the same time judges the special promise; then the will or heart, which lays hold of what is promised.

units.la: Naturæ partes sunt notitia cum judicio mentis, apprehensio quædam voluntatis & cordis. Ex his jam dictis, hujus Fidei definitionem hanc colligo: ut sit Fides miraculosa, specialis promissionis, sive revelationis de miraculo edendo, mentis cognitio, & voluntatis apprehensio. Hactenus de Fide miraculosa, omninoque de vera Fidei doctrina.
units.tr: The parts of its nature are knowledge joined with the judgment of the mind, and a certain apprehension of the will and heart. From what has now been said I gather this definition of this faith: miraculous faith is a knowledge of the mind and an apprehension of the will concerning a special promise or revelation of a miracle to be worked. So far concerning miraculous faith, and indeed concerning the true doctrine of faith.

units.la: Adversariorum de Fide sententia.
units.tr: The opponents' view of faith.

units.la: CAP. 31.
units.tr: CHAPTER 31.

units.la: Sequitur nunc ut videamus paucis quid adversarij de Fide sentiant. Primùm, diversas Fidei acceptiones non agnoscunt: unam tantum Fidem tradunt, eamque justificantem appellant, hoc est, ut illi vocem definiunt, disponentem nos ad justitiam postea suo tempore infundendam. Sic sentit Bellarminus in tractatu suo de Fide.
units.tr: Let us now see briefly what the opponents think about faith. First, they do not recognise different senses of faith. They teach only one faith, and they call it justifying, that is, in their definition of the word, faith that disposes us for righteousness, which is to be infused afterwards in its own time. Bellarmine holds this view in his treatise on faith.

units.la: In doctrina hujus Fidei, quam justificantem vocant, primùm differentiunt à nobis quòd ad objectum ejus. Objectum Fidei non inficiantur quidem esse Dei misericordiam in Christo Iesu, oblatam in Evangelio, hoc est, esse Evangelium, & promissiones gratuitas de Christo, deque misericordia Dei in ipso. Verùm objectum volunt esse, non tantum Evangelij verbum, sed vniversum ex æquo Dei verbum.
units.tr: In the doctrine of this faith, which they call justifying, they differ from us first over its object. They do not deny that the object of faith is the mercy of God in Jesus Christ offered in the gospel, that is, the gospel itself and the free promises concerning Christ and God's mercy in him. But they want the object to be not only the word of the gospel, but the whole word of God, equally.

units.la: Ad hanc sententiam suam confirmandam, adducunt definitionem illam Fidei, quæ tradita est Heb. 11. Fides, inquit Apostolus, est ὑπόστασις rerum quæ sperantur, & ἔλεγχος rerum quæ non videntur. Hæc, inquiunt, definitio est Fidei justificantis: Atqui hæc definitio patet non tantùm ad Christum, promissiones Dei, omninòque Evangelium de ipso; verùm patet ad totum verbum Dei, & omnia quæ verbo Dei continentur: Verbi gratia, patet ad verbum Dei quod est de mundi creatione ut apparet ex ver. 3. qui sequitur eodem cap.: Per Fidem intelligimus constructum fuisse mundum verbo Dei: Hinc concludunt Fidem justificantem pro objecto suo habere vniuersum Dei verbum. Sed ad hæc respondemus, non definiri illo loco ab Apostolo fidem tantum justificantem, sed eam definitionem communem esse omnibus Fidei acceptionibus, ut satis apparet ex illa exemplorum inductione, quæ illo loco & capite sequitur.
units.tr: To confirm this view they cite the definition of faith given in Heb. 11. "Faith," says the Apostle, "is substance [ὑπόστασις] of things hoped for, and evidence [ἔλεγχος] of things not seen." This, they say, is the definition of justifying faith. But this definition plainly extends not only to Christ, to God's promises, and to the gospel concerning him, but to the whole word of God and all that is contained in it. For example, it extends to the word of God concerning the creation of the world, as appears from verse 3 of the same chapter, which follows: "By faith we understand that the world was framed by the word of God." Hence they conclude that justifying faith has for its object the whole word of God. But to this we reply that the Apostle does not here define justifying faith alone. This definition is common to all senses of faith, as is sufficiently clear from the enumeration of examples that follows in that place and chapter.

units.la: Neque valet illud eorum argumentum quod petunt ex serie contextus: Definitur, inquiunt, ea Fides de qua loquutus est Apostolus ultimis verbis cap. præcedentis, Iustus autem ex fide vivet &c. At ibi loquutus est Apoft. de Fide justificante, ergo definita est Fides justificans. Respondeo, Definitio haec, fateor, est Fidei justificantis, sed non ejus tantùm; verùm communis ei cum aliis Fidei acceptionibus: ut cum Fide historica, & miraculosa &c. ut apparet ex inductione quae sequitur. Cum igitur non sit ista definitio Fidei tantùm justificantis, sequitur ex hac definitione non confici quod volunt, nempe, Fidei justificantis objectum ex aequo esse universum Dei verbum. Sit igitur ejus objectum proprie id quod ipsa apprehendit: id autem est Evangelium, & verbum de Christo.
units.tr: Nor does their argument from the sequence of the context hold. "The faith defined," they say, "is that of which the Apostle spoke in the last words of the preceding chapter: 'The just shall live by faith,' etc. But there the Apostle spoke of justifying faith; therefore justifying faith is defined." I reply: I grant that this definition is of justifying faith, but not of it alone. It is common to it along with the other senses of faith, such as historical and miraculous faith, and so on, as appears from the enumeration that follows. Since this definition is not of justifying faith alone, it follows that from it they cannot establish what they want, namely that the object of justifying faith is equally the whole word of God. Let its object, then, properly be what it itself apprehends. That is the gospel and the word concerning Christ.

units.la: Deinde in hoc ipso speciali objecto, nempe, Dei misericordia in Christo, a nobis differunt. Nos enim dicimus atque affirmamus, objectum Fidei justificantis esse, non generalem misericordiam tantùm, non generalem promissionem de Christo tantùm, sed multò magis specialem misericordiam, specialem promissionem: hoc est, misericordiam non promisit cuique omnibus, verùm peculiariter mihi vel tibi in Evangelio oblatam. Nam etsi promissiones & sententiae Evangelicae generaliter concipiantur; tamen certum est specialiter à singulis accipiendas esse, ac si singulis essent dictæ, verbi gratia: Ioh.3. generaliter concipitur promissio fœderis gratuiti, his verbis, Quisquis credit in Filium non peribit, sed habebit vitam æternam. Generaliter quidem concipitur hæc promissio, verum particulariter & singulariter à singulis est intelligenda, ac si fuisset dictum mihi, aut tibi; Si tu credideris in Filium, non peribis, sed habebis vitam æternam. Apost.1.Timoth.1. generale hanc sententiam, nempè, Christum Iesum venisse in mundum vt peccatores servaret, nō secus accipit, atque si de seipso tantùm fuisset pronunciata: unde eam ad sese peculiariter applicat, assumens nominatim se peccatorem esse, & concludens, saltem tacitè, Christum venisse in mundum ad se nominatim servandum.
units.tr: Next, we differ from them even about this special object, namely God's mercy in Christ. For we say and affirm that the object of justifying faith is not merely general mercy or a general promise concerning Christ, but much more a special mercy and a special promise. That is, it is mercy not promised to everyone indiscriminately, but offered in the gospel particularly to me or to you. For although the evangelical promises and sayings are framed in general terms, it is certain that each of them is to be received particularly by each person, as if it were spoken to each one. For example, Ioh. 3. frames the promise of the free covenant in general terms, in these words: "Whoever believes in the Son will not perish, but will have eternal life." This promise is indeed framed generally, but it must be understood particularly and singly by each person, as if it had been said to me or to you: "If you believe in the Son, you will not perish, but will have eternal life." In 1 Tim. 1 (Timoth. 1.) the general sentence, namely that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, is received no differently than if it had been pronounced of himself alone. Hence he applies it to himself peculiarly, naming himself a sinner, and concluding, at least tacitly, that Christ came into the world to save him by name.

units.la: Hujus rei judicium faciendum est ex promissionibus illis specialiter factis in Evangelio certis quibusdam hominibus: vt Paralitico, Matth.9. Peccatrici mulieri, Luc.7. Adulteræ, Ioh.8. Zachæo, Luc.19. Latroni, Luc.23. Nam Spiritus Christi, dum profertur aliqua generalis promissio vel sententia de Christo, deque ejus misericordia, non minùs nunc specialiter eam applicat singulis, intus in corde cujusq; loquens, quàm tunc Christus ftus viva voce applicavit promissiones illas particulares certis quibusdam personis.Rom. 3.cum justitia Dei dicitur pertinere ad omnes credentes, idque fine distinctione, plane significatur justitiam illam cujuscunque fortis & conditionis hominibus offerri, adeoq; etiam singulis proponi. 1. Tim. 2. postquam monuit pro quibusvis hominibus orandum, subjecit velle Deum omnes seruari, & ad agnitionem veritatis venire. Ex quo sequitur à Deo haberi rationem in promulgando Evangelio, non tantum confertim vniversorum; sed etiam distinctè singulorum: quam etiam rationem vult ipse à nobis haberi in precibus nostris.
units.tr: The judgment on this matter must be drawn from those promises made in the gospel specially to certain particular persons: to the paralytic, Matth. 9.; to the sinful woman, Luc. 7.; to the adulteress, Ioh. 8.; to Zacchaeus, Luc. 19.; to the thief, Luc. 23. For when some general promise or saying concerning Christ and his mercy is put forward, the Spirit of Christ applies it no less specially to each person now, speaking inwardly in each one's heart, than Christ by his living voice then applied those particular promises to certain persons. When Rom. 3. says that the righteousness of God pertains to all who believe, and that without distinction, it is plainly signified that this righteousness is offered to men of every sort and condition, and so is set before each one individually. And 1. Tim. 2., after urging that prayers be made for men of every kind, adds that God wills all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. From this it follows that God takes account, in publishing the gospel, not only of all in a body but also distinctly of each individual. He wills that we too take this account in our prayers.

units.la: Quid multis opus est? nam fi nihil aliud effet, quod hoc doceret, Sacramentorum adminiftratio vel sola, fatis argumenti in fe habet ad ostendendum misericordiam Dei in Christo, specialiter singulis offerri: In sacramento enim utroque, sigilla illius misericordiæ, singulis sigillatim dantur & offeruntur. Atque hæc sufficiant ad ostendendum specialem, quæ dicitur, misericordiam, objectum esse proprie justificantis Fidei, contrà quam sentiunt adversarij.
units.tr: Why need there be more? Even if nothing else taught this, the administration of the sacraments alone has enough in itself to show that the mercy of God in Christ is offered specially to each individual. For in both sacraments the seals of that mercy are given and offered to each one singly. Let these suffice to show that the special mercy, as it is called, is properly the object of justifying faith, contrary to what the opponents hold.

units.la: Posita pro objecto Fidei justificantis generali misericordia,sequitur fidè, ex adversariorū sententia,generalem esse, non autē speciālem assensum. Nam cum generalis tantum est misericordia generaliter Ecclesiæ proposita, non autem particulariter singulis membris ipsius oblata, qui potest singularis aliquis homo sibi vendicare particulariter, quod particulariter non est dictum & oblatum? Sed nos affirmamus Fidem justificantem esse, qua vnusquisq; fidelis peculiariter, nō tantùm as- sentitur promissioni tanquā de se verè: sed etiam rem promissam corde apprehendit, sibiq; propriam vendicat. Demonstrato enim eo quòd misericordia Dei specialiter offeratur cuiq;, sequitur Fidem oportere speciale esse.
units.tr: If general mercy is posited as the object of justifying faith, it follows, on the opponents' view, that assent is general and not special. For since mercy is only general, proposed generally to the Church and not offered particularly to its individual members, how can any single man claim for himself particularly what was not said and offered to him particularly? But we affirm that justifying faith is that by which each believer peculiarly not only assents to the promise as true of himself, but also apprehends the promised thing in his heart and claims it as his own. For once it is shown that God's mercy is offered specially to each person, it follows that faith must be special.

units.la: Sed ad hoc quoque ostendendum succurrunt Scripturæ testimonia penè infinita: nos tantùm paucis erimus contenti. Gal. 2. 10. Et vitam quam nunc vivo in carne,vivo per fidè Filij Dei, qui dilexit me, & tradidit semetipsum pro me. Vide hîc vt per fidem peculiariter ad sese applicet filiū Dei, vitam ipsius, dilectionem ipsius,denique mortem ipsius: neque est quod quis dicat hoc licuisse Apostolo qui ejus rei extraordinariam aliquam revelationem habuit, nō autem licere vulgo Christianorum: quandoquidem Apost. hoc loco sustineat personam cujusuis Christiani ac fidelis hominis. Rom. 8. Nam mihi persuasum est, inquit, neque mortem, neque vitam, &c. Nota hic fiduciam specialem & particularem applicationem designari per verbum singularis numeri. Præterea illud quod ex Habacuc citatur ab Apostolo, Iustus ex Fide vivet, satis indicat specialem Fidem : ea enim significaturvnumquemq; justum viuere sua fide, hoc est, speciali assensu, & applicatione justitiæ Dei in Christo. Mat. 9. commendata est specialis Fides Paralytico; cui dictum est: Confide fili, remissa sunt tibi peccata tua. Ioh. 3. cùm dicitur, Qui credit in Filium habet vitâ æternam, significatur illa ipsa specialis Fides, quæ est vniuscujusque particulariter assentietis, & ad sese applicantis specialiter sibiipsi ob latam vitam æternam. Quid multis opus est? Idipsum docet illud(Credo)quod in Symbolo Apost. reperitur: nam (Credere) ibi est, in specie & indiuiduo credere.
units.tr: To show this, the testimonies of Scripture come to hand in almost endless number. We shall be content with a few. Gal. 2. 10.: "And the life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me." See here how through faith he applies to himself peculiarly the Son of God, his life, his love, and finally his death. Nor can anyone say that this was permitted to the Apostle, who had some extraordinary revelation of it, but is not permitted to the common run of Christians. For the Apostle in this place speaks in the person of any Christian and believer. Rom. 8.: "For I am persuaded," he says, "that neither death nor life, etc." Note here that special trust and particular application are signified by the verb in the singular number. Moreover, what the Apostle cites from Habakkuk, "The just shall live by faith," sufficiently indicates special faith. For it signifies that each just person lives by his own faith, that is, by special assent and application of God's righteousness in Christ. In Mat. 9. special faith is commended in the paralytic, to whom it was said: "Take heart, son; your sins are forgiven." When Ioh. 3. says, "He who believes in the Son has eternal life," that very special faith is signified which is the particular assent of each person, applying to himself specially the eternal life offered to him. Why need there be more? The Apostles' Creed teaches the same thing by the word (I believe) found in it. For "to believe" there is said of the species and of the individual.

units.la: Ex generali misericordia, & generali Fide adversariorum, sequitur Fidei particularis ac propriæ gratiæ incertitudo, quam ipsi debere esse defendunt. Nam quod incertitudo sequatur necessario ex illa generalitate, primùm misericordiæ, deinde Fidei, facilè conspicitur. Cum enim nō specialiter, sed generaliter misericordia proponitur & offertur,& generalis tantùm est assensus Fidei, quì possum ego certus esse misericordiæ illius, quòd certò ad me nominatim pertineat.
units.tr: From the general mercy and the general faith of our opponents there follows an uncertainty of particular and proper grace, which they maintain ought to exist. That uncertainty follows necessarily from that generality, first of mercy and then of faith, is easily seen. For when mercy is set forth and offered not specifically but generally, and faith's assent is only general, how can I be certain of that mercy, that it belongs to me by name?

units.la: Quòd autem Fidei sit certitudo, contrà quàm illi sentiunt; primùm facilè apparet ex ijs quæ dicta sunt de speciali misericordia, & Fide speciali. Nam cum misericordia offertur particulariter mihi,tibi &c.& ego vicissim particulariter ei assentior: jam ego certus sum de hac misericordia, quod mea sit,præsertim cū eam jam possideam per Fidem, &specialē applicationem. Per Fidem enim inhabitat Christus in cordibus nostris, hoc est,jam possidemus Christum,eoque fruimur quasi præsente. De hac certitudine speciali vide Rom.4 16. Ex Fide est hæreditas,vt sit per gratiam,ut firma sit promissio toti semini. Et ibidem postea ver.18. Qui Abraham contra spem sub spe credidit. Sed de hac relocus est ad Hebr. 6.18. maximè insignis: Vt per duas res immutabiles in quibus fieri non potest ut mentitus sit Deus, validam consolationem habeamus qui cursum eo corripuimus,vt spem propositam obtineamus: Vbi vides Deum promisisse primùm, deinde jurejurando sese obstriuxisse strinxisse, hoc est, indicasse immutabilitatem consilij sui in nobis servandis per duas res immutabiles, eo fine vt validam consolationem habeamus. Valida autem hæc consolatio nō est nisi ex firmo certoque assensu nostro, quo nos assentimur veritati promissionis divinæ. Si enim vacillet & incertus sit assensus noster, profecto non potest ex assensu existere valida consolatio: deinde vt sit valida consolatio, non sufficit certitudo assensus nostri generalis aliqua, verum necesse est certitudo assensus specialis, & (vt sic dicam) individualis sit: qua nimirùm ego certus sum id quod promittitur de me verum esse. Quæ enim potest esse consolatio omninò, nedum valida consolatio, cū ego certus sum promissionem de Christo ad Ecclesiam tantùm in genere, nō etiam ad meipsum in specie pertinere: Imò verò, ea ipsa reaugetur dolor, quòd quis beneficia Christi ad alios pertinere videat, nihil autem ad se.
units.tr: That there is, contrary to what they think, a certainty of faith is first made plain from what has been said about special mercy and special faith. For when mercy is offered to me particularly, to you and so on, and I in turn particularly assent to it, then I am already certain of this mercy, that it is mine, especially since I now possess it through faith and special application. For through faith Christ dwells in our hearts; that is, we already possess Christ and enjoy him as though he were present. On this special certainty see Rom. 4.16. "It is of faith, that the inheritance may be by grace, so that the promise may be sure to all the seed" (Rom. 4.16). And a little later in the same place, verse 18: "Who against hope believed in hope." But the passage most notable on this point is Heb. 6.18: "that by two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold on the hope set before us." Here you see that God first promised and then bound himself by an oath, that is, he showed the immutability of his purpose to keep us, by two immutable things, with the aim that we might have a strong consolation. But this consolation is not strong unless it rests on our firm and certain assent, by which we assent to the truth of the divine promise. For if our assent wavers and is uncertain, a strong consolation cannot arise from it. Further, for the consolation to be strong, some general certainty of our assent is not enough; a certainty of special assent, which is, so to speak, individual, is necessary, by which I am certain that what is promised is true of me. For what consolation can there be at all, let alone a strong one, when I am certain that the promise of Christ pertains to the Church only in general, and not to myself in particular? Indeed, the very grief is increased when a man sees the benefits of Christ pertaining to others and nothing to himself.

units.la: Verùm vt hoc quod dicimus de certitudine & incertitudine manifestius sit, paulò altiùs nonnihil erit repetendum. In genere itaq; certitudo vel est rei ipsius, vel personæ. De certitudine rei ejusque firma veritate nulla quæstio est. Certitudo personæ rem obječtā apprehendentis, nihil aliud est, quàm firmitas judicij
units.tr: But so that what we say about certainty and uncertainty may be clearer, we must go back somewhat further. In general, then, certainty belongs either to the thing itself or to the person. Concerning the certainty of the thing and its firm truth there is no question. The certainty of the person apprehending the object is nothing other than the firmness of judgement.

units.la: [illegible, ~3 letters] judicij, siue assensus mentis assentientis veritati alicujus rei vel sententiæ. Quare certitudo nihil aliud est, quàm proprietas quædam judicij, vel assensus mentis nostræ. Cum autem assensus mentis duplex sit, vel generalis, cùm generaliter assentior veritati alicujus sententiæ quod vera sit: verbi gratia, de vniuersa Ecclesia, vel est specialis, cum specialiter assentior veritati alicujus sententiæ, quòd eaverasit, etiam de me; & de indiuiduo: cum, inquam, duplex sit assensus mentis, sequitur duplicem esse certitudinem, vnam generalem, generalis nimirùm assensus: alteram specialem, specialis nimirùm assensus proprietatem.
units.tr: ...firmness of judgement, or the assent of a mind assenting to the truth of some thing or proposition. Hence certainty is nothing other than a property of judgement or of our mind's assent. Now since the assent of the mind is twofold, either general, when I assent generally to the truth of some proposition, that it is true, for example, of the whole Church, or special, when I assent specially to the truth of some proposition, that it is true also of me, and of the individual; since, I say, the assent of the mind is twofold, it follows that there is a twofold certainty: one general, that is, of general assent, and the other special, that is, the property of special assent.

units.la: Nunc vt ad rem & statum controuersiæ veniamus, de generali certitudine non est quæstio: verùm de speciali certitudine assensus specialis, quæ vocat certitudine gratiæ, sive misericordiæ specialis, tota est controuersia. Nos enim certitudinem specialis gratiæ affirmamus atq; defendimus: Illi autem hanc ipsam specialis gratiæ certitudinem oppugnant, sed quibus quæso argumentis? Primùm, inquiunt, in Evangelio nulla vsquam speciali homini vel individuo, specialiter offertur vel promittitur misericordia, Ergo non potest esse certitudo specialis gratiæ. Respondeo, & inverto argumetum. In Evangelio promittitur & offertur gratia non tantum in genere vniversis, sed in specie singulis, sicut antea docuimus: quamobrem requiritur in vnoquoque speciali gratiæ certitudo.
units.tr: Now, to come to the matter and state of the controversy: there is no dispute about general certainty. The whole controversy concerns special certainty, the certainty of special assent, which is called certainty of grace, or of special mercy. For we affirm and defend the certainty of special grace; but they attack this very certainty of special grace. On what arguments, I ask? First, they say, nowhere in the Gospel is mercy offered or promised specially to any individual man. Therefore there cannot be a certainty of special grace. I answer, and I turn the argument around: in the Gospel grace is promised and offered not only generally to all, but specifically to each, as we taught before. Therefore in each individual a certainty of grace is required.

units.la: Ad ea quæ diximus de speciali misericordia specialiter singulis oblata, hæc pauca addo quo ea res tota clarius conspiciatur, & quo ex ipso sensu atque experientia à Deo singulis offerri gratiam discamus. Spiritus Christi est vicarius Christi solus in terris, qui docet nos & instruit in iis quæ Christus est loquutus, & quæ in Evangelio scripta sunt. Docet autem hic Spiritus non tantùm generaliter promissiones & sententias Evangelij de Christo, ipsiusque beneficijs, veras esse de tota Ecclesia, sed multò magis veras esse de eo homine singulari & individuo, quem ipse intùs docet. Et cum Spiritus adoptionis testatur cum spiritu nostro nos esse filios Dei, vt loquitur Apostolus, Rom. 8. Hoc Spiritus sancti testimonium non est generale de tota Ecclesia, quòd qui in Ecclesia sunt, filij sint Dei: sed speciale est testimonium de me, de te, quòd ego filius sum Dei, tu filius es Dei. Præterea 1. Cor, 2. de Spiritu dicitur, quod scrutetur etiam profunditates Dei, hoc est, Spiritus qui datur vnicuique & qui
units.tr: To what we have said about special mercy offered specially to each, I add these few words, so that the whole matter may be seen more clearly, and so that from the very sense and experience we may learn that grace is offered by God to each. The Spirit of Christ is the sole vicar of Christ on earth, who teaches and instructs us in those things which Christ has spoken and which are written in the Gospel. Now this Spirit teaches not only that the promises and sayings of the Gospel about Christ and his benefits are true of the whole Church in general, but much more that they are true of that single and individual man whom he teaches inwardly. And when the Spirit of adoption bears witness with our spirit that we are the children of God, as the Apostle says, Rom. 8. This testimony of the Holy Spirit is not general, about the whole Church, that those who are in the Church are children of God; it is a special testimony about me and about you, that I am a child of God, and you are a child of God. Further, in 1 Cor. 2. it is said of the Spirit that he searches even the depths of God; that is, the Spirit who is given to each and who dwells in each searches out that grace and mercy in Christ Jesus which lies hidden in the depth, and makes it known to each.

units.la: {y} & qui habitat in unoquoq;, scrutetur illam, quæ in profunditate latet, gratiam atque misericordiam in Christo Iesu, eamque unicuique innotescere faciat. Nam Spiritus Dei in me habitans revelat mihi quod in ipso Dei corde est reconditum. Iam quæro, utrùm revelet mihi misericordiam aliquam generalé duntaxat, in genere tantùm ad Ecclesiam pertinentem, an verò revelet mihi specialem illâ in Deo reconditam misericordiam, ad me pertinentem peculiariter? Profectò, nemo omnium est, cui Spiritus hic in ipso habitans quidquam gratiæ in Deo latentis unquam revelávit, qui non constáter affirmet per Spiritum sanctum revelari unicuique misericordiam, nō quidem generalem, hoc est, nescio quam ideam; sed specialem ad se specialiter pertinentem. Quare mihi tantùm ψυχικοὶ & animales, non autem πνευματικοὶ & spirituales videntur isti generalis duntaxat misericordiæ propugnatores: de quibus illud Apostoli vere dici potest, Animalis homo non percipit ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei.
units.tr: For the Spirit of God dwelling in me reveals to me what is hidden in the very heart of God. Now I ask: does he reveal to me only some general mercy, pertaining to the Church merely in general, or does he reveal to me that special mercy hidden in God, pertaining to me in a peculiar way? Surely there is no one to whom this Spirit dwelling within has ever revealed anything of the grace hidden in God who would not firmly affirm that the Holy Spirit reveals to each person mercy, not a general mercy, that is, some idea or other, but a special mercy pertaining to him specially. So these defenders of merely general mercy seem to me to be not spiritual [πνευματικοὶ] but merely natural [ψυχικοὶ], animal men, of whom that saying of the Apostle can truly be said: "The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God."

units.la: Secundò, non expedit, inquiunt, ut unusquisque certus sit gratiæ, justitiæ, salutis propriæ; certitudo enim gignit superbiam, incertitudo verò humilitatem. Respondeo: Certitudo donum est Spiritus regenerantis, quod in solos electos confertur. Loquor de vera solidaque certitudine speciali, quae est fidei verę & justificantis. An igitur citra blasphemiam dici potest, Spiritum sanctum & Fidem justificantem causam esse mali omnium peffimi, hoc est, superbiae? Quin potius incertitudo hominis est plane superbiae adversus Deum, etiam promittentem & offerentem speciale m misericordiam, etiam jurantem.
units.tr: Secondly, they say, it is not expedient for each person to be certain of his own grace, righteousness, and salvation; for certainty begets pride, while uncertainty produces humility. I answer: certainty is a gift of the regenerating Spirit, which is conferred only on the elect. I speak of true and solid special certainty, which belongs to true and justifying faith. Can it then be said, without blasphemy, that the Holy Spirit and justifying faith are the cause of the worst of all evils, that is, of pride? Rather, a man's uncertainty is plainly pride against God, even when God promises and offers special mercy, even when he swears to it.

units.la: Tertiò, inquiunt, certitudo specialis misericordię, specialis est certorum quorundam hominum prærogativa, quibus Deo visum est revelare extra ordinem specialem & ipsis propriam misericordiam. An igitur specialis prærogativa, quę nō nisi certorum est & perpaucorum hominum, in communibus Dei donis est numeranda? Respondeo, falsum est certitudinem specialis gratiae prærogativam esse specialem certorum quorundam hominum: Nam si fides justificans in bonis & donis communibus quibuscunq; Christianis numeretur, certitudo autem ista specialis sit fidei justificantis, qua fronte audet quis hoc donum specialis certitudinis negare etiā vulgo Christianorum hominum? An quia certis & pancis aliquot illud est revelatum, quod ipsis remissa sin t
units.tr: Thirdly, they say, certainty of special mercy is the special prerogative of certain men, to whom it has pleased God to reveal their own particular mercy outside the ordinary way. Is a special prerogative, which belongs only to certain and very few men, to be counted among the common gifts of God? I answer: it is false that the certainty of special grace is the special prerogative of certain men. For if justifying faith is counted among the common gifts bestowed on all Christians, and this special certainty belongs to justifying faith, with what face does anyone dare to deny this gift of special certainty even to the common run of Christian men? Or because it has been revealed to a few certain persons that their sins are forgiven, as to that paralytic, as to the sinful woman, as to Zacchaeus, as to the thief, is this gift of certainty therefore only special and extraordinary?

units.la: {y} Quod est donum. sint peccata sua, ut Paralytico illi, ut peccatrici mulieri, at Zachæo, ut Latroni, ideò hoc certitudinis donum non nisi speciale & extraordinarium est: imò jam diximus non minùs promitti nunc & offerri speciale m Dei misericordiâ etiam singulis, & individuis, ut mihi, ut tibi, quàm tum olim illis hominibus expressis Christi verbis oblata est.
units.tr: As for the gift, that their sins were forgiven, as with that paralytic, the sinful woman, Zacchaeus and the thief, this gift of certainty is therefore special and extraordinary only. Indeed, as we have already said, God's special mercy is no less promised and offered now to each and every individual, to me and to you, than it was once offered in Christ's own words to those particular men.

units.la: Quartò, sanctissimi quique, (inquiunt) flebili voce in ipso mortis puncto incertitudinem salutis suæ prodiderunt, & quotidie produnt: Ergo non est ea misericordiæ & vitæ certitudo, quam nos dicimus esse. Resp. Multùm discriminis est inter id quod est, & id quod esse debet: hoc argumentum tantùm concludit id quod est, hoc est, incertitudinem esse: non autem concludit incertitudinem esse debere, imò contra concludit, non debere esse: Qui enim flent & dolent propter incertitudinem salutis propriæ, eo ipso arguùt, non debere esse incertitudinem: At adversarij incertitudinem salutis propriæ in præcipuis virtutibus Christianis numerant. Deinde respondeo, ex ea ipsa querimonia sanctorum hominum extremam animam agentium, nō minùs sequi certitudiné specialis misericordiæ, quàm incertitudinem. Nam vox ea existit iftit ex luƈta illa, quę est inter Spiritum & carnem, fidem & infidelitatem, certitudinem & incertitudinem. Quamobrem non minùs argumentum est certitudinis, quàm incertitudinis, imò arguit in luƈta illa superiorem esse certitudinem.
units.tr: Fourthly, the holiest of men, they say, have uttered with a tearful voice, at the very moment of death, their uncertainty of salvation, and they utter it daily. Therefore this is not the certainty of mercy and life that we say exists. I reply: there is a great difference between what is and what ought to be. This argument proves only what is, namely that there is uncertainty, but it does not prove that uncertainty ought to be; on the contrary, it proves that it ought not to be. For those who weep and grieve over the uncertainty of their own salvation thereby show that there ought not to be uncertainty. Yet our opponents count uncertainty of one's own salvation among the chief Christian virtues. Next, I reply that from that very complaint of holy men struggling at the point of death, a certainty of special mercy follows no less than uncertainty. For that cry arises out of that struggle which exists between the Spirit and the flesh, faith and unbelief, certainty and uncertainty. Therefore it is no less an argument for certainty than for uncertainty; indeed it shows that in that struggle certainty is the stronger.

units.la: Quinto, optimi quique, aiunt, possunt deficere à fide & gratia: Ergo quæ potest esse certitudo specialis misericordiæ & salutis? R. Qui fide tantùm & gratia temporaria prædití sunt, ij quidem, & possunt deficere, & deficiunt: at qui fide vera & justificante, ac gratia regenerante donati sunt, neque totaliter, ut sic dicam, neque finaliter deficere possunt. Id autem fit non ratione ipsorum hominum; sua enim natura propési sunt ad finalem & totalem defectionem (qua sunt infirmitate & fragilitate), verùm fit ex natura, ut sic dicam, illius gratiæ & doni Dei, quod datur in Christo Iesu: Dona enim & vocatio Dei ejusmodi sunt, ut ipsorum poenitere non possit. Rom. 11.
units.tr: Fifthly, the best of men, they say, can fall away from faith and grace. Then what certainty of special mercy and salvation can there be? I reply: those who are endowed only with faith and temporary grace can indeed fall away, and do fall away. But those who have been given true, justifying faith and regenerating grace can neither wholly, so to speak, nor finally fall away. This is not due to the men themselves, for by their own nature they are prone to final and total defection (through their weakness and frailty). Rather it comes from the nature, so to speak, of that grace and gift of God which is given in Christ Jesus. For God's gifts and calling are of such a kind that he cannot repent of them. Rom. 11.

units.la: Sexto, obijciunt Scripturæ testimonia, hæc præsertim quæ commendat nobis curam, sollicitudinem, studium in retinenda & conservanda gratia. Qui stat, videat ne cadat. 1.Cor. 10.12. Item 2. Cor.6.1. Paulus hortatur Corinthios ne frustrà gratiam receperint. Chriftus denique monet vt vigilemus & oremus: vt nihil dicam de ijs locis quibus commendatur nobis timor, vt Rom. 11. Tu per fidem stas, ne effertor animo, sed time, & alibi, Cum timore & tremore operemini salutem vestram. Ex his, inquiunt, & similibus locis sequitur dubitatio de propria gratia & salute: quorsum enim sic praecipiceretur, nisi posset fieri vt quis deficeret a fide & gratia, ac proinde deberet dubitare de propria gratia & salute? Respondeo: Ex his & similibus locis sequitur, non esse perseverantiam in gratia, nisi adsit cura, solicitudo, studium retinendae gratiae. Nam cura & solicitudo Deo sic ordinante, apponitur gratiae tanquam custos & vigil, prohibens ne homo incidat in carnalem securitatem, quae gratiae inimica est: atque solicitudo ista, & cura datur cum gratia, estq; ipsa Dei quaedam gratia specialis, & gratiae comes: quae nunquam ab ejus latere discedit: vbi enim est gratia, ibi perpetuo est aliqua certe solicitudo & cura retinendae illius gratiae, quae tota nunquam plane amittitur, quemadmodum ipsa gratia nunquam tota plane deperditur. Est enim perpetuo ipsi gratiae proportionalis. Cum enim magna gratia est, solicitudo magna est: cum vero parva gratia, solicitudo parva est. Cum autem Deus sciat quàm necessaria sit ista solicitudo, quæ gratiæ comes & conservatrix est, ideò totiesin Scripturis excitat nos ad solicitudinem, eamque nobis commendat. Atque omnes istæ exhortationes nihil aliud sunt, quàm voces totidem & quasi clamores, quibus solicitudo ista, quam vigilem esse diximus, & custodem gratiæ, excitatur & provocatur ad officium suum faciendum, hoc est, ad custodiendum gratiam, & abercendum securitatem carnalem, quæ inimica est gratiæ, quæque, nisi excubaret solicitudo, ipsam gratiam, vt fidem, regenerationem, justitiam, & vitá, prorsus aboleret. Ergo ex his & ejusmodi locis sequitur solicitudo, non dubitatio, virtus, non vitium. Dubitatio enim in malis pessimis, & Deo atque homini inimicissimis, semper numerata est in Scripturis.
units.tr: Sixthly, they object the testimonies of Scripture, especially those which commend to us care, anxiety and zeal in holding and preserving grace: "Let him who stands take heed lest he fall" 1 Cor. 10.12. Likewise 2 Cor. 6.1., where Paul urges the Corinthians not to have received grace in vain. Christ finally warns us to watch and pray. I say nothing of those passages in which fear is commended to us, such as Rom. 11., "By faith you stand; do not be proud, but fear", and elsewhere, "Work out your salvation with fear and trembling." From these and similar passages, they say, it follows that there is doubt about one's own grace and salvation. For why would such precepts be given, unless it could happen that someone fall away from faith and grace, and therefore ought to doubt his own grace and salvation? I reply: from these and similar passages it follows that there is no perseverance in grace unless care, anxiety and zeal for retaining grace are present. For care and anxiety, God so ordaining, are set alongside grace as its guardian and watchman, preventing a man from falling into carnal security, which is the enemy of grace. This anxiety and care is given together with grace; it is itself a certain special gift of God and the companion of grace, which never leaves its side. For where grace is, there is always some anxiety and care to retain that grace, which, as a whole, is never altogether lost, just as grace itself is never entirely destroyed. For this anxiety is always proportionate to grace itself. When grace is great, anxiety is great; when grace is small, anxiety is small. Since God knows how necessary this anxiety is, which is the companion and preserver of grace, he therefore so often stirs us up to anxiety in the Scriptures and commends it to us. And all these exhortations are nothing but so many voices, as it were cries, by which that anxiety, which we have said is the watchful guardian of grace, is roused and provoked to do its duty, that is, to guard grace and to drive away carnal security, which is hostile to grace, and which, were anxiety not keeping watch, would utterly destroy grace itself, along with faith, regeneration, righteousness and life. Therefore from these and similar passages there follows anxiety, not doubt; a virtue, not a vice. For doubt has always been counted in the Scriptures among the worst evils, most hostile to both God and man.

units.la: Nunc dicamus de subjecto fidei justificantis quodnam sit illud ex sententia adversariorum. Subjectum fidei statuunt mentem tantum, & in mente facultatem proprie vnam, quæ est judicandi, siue assentiendi veritati alicujus sententiæ. De voluntate & corde nihil loquuntur, cum tamen fides justificans præcipuè sit cordis, quemadmodum supra dixi-mus.
units.tr: Now let us speak of the subject of justifying faith, according to our opponents' view of what it is. They locate the subject of faith in the mind alone, and in the mind they posit essentially one faculty, that of judging, or of assenting to the truth of some proposition. They say nothing about the will and the heart, although justifying faith is chiefly of the heart, as we said above.

units.la: Partes naturæ fidei justificantis non tot faciunt, quot nos. Nam quod ad notitiam, quæ prima pars est fidei justificantis, eam, vel non necessariam esse omnino dicūt, vel obscuram aliquam sufficere: id quod primum hac ratione ostendunt. Duplex, inquiunt, assensus est mentis quo assentimur veritati alicujus sententiæ. Prior assensus est cum ei propter rationem & causam aliquam assentimur: qui vocatur scientia: hic assensus postulat necessariò præcedentem ejus rei notitiam, cujus veritati assentimur. Posterior assensus est, cum non propter rationem aliquam, sed propter authoritatem dicentis assentimur veritati alicujus sententiæ: hic assensus fides appellatur: ejus autem rei notitiam cui assentitur præcedentem non requirit, contentus nuda, solaque dicentis authoritate. Ex hac assensus distinctione atque differentia sequitur, inquiunt, in fide non opus esse notitia, cum fides assensus sit quo veritati alicujus sententiæ assentimur, non quidem ratione aliqua & causa, sed dictis authoritate adducti.
units.tr: They do not make the parts of the nature of justifying faith as many as we do. For as regards knowledge, which is the first part of justifying faith, they either say that it is not necessary at all, or that some obscure knowledge is sufficient. They show this first by the following argument. There are two kinds of assent of the mind, they say, by which we assent to the truth of some proposition. The first assent is when we assent to it on account of some reason and cause; this is called knowledge. This assent necessarily requires a prior knowledge of the thing whose truth we assent to. The second assent is when we assent to the truth of some proposition not on account of some reason, but on account of the authority of the one speaking; this assent is called faith. It does not require a prior knowledge of the thing assented to, being content with the bare authority of the speaker alone. From this distinction and difference between assents, they say, it follows that in faith there is no need of knowledge, since faith is an assent by which we assent to the truth of some proposition, not indeed on account of some reason and cause, but led by the authority of the words.

units.la: Ad hanc rationem respondemus: ac primùm quidem concedimus hanc assensuum differentiam: verùm negamus assensum eum qui fit propter authoritatem dicentis, non opus habere notitia antecedente. Nam vt sit fides justificans, requiritur vt id quod dicitur etiam ab ipso Deo, à nobis aliquo modo intelligatur. Neque etiam id à nobis Deus postulat, vt verbis ac voci ipsius non intellectis, propter authoritatem nudam testantis, assentiamur.
units.tr: To this argument we reply: first, we indeed grant this difference of assents; but we deny that the assent which is made on account of the authority of the speaker has no need of prior knowledge. For in order that it be justifying faith, it is required that what is said, even by God himself, be understood by us in some way. Nor does God demand of us that we assent, without understanding his words and voice, merely on account of the bare authority of the one testifying.
