units.la: Deinde argumentantur ex definitione illa fidei quæ est Heb.11. Fides est ὑπόστασις rerum quæ sperantur, & ἔλεγχος rerum quæ non videntur. Hic, inquiunt, videmus fidem rerum ignoratarum, vtpote sperandarum, & earum quæ non videntur? At inquam, duo hæc verba ὑπόστασις & ἔλεγχος satis arguunt eas ipsas res quæ sperantur & non videntur, aliquo modo interea præsentes subsistere, & à nobis cospici. Vnde Paulus 2.Cor.4. Dum spectamus, inquit, non ea quidem quæ cernuntur, sed ea quæ non cernuntur. Hic vides etiam ea quæ non cernuntur, neque objiciuntur oculis hisce corporeis, cerni tamen ac spectari oculis fidei spiritualibus. Atque hæc eorum sententia est de fidei notitia, quæ eo spectat vt stabiliatur fides illa, quam ipsi implicitam vocant.
units.tr: Then they argue from that definition of faith in Heb. 11. "Faith is ὑπόστασις [substance] of things hoped for, and ἔλεγχος [proof] of things not seen." Here, they say, we see faith in things unknown, inasmuch as they are hoped for, and in things that are not seen. But I reply that these two words, ὑπόστασις [substance] and ἔλεγχος [proof], sufficiently show that the very things which are hoped for and not seen do in some way already subsist present, and are beheld by us. Whence Paul, 2 Cor. 4.: "While we look," he says, "not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen." Here you see that things which are not seen, and are not presented to these bodily eyes, are nevertheless seen and beheld by the spiritual eyes of faith. This is their view of the knowledge of faith, which aims at establishing that faith which they call implicit.

units.la: Quod ad assensum illum, què diximus secundam esse partem fidei justificantis, naturam quidem fidei in solo illo assensu, qui est ratione veritatis, collocant: nam de assensu sive judicio bonitatis nihil loquuntur: & judicium illud veritatis quod statuunt, generale tantum faciunt: quo nimirum quis judicat sententiam aliquam veram esse, non de se, sed in genere de tota Ecclesia, cum tamen judicium illud, tam veritatis quam bonitatis quod fidei est, particulare magis sit, adeoque etiam singulare, quod in Scripturis πληροφορια nuncupatur, ut supra docuimus.
units.tr: As for that assent which we said is the second part of justifying faith, they place the nature of faith solely in the assent that rests on the truth of the matter. They say nothing about assent or judgment concerning goodness, and the judgment of truth they posit is only a general one, by which someone judges a certain doctrine to be true, not for himself, but in general, for the whole Church. Yet the judgment of faith, both of truth and of goodness, is rather particular, and therefore even singular, which the Scriptures call plērophoria [πληροφορια], as we showed above.

units.la: Quod ad tertiam fidei partem, quam fiduciam cordis appellamus, eam non agnoscunt: Nam fiduciam nihil aliud esse dicunt quam spem corroboratam, & effectum quoddam fidei, cum tamen fiducia, quae graecis παρρησια dicitur, motus quidam voluntatis & cordis sit non quidem exspectans, verum in praesentia apprehendens aliquid boni, eoque tanquam praesenti nitens atque gaudens. Praeterea, eiusdem sunt originis πειθω & πεποιθησις: utrumque enim est a verbo πειθω, quod persuadere significat. Ad haec, verbum πεπεισμαι ab Apostolo pro persuaderi, credere, non autem pro sperare accipitur. Rom. 8. πεπεισμαι persuasum habeo, neque vitam, neque mortem, neque praesentia, neque futura, &c. Phil. 1. πεποιθα Persuasus sum quod qui incepit in vobis opus
units.tr: As for the third part of faith, which we call the confidence of the heart, they do not acknowledge it. For they say that confidence is nothing other than hope strengthened, and a certain effect of faith. Yet confidence, which is called parrēsia [παρρησια] in Greek, is a certain motion of the will and heart, not waiting for something good but grasping it in the present, and resting and rejoicing in it as present. Moreover, peithō [πειθω] and pepoithēsis [πεποιθησις] have the same origin, for both come from the verb peithō, which means to persuade. Besides, the Apostle takes pepeismai [πεπεισμαι] to mean to be persuaded or to believe, not to hope. Rom. 8: pepeismai, I am persuaded that neither life nor death, nor things present nor things to come, etc. Phil. 1: pepoitha [πεποιθα], I am persuaded that he who began a good work in you...

units.la: {*} Not further legible. pus bonum,&c. 2.Cor.5. Scientes terrorem illum Domini [Greek] homines ad Fidem adducimus. Concedo, nonnunquam capitur nomen [Greek] pro confidentia, quæ fidei est consequens, & fiduciæ quædam proprietas, qua fit vt qui credit, aut fiduciam habet, nitatur eo in quo fiduciam suam collocat. De hac acceptione [Greek] lege Eph.3. 12. In quo habemus libertatem & aditum cū fiducia [Greek] per fidem ipsius.
units.tr: {*} Not further legible. ...the good work, etc. 2 Cor. 5: Knowing the terror [phobon φόβον] of the Lord, we persuade men to the faith. I grant that the name pepoithēsis [πεποιθησις] is sometimes taken for confidence, which is a consequence of faith, and a certain property of trust, by which it comes about that whoever believes, or has confidence, rests on that in which he places his confidence. For this sense of parrēsia [παρρησια] see Eph. 3:12: In whom we have boldness and access with confidence [parrēsia παρρησια] through his faith.

units.la: Ex his quæ diximus facile est justificantis Fidei definitionem ex eorum sententia colligere: quibus nihil aliud est fides justificans, quam qua quis in genere assentitur veritati verbi Dei, idque propter authoritatem dicentis. Quæquidem definitio quid aliud quæso est, quàm generalis fidei notio, & communis omnibus Fideiacceptionibus, quæ supra à nobis adductæ sunt.
units.tr: From what we have said it is easy to gather, from their opinion, the definition of justifying faith: for to them justifying faith is nothing other than that by which someone assents in general to the truth of God's Word, and that on account of the authority of the one speaking. What, I ask, is this definition but the general notion of faith, common to all the meanings of faith that we have cited above?

units.la: Ex hac definitione Fidei justificantis colligunt, & verè quidem, Fidem justificantem posse inesse etiam in impio, & flagitiosissimo quoque: In eo enim potest esse generalis hic assensus, qui ne Dæmonijs quidem negari potest, teste Iacobo. Dæmonia, inquit, credunt, & contremiscunt: Fidem tamen justificantem & veram hanc vocant, licet non viyam. Nam inter veram & vivam distinguunt. Veram dicunt etiam eam quae non operatur per charitatem, etiam mortuam: vivam vero vocant eam, quae operatur per charitatem, tanquam per formam suam, non autem instrumentum; unde alio nomine fidem formatam eam vocant.
units.tr: From this definition of justifying faith they conclude, and truly so, that justifying faith can be present even in the ungodly and the most wicked. For in such a person there can be this general assent, which cannot even be denied to the demons, as James witnesses: The demons, he says, believe and tremble. Yet they call this faith justifying and true, though not living. For they distinguish between true and living. They call faith true even when it does not work through charity, even if it is dead; but they call it living when it works through charity, as through its form and not as through an instrument. For this reason they also call it formed faith.

units.la: At nos distinctionem hanc fidei verae & vivae plane negamus: veram enim fidem & vivam fidem pro eodem capimus: quemadmodum idem est homo verus & vivus: & ut verus sive vivus homo sic appellatur ab anima sive forma sua: ita quoque vera sive viva fides sic appellatur ab anima sive forma sua, quae est sita in ἀληθοφανίᾳ & πεποίθησει quā diximus, citra quam fides nihil aliud est, quam quasi cadaver quoddam, quemadmodum homo sine anima, non tam homo est, quam cadaver & corpus mortuum.
units.tr: But we utterly reject this distinction between true faith and living faith. For we take true faith and living faith to be the same thing, just as a true man and a living man are the same. And as a man is called true or living from his soul or form, so too faith is called true or living from its soul or form, which consists in alēthophania [ἀληθοφανίᾳ] and pepoithēsei [πεποίθησει], which we have mentioned. Apart from these, faith is nothing other than a kind of corpse, just as a man without a soul is not so much a man as a corpse and dead body.

units.la: At illi ex Iacobo cap. 2. versu ultimo, conantur probare fidem etiam mortuam & non vivam, veram tamen esse. Quemadmodum se habet corpus ad Spiritum, ita se habet fides ad opera: Atqui corpus sine Spiritu verum est corpus, licet non vivum: Ergo, fides sine operibus vera est fides, etsi non viva. Respondeo, Sophisma hoc esse: nam comparatio corporis & fidei, quam instituit Iacobus, non est in veritate, verùm in morte: & Iacobus ex illa propositione assumit & concludit: At corpus sine spiritu mortuum est: quare etiá fides sine operibus mortua est. Nã inter fidë & corpus hoc discriminis est: Corpus vnû idemq; & mortuum esse potest & verum: at verò fides non est simul vera & mortua, quemadmodum homo non est simul verus & mortuus. Vtenim homo quiddam compositum est ex corpore suo & anima sua: ita fides cópositum quiddam est ex corpore quasi suo, & anima quasi sua, cujus quidë indices sunt actiones. Quamobrem apud Iacobum comparatio facta est simplicis & cópositi: simplicis, quod corpus est animæ expers; compositi, quæ fides est. Comparatio autem ea valet in eo in quo facta est, nempè, in morte vtriusq;, non autè in alijs. Atq; hæc hactenus de Fide justificate ex adversariorum sententia: omninòque de doctrina fidei dicta sunto.
units.tr: But they, from James chapter 2, last verse, try to prove that faith which is dead and not living is nevertheless true. As the body is related to the spirit, so faith is related to works. But a body without the spirit is a true body, though not living; therefore faith without works is true faith, though not living. I reply that this is a sophism. For the comparison James draws between the body and faith is not in respect of truth but of death, and James takes from that proposition and concludes: but a body without the spirit is dead; therefore faith too without works is dead. For there is this difference between faith and the body: a body can be one and the same both dead and true, but faith is not at once true and dead, just as a man is not at once true and dead. For a man is a composite made of his body and his soul; so faith is a composite made of what is, as it were, its body and what is, as it were, its soul, of which the indications are its actions. Hence in James the comparison is of the simple and the composite: simple, because the body is devoid of soul; composite, which is faith. But the comparison holds in that respect in which it was made, namely in death of both, and not in other respects. So far, then, concerning justifying faith according to the opinion of our opponents; and with that, what is to be said about the doctrine of faith has been said.

units.la: De Spe. Cap.32.
units.tr: On Hope. Chapter 32.

units.la: Idem sequitur spes: nam apprehensio illa Iesu Christi cum beneficijs suis, in verbo & sacramentis oblati, quæ fidei est, spem nobis facit nos aliquando Christo præsente fruituros. Apostolus Rom.5. dicit Experientiam gignere spem. Fide autem experimur, &, vt loquitur Petrus, gustamus quam benignus sit Dominus: quare necesse est fides gignat spē.
units.tr: Hope follows in the same way. That apprehension of Jesus Christ with his benefits, offered in the word and the sacraments, which belongs to faith, makes us hope that we shall at some time enjoy Christ's presence. The Apostle says in Rom.5. that experience produces hope. By faith, however, we experience, and, as Peter says, we taste how gracious the Lord is. So it is necessary that faith produces hope.

units.la: Vt igitur de spe dicamus: primùm omniū videndum est, quod sit ejus objectum. Fidei & spei objectum idem est re, nempe, Iesus Christus cum beneficijs suis. Heb.11. dicitur fides ὑπόστασις rerum quæ sperantur. Vicissim dici potest, spem esse rerum quæ creduntur, vel quæ per fidem jam subsistunt & exstant aliquo certè modo. Ex his apparet idem esse re fidei & spei objectum.
units.tr: To speak about hope, we must first of all see what its object is. The object of faith and of hope is the same in reality, namely Jesus Christ with his benefits. In Heb.11. faith is called the substance [ὑπόστασις] of things hoped for. Conversely, it can be said that hope is of things believed, or which already subsist and exist in some definite way through faith. From these things it is clear that the object of faith and of hope is the same in reality.

units.la: Ratione tamen differt objectum spei, ab objecto fidei. Præcipuum discrimen est, quòd objectum Fidei sit Christus in verbo & sacramento, sive verbum de Christo, & sacramentum quod ipsum adumbrat: quare objectum Fidei est imago quasi quædam Christi, quæ nobis in speculo verbi & sacramenti inspicienda proponitur. Unde 2.Cor.3. dicimur reteēta facie intuentes quasi in speculo, transformari in eandem imaginem, nempè, cum ea quam in speculo illo intuemur.
units.tr: Yet the object of hope differs in aspect from the object of faith. The principal difference is that the object of faith is Christ in the word and sacrament, or the word about Christ and the sacrament which foreshadows him. So the object of faith is, as it were, an image of Christ, set before us to be looked at in the mirror of word and sacrament. Hence in 2.Cor.3. we, with unveiled faces beholding as in a mirror, are said to be transformed into the same image, namely the one we gaze upon in that mirror.

units.la: Objectum autem spei, est Christus cum beneficijs suis, non quidem in verbo aut Sacramento apparens, verùm apparens sicuti est,& in sua ipsius,vt sic dicam,persona.Nam spes non est imaginis illius Christi, quam intuemur in speculo per fidem;verùm est ipsius faciei Christi,quam speramus nos visuros tandem aliquando. Philip.3.20. Vnde etiam Seruatorem expectamus Dominum Iesum Christum. Tit.2. Expectantes beatam illam spem, & illustrem illum aduetum magni illius Dei, & seruatoris nostri, Iesu Christi. 1.Ioh.3.2. Quoniam videbimus eum sicuti est: quisquis autem habet hanc spem in eo sitam, hoc est, qui sperat se visurum eum sicuti est. Ex his concipitur spem esse faciei ipsius Iesu Christi. Tria sunt quae versantur circa vnum Christum, Fides, spes, aspectus: verùm ratione alia atque alia. Nam fides proprie est imaginis ipsius: spes est faciei, sed venturae & apparituræ: aspectus similiter est faciei, sed praesentis.
units.tr: The object of hope, however, is Christ with his benefits, not appearing in the word or sacrament, but appearing as he is, and, so to speak, in his own person. For hope is not of that image of Christ which we look upon in the mirror through faith; it is of the very face of Christ, which we hope to see at last at some time. Philip.3.20. Hence we also wait for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ. Tit.2. Waiting for that blessed hope and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour, Jesus Christ. 1.Ioh.3.2. Since we shall see him as he is; and everyone who has this hope set on him, that is, who hopes that he will see him as he is. From these things it is understood that hope is of the very face of Jesus Christ. Three things concern the one Christ: faith, hope, and sight, but each in a different respect. For faith is properly of his image; hope is of his face, but of it as yet to come and to appear; sight is likewise of his face, but of it as present.

units.la: Secundum discrimen inter obiectum fidei & spei, ex primo illo consequens est, est autem quod fides sit rerum praesentium, Christi & beneficiorum ipsius; vel potius imaginis istarum rerum, quam praesentem intuemur in speculo verbi & sacramenti. Vnde Hebr.11. dicitur ὑπόστασις & ἔλεγχος, quae verba praesentiam eorum quae creduntur significant. Spes autem est rerum futurarum ac venturarum: nam spes fi cernatur, non est spes, hoc est, si sit rerum præsentium, non amplius est spes. Quod enim videt quis cur & speret? Rom.8.24. Præterea spes est faciei ipsius, quæ nondum videtur.
units.tr: The second difference between the object of faith and of hope follows from the first. Faith is of things present, Christ and his benefits, or rather of the image of these things, which we see present in the mirror of word and sacrament. Hence in Hebr.11. it is called substance [ὑπόστασις] and evidence [ἔλεγχος], words which signify the presence of the things believed. Hope, however, is of things future and yet to come. For if hope is seen, it is not hope; that is, if it concerns present things, it is no longer hope. For why does anyone hope for what he sees? Rom.8.24. Moreover, hope is of the face which is not yet seen.

units.la: Tertium discrimen ex primo quoque sequitur. Nam fides est rei ex parte tantum, cū sit imaginis, & quasi umbræ: &, ut sic dicam, arrhabonis, quæ pars est summæ: Vide 1. Cor. 13. Ex parte cognoscimus. Spes vero est rei totius, est faciei, est complementi, est denique perfectæ summæ, cujus spem nobis facit arrha illa, quam fides apprehendit. Atque hæc de objecto spei.
units.tr: The third difference follows from the first as well. Faith is of the thing only in part, since it is of the image, and as it were of a shadow, and, so to speak, of an earnest, which is a part of the whole sum: see 1. Cor. 13. We know in part. Hope, however, is of the whole thing. It is of the face, of the fulfilment, and finally of the complete sum, the hope of which is given to us by that earnest which faith apprehends. And so much for the object of hope.

units.la: Sequitur subjectum, quod non est mens aut mentis aliqua facultas, sive ea intelligendi, sive judicandi sit: non item voluntas quæ rationalis est; nam in his sedem suam posuit fides. Spes autem contenta inferiori quasi subsellio subsidit in corde. Est enim cordis affectus, quemadmodum metus qui ei opponitur. De natura ejus ut dicamus, non est notitia, non est judicium sive assensus, non est denique apprehensio sive fiducia: ista enim omnia fidei sunt, sed est expectatio quæ fidem sequitur, & per fidem gignitur.
units.tr: Next comes the subject, which is not the mind or any faculty of the mind, whether of understanding or of judging. Nor is it the will, which is rational, for faith has placed its seat in these. Hope, however, sits down lower, as it were on a bench beneath them, in the heart. For it is an affection of the heart, just as fear, which is opposed to it, is. As to its nature, it is not knowledge, not judgement or assent, and not finally apprehension or trust; for all these belong to faith. It is an expectation which follows faith and is begotten through faith.

units.la: Proprietas spei est, non certitudo propriè quæ est fidei, siue assensus illius qui est in fide: Fides enim proprie certa dicitur: Spes autem non proprie certa dicitur, verùm certa dicitur propter Fidei certitudinem. In Scriptura reperio ὑπομονὴν patientiam, spei attributam esse tanquam ipsius proprietatem quandam. Rom. 8. 25. Si verò quod non videmus, speramus, nempe, per patientiam expectamus. Heb. 6. de Abrahamo dicitur quod cum patienter expectasset, promissum sit assequutus. 1. Thess. 1. 3. mentio fit ὑπομονῆς τῆς ἐλπίδος tolerantiæ spei, vel toleratis spei. Est autem hæc ὑπομονὴ, quæ spes sustinet omnes incursus atq; impetus rerum adversariarum, & quasi manet sub iis. Promissiones enim rerum coelestium factæ sunt omnes cum exceptione temporalium afflictionum. Quāobrem quisquis sperat se assequuturum res illas coelestes promissas, necesse est se comparet ad ferendas & sustinendas omnes calamitates quæ in hac vita incidunt. Quamobrem patientia spei adeò necessariò conjuncta est, ut non possit esse spes sine ea.
units.tr: The property of hope is not certainty properly so called, which belongs to faith, that is, the assent of the one who is in faith. For faith is properly called certain; hope is not properly called certain, but is called certain on account of the certainty of faith. In Scripture I find patience [ὑπομονήν] ascribed to hope as a certain property of its own. Rom. 8. 25. But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it through patience. Heb. 6. It is said of Abraham that, having waited patiently, he obtained the promise. 1. Thess. 1. 3. Mention is made of the endurance of hope [ὑπομονῆς τῆς ἐλπίδος], or endurance which hope bears. This endurance is what hope sustains: it withstands all the assaults and onsets of adverse things, and as it were remains firm under them. For all the promises of heavenly things were made with the exception of temporal afflictions. Therefore whoever hopes that he will obtain those promised heavenly things must prepare himself to bear and endure all the calamities that befall in this life. Hence the patience of hope is so necessarily joined to it that there cannot be hope without it.

units.la: Ex his quæ diximus colligi potest spei definitio: ut sit spes patiens cordis expectatio quæ est faciei, sive complemeti promissionis. Notandum definitionem hanc esse spei ut nomē hoc accipitur pro opere & functione spei, quæ propriè proprie significat cordis affectum, & eum qui dem sanctificatum; neque id tantùm, sed etiā evectum supra naturam. Neque enim dum regeneramur per Spiritum Christi, tantùm recuperamus deperditam illam in Adamo naturæ sanctitatem: verùm in regeneratione non est facultas mentis, vel affectio cordis nostri, cui non inditur ἐνέργεια, vel qualitas aliqua supernaturalis, ad exercendas functiones supernaturales. Regeneratio enim nostri non tam fit ad imaginem illam quæ in Adamo fuit ante lapsum sancta & integra, quàm ad imaginē Christi. 1.Cor. 15. 49. Gestabimus etiā imaginem cœlestis subaudi hominis: Unde motus cordis nostri inenarrabiles & ineffabiles vocantur. Rom. 8. Suspiria inenarrabilia dicuntur. 1. Pet. 1. Gaudium vocatur ineffabile & gloriosum: & facultates mentis atque affectiones cordis regenitæ feruntur in ea quæ sunt incomprehensibilia, & quæ per naturam etiā sanctam Adami comprehendi, credo, non potuerunt: ut sunt inpervestigabiles illæ opes Christi. Eph. 3. 8. ut est charitas illa Christi omni cognitione superior, ibidem 19. ut sunt illa quæ oculus non vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in mentem hominis venerunt. 1. Cor. 2. 9. Sed de his jam diximus in doctrina de Fide.
units.tr: From what we have said, a definition of hope can be gathered: hope is a patient expectation of the heart, which is of the face, or of the fulfilment of the promise. It should be noted that this definition takes the word hope for the work and function of hope, which properly signifies an affection of the heart, and a sanctified one at that; and not only sanctified, but also raised above nature. For when we are regenerated by the Spirit of Christ, we do not merely recover that holiness of nature which was lost in Adam. Rather, in regeneration there is no faculty of the mind or affection of our heart into which an energy [ἐνέργεια] or some supernatural quality is not infused, for exercising supernatural functions. For our regeneration is not so much made according to that image which was holy and whole in Adam before the fall, as according to the image of Christ. 1.Cor. 15. 49. We shall also bear the image of the heavenly one. Hence the motions of our heart are called unspeakable and ineffable. Rom. 8. Groanings are said to be unutterable. 1. Pet. 1. Joy is called ineffable and glorious. The faculties of the mind and the affections of the regenerate heart are carried toward things which are incomprehensible, and which, I believe, could not be grasped even through the holy nature of Adam: such as the unsearchable riches of Christ. Eph. 3. 8. Such as the love of Christ, which surpasses all knowledge, ibid. 19. Such as those things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor which have entered into the heart of man. 1. Cor. 2. 9. But we have already spoken of these in the doctrine on faith.

units.la: Hoc postremò de spe observandum, quòd plures sint ipsius gradus: est enim spes quædam intetior, quæ ἀπόκαρδοκία vocatur ab Apostolo Rom. 8. 19. ubi habes ἀπόκαραδοκίαν sive solicitam observationem creaturæ. Phil. 1. Paulus ἀπεκδέχεται, sive intenta expectationem suam profitetur. Atq; hæc de spe ex nostra sententia.
units.tr: Finally, this should be observed about hope: there are several degrees of it. For there is a certain more intense hope, which the Apostle calls eager expectation [ἀπόκαρδοκία] in Rom. 8. 19. where you have eager expectation [ἀπόκαραδοκίαν], that is, the anxious watching of the creature. In Phil. 1. Paul says he eagerly awaits [ἀπεκδέχεται], that is, he professes his intent expectation. And so much for hope according to our view.

units.la: Quid de ea sentiant adversarij paucis admonebimus. Objectum spei statuunt eas res quæ peculiariter ad sperantem pertinent: hoc enim discrimen faciunt inter spem & fidem, quod fides sit generalis misericordiæ, non propriæ: spes vero sit propriç. Sed discrimen hoc falsum: nam tam fides quàm spes est propriæ gratiæ, ac misericordiæ. Subjectum spei nobiscum dicunt esse cor: virtutem enim cordi infusam tradunt spem esse.
units.tr: What the opponents think about it we will briefly point out. They state the object of hope to be those things which pertain peculiarly to the one hoping. For they make this distinction between hope and faith: faith is of general mercy, not of a particular mercy, whereas hope is of a particular one. But this distinction is false, for both faith and hope are of particular grace and mercy. They say with us that the subject of hope is the heart, for they teach that hope is a virtue infused into the heart.

units.la: Naturam ponunt non in cognoscendo, non in judicando, sed in expectando. Bellarminus discrimen facit inter sperare, & expectare. Speramus (inquit) quæ non certò scimus nos assequuturos esse: expectamus vero quæ certò scimus nos consequuturos. Vnde beatæ animæ in cœlis dicuntur expectare resurrectionem corporum suorum, quia certò sciunt eam futuram. Sed Paulus Rom. 8. pro eodem videtur sumere sperandi & expectandi verbum. Si quod non videmus speramus, nempe igitur per patientiam expectamus. Videsz Paulo idem esse ἐλπίζειν & ὑπομένειν,
units.tr: They place the nature of hope not in knowing or judging, but in expecting. Bellarmine distinguishes between hoping and expecting: "We hope for things which we do not know for certain that we shall attain, but we expect things which we know for certain we shall obtain. Hence the blessed souls in heaven are said to expect the resurrection of their bodies, because they know for certain that it will come." But Paul in Rom. 8 seems to use the words "hope" and "expect" for the same thing: "If we hope for what we do not see, then we wait for it with patience." You see that for Paul hoping [ἐλπίζειν] and enduring [ὑπομένειν] are the same.

units.la: Proprietatem spei faciunt certitudinem: spem enim certam esse dicunt. verùm hanc certitudinem intellectus esse docent. Nam intellectus est qui certò scit salutem obventuram: & propter certitudinem intellectus, spes dicitur certa, & cor sperat certò futuram salutem. Ergo certitudo hæc non est proprie in spe, sed spes eam præsupponit. Certitudinem hanc non simpliciter & absolutam esse dicunt: Nemo enim (inquiunt) simpliciter & absolutè certus est de salute sua, vel certò scit se salutem consecuturum: imò contrà spei incertitudinem simpliciter & absolutè esse tradunt: & qui sperat (inquiunt) simpliciter & absolutè incertus est de salute sua: certus autem est de salute sua is qui sperat, non simpliciter & absolutè, verùm <bl>καλῶς</bl> secundum quid, & aliquo respectu: Primùm, respectu fundamenti spei, hoc est, promissionis Dei quæ fallere non potest, & propter quam, si non essent aliæ certitudinis causæ, simpliciter & absolutè dici posset quis certus esse de salute sua. Verùm cum sint aliæ certitudinis causæ præter promissionem onem Dei, non potest quis simpliciter & absolutè certus esse de salute sua, propter solam promissionem Dei, ipsiusque infallibilem veritatem. Deinde certus dicitur aliquis de salute sua respectu charitatis, quam dicunt esse spei formam: Qui enim habet charitatem hac ex parte & hoc respectu, certus est de sua salute: nam charitas est certa salutis causa: & si fieri posset ut quis nunquam excideret charitate, vel propter eam solam posset esse certus simpliciter & absolutè de salute sua. Verùm cum possit quis excidere charitate, eamq; amittere, ideò ne propter charitatem quidem simplex est spei certitudo. Hæc est ergo eorum sententia spem similiter incertam esse, certam autem esse aliquot respectibus: primùm respectu promissionis, deinde respectu charitatis ac proinde certitudinem spei admixtam esse perpetuò incertitudini. Nam quo tempore certa est propter promissionem Dei, eodem tempore incerta est propter alias causas quæ in nobis ipsis sunt: ut ratione respipiscentiæ nostræ, ratione operum & meritorum nostrorum, quæ requiruntur quoque ad spei certitudinem efficiendam. Rursus quo tempore certa est propter charitatem, eodem tempore incerta est propter mutabilitatem illius charitatis.
units.tr: They make certainty the property of hope, for they say that hope is certain. But they teach that this certainty belongs to the intellect. For it is the intellect that knows for certain that salvation will come, and because of the certainty of the intellect hope is called certain, and the heart hopes with certainty for future salvation. So this certainty is not properly in hope, but hope presupposes it. They say that this certainty is not simple and absolute. For no one (they say) is simply and absolutely certain of his salvation, or knows for certain that he will attain salvation. Rather, they teach that uncertainty is simply and absolutely the mark of hope: the one who hopes (they say) is simply and absolutely uncertain of his salvation. He who hopes is certain of his salvation not simply and absolutely, but "rightly" [καλῶς], in a certain respect and in some regard. First, with respect to the ground of hope, that is, the promise of God, which cannot deceive, and on account of which, if there were no other causes of certainty, a man could be said simply and absolutely to be certain of his salvation. But since there are other causes of certainty besides the promise of God, a man cannot be simply and absolutely certain of his salvation on the sole ground of God's promise and his infallible truth. Next, a man is said to be certain of his salvation with respect to charity, which they say is the form of hope. For one who has charity, in this respect and in this regard, is certain of his salvation, since charity is a sure cause of salvation. And if it could happen that a man never fell from charity, or lost it, he could be simply and absolutely certain of his salvation on the basis of charity alone. But since a man can fall from charity and lose it, the certainty of hope is not simple even on account of charity. This, then, is their opinion: hope is uncertain in the same way, and is certain only in certain respects: first, with respect to the promise, and then with respect to charity; and so the certainty of hope is always mingled with uncertainty. For at the same time that it is certain because of God's promise, it is uncertain because of other causes that lie in ourselves, such as our repentance, and our works and merits, which are also required to produce the certainty of hope. Again, at the same time that it is certain because of charity, it is uncertain because of the changeableness of that charity.

units.la: Hæc est eorum sententia.
units.tr: This is their opinion.

units.la: Nos autem sic statuimus certam dici spem propter fidem antegredientem, & fidei πληροφορίαν. Nam certitudo proprie est fidei, & fides est qua certò scimus singuli salutem ad nos pertinere: Hinc firmitas spei, ejusque certitudo. Deinde certitudinem hanc spei, quæ est propter fidem, dicimus simplicem & absolutâ esse: negamusque spem hoc respectu certam esse, illo autem respectu incertâ esse, id quod isti dicunt: sed affirmamus omni respectu eâ certam esse, saltem esse debere, respectu promissionis Dei, respectu charitatis, omninòq; regenerationis, respectu perseverâtiæ noştrę, & sic de cæteris: Nam omnia ista certa sunt ac solida quibus spes nititur, & propter quæ certa dicitur; nituntur-que ista Dei ipsius immutabilitate, sive ea extra nos sint, ut Dei promissio; sive in nobis sint, ut charitas, omninòque regeneratio: Gratia enim semel data in Christo Iesu totaliter, ut sic dicam, & finaliter amitti non potest.
units.tr: We, however, hold that hope is called certain on account of the preceding faith and the full assurance [πληροφορία] of faith. For certainty properly belongs to faith, and faith is that by which each one of us knows for certain that salvation pertains to him. Hence comes the firmness of hope and its certainty. Moreover, we say that this certainty of hope, which rests on faith, is simple and absolute. We deny that hope is certain in one respect and uncertain in another, as they say. Rather, we affirm that it is certain in every respect, or at least ought to be: with respect to God's promise, with respect to charity, and altogether with respect to regeneration, with respect to our perseverance, and so on for the rest. For all those things on which hope rests, and on account of which it is said to be certain, are certain and solid. They rest on the immutability of God himself, whether they lie outside us, as God's promise does, or within us, as charity and regeneration altogether do. For grace once given in Christ Jesus cannot be lost totally, so to speak, and finally.

units.la: Adversarij causam aliquam certitudinis in nobis nostrisque viribus, & in operibus atq; meritis collocant. Ideòque non mirum est si dicant spem non esse simpliciter, absolutèq; certam: Nam profectò his rebus in quibus ipfi collocant causam certitudinis spei aliquam imò præcipuam, nihil incertius.
units.tr: The adversaries place some cause of certainty in ourselves, in our own strength, and in works and merits. So it is no wonder if they say that hope is not simply and absolutely certain. Indeed, nothing is more uncertain than those things in which they locate some cause of the certainty of hope, or rather the chief cause.

units.la: De spei absoluta certitudine testimonia Scripturæ sunt. Pfal.31. Inte Domine speravi, non confundar in æternum. Qui confidit in Domino sicut mons Sion in æternum non commovebitur. Rom.5. Gloriamur sub spe gloriæ Dei. Et postea, Spes non pudefacit. Rom.8. Spe servati fumus. Philip.1. Secundum intentam expectationem, & spem meâ, quòd nullain re pudefiam. Rom.9. Omnis qui credit in eo non pudefiet. Atque hæc de spe hactenus.
units.tr: Scripture gives testimonies to the absolute certainty of hope. Psal. 31: "In you, Lord, I have hoped; let me never be put to shame." "Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion, which shall never be moved." Rom. 5: "We rejoice in the hope of the glory of God." And afterwards: "Hope does not disappoint." Rom. 8: "We have been saved by hope." Phil. 1: "According to my earnest expectation and hope, that in nothing I shall be put to shame." Rom. 9: "Everyone who believes in him shall not be put to shame." So much for hope up to this point.

units.la: De Charitate. Cap.33.
units.tr: On Love. Chapter 33.

units.la: IN præcipuis Fidei effectibus proximè fecundû spem, numeratur charitas: & Paulus 1.Cor.13. tria præcipua Spiritus fan�000ti dona simul numerat, fidem, spem, charitatem. Tria sunt, inquit, fides, spes, charitas, maxima autem horum est charitas. Hæc quæ conjunxit Apoftolus, nos non sejungimus, præsertim cum amor Dei vinculum quoddam fit, vnà cum vinculo illo fidei, quod primarium est ac principale, nos cum Deo vniens. Atque ideò Petrus cum Christo absente collocatin dilectione & fide. His adducti rationibus nos tertio post fidem loco, in doctrina vocationis effi-
units.tr: Among the chief effects of faith, love is numbered next after hope. Paul, in 1 Cor. 13, lists together the three chief gifts of the Holy Spirit: faith, hope, and love. "There are three," he says, "faith, hope, and love, but the greatest of these is love." We do not separate what the Apostle has joined. Love of God is a kind of bond, and together with that chief and principal bond of faith it unites us with God. For this reason Peter places love and faith together in regard to Christ, though he is absent. Led by these reasons, we treat of love third after faith, in the doctrine of effectual calling.

units.la: [illegible, ~5 letters] The Greek word aster "Petrus" is printed in Greek letters and is illegible here. efficacis, de charitate agimus.
units.tr: [illegible] ... of effectual calling, we treat of love.

units.la: Existit autē charitas sive dilectio ex illa tam suavi apprehensione, & quasi gustu Domini: Gustus enim ille excitat in corde ineffabilem amorē Domini,&,propter ᴐominū,proximi: excitata per fidē jam charitas, evadit fidei instrumetū,per quod ipsa operatur alia quoque Spiritus sancti dona, vt scientiæ, vt prophetiæ, vt linguarum donū,ut miraculorum donum. Sunt ista quoq; totidem fidei justificantis instrumenta & organa, per quæ ipsa operatur, verùm primarium fidei instrumetum est charitas. Vnde Galat.5. dicitur fides per charitatē agere, & charitas cum suis operibus omnium signorum & testimoniorum fidei certissimū est signum ac testimonium.
units.tr: Love or affection arises from that sweet apprehension of the Lord, and as it were a taste of him. For that taste stirs up in the heart an ineffable love of the Lord and, for the Lord's sake, of the neighbour. Once aroused through faith, love becomes an instrument of faith, through which faith itself works the other gifts of the Holy Spirit: knowledge, prophecy, the gift of tongues, and the gift of miracles. These are also so many instruments and organs of justifying faith through which faith works. Yet the primary instrument of faith is love. Hence Gal. 5 says that faith works through love, and love, with its works, is the most certain sign and testimony of all the signs and testimonies of faith.

units.la: Hæc si comparetur cum alijs donis Spiritus sancti,omnibus est præferenda, tertium enim locum obtinet post fidem. Ergo si fidem & spem excipias, charitas inter dona Spiritus sancti primum locum obtinet,estque sequentium donorum omnium quasi anima.Ideoq; Apost.1.Cor.12.13. posteaquam varia Spiritus sancti dona recensuit,dixit ea absque charitate vel mortua esse, vel nihil esse, vel nihil prodesse: quo significavit omnes alias virtutes nihil solidi in se habere, si à charitate separénparentur : verùm esse tantùm virtutum quædam simulachra. Non immeritò igitur dicetur charitas aliarum omnium virtutum sequëtium esse anima.
units.tr: If love is compared with the other gifts of the Holy Spirit, it is to be preferred to them all, for it holds the third place after faith. So, if you leave out faith and hope, love holds the first place among the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and it is as it were the soul of all the gifts that follow. Therefore, after the Apostle (1 Cor. 12–13) had listed the various gifts of the Holy Spirit, he said that without love they are either dead, or nothing, or profit nothing. By this he signified that all other virtues have nothing solid in themselves if they are separated from love, but are only certain images of virtues. Not undeservedly, then, is love said to be the soul of all the other virtues that follow.

units.la: . Hac charitatis prærogativa si contenti suissent adversarij, non aberrasscnt: verùm cum eam quoque fidei animam & formam faciant hîc graviter peccant, cum potiùs è contra fides sit charitatis anima, cum citra fidem non sit in homine nisi charitatis quoddam simulachrum. Quare tum charitatis, tum aliarum omnium virtutum principalis anima est fides Christi, sine qua omnia ficta, fucata, denique peccata sunt: Quod enim ex fide non est, peccatum est.
units.tr: If the opponents had been content with this prerogative of love, they would not have gone astray. But because they also make love the soul and form of faith, they err gravely here, since rather, on the contrary, faith is the soul of love, for apart from faith there is in man only a kind of image of love. Therefore the principal soul both of love and of all the other virtues is the faith of Christ, without which everything is feigned, counterfeit, and in the end sin. For whatever is not of faith is sin.

units.la: Charitatis objectum primarium idem est cum objecto fidei & spei: quod enim fide primùm apprehendimus, deinde spe expectamus, illud charitate diligimus. Secundarium charitatis objectum est proximus, quæ propter Dominum diligimus. Subjectum charitatis est cor: Corde enim amamus.
units.tr: The primary object of love is the same as the object of faith and hope: what we first apprehend by faith and then await by hope, that we love. The secondary object of love is the neighbour, whom we love for the Lord's sake. The subject of love is the heart, for we love with the heart.

units.la: Natura ejus non est in cognitione, non est in expectatione, sed in dilectione. In dilectione autem duo sunt: primùm studium conservādi eam rem quam diligimus: deinde appetitio vniendi, conjungendiq; nos cum ipsa: Vtrumq; hoc cernitur in dilectione primùm Dei, deinde proximi.
units.tr: Its nature lies not in knowledge or in expectation, but in affection. In affection there are two things: first, the zeal to preserve the thing we love; second, the desire to join and unite ourselves with it. Both of these are seen in love, first of God, then of the neighbour.

units.la: Proprietates charitatis consequentes multæ enumeratæ sunt 1. Cor. 13. 4. & deinceps. Nam vbi charitas est ibi virtutum est cumulus : neque charitas vnquam sola est in quoquam, sed comites habet & quasi pedissequas alias virtutes non paucas.
units.tr: The consequent properties of love are listed in 1 Cor. 13:4 and following. For where love is, there is an abundance of virtues, and love is never alone in anyone, but has with it, as companions and as it were attendants, many other virtues.

units.la: Ex suprà dictis definitio ejus certè aliqua colligi potest: ut sit charitas studium conservādi rem amatam, sive Deum, sive hominem, cum appetitione vniendi nos cum ea. Est enim charitas illud vinculum, sic enim vocatur ab Apost. quo membra corporis inter se vniuntur: atque etiam suo loco & modo nos cum Deo & Christo vnit, licet fidei præcipuè tribuatur illa xoινωνία Christi capitis, & corporis ipsius. Atque ista ratione justificationem antecedit, estque in efficaci vocatione vnà cum fide, spe, & resipiscentia. Cujus quidem rei consideratio inter cætera effecit, vt nos in doctrina vocationis, de ea post fidem & spem ageremus: fides enim in qua positam esse dicimus secundam efficacis vocationis partem, inseparabiles quasi comites habet, spem, charitatem, & refipiscentiam. Post quę licet non temporis, tamen naturę ordine sequitur
units.tr: From what has been said above, a definition of love can certainly be drawn: love is the zeal to preserve the beloved thing, whether God or man, with the desire to unite ourselves with it. For love is that bond, so the Apostle calls it, by which the members of the body are united with one another; and it also unites us with God and Christ in its own place and manner, although that fellowship [κοινωνία] with Christ the head and with his body is chiefly ascribed to faith. On this ground love precedes justification, and in effectual calling it is joined with faith, hope, and repentance. This consideration, among other things, led us to treat of love in the doctrine of calling, after faith and hope. For faith, in which we say the second part of effectual calling consists, has as its inseparable companions hope, love, and repentance. After these, though not in time, justification follows in the order of nature.

units.la: 4 quitur justificatio. Alia autem ratione charitas justificationem sequitur, & ad gratiam regenerationis pertinet: Sed de hoc suo loco erit dicendum.
units.tr: Justification follows love in another way, and love belongs to the grace of regeneration. But this will be said in its own place.

units.la: Nunc ut redeamus: definitio illa quam attulimus, est non tam charitatis ipsius, quàm operis & functionis charitatis. Nam charitas proprie affectus est, & quidem sanctificatus: neque id modo, sed etiam supra naturam evectus, ad diligendum ea quæ supra naturam sunt, & quæ superant naturalem omnem dilectionem: ut enim fides est eorum quæ superant naturalem omnem cognitionem atque apprehensionem, & spes est eorum quæ superant naturalem omnem expectationem: sic charitas est eorum quæ superant naturalem omnem dilectionem. Nam, ut antea non semel admonuimus, regeneratio ista nostri in Christo Iesu, non tam est ad imaginem Adami eam, quæ fuit ante lapsum, quam ad imaginem Christi, qui homo est spiritualis & coelestis, & in quo habemus non tantum sanctitatem, ut sic loquar, naturalem: sed etiam coelestem quandam & supernaturalem ἐνέργειαν, & efficaciam inditam omnibus animi nostri facultatibus & affectionibus. Verum supernaturalis ista conditio nostra nondum conspicitur, fpiritur, neque etiam fatis sentitur aut percipitur à nobis ipsis, sed in altera vita conspicietur, in qua demùm gestabimus imaginem coelestis illius hominis, 1.Cor.15.49. Nunc filij Dei sumus, sed nondum patefactū est quod erimus: scimus autem fore ut cum ipse patefactus fuerit, similes ei simus. 1.John.3.2.
units.tr: Now to return: the definition we have given is not so much of love itself as of the work and function of love. For love is properly an affection, and indeed a sanctified one, and not only that but also raised above nature, to love the things that are above nature and that surpass all natural affection. For just as faith is of those things that surpass all natural knowledge and apprehension, and hope is of those things that surpass all natural expectation, so love is of those things that surpass all natural affection. For, as we have more than once remarked before, this regeneration of ours in Christ Jesus is not so much according to the image of Adam as he was before the fall, as according to the image of Christ, who is the spiritual and heavenly man, and in whom we have not only a natural holiness, as I may say, but also a heavenly and supernatural energy and efficacy infused into all the faculties and affections of our mind. Yet this supernatural condition of ours is not yet seen, nor breathed, nor sufficiently felt or perceived by ourselves; it will be seen in the other life, in which at last we shall bear the image of that heavenly man (1 Cor. 15:49). Now we are the sons of God, but it has not yet been revealed what we shall be; we know, however, that when he is revealed we shall be like him (1 John 3:2).

units.la: Adversarij toti sunt in prædicandis laudibus charitatis, atque etiam nimij sunt in charitate efferenda. Nam spolijs fidei justificantis eam ditant: & non suis, sed furtivis coloribus depingunt, dum justificationem & salutē hominis fidei detractam, charitati deferunt: id quod videbimus cum vētum fuerit ad doctrinam justificationis. Atque hæc hactenus de charitate dicta sunto.
units.tr: The opponents are wholly occupied in praising love, and indeed they are excessive in extolling it. For they enrich it with the spoils of justifying faith, and they paint it not in its own colours but in borrowed ones, while they transfer to love the justification and salvation of man, which have been taken away from faith. We shall see this when we come to the doctrine of justification. So much for what we have said about love.

units.la: De Resipiscentia. Cap. 34.
units.tr: On Repentance. Chap. 34.

units.la: FIdem sequitur Resipiscentia, ut effectus causam suam. Nam dolorille, qui est secundum Deum, efficitque refipiscentiam, fidei fœtus est, id quod posteā videbimus. Hujus beneficij varia sunt in variis linguis & idiomatis nomina. Hebrei vocant [TESCHVBHAH] Græci μετανοιαν & μεταμελειαν appellant. Μετανοια est à verbo μεταvoεῖν quòd significat post factum sapere, sententiam retractare, consilium immutare, ad sanam mentem redire. Unde μετάνοια est sapientia post factum, sententiæ retractatio, consilij immutatio. Μεταμέλεια est à vocabulo μελάμελει, quod significat post factum solicitum esse & anxium: unde μεταμέλεια est post factum solicitudo, & cordis anxietas. Differt itaq; μετάνοια à μεταμέλεια quòd μέλεια proprie sit mentis, μεταμέλεια vero cordis. Differunt etiam quòd μετάνοια complectatur totum beneficium resipiscentiæ: (nam mutatio consilij quæ hoc nomine significatur, præsupponit necessariò dolorem cordis, & μεταμέλειαν, hoc est, post factum contritionem & solicitudinē:) Μεταμέλεια vero magis restringatur ad partem tantum huius beneficij significandam, nempe primam, quæ est in dolore, contritione, & solicitudine cordis post factum: neq; enim ita necessarium est ut ubi μεταμέλεια est, ibi continuò fit μετάνοια: quemadmodum necessarium est, ut ubi μετάνοια est, ibi quoque fit μεταμέλεια.
units.tr: Repentance follows faith as an effect follows its cause. For the sorrow that is according to God, which produces repentance, is the offspring of faith, as we shall see later. This blessing has various names in various languages and idioms. The Hebrews call it [TESCHVBHAH]. The Greeks call it metanoia and metameleia. Metanoia comes from the verb metanoein, which means to become wise after the event, to change one's opinion, to alter one's purpose, to return to a sound mind. Hence metanoia is wisdom after the event, a change of opinion, an alteration of purpose. Metameleia comes from the word melamelei, which means to be anxious and troubled after the event; hence metameleia is anxious care after the event and anguish of heart. Metanoia therefore differs from metameleia in that meleia properly belongs to the mind, while metameleia belongs to the heart. They also differ in that metanoia embraces the whole blessing of repentance (for the change of purpose signified by this name necessarily presupposes sorrow of heart, that is, metameleia, contrition and anxious care after the event), whereas metameleia is more restricted to signifying only the first part of this blessing, namely the sorrow, contrition and anxiety of heart after the event. For it is not necessary that where metameleia is, metanoia immediately follows; but it is necessary that where metanoia is, metameleia is also present.

units.la: Tertium discrimen tradunt quidam inter hæc nomina, quòd μετάνοια proprie, & tantū sit piorum & electorum. Nam soli electi proprieac veré post perpetratum malum sapiūt, mentem & consilium immutant, ad mentis sanitatem redeunt. Μεταμέλεια vero non solùm piorum sit & electorum, sed etiam impiorum & reproborum, in quos cadit post malum perpetratum, cordis solicitudo & anxietas, atque dolor, non quidem propter peccatum admissum, sed propter peccati poenam. Sciendum autem quod cum μετανοια impijs tribuitur, hoc nomine intelligatur, non quidem solicitudo & dolor ille qui est secundum Deum, verum dolor mundi, & dolor qui est ad mortem: hoc enim sensu tribuitur Iudae Mat. 27. vbi dicitur, μεταμεληθεὶς ὁ Ἰούδας. Cum vero pijs tribuitur, significatur eo, non tam dolor qui est propter poenam peccati, quàm qui est propter ipsum peccatum, & offensum Deum. De graecis appellationibus hactenus.
units.tr: Some give a third distinction between these names: that metanoia properly belongs only to the pious and the elect. For only the elect truly and properly become wise after the evil committed, change their mind and purpose, and return to soundness of mind. Metameleia, however, belongs not only to the pious and the elect but also to the impious and the reprobate, on whom there falls, after the evil committed, anxiety, distress of heart and sorrow, not indeed on account of the sin committed but on account of its punishment. It should be noted, however, that when metanoia is attributed to the impious, the name is understood not of that anxiety and sorrow which is according to God, but of the sorrow of the world and the sorrow that leads to death. In this sense it is attributed to Judas in Mat. 27., where it is said: metameletheis ho Ioudas [μεταμεληθεὶς ὁ Ἰούδας]. But when it is attributed to the pious, it signifies not so much the sorrow that is on account of the punishment of sin as that which is on account of sin itself and the offended God. So much for the Greek names.

units.la: Latinae sunt, Conversio, Resipiscentia, & Poenitentia. Conversio proprie respondet Hebraeae voci [TESCHVEHAH] estque verbum quo vsi sunt Prophetae in veteri Testamento, Converte me Domine & convertar. Ieremiae 31. quemadmodum Christus & Apostoli ipsius in novo Testamento utuntur verbis μετάνοια & μετανοεῖν, Refipiscētiȩ, & Poenitentiae. Resipiscentia proprie respondet graeco nomini μετάνοια: Nam resipiscere est post factum incipere sapere. Poenitentia proprie respondet graeco nomini μεταμέλεια dicitur enim à pœnitere five pœna : nam in pœnitentia dolor ille & anxietas cordis pœna est Nomen pœnitentiæ plane eodem modo dif-fert à nomine refipifcentiç,quo nomen μεταμελείας differt à nomine μέλαvoιας. Nam vt de alijs differentijs taceam, nomen pœnitentiæ significat proprie vnam tantum partem hujus beneficij, nempe dolorem, folicitudinem, & anxietatem post factum: nomen vero refipifcentiæ totum beneficium completitur : Nã mutatio consilij, & sapientia post factum, neceffario præfupponit dolorem cordis,tanquã efficientem causam. Vetus versio latina vtrûque græcum verbum & μέλαvοιας & μεταμέλειας vbique reddit pœnitentiam.
units.tr: The Latin names are conversio, resipiscentia and poenitentia. Conversio properly corresponds to the Hebrew word [TESCHVEHAH], and it is the verb the prophets used in the Old Testament: "Convert me, O Lord, and I shall be converted," Ieremiae 31. Just as Christ and his apostles in the New Testament use the words metanoia and metanoein, so we use resipiscentia and poenitentia. Resipiscentia properly corresponds to the Greek word metanoia, for resipiscere means to begin to be wise after the event. Poenitentia properly corresponds to the Greek word metameleia, for it is named from poenitere or poena, since in repentance that sorrow and anxiety of heart is a punishment. The name poenitentia differs from the name resipiscentia in exactly the same way that metameleias [μεταμελείας] differs from metanoias [μετανοίας]. For, to pass over other differences, the name poenitentia properly signifies only one part of this blessing, namely the sorrow, anxious care and distress after the event; the name resipiscentia, however, comprises the whole blessing, for the change of purpose and wisdom after the event necessarily presupposes sorrow of heart as its efficient cause. The old Latin version renders both Greek words, metanoia and metameleia, everywhere as poenitentia.

units.la: Adversarij vero pœnitentiæ vocem ubiq; retinendam esse acriter contendunt; nempe ut sacramentum pœnitentiæ, quod vocant, defendant, vel ex ipso nomine suo,politum esse in pœna & afflictione externa & corporali. A nostris magis receptum est nomen refipifcentiæ,quoties hoc beneficiû volunt fignificare.De appellationibus itaq; hujus beneficij hactenus.
units.tr: Our opponents, however, strongly contend that the word poenitentia must be retained everywhere, namely in order to defend what they call the sacrament of penance, which, they say, rests by its very name on punishment and external, bodily affliction. Among our people the name resipiscentia is more commonly received whenever they wish to signify this blessing. So much for the names of this blessing.

units.la: Partes ejus in genere nominantur:primùm dolor, deinde ex dolore mutatio mentis ac consilij,quæ proprie nomine μέλαvοιας five refipiscentiæ significatur. De dolore igitur & prima resipiscentiæ parte primo loco erit nobis dicendum. Dolor in resipiscentia duplex est: Primùm est dolor propter pœnam peccati, qui 2.Cor. 7. vocatur dolor mundi, item dolor qui est ad mortem: Deinde est dolor propter ipsum peccatum & offensum Deum, qui ab Apostolo ibidem vocatur dolor secundum Deum. De vtroque isto dolore dicamus seorsim.
units.tr: Its parts are named in general: first sorrow, then from sorrow a change of mind and purpose, which is properly signified by the name metanoia or resipiscentia. So we must speak first of sorrow, the first part of resipiscence. Sorrow in repentance is twofold. First is the sorrow on account of the punishment of sin, which in 2.Cor. 7. is called the sorrow of the world, and also the sorrow that leads to death. Then there is the sorrow on account of sin itself and the offended God, which the Apostle in the same place calls godly sorrow. Let us speak of each of these separately.

units.la: Doloris igitur prioris qui est propter pœnam, efficiens principalis est Spiritus sanctus, qui Rom. 8. vocatur Spiritus servitutis ad metum, hoc est, qui testatur nobis de servili ac misera extra Christum conditione nostra, ac proindè metum & horrores incutit. Instrumentum per quod operatur Spiritus in cordibus nostris hunc dolorem, est Legis prædicatio, cuius compendium est in illo Syllogismo, de quo in doctrina de fide dictum est; cuius quidem propositio est: Maledictus qui non manserit in omnibus quæ scripta sunt in Libro Legis huius, vt faciat ea. Ex quia assumit conscientia cuiusque: At ego non mansi in iis: & concludit, Ergo ego maledictus sum. Hinc dolor ille cordis, vel potiùs horror, non tam propter peccatum, quod est in Assumptione, quàm propter pœnam maledictionis, quæ est in Conclusione. Atque hic est ille qui vocatur conscientiæ stimulus, quo quidè illata illa conclusione, miserum, non tam stimulat, quàm transfigit. Dolor hic qui est ex Lege, nisi interveniret Evangelij gratia, hominem in desperationem ageret. Atque hæc de priori illo dolore.
units.tr: The principal efficient cause of the former sorrow, which is on account of punishment, is the Holy Spirit, who in Rom. 8. is called the Spirit of bondage unto fear, that is, who testifies to us of our servile and wretched condition outside Christ, and therefore strikes us with fear and horrors. The instrument by which the Spirit works this sorrow in our hearts is the preaching of the Law, whose summary is in that syllogism discussed in the doctrine of faith. Its major premise is: Cursed is he who does not continue in all the things written in this book of the law, to do them. From this the conscience of each person takes the minor: But I have not continued in them; and it concludes: Therefore I am cursed. Hence that sorrow of heart, or rather horror, arises not so much on account of the sin which is in the minor as on account of the punishment of the curse which is in the conclusion. This is what is called the goad of conscience, which, once that conclusion has been brought in, does not so much prick the wretched man as pierce him through. This sorrow, which comes from the Law, would drive a man to despair unless the grace of the Gospel intervened. So much for that former sorrow.

units.la: Posterioris efficiens principalis est idem ille Dei spiritus, sed alio modo sese habens, nā jam evadit Spiritus adoptionis, per quem clamamus Abba Pater, Rom.8. hoc est, qui testatur de adoptione nostri in Christo, ac proinde dilatat guttur simul & os nostrum, ad Deū familiariter invocandum, tanquam patrem nostrum. Instrumentum per quod operatur Spiritus in cordibus nostris hunc dolorem, est Evangelij prædicatio, cujus summa continetur in illo Syllogismo, de quo diximus in doctrina de fide. Propositio Syllogismi. Qui crediderit justificabitur & vivet: Ex qua assumit fides, At ego credo: & concludit: Ergo justitia & vita ad me pertinent. In hac conclusione est quidem materia lætitiæ, fateor, & ineffabilis gaudij, sed tam verum est in ea esse materiam doloris: qui, cognita jam tanta Dei in Christo misericordia, concipitur propter offensum tam misericordem & clementem patrem. Est itaque laetitia dolori admixta, & cum gaudio fidei ineffabili ac glorioso conjuncta sunt suspiria inenarrabilia. Sic igitur dictum sit de posteriori illo dolore.
units.tr: The principal efficient cause of the latter is that same Spirit of God, but in another mode, for now he becomes the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry "Abba, Father," Rom.8. that is, who testifies of our adoption in Christ, and therefore enlarges both throat and mouth to call upon God familiarly as our Father. The instrument by which the Spirit works this sorrow in our hearts is the preaching of the Gospel, whose substance is contained in that syllogism which we mentioned in the doctrine of faith. The major premise of the syllogism: He who believes will be justified and will live. From this faith takes the minor: But I believe; and it concludes: Therefore righteousness and life belong to me. In this conclusion there is indeed, I grant, the matter of joy and of inexpressible gladness; but it is just as true that there is in it the matter of sorrow, which, now that such great mercy of God in Christ is known, is conceived on account of having offended so merciful and gracious a Father. Joy is therefore mixed with sorrow, and unutterable sighs are joined to the inexpressible and glorious joy of faith. So much be said of that latter sorrow.

units.la: Nunc videndum quomodo utrque affectus sit ad resipiscentiam. Prior ille dolor qui ex Lege est, & propter peccati poenam concipitur, fateor, non est pars resipiscentiae & conversionis ad Deum: nam sua natura magis nos a Deo avertit, quam ad Deum convertit, & re ipsa improbos plane avertit a deo tanquam terribili judice. In resipiscentia tamen usum suum obtinet: nam electos praeparat sensu miseriae suae, ad gratiam illam & misericordiam, quae in Evangelio proponitur.
units.tr: Now we must see how each affection relates to resipiscence. The former sorrow, which comes from the Law and is conceived on account of the punishment of sin, is not, I grant, a part of resipiscence and conversion to God: for by its nature it turns us away from God rather than converting us to God, and in fact it entirely turns the wicked away from God as a terrible judge. Nevertheless it has its use in resipiscence: for it prepares the elect, by a sense of their misery, for that grace and mercy which is set forth in the Gospel.

units.la: Posterior dolor qui secundum Deum est & per Evangelium efficitur, proprie pars est resipiscentiae, & efficit mentis illam & consilij immutationem. Unde Apost. 2.Cor.7. Dolor qui secundum Deum est efficit resipiscentiam. Hactenus dictum est de prima huius beneficij parte, quae cernitur in dolore.
units.tr: The latter sorrow, which is according to God and is produced through the Gospel, is properly a part of resipiscence, and it brings about that change of mind and purpose. Hence the Apostle in 2.Cor.7. says: sorrow which is according to God produces repentance. So far has been said of the first part of this blessing, which is seen in sorrow.

units.la: Sequitur altera quae proprie μετανοια & resipiscetiae verbo ab Apost. vocata est 2.Cor. 7. Dolorem igitur illum qui est secundum Deum, sequitur insignis quaedam mutatio in mente, in voluntate, in corde. Primum autem est mutatio mentis. Quod ad mentis cognitionem sive agnitionē attinet, ea praecessit dolorem illū de quo diximus; & agnitio est primum peccati & miseriæ per Legem, deinde misericordiæ per Evangelium accensa. Ergo mutatio mentis quæ sequitur dolorem, est facultatis judicantis, sive judicij mentis, quod etiam consilium & propositum mentis vocatur. Act. 11. 23. Ut propósito cordis permanerent in Domino. Mutatur autem judicium sive consilium mentis in hunc modum: mens malum illud quod perpetratum est improbat: bonum vero faciendum in posterum approbat. Duæ igitur partes sunt mutationis judicij sive consilij: prima est improbatio mali perpetrati: secunda est approbatio boni perpetrandi.
units.tr: There follows the second element, which is properly called μετάνοια (metanoia) and which the Apostle calls by the word "repentance" (resipiscentia) in 2 Cor. 7. After that sorrow which is according to God there follows a remarkable change in the mind, in the will and in the heart. The first is a change of mind. As for the knowing or recognition of the mind, this went before the sorrow of which we have spoken; and recognition is first of sin and misery through the Law, and then, kindled by the Gospel, of mercy. Therefore the change of mind which follows sorrow belongs to the faculty of judgement, or the judgement of the mind, which is also called the counsel and purpose of the mind. Acts 11:23: "that with purpose of heart they should cleave to the Lord." The judgement or counsel of the mind is changed in this way: the mind disapproves of the evil that has been committed, and approves of the good that is to be done in future. There are therefore two parts of the change of judgement or counsel: the first is disapproval of the evil committed; the second is approval of the good to be done.

units.la: Post mutationem judicij sive consilij mentis nostræ, sequitur mutatio voluntatis in hunc modum. Voluntas malum illud quod perpetratum est repudiat, sive ab eo declinat, bonū autem faciendum in posterum eligit, sive ad id inclinat. Duæ igitur sunt partes huius mutationis: prima est declinatio à malo perpetrato, secunda inclinatio ad bonum perpetrandum. Mutationem voluntatis excipit mutatio cordis, quæ hoc modo perficitur: Cor malum illud jam perpetratum odit atque detestatur, bonum autem perpetrandum amat & persequitur. Duæ igitur partes sunt hujus mutationis: prima est detestatio mali perpetrati, secunda est dilectio boni perpetrandi.
units.tr: After the change of the judgement or counsel of our mind there follows a change of the will in this way. The will rejects the evil already committed, or turns away from it, and chooses the good to be done in future, or inclines towards it. There are therefore two parts of this change: the first is turning away from the evil committed, the second is inclination towards the good to be done. The change of the will is followed by a change of the heart, which is brought about in this way: the heart hates and abhors the evil already committed, but loves and pursues the good to be done. There are therefore two parts of this change: the first is detestation of the evil committed, the second is love of the good to be done.

units.la: In genere igitur duæ sunt partes μετανοίας quæ sequitur dolorem: prima est mutatio à malo & peccato commisso, secunda est mutatio ad bonum in posterum faciendum: Vulgo has partes vocant mortificationem, & vivificationem, sed nescio quam recte & juste. Mortificatio enim & vivificatio partes sunt proprie regenerationis, quæ differt à μετανοια, ut postea videbimus.
units.tr: In general, then, there are two parts of the repentance which follows sorrow: the first is a change from the evil and sin committed, the second is a change towards the good to be done in future. Commonly people call these parts mortification and vivification, but I do not know how correctly and justly. For mortification and vivification are properly parts of regeneration, which differs from μετάνοια, as we shall see later.

units.la: Ex prædictis quoque intelligimus qui sint termini μετανοίας, à quo, & ad quem. Terminus à quo est factum malum, sive peccatum commissum: terminus ad quem est bonum faciendum in posterum. Ergo μετάνοια est inter duo facta, præteritum & futurum, eoque differt à regeneratione, cujus termini sunt, non facta & actiones, sed qualitates, nempe, naturæ corruptio sive vetus homo, sanctitas sive novus homo. Sed de hoc quoque postea, cum agetur de differentia μετανοίας & παλιγγενεσίας.
units.tr: From what has been said we also understand what the termini of μετάνοια are, from which and to which. The terminus from which is the evil deed, or the sin committed; the terminus to which is the good to be done in future. Repentance therefore lies between two deeds, the past and the future, and by this it differs from regeneration, whose termini are not deeds and actions but qualities, namely the corruption of nature or the old man, and holiness or the new man. But of this too we shall speak later, when we treat of the difference between μετάνοια and παλιγγενεσία.

units.la: Vides itaque post dolorem illum insignem fieri in toto hominis animo mutationem. Vides deinde ex ijs quae diximus de hoc resipiscentiae beneficio, refipiscentiam incipere à corde, progredi per rationales facultates mentis & voluntatis, & postremò in cor recidere atq; desinere. Deniq; ex ijs quae dicta sunt, & ex partium explicatione facile colligi potest, refipiscentię aliqua definitio ex ipsis partibus sumpta: ut sit Refipiscetia, post factum & malum jam perpetratū, dolor propter offensum Deum, & ex dolore mutatio quaedam totius animi à malo in bonum. Effectus refipiscentiae est in externa vita, utpote vitę emendatio. Edite fructus dignos resipiscentia. Mat.3.8.
units.tr: You see, then, that after that remarkable sorrow a change takes place in the whole mind of the man. You see further, from what we have said about this benefit of repentance, that repentance begins from the heart, proceeds through the rational faculties of mind and will, and at last returns to the heart and ends there. Finally, from what has been said, and from the explanation of the parts, a definition of repentance can easily be gathered from the parts themselves, as follows: Repentance is, after a deed done and an evil already committed, sorrow on account of having offended God, and from that sorrow a certain change of the whole soul from evil to good. The effect of repentance is in outward life, namely the amendment of life. "Bring forth fruits worthy of repentance" (Matt. 3:8).

units.la: Quaestio est de Resipiscentia, an sit eadem cum regeneratione, sive renovatione? nam communis Theologorum sententia est, quod non sint distincta reipsa beneficia refipiscentiae & regenerationis. Nobis tamen videtur discrimen esse inter haec duo, & ijs quoque videbitur, qui volent diligentius fines beneficiorum Dei regere. Nam resipiscentia ad locum de vocatione efficaci pertinet, & fidei, quae est altera pars vocationis efficacis, essectus est. Quotquot enim credunt, ij resipiscunt, mutant consilium, & ad sanam mentem redeunt. unt. Regeneratio vero initium est glorificationis nostri, & inchoatio novæ creaturæ. Resipiscentia justificationem antecedit, quemadmodum fides & spes. De Baptista enim dicitur, quod prædicaverit Baptisma resipiscentiæ ad remissionem peccatorum. Marci 3.4. Luc.3.3. Regeneratio vero justificationem sequitur, justificati enim accipimus Spiritum sanctificationis, quo renovamur, & nova quasi creatio nostri inchoatur in hac vita. Resipiscentia causa est; Regeneratio vero effectus: Ideo enim nos renovat in Christo Deus, & novos homines facit; quia pœnitet nos vitæ pristinæ, & post peccatum commissum incipimus sapere. Medio tamen loco inter resipiscentiam & regenerationem, intervenit justificatio, qua nos Deus, ex mera sua misericordia, pro justis habet ac censet. Resipiscentiæ nomen includit dolorem, nomen vero regenerationis lætitiam potius. Denique resipiscentiæ termini, a quo, & ad quem, sunt facta, malum sive peccatum jam commissum, bonum faciedum: Regenerationis vero termini sunt qualitates, inhærens corruptio, & sanctitas quæ introducitur: vetus homo & novus homo.
units.tr: The question is whether repentance is the same as regeneration, or renewal. For the common opinion of the theologians is that the benefits of repentance and regeneration are not really distinct. Yet to us there seems to be a difference between these two, and it will seem so also to those who wish to examine more carefully the limits of God's benefits. For repentance pertains to the locus on effectual calling, and is an effect of faith, which is the other part of effectual calling. For all who believe repent, change their counsel, and return to a sound mind. But regeneration is the beginning of our glorification and the inauguration of a new creature. Repentance goes before justification, just as faith and hope do. For of the Baptist it is said that he preached the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins (Mark 1:4; Luke 3:3). But regeneration follows justification: for having been justified we receive the Spirit of sanctification, by whom we are renewed, and a kind of new creation of ourselves is begun in this life. Repentance is the cause; regeneration is the effect. For God renews us in Christ and makes us new men for this reason: because we repent of our former life, and after the sin committed we begin to be wise. Yet between repentance and regeneration there intervenes justification, by which God, out of his pure mercy, holds and counts us as righteous. The name of repentance includes sorrow; the name of regeneration rather includes joy. Finally, the termini of repentance, from which and to which, are deeds, the evil or sin now committed, and the good to be done; but the termini of regeneration are qualities: the inherent corruption, and the holiness which is introduced; the old man and the new man.

units.la: At dices in resipiscentia est mutatio a malo ad bonum, mutatio, inquam, mentis & cordis? Respondeo, in ipsa quoque vocatione efficaci & fide incipit animi humani mutatio: omnes tamen distinguunt vocationem & fidem a regeneratione: cur non similiter distinguenda resipiscentia, quae fidem consequitur & efficacem vocationem, a regeneratione? Neque enim omnis mutatio animi humani statim censenda est regeneratio: verum quaedam sunt mutationes animi humani, quae antegrediuntur regenerationem, & quae animum adeoque totum hominem ad regenerationem praeparant, hoc est, ad novam illam creationem: in quo genere est resipiscentia. Ista sunt distinguenda naturae ordine, non autem temporis: nam eodem temporis momento & credimus sive efficaciter vocamur, & resipiscimus, & justificamur, & denique regeneramur.
units.tr: But you will say: in repentance there is a change from evil to good, a change, I say, of mind and heart? I answer: in effectual calling itself and in faith too a change of the human soul begins; yet all men distinguish calling and faith from regeneration. Why should repentance, which follows faith and effectual calling, not likewise be distinguished from regeneration? For not every change of the human soul is at once to be counted as regeneration; rather there are certain changes of the human soul which precede regeneration, and which prepare the soul, and so the whole man, for regeneration, that is, for that new creation; and repentance is of this kind. These must be distinguished by the order of nature, but not by the order of time: for in one and the same moment of time we both believe, or are efficaciously called, and repent, and are justified, and finally are regenerated.

units.la: Quousque possit impius progredi in Resipiscentia.
units.tr: How far the ungodly man can advance in repentance.

units.la: CAP. 35.
units.tr: Chapter 35.

units.la: EXplicata jam resipiscentia quae electorum & piorum est propria, videndum est quousque possit reprobus & impius progredi in resipiscentia. Omnium improborum sive impiorum non statim est vnus idemque progressus: verùm ex impijs alij minorem, alij majorem in resipiscentia faciunt progressum. Primùm dicemus de ijs, qui minimum faciût omnium progressum.
units.tr: Having now explained the repentance that is proper to the elect and the godly, we must consider how far the reprobate and the ungodly can advance in repentance. Not all the wicked or ungodly make the same progress. Some of them advance less in repentance, others more. I shall speak first of those who make the least progress of all.

units.la: In hos igitur primùm cadit dolor, sive potiùs horror, qui est ex Lege: idque non propter peccatum, vel offensum Deum proprie & per se, verùm propter peccati pœnâ proprie, propter peccatum autem per accidens, quia peccatum pœna sequitur. Post dolorem in ijs sequitur in mente improbatio quædam faciNoris perpetrati, verùm propter pœnâ: quòd vero ad boni faciendi approbationem attinet eo vsque non perveniunt. Sequitur deinde in voluntate declinatio à malo perpetrato, sed propter pœnam, interea voluntate ad bonum faciendum non inclinant. Voluntatis istam inchoatam mutationem, sequitur in corde mali perpetrati detestatio, sed quæ est propter pœnam: verùm cor nô progreditur ad amorem justitiæ sive boni faciendi. Quod ad externam vitam, in ea nulla sequitur mutatio, sive emendatio.
units.tr: In these, first, comes sorrow, or rather horror, which arises from the Law. This is not because of sin, or because they have offended God properly and in themselves, but because of the punishment of sin, which is properly what they fear; sin itself they dread only incidentally, because punishment follows sin. After this sorrow there follows in them a certain disapproval of the wrong they have committed, in their mind, but only on account of the punishment; as for approving of doing good, they do not reach that far. Next there follows in the will a turning away from the evil committed, but again on account of the punishment; meanwhile, they are not inclined in their will to do good. Upon this beginning of change in the will there follows, in the heart, a detestation of the evil committed, but this too is on account of the punishment; the heart does not advance to the love of righteousness or of doing good. As for their outward life, no change or amendment follows in it.

units.la: In hoc genere fuit Iudas proditor, de cujus pœnitentia lege Mat.27. vbi primùm dicitur, quòd Iudam fàcti sui pœnituerit. Nota
units.tr: Judas the traitor belongs to this class. Concerning his repentance, read Matt. 27., where it is first said that Judas repented of what he had done.

units.la: ij in hoc verbo dolorem & cordis anxietatem. Tum dicitur eum retulisse triginta argenteos numinos ad principem sacerdotum: ex quo necessario colligenda est aliqua mentis, voluntatis, & cordis mutatio: ut etiam ex ipsius confessione liquet, quia dixit postea: Peccavi prodito sanguine innoxio: nam vox haec arguit aliquam peccati improbationem, repudiationem, detestationem, licet non sinceram, sed eam quae fuit peccati per accidens, poenae vero per se. Denique ex eo quod abjecerit argenteos nummos in templum, conspicitur interna aliqua rejectio mali, improbatio, repudiatio, detestatio. Quod autem nulla vitae emendatio sequuta sit hanc animi mutationem, ex eo apparet, quod continuo recedens sese strangulaverit.
units.tr: Note in this word sorrow and anguish of heart. Then it is said that he brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests. From this some change of mind, will and heart must necessarily be inferred, as is also clear from his own confession, for he said afterwards: "I have sinned in betraying innocent blood." For this word shows some disapproval, rejection and detestation of sin, although not a sincere one, but one that belonged to the sin only incidentally and to the punishment in itself. Finally, from the fact that he threw the silver coins into the temple, some inner rejection of evil is seen, a disapproval, repudiation and detestation of it. That no amendment of life followed this change of mind is clear from the fact that, going away at once, he hanged himself.
