units.la: Sunt alij deinde ex impijs qui paulo majorem isto faciunt progressum in μετανοια, & in quos cadit animi mutatio aliqua in bonum: mentis approbatio boni; voluntatis electio boni; cordis dilectio boni: sed ista non sincera sunt, verum ex formidine poenae sunt: Quod ad vitae externae emendationem, eam quoque inchoant: verum, ut ait Propheta, Bonitas eorum abit quasi nubes matutina, & ros mane stillans. Amos 6.
units.tr: Next there are others among the ungodly who make a somewhat greater progress in repentance [μετάνοια], and in whom some change for the better takes place: their mind approves of the good, their will chooses the good, their heart loves the good. But these things are not sincere; they arise from fear of punishment. As for amendment of outward life, they begin that too; yet, as the Prophet says, "Their goodness passes away like a morning cloud and like the dew that falls early in the morning" (Amos 6).

units.la: In hoc genere erat Saul, 1.Sam.15. Achab 1.Reg.21. In hoc quoque genere videtur suisse Esau: de cujus reprobatione vide Heb. 12. quo loco ascribitur ei hoc ipsum nomen μετανοίας quod proprie electis & piis tribui solet. Dolor Esau apparet ex lachrymis, quarum ibi mentio fit: Mutatio etiam in bonum aliqua animi apparet ex eo quod dicitur, cum voluisse assequi benedictionem, exquisivisse benedictionem: Sed nihil in eo sinceri fuit, nam statim post redijt ad ingenium suum.
units.tr: Saul belonged to this class, 1 Sam. 15.; so did Ahab, 1 Kings 21. Esau also seems to have been of this kind. On his rejection see Heb. 12., where that very name of repentance [μετανοίας] is ascribed to him, which is usually given properly to the elect and the godly. Esau's sorrow appears from the tears mentioned there. Some change of mind towards good also appears from the statement that when he wished to obtain the blessing, he sought it. But there was nothing sincere in him, for soon afterwards he returned to his own disposition.

units.la: Qui autem eximipijs maximum in μετανοίας progressum faciunt, sunt ij qui fidem temporariam obtinent, quorum dolor est etiam ex Evangelio, & agnitione misericordiæ Dei in Christo; animi autem eorum mutatio in bonum est aliquo modo propter ipsum bonum: Nam Dei in Christo suavitate aliquo modo degustant, eoq; delectantur. Quod ad vitæ externæ emendationem, ea in ijs est paulò magis diuturna, quàm in alijs suprà dictis. Est etiam multorum peccatorum emendatio.
units.tr: Those, however, who make the greatest progress in repentance [μετανοίας] among the ungodly are those who have a temporary faith. Their sorrow comes also from the Gospel and from the knowledge of God's mercy in Christ. Their change of mind towards good is in some measure for the sake of the good itself, for they taste in some way the sweetness of God in Christ and take delight in it. As for amendment of outward life, in them it lasts somewhat longer than in those mentioned above. There is also amendment of many sins.

units.la: In hoc genere videtur fuisse Herodes, de quo Marci 6. 29. sic scriptum est. Herodes metuebat Iohannem, sciens eum esse virum justum ac sanctum, & observabat eum, auditoque eo multa faciebat, & libenter eum audiebat.
units.tr: Herod seems to have belonged to this class, concerning whom it is written thus in Mark 6:20: "Herod feared John, knowing that he was a just and holy man, and he kept him safe; and when he heard him he did many things and heard him gladly."

units.la: Atque hæc de impiorum in μετανοia progressu triplici, omninoque de vera resipiscentiæ doctrina.
units.tr: So much concerning the threefold progress of the ungodly in repentance [μετάνοια], and in general concerning the true doctrine of repentance.

units.la: De Pœnitentia quid sentiant Papistæ.
units.tr: What the Papists think about penance.

units.la: CAP. 36.
units.tr: Chapter 36.

units.la: SEquitur nunc ut videamus quid de pœnitentia sua (nam resipiscentiæ nomen repuunt) sentiant adversarij. Ex infinitis erroribus paucos aliquot enumerabimus, & paucis eos refutabimus. Primùm, pœnitentiam sacramentum esse dicunt. At, inquam, quod habet sensibile signum, si sacramentum sit? Respondent signum esse partim actum pœnitentis, partim verba Sacerdotis quibus absolvit pœnitentem. At, inquam, signum in sacramento non tantùm debet esse audibile, sed etiam visibile: oportet etiam sit elementum quoddam, non tantùm ritus: ut in Baptismo & cœna Domini, præter ritus sunt elementa, aqua, panis, vinum. Sed de hoc errore satis.
units.tr: Now let us see what our opponents think of their penance (for they reject the name of repentance). I shall list a few of their countless errors and refute them briefly. First, they say that penance is a sacrament. But, I ask, what has a sensible sign, if it is to be a sacrament? They answer that the sign is partly the act of the penitent, partly the words of the priest by which he absolves the penitent. But I reply that a sign in a sacrament must not only be audible but also visible; it must also be some element, not merely a rite. In Baptism and the Lord's Supper, besides the rites there are elements: water, bread and wine. But enough on this error.

units.la: Deinde vsum pœnitentiæ affirmant hunc esse, ut peccatum mortale post Baptismum admissum aboleat, & ex amico Dei inimicum factu, rursum amicum faciat, hoc est, justum. Ad hoc respondeo. Ad hominem, qui post Baptismum peccavit, quasi restituendum reparandum, non opus esse alio sacramento, quā Baptismo, cujus vis in tota vita hominis perpetua est ad ablutionē peccati & regenerationē: Falsum enim est Baptismo tantū ablui peccata commissa ante ipsum Baptismum, cū Baptismus ad totam hominis vitam pateat, ipsiusque recordatio efficax sit ad remissionem peccatorum & regenerationem, etiam tūm cūm quis agit extremam animam, & è vivis discedit.
units.tr: Next they affirm that the use of penance is this: that it wipes out a mortal sin committed after Baptism, and makes a man who has become an enemy of God from a friend again a friend, that is, righteous. To this I reply: a man who has sinned after Baptism does not need another sacrament, as though he had to be restored and repaired, other than Baptism, whose power lasts throughout the whole of a man's life for the washing away of sin and for regeneration. For it is false that only the sins committed before Baptism itself are washed away by Baptism, since Baptism extends to the whole life of man, and its remembrance is effective for the forgiveness of sins and for regeneration, even when a man is breathing his last and departing from the living.

units.la: Tertiò dicunt in veteri Testamento, & ante Christi resurrectionem, aliam fuisse poenitentiam ab ea, quæ est post resurrectionem Christi: illam enim non fuisse Sacramentum, hanc verò esse. Respondeo, poenitentiæ & conversionis ad Deum una eademque est doctrina, quā omnes Prophetæ, Iohannes Baptista, Christus promissus ac missus, & sancti Apostoli prædicârunt.
units.tr: Thirdly, they say that in the Old Testament, and before the resurrection of Christ, there was another penance from that which is after the resurrection of Christ: for the former was not a sacrament, but the latter is. I reply: there is one and the same doctrine of penance and of conversion to God, which all the Prophets, John the Baptist, the promised and sent Christ, and the holy Apostles preached.

units.la: Quartò, poenitentiæ principalem efficientem causam tradunt, libertatem arbitrij, & naturæ vires, excitatas per gratiam prævenientem: Gratiam verò tantū adjutricem & cooperatricem? Respondeo, Imò contra resipiscentiæ principalis efficiens est Spiritus sive gratia; instrumentum verò, sunt facultates animi nostri, non quales sunt natura, sed per Spiritum sanctificatæ, id quod intelligi potest vel ex uno hoc testimonio. Coverte me Domine & convertar. Ierem. 31. vbi principalis efficientia ipsi Domino, ipsiusque gratiæ tribuitur. De nobis autem dicitur, quòd actiâ Spiritu, agamus.
units.tr: Fourthly, they hold that the principal efficient cause of penance is free will and the powers of nature, stirred up by prevenient grace, while grace is only a helper and cooperator. I reply: on the contrary, the principal efficient cause of repentance is the Spirit, or grace; the instrument, however, is the faculties of our mind, not as they are by nature, but as sanctified by the Spirit. This can be understood even from this one testimony: "Turn me, O Lord, and I shall be turned" (Jer. 31), where the principal efficiency is attributed to the Lord himself and to his grace. It is said of us that, acted upon by the Spirit, we act.

units.la: Quintò, pœnitentiam dividunt essentialiter in actus pœnitentis, tanquam materiam, & in absolutionem Sacerdotis, tanquam formam. Respondeo, nullam esse necessitatem cur pœnitentia sic transigatur inter pœnitentem sive confitetem peccatorem, & absolventē Sacerdoté. Potest enim peccator, quæ pœnitet peccati sui, privatim confiteri Deo suo, & ab eo etiam citra absolutionis aliquâ formulam à Sacerdote conceptam, absolvi. Resipiscimus quotidie, neque tamen sic res transigitur, neq; opus est ut sic transigatur, inter peccatorem resipiscentem, & Sacerdotem sive Ministrum absolventem. Quamobrem non est restringenda resipiscentia ad hanc formulam, & ad hunc quasi dialogismum, qui est inter peccatorem resipiscentem, & Sacerdotem absolventem.
units.tr: Fifthly, they divide penance essentially into the acts of the penitent, as the matter, and the absolution of the priest, as the form. I reply: there is no necessity why penance should be carried out in this way between the penitent, or the sinner confessing, and the absolving priest. For a sinner who repents of his sin can confess privately to his God and be absolved by him, without any formula of absolution composed by a priest. We repent every day, and yet the matter is not so transacted, nor is it necessary that it be so transacted, between the repentant sinner and the priest or minister who absolves. Therefore repentance is not to be restricted to this formula and to this kind of dialogue which takes place between the repentant sinner and the absolving priest.

units.la: Sextò, pœnitentiam dividunt materialiter in Contritionem, Confessionem, Satisfactionem: nam hæ tres partes ad actus pœnitentis pertinent, qui actus poenitentis efficiunt materiam sacramenti poenitentiae. Respondeo, quod ad contritionem, quae nihil aliud est quàm dolor cordis, eam quidem admittimus, sed citra opinionem meriti alicujus, quod ab ipsis contritioni attribuitur.
units.tr: Sixthly, they divide penance materially into contrition, confession and satisfaction, for these three parts belong to the acts of the penitent, and these acts of the penitent make up the matter of the sacrament of penance. I reply: as for contrition, which is nothing other than sorrow of heart, we indeed admit it, but without the notion of any merit which they attribute to contrition itself.

units.la: Quod ad confessionem, primùm dicimus eam non esse proprie partem resipiscentiae, sed signum externum resipiscentiae, quae interius in animo peragitur; in signis enim numerantur confessio oris, lachrymae, corporis humiliatio, & alia id genus. Deinde dicimus confessionem illam eorum auricularem, in qua oportet enumerentur omnia etiam privata hominis delicta, quantum per memoriam poteft fieri, & insusurrentur in aurem Sacerdotis: hujusmodi, inquam, confessionem affirmamus esse inventum humani cerebri, cujus nullum vel mandatum vel exemplum extat in tota Scriptura. Imò verò voluntas Dei est, ut ex privatis peccatis multa, quorum nos ipsi nobis tantum fumus conscij, celentur, ac de ijs taceatur: quemadmodum ipse Deus operit multitudinem privatorum peccatorum, pro ea, qua nos prosequitur, charitate & misericordia in Christo Iesu. Requiritur tamen ut privatim nos poeniteat, quoties memoriae nostræ recurrunt.
units.tr: As for confession, first, we say that it is not properly a part of repentance but an external sign of the repentance that is carried out inwardly in the mind. For among the signs are counted the confession of the mouth, tears, the humbling of the body, and others of that kind. Second, we say that their auricular confession, in which all of a person's private sins must be enumerated, as far as memory allows, and whispered into the ear of the priest, is, I say, something we affirm to be an invention of the human brain, for which there is neither command nor example anywhere in Scripture. Indeed, it is God's will that many private sins, of which we ourselves are conscious only to ourselves, should be hidden and passed over in silence, just as God himself covers the multitude of private sins out of that charity and mercy which he shows us in Christ Jesus. Nevertheless, it is required that we repent privately whenever those sins come back to our memory.

units.la: Quod denique ad satisfactionem attinet, qua, ut ipsi docent, nos per nos ipsi satisfacimus iræ atque justitiæ Dei, idque temporalibus pœnis, pro peccatis à nobis admissis, hàc prorsus damnamus, ut quæ deroget Christi merito & satisfactioni, qua sola satisfit iræ ac justitiæ Dei pro peccatis nostris. Quod autem ad temporarias istas afflictiones piorum, non sunt exquidem satisfactiones pro peccatis eorum, verùm per eas Deus mortificat reliquias istas peccati, & ijs nos ad seriam resipiscentiâ stimulat, deterret etiam à peccato in posterùm perpetrando: denique, ut diligentibus Deum omnia cooperantur in bonum, sic hæ non tàm pœnæ quàm afflictiones & cruces cooperantur pijs in bonum. Neque valet illa distinctio pœnarum temporalium & æternarum: Nam certum est quòd quicunque temporaliter puniuntur propter peccata sua, hoc est, eo nomine, ij quoque in æternum puniendi sint propter peccata sua. Vnde temporales pœnæ impiorum in hac vita initium sunt æternarum pœnarum in altero sæculo luendarum.
units.tr: As for satisfaction, by which, as they themselves teach, we satisfy by our own efforts the wrath and justice of God, and that by temporal punishments for the sins we have committed, we utterly condemn this, since it detracts from the merit and satisfaction of Christ, by which alone the wrath and justice of God is satisfied for our sins. As for the temporary afflictions of the godly, these are indeed not satisfactions for their sins, but through them God mortifies those remnants of sin, stirs us up to serious repentance, and deters us from committing sin in future. Finally, as all things work together for good for those who love God, so these are not so much punishments as afflictions and crosses which work together for good for the godly. Nor does that distinction between temporal and eternal punishments hold. For it is certain that whoever are punished temporally on account of their sins, that is, for that reason, are also to be punished eternally on account of their sins. Hence the temporal punishments of the wicked in this life are the beginning of the eternal punishments to be paid in the next age.

units.la: Hæc hactenus de Resipiscentia.
units.tr: So much for repentance.

units.la: De Libero arbitrio humano.
units.tr: On Human Free Choice.

units.la: CAP. 37.
units.tr: CHAP. 37.

units.la: DOctrinam de fide, spe,& resipiscentia, sequitur doctrina de libero arbitrio, hac occasione, quòd nimirùm adversarij, fidem, spem, refipiscentiam, sive, ut ipsi vocant, poenitentiam, tribuant libertati voluntatis nostrę tanquam principali agenti, gratię verò secundum locum in fide, spe, & poenitentia efficienda assignent: Postquàm enim, aiunt, à praeveniente gratia jam excitatum est liberum arbitrium, homo beneficio liberi arbitrij sui ipse credit, ipse sperat, ipse poenitetia ducitur peccati sui. Quod verò ad gratiam, ea tantùm cooperatrix est, inquiunt illi, & adjutrix liberi arbitrij, quod principaliter operatur in credendo, sperando, & poenitendo. Sed ad hoc respondimus jam priùs in doctrina de resipiscentia, & posteà respondebimus paulò apertiùs. Nunc veniendum ad doctrinam liberi arbitrij, postequam quę fit occasio cur locis fidei, spei, & poenitentię subijciamus locum hunc de libero arbitrio, jam vidimus.
units.tr: After the doctrine of faith, hope and repentance, the doctrine of free choice follows, for this reason: our opponents attribute faith, hope, repentance (or, as they call it, penance) to the freedom of our will as the principal agent, and assign only a secondary place to grace in bringing these about. For, they say, once free choice has been roused by preventing grace, a man believes by the benefit of his own free choice, hopes by himself, and is led by himself to repent of his sin. As for grace, they say, it is only a co-operator and helper of free choice, which works principally in believing, hoping and repenting. But we have already answered this in the doctrine of repentance, and we will answer more clearly afterwards. Now we must come to the doctrine of free choice, since we have already seen the occasion for placing this topic on free choice after the topics of faith, hope and repentance.

units.la: Voluntas humana, facultas est animi rationalis, proxima post mentem, quæ primùm intelligit, deinde judicat. Ejus functio est in volendo,nolendo,eligendo,repudiando,fufpédendo ea quæ jam priûs à mente intellecta & judicata sunt. Ejus obiecta sunt, bona simpliciter,mala simpliciter, ἀδιάφορα. Bona simpliciter voco,quę expressa aliqua Dei lege jubētur. Mala simpliciter voco, quæ expressa aliqua Dei lege vetantur. Adiaphora denique,quę nulla lege Dei vel jubentur, vel vetantur per se: quòd si jubeantur vel vetentur aliqua Dei Lege,id per accidēs fit, nempe, quatenus vel promovent, vel impediūt ædificationē proximi. Hæc voluntatis objecta subdivido in fines,& in media ad fines tendētia. Functiones voluntatis sic applico ad fines & ad media: Tàm media,quàm fines dicimur velle & nolle: velle enim & nolle generalia sunt: mediorum autem tantum est electio, repudiatio, & suspensio: hæc enim specialia sunt. De voluntate hactenus pro hujus instituti ratione.
units.tr: The human will is a faculty of the rational soul, next after the mind, which first understands and then judges. Its function is to will, to nill, to choose, to reject, and to suspend those things which have already been understood and judged by the mind. Its objects are good things absolutely, evil things absolutely, and Adiaphora. I call good things absolutely those which are commanded by some express law of God. I call evil things absolutely those which are forbidden by some express law of God. Finally, Adiaphora are those which are neither commanded nor forbidden in themselves by any law of God; but if they are commanded or forbidden by some law of God, this happens incidentally, namely insofar as they promote or hinder the edification of the neighbour. I divide these objects of the will into ends and means tending towards the ends. I apply the functions of the will to ends and means in this way: both means and ends are said to be willed and nilled, for willing and nilling are general acts; but only means are chosen, rejected or suspended, for these are specific acts. So much about the will, as far as the plan of this work requires.

units.la: Voluntati proprietas quædam assignatur quę Latinis vocatur libertas,potestas: Græcis, ἐξουσία. Rom.9. vbi de potestate figuli in lutum agitur. 1.Cor.7. ἐξουσίαν ἔχει ἰδίου θελήματος: hoc idem est ac si dixisset ἐχει ἐξουσίαν θελήματος; habet libertatem sive potestatem voluntatis. Vulgari nostro idiomate dicitur Soveranitie. Hæc libertas voluntatis est potestas quasi-reregia, & in græco eandem appellationem cū potestate regia & magistratus sortita est. Vide Rom. 13. Omnis anima subjecta esto ὑπερεχούσαις supereminentibus. Propter hanc voluntas in anima humana regina quædam habetur, & ab hac ἀυτεξούσιος, hoc est, sui juris, ipsa denominatur.
units.tr: A certain property is assigned to the will, which in Latin is called liberty or power, and in Greek ἐξουσία [power]. See Rom. 9., where the power of the potter over the clay is discussed; and 1 Cor. 7.: he has authority over his own will [ἐξουσίαν ἔχει ἰδίου θελήματος]. This is the same as if it had said: he has authority of the will [ἐχει ἐξουσίαν θελήματος]; that is, he has liberty or power of the will. In our vernacular it is called sovereignty. This liberty of the will is a power that is almost royal, and in Greek it has received the same name as royal power and the power of the magistrate. See Rom. 13.: let every soul be subject to the higher powers [ὑπερεχούσαις]. For this reason the will is regarded as a kind of queen in the human soul, and from it the soul is named self-ruling [ἀυτεξούσιος], that is, its own master.

units.la: Est autem libertas, ut ad ejus definitionem aliquam veniamus, qua cum aliquid voluntati tanquam Reginæ cuidam obijcitur, siue id bonum sit, siue malum, sive ἀδιάφορον; jam voluntas illud potest suo quodam jure vel nolle, vel velle, vel eligere vel repudiare, vel suspendere. Unde vulgò à Scholasticis definitur potentia in vtrumlibet, vel in oppositá, hoc est, in utramlibet partem contradictionis, vel in contraria, ut sunt eligere, repudirre. Sic vulgò definitur voluntatis libertas: Verùm ego hanc definitionem magis probo, ut scilicet sit libertas voluntatis, respectu rerum bonarum & malarum (nam de ijs controvertitur) sit, inquam, potestas voluntatis, sive jus quoddam ipsius, quo ex interno quodam & suo principio, citra coactionem, vult tantum quod bonum est, eligit quod bonū est, non vult quod malum est, repudiat quod malum est. Uno verbo libertas est, potestas ad bonum, non ad malum.
units.tr: Now, to come to a definition of liberty: liberty is that by which, when something is set before the will as before a queen, whether it be good, evil or indifferent, the will can then by its own right either will it or nill it, or choose it or reject it, or suspend judgment on it. Hence the Scholastics commonly define it as a power towards either side, or towards opposites, that is, towards either part of a contradiction, or towards contraries, such as choosing and rejecting. This is the common definition of the liberty of the will. But I prefer this definition: that the liberty of the will, with respect to good and evil things (for it is about these that the dispute is), is a power or a certain right of the will, by which, from its own internal principle and without compulsion, it wills only what is good, chooses what is good, does not will what is evil, and rejects what is evil. In a word, liberty is a power towards good, not towards evil.

units.la: Ego,ut probem hanc libertatis definitionem adducor primùm exemplo libertatis ipsius Dei, qui omnium confessione liberrimè vult & facit omnia: Libertas tamè Dei nō sic definitur,ut sit potestas quædam,qua ita vult bonum vt possit illud nolle, qua ita non vult malum,ut possit illud velle: sed libertas Dei est,qua suo jure, & citra coactionem, potest velle tantùm quod bonum est, nolle quod malum est. Deinde exemplo beatorum Angelorum idem patet, quorum libertas est ad bonum tantùm, non autem in utrumlibet: hoc est, non ita volùt bonum ut possint illud nolle : sic enim reguntur & confirmantur à Deo, ut ad bonum tantùm propédeat eorum voluntas,& à malo abhorreat.Denique idem ostenditur exemplo Adami,& conditionis ejus quæ fuit ætc ipsius lapsum: Nam tùm profestò voluntatis ipsius libertas fuit ad bonum tantùm volendum,non autem libertas fuit in utrumlibet,hoc est,non ita voluit bonum, ut potuerit illud nolle, nisi potentiam remotam intelligas:Nos autem libertatis nomine proprie propinquam accipimus.
units.tr: I am led to prove this definition of liberty, first, by the example of the liberty of God himself, who, by the confession of all, most freely wills and does all things. Yet the liberty of God is not defined as a power by which he so wills the good that he could also nill it, or so does not will evil that he could also will it. Rather, the liberty of God is that by which, by his own right and without compulsion, he can will only what is good and nill only what is evil. Next, by the example of the blessed angels the same thing is evident: their liberty is towards good only, not towards either side; that is, they do not will the good in such a way that they could nill it. For they are so governed and confirmed by God that their will tends towards good alone and shrinks from evil. Finally, the same is shown by the example of Adam and the condition he had before his fall. For then the liberty of his will was only to will the good, not a liberty towards either side; that is, he did not will the good in such a way that he could have nilled it, unless you understand a remote power. But we properly take liberty to mean a proximate power.

units.la: Remotam potentiam eam voco quæ materiæ est consequens, ut est potentia ridendi in corpore humano antequam formam & animam accipiat. Propinquam voco, potentiam quæ formæ consequens est, vt est potentia ad ridendum hominis jam animati: Sic in voluntate humana est potétia remota & quasi materiæ: est etiam propinqua, & quasi formæ: Nos autè, vti paulò ante admonuimus, libertatis nomine non remotam illam, quæ materiæ est, sed propinquam quæ formæ est consequens intelligimus: formæ nomine intelligimus sanctitatem illam, quæ est ad Dei imaginem, & quæ est anima quasi animæ nostræ, & citra quam anima nostra quasi mortua est. Vnde ab Apost. Eph.2. citra hanc sanctitatem dicimur in peccatis & offensis mortui. Ex his concludo libertatem voluntatis proprie esse potestatem, sive potentiam propinquam, & sanctitatis, tanquam formæ, & quasi animæ voluntatis, consequentem: qua fit vt incoatè voluntas tantum inclinet ad bonum, declinet à malo. Hæc enim libertas voluntatis humanæ est ad similitudinem & imaginem libertatis ipsius Dei.
units.tr: I call a remote power that which follows matter, as the power of laughing belongs to the human body before it receives form and soul. I call a proximate power that which follows form, as the power to laugh belongs to a man who is already animated. So in the human will there is a remote power, which is as it were of matter; and there is also a proximate power, which is as it were of form. But we, as we admonished a little earlier, understand by liberty not that remote power which follows matter, but the proximate power which follows form. By form we understand that holiness which is according to the image of God, and which is as it were the soul of our soul, and without which our soul is as it were dead. Hence the Apostle says in Eph. 2. that without this holiness we are called dead in sins and trespasses. From these things I conclude that the liberty of the will is properly a power, or proximate power, which follows holiness as form and as the soul of the will; by which it comes about that the will, in an incipient way, inclines only to good and turns away from evil. For this liberty of the human will is according to the likeness and image of the liberty of God himself.

units.la: Libertati huic opponitur Coactio, quæ est ab externo aliquo agente, & contraria est voluntatis naturæ: Voluntas enim non est, si coacta fit, neq; voluntas cogi dicitur, licet homo ipse cujus est ea cogi dicatur. Dico li-bertati bertati oppositam esse coactionem, non autem necessitatem: Nam quae libere volumus, vel nolumus, ea ex necessitate volumus, vel nolumus; primum ex necessitate divini decreti, deinde etiam ex necessitate formae aduentitiae ipsius voluntatis, ut sanctitatis, corruptionis, utriusque: Homo enim cum sanctus erat in creatione, manente sanctitate illa, ex necessitate volebat bonum, nolebat malum: sic beati Angeli ex necessitate quadam volunt bonum, nolunt malum; & tandem glorificatus homo ex necessitate quadam inclinabit ad bonum, declinabit a malo: sic homo corruptus totus ante regenerationem fui, ex necessitate quadam vult malum, non vult bonum; & tamen suo quodam modo libere vult, licet haec non sit vera libertas, ut postea videbimus: denique homo renatus partim ex necessitate vult bonum, nempe, qua renatus est, partim ex necessitate vult malum, nempe, qua corruptus est; utrumque autem libere vult: Nam distinguendum est inter necessitatem & coactionem; cum necessitas coactione latius pateat, & coactum fit necessarium, non autem e contra, necessarium fit coactum. Haec de libertate voluntatis in genere.
units.tr: Compulsion is opposed to this liberty. It comes from some external agent, and is contrary to the nature of the will; for if the will is compelled, it is no longer a will, and it is not said that the will is compelled, although the man to whom the will belongs is said to be compelled. I say that compulsion, not necessity, is opposed to liberty. For what we will or nill freely, we will or nill from necessity: first from the necessity of the divine decree, and then also from the necessity of the form added to the will itself, such as holiness, corruption, or either of these. For man, when he was created holy, while that holiness remained, willed the good and nilled evil from necessity. So the blessed angels will the good and nill evil from a certain necessity. And finally, the glorified man will incline to good and turn away from evil from a certain necessity. So man, wholly corrupt before his regeneration, wills evil and does not will good from a certain necessity; and yet in a certain way he wills freely, although this is not true liberty, as we shall see later. Lastly, the regenerate man wills good partly from necessity, namely because he has been regenerated, and wills evil partly from necessity, namely because he is corrupt; yet he wills both freely. For we must distinguish between necessity and compulsion: necessity extends more widely than compulsion, and what is compelled is necessary, but not conversely, what is necessary is not thereby compelled. So much for the liberty of the will in general.

units.la: Nunc applicanda est ea ad varias hominis conditiones. Quadruplex omnino status homiminis venit considerandus. 1. status innocentiæ ante lapsum. 2. status corruptionis post lapsum. 3. status regenerationis. 4. status glorificationis. De primo itaque statu primum quæritur, An homo in statu innocentiæ habuerit libertatem voluntatis? Resp. Si libertatis priorem illam definitionem sequaris, quæ est potentia in utrumlibet, habuit quidem, fateor, in adiaphoris libertatem, in rebus vero bonis simpliciter & malis, non habuit homo in statu innocentiæ cum voluntatis libertate, qua, cum voluit bonum, potuit illud nolle, cum noluit malum, potuit illud velle: nisi potentiam remotam intelligas: nam potentiam propinquam ad bonum tantum habuit, propter formam sanctitatis & bonitatis in voluntate, quæ fuit ad Dei imaginem. Sin sequaris posteriorem libertatis definitionem, quæ est, cum voluntas ex interno suo principio, citra coactionem externi agentis, fertur in id quod bonum est tantum: si, inquis, hanc definitionem sequaris, respondeo hominem in statu innocentiæ libertatem voluntatis habuisse.
units.tr: Now these points must be applied to the various conditions of man. There are altogether four states of man to be considered: (1) the state of innocence before the fall; (2) the state of corruption after the fall; (3) the state of regeneration; (4) the state of glorification. Concerning the first state, the first question is: did man in the state of innocence have liberty of the will? Answer: if you follow the earlier definition of liberty, which is a power towards either side, I grant that he did have liberty in indifferent things; but in things good and evil absolutely, man in the state of innocence did not have liberty of will in the sense that, when he willed the good, he could have nilled it, and when he nilled evil, he could have willed it, unless you understand a remote power. For he had only a proximate power towards good, on account of the form of holiness and goodness in the will, which was according to the image of God. But if you follow the latter definition of liberty, which is that when the will, from its own internal principle and without compulsion from an external agent, is borne towards that which is good only, then, you say, if you follow this definition, I answer that man in the state of innocence had liberty of the will.

units.la: De secundo statu hominis quæritur, an homo in statu corruptionis habeat nunc voluntatis libertatem? Resp. si priorem libertatis definitionem sequaris, non nego quidem eum in adiaphoris habere libertatem: At in rebus simpliciter bonis & malis non habet eam: Nam homo qui totus corruptus est, no in ravult malu, ut possit illud nolle: nec ita non vult bonum ut possit illud velle: nisi potentiam intelligas remotam: Nam in homine corrupto potentia propinqua voluntatis ad malum duntaxat est, propter formam corruptionis & impuritatis, quae totam voluntatem occupat: Sin posteriorem libertatis definitionem sequaris, profecto libertatem voluntatis illam, quae est ad imaginem libertatis Dei ipsius, estque potestas sive potentia propinqua, qua citra coactionem fertur ad id duntaxat quod bonum est, homini corrupto & ipsius voluntati tribuere non possumus. Potestas enim ad malum libertas vere dici non potest, quin potius servitus quaedam est dicenda: Et re vera hominis non renati, non liberum, sed servum est arbitrium: Quia autem vult non renatus malum, non coacte, sed sponte sua, aliquo modo libertatis nomen ipsius voluntati potest attribui.
units.tr: Concerning the second state of man, the question is whether man in the state of corruption now has freedom of the will. Answer: if you follow the former definition of freedom, I do not deny that he has freedom in indifferent matters. But in things simply good and evil he does not have it. For a man who is wholly corrupt does not so will evil that he is able not to will it, nor does he so refuse good that he is able to will it, unless you understand a remote power. For in a corrupt man the proximate power of the will extends only to evil, on account of the form of corruption and impurity which occupies the whole will. But if you follow the latter definition of freedom, the freedom that is according to the image of God's own freedom, which is a power or proximate faculty by which the will is carried, without compulsion, towards that alone which is good, we cannot attribute this to a corrupt man and his will. For a power towards evil cannot truly be called freedom; it should rather be called a kind of servitude. Indeed, the will of a man not reborn is not free but a slave. Yet because the unregenerate man wills evil not under compulsion but of his own accord, the name of freedom can in some sense be attributed to the will itself.

units.la: Hic adversarij a nobis dissentiunt, & libertatem voluntatis homini non renato adscribunt, qua etiam potentia propinqua bonum velle potest, licet ante prævenientem gratiam hæc libertas sive potentia propinqua consopita jaceat: est tamen, inquiunt, reipsa, queadmodum homo consopitus homo est, & vivus est. Ex hoc sequitur necessario, aliquam in voluntate hominis non renati sanctitatem, & rectitudinem esse: Nam non est potentia voluntatis propinqua ad bonum, nisi præsente sanctitatis & rectitudinis forma, quæ est quasi anima voluntatis, efficitque potentiam hanc propinquam in voluntate, ad bonum.
units.tr: Here our opponents differ from us, and they ascribe to the unregenerate man a freedom of the will by which even a proximate power can will good, although before prevenient grace this freedom or proximate power lies dormant. Yet, they say, it is real, just as a man who is asleep is still a man and is alive. From this it necessarily follows that there is some holiness and rectitude in the will of the unregenerate man. For there is no proximate power of the will towards good unless the form of holiness and rectitude is present, which is as it were the soul of the will and makes this proximate power towards good to be in the will.

units.la: Bis igitur errant: Primùm ideò, quòd aliquam sanctitatem & rectitudinem in voluntate hominis non renati post lapsum reliquâ esse volunt: Deinde quòd potentiam voluntatis propinquam, quæ præsentiam formæ sanctitatis necessario sequitur; potentiam, inquam, propinquam ad bonum, in voluntate esse volunt: Nam quòd ad sanctitatem & rectitudinem, certum est eam universam deperditam esse in lapsu hominis, & per Christum Iesum totam, quantacunque est, reparari, & quasi denuò creari: unde nova creatura vocatur: quæ, si aliqua ex parte vetus est, cur nova dicitur? et si remanserit post lapsum in homine aliqua sanctitas, quæ anima est animæ nostræ, cur homo post lapsum ante regenerationem prorsus mortuus dicitur, non semi-mortuus? Testimonijs Scripturæ, quæ pro hac re afferri possunt infinita, nunc supersedemus. Quod ad libertatem, sive potentiam propinquam, quam ascribunt voluntati hominis non renati, quot Scripturæ testimonia eam refellunt: Iohn. 6. 44. Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi pater, qui misit me, traxerit eum. Rom. 8. 7. Legi Dei non subjicitur, nam nec potest quidem. 1. Cor. 2. 14. Animalis homo non est capax eorum, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei; sunt enim ei stultitia, nec potest ea cognoscere. Hæc Scripturæ loca, & alia hujusmodi, intelligenda sunt de potentia propinqua quæ est ad bonum; quam ideo negat Scriptura homini corrupto, quia nulla prorsus in eo est sanctitas post lapsum reliqua: Nam quod ad potentiam, quam diximus remotam esse etiam ad bonum, quæ materiæ non formæ consequens est, nos non negamus eam esse in voluntate hominis non renati: quæ & ipsa statim fit ex remota, propinqua, ubi primùm introducta est aliqua sanctitas in voluntatem hominis, per Spiritum Iesu Christi: Cum itaque remotam hanc potentiam relinquamus voluntati hominis non regeniti, hoc est, materiæ quandam potentiam, non est quòd aduersarij objiciant nos ex hominibus totidem stipites & truncos facere, dum negamus ijs libertatem, quam vocant, arbitrij: nam materiæ hæc potentia ad bonum, quâ nos concedimus voluntati hominis non regeniti, non est in stipite & in trunco.
units.tr: They therefore err twice: first, because they want some holiness and rectitude to remain in the will of the unregenerate man after the fall; second, because they want the proximate power of the will, which necessarily follows the presence of the form of holiness, to be in the will, a proximate power, I say, towards good. For it is certain that all holiness and rectitude was lost in the fall of man, and that through Jesus Christ it is wholly restored, however much there is, and as it were created anew; hence it is called a new creature. If it is in any part old, why is it called new? And if some holiness remained in man after the fall, which is the soul of our soul, why is man after the fall and before regeneration called wholly dead, not half-dead? We may now pass over the countless testimonies of Scripture that could be brought for this. As for the freedom, or proximate power, which they ascribe to the will of the unregenerate man, how many passages of Scripture refute it: John 6. 44. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. Rom. 8. 7. It is not subject to the law of God, for indeed it cannot be. 1 Cor. 2. 14. The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know them. These passages of Scripture, and others of the same kind, are to be understood of the proximate power towards good, which Scripture denies to a corrupt man because no holiness at all remains in him after the fall. As for the power which we said is remote even towards good, which follows matter and not form, we do not deny that it is in the will of the unregenerate man. This too becomes proximate from remote as soon as some holiness is first introduced into the will of man through the Spirit of Jesus Christ. Since we therefore leave this remote power to the will of the man not yet regenerated, that is, a certain power of matter, there is no reason for our opponents to object that we make men into so many stocks and blocks when we deny them what they call freedom of choice. For this power towards good, which we concede to the will of the unregenerate man, is not in a stock or a block.

units.la: Sciendum est hoc loco, quod dum negamus nō renato potentiam propinquam, hoc est, libertatem ad bonum, nomine boni intelligamus bonum, quâ est bonum: nam etiam non renatus potest velle id quod bonum est in se, ut conservationem patriæ, justitiam, æquitatem, &c. Verùm id quod in se bonû est, malum fit quodam modo respectu hominis non renati, qui non bene vult id quod bonû est in se, hoc est, neque eo modo, neque eo fine vult, quo debet illud velle, cum ipse non sit bonus & mundus: Immundis autem omnia immunda, ut mundis omnia munda.
units.tr: It must be noted here that when we deny the unregenerate man a proximate power, that is, freedom towards good, we understand by good the good as it is good. For even the unregenerate man can will what is good in itself, such as the preservation of the fatherland, justice, equity, and so on. But what is good in itself becomes in a certain way evil with respect to the unregenerate man, who does not will well what is good in itself. That is, he does not will it in the manner or for the end in which he ought to will it, since he himself is not good and clean. "To the unclean all things are unclean, as to the clean all things are clean."

units.la: Sciendum rursus est, nos in hoc negotio libertatis arbitrij, eandem rationem facere bonorum cujuscunque demum generis, sive ea naturalia sint, sive humana & civilia, sive denique spiritualia: nam ad nullum bonum, quâ bonum est, & Deo gratum, ipsiusque legi consentiens libertatem sive potentiam propinquâ habet homo non renatus, licet natura magis aliena sit ejus voluntas ab illis spiritualibus, quorum animalis homo non est capax, & queᵢ, ut ait Apostolus, non potest cognoscere, imò ipsi stultitia sunt. Spiritualia bona voco fidem, spem, resipiscentiam, justificationem, vitam denique æternam. Non est igitur quod adversarij fidem, spem, resipiscentiam asscribant libertati voluntatis nostræ, hoc est, viribus naturalibus, tanquam principali earum efficienti: Quasi verò nos natura duce & potestia sive libertate naturali, credamus, speremus, & convertamus nos ad Deum.
units.tr: Again it must be noted that in this matter of freedom of choice we make the same reckoning for goods of whatever kind they are, whether natural, or human and civil, or finally spiritual. For the unregenerate man has no proximate freedom or power towards any good as good, that is, pleasing to God and agreeing with his law, although his will is by nature more alien to those spiritual things of which the natural man is not capable, and which, as the Apostle says, he cannot know; indeed they are foolishness to him. I call spiritual goods faith, hope, repentance, justification, and finally eternal life. There is therefore no reason for our opponents to ascribe faith, hope, and repentance to the freedom of our will, that is, to natural powers, as their principal efficient cause, as if we, with nature as our guide and by natural power or freedom, believed, hoped, and turned ourselves to God.

units.la: Quo autem hæc res manifestior evadat, duo esse rerum bonarum genera intelligendum est: unum est rerum bonarum humanarum, alterum est rerum bonarum divinarum & spiritualium. Res bonæ humanæ vel Ethicæ sunt, & ad privatum quemque pertinent; vel œconomicæ sunt, & ad familiam pertinent: vel denique politicæ sunt, & ad universam Rempublicam & civitatem spectant. Res bonas spirituales voco, ut fidem, spem, resipiscentiam, justificationem, sanctificationem, vitam æternam. Ad utrumque hoc rerum bonarum genus, voluntas humana nō est similiter affecta: nam ad res humanas, sive humana bona, paulò propensior est: verbi gratia, ad temperantiam, fortitudinem, liberalitatem, justitiam, natura inclinat: licet hæc ipsa quæ in se bona sunt, neque eo quo debet modo, neque eo quo debet fine, velit, & eligat: quò fit, ut ea quæ in se bona sunt, non renati respectu, mala fiant, & peccata. Quod ad res spirituales, voluntas humana ab ijs alienior est, & cum sese offerunt voluntati, ipsa ab ijs natura tota abhorret.
units.tr: So that this matter may become plainer, it must be understood that there are two kinds of good things: one is human good things, the other is divine and spiritual good things. Human goods, whether ethical, pertain to each individual; or they are economic and pertain to the household; or finally they are political and concern the whole commonwealth and state. I call spiritual goods such things as faith, hope, repentance, justification, sanctification, and eternal life. The human will is not similarly disposed towards both kinds of good. It is rather more inclined towards human goods: for example, nature inclines us to temperance, fortitude, liberality, and justice, although the will does not will and choose these things, which are good in themselves, in the manner it ought or for the end it ought. Hence it happens that things which are good in themselves become evil and sins with respect to the unregenerate. As for spiritual things, the human will is more alien to them, and when they present themselves to the will, it shrinks from them entirely by nature.

units.la: Res hæc exemplo & experientia evadet manifestior. Duo quædam sunt bona, nempe, justitia per opera, & justitia per fidem, quæ Dei justitia vocatur: omnes nos experimur voluntatem natura propendere ad justitiam illa quæ est per opera, & quæ humanum quoddam bonum est: hinc fit ut hodierno die totus fere mundus naturam sequutus, quærat justificari per opera bona: At vero voluntas eadem abhorret tota à justitia illa quæ est per fidem, cum spirituale quoddam bonum sit: hinc fit ut tam pauci quærant justificari per fidem, solamque Dei in Christo misericordiam.
units.tr: This will become clearer by example and experience. There are two goods, namely justice through works and justice through faith, which is called the righteousness of God. We all experience that the will by nature inclines to that justice which is through works, which is a certain human good. Hence it happens that today almost the whole world, following nature, seeks to be justified by good works. But the same will shrinks entirely from that justice which is through faith, since it is a certain spiritual good. Hence it happens that so few seek to be justified by faith and by God's mercy in Christ alone.

units.la: Ex hoc & aliis similibus exemplis patet voluntatem humanam, ad bona quidem humana na natura propensiorem esse, à bonis vero spiritualibus totam abhorrere: licet ipsa ad nullum omnino bonum quà bonum est, propendeat: nam ne ad hæc ipsa quidem humana bona, quà bona sunt, & Deo grata propendet cum neque eo modo, neque eo fine quo debet, ea velit'. Quatenus igitur ea vult quæ in se bona sunt, peccata sunt, Deoque ingrata. Differunt tamen ab ijs malis & peccatis, quæ etiam in se & essentia sua mala sunt, cujusmodi sunt homicidium, adulterium, furtum &c. in quibus fateor, plures sunt peccati gradus: In his enim peccatur & in essentia ipsarū rerum, & in modo agendi, & in fine: & ad hæc propensior est natura sua voluntas hominis non renati, quàm ad ea, quæ in se bona sunt. Primū enim, prono impetu fertur ad ea quę in se mala sunt: deinde propensionem aliquā habet ad res humanas in se bonas: postremò, à rebus bonis spiritualibus tota abhorret ante regenerationem. Rursus concludo, humana bona quatenus ea vult homo non renatus, mala fieri quodam modo, & hominem non renatum in ijs expetendis peccare; id quod etiam verum est in adiaphoris, quæ in se neque bona neque mala sunt: Nam quatenus ea vult homo non renatus, eatenus mala fiunt, & peccat eat non renatus dum vult, & expetit etiam quod sua natura indifferens est, quia id vult, neque eo modo, neque eo fine quo debet.
units.tr: It is clear from this and other similar examples that the human will is more inclined to good things in the human sphere by nature, but wholly averse from spiritual goods, although it does not incline at all to any good as good. For it does not even incline to these human goods as good and pleasing to God, since it does not will them in the way it ought, nor for the end for which it ought. Insofar, therefore, as it wills those things which are good in themselves, it wills sins, and things displeasing to God. Yet these differ from those evils and sins which are evil in themselves and in their essence, such as murder, adultery, theft, and so on. In these, I admit, there are several degrees of sin: for in them one sins both in the essence of the things themselves, and in the manner of acting, and in the end. And the will of the unregenerate man is by its nature more inclined to these than to things that are good in themselves. For first, it is carried with headlong impulse to things that are evil in themselves; then it has a certain inclination towards human things that are good in themselves; lastly, before regeneration it is wholly averse from spiritual good things. Again I conclude: human goods, insofar as the unregenerate man wills them, become evil in a certain way, and the unregenerate man sins in desiring them; which is also true of adiaphora, things that are in themselves neither good nor evil. For insofar as the unregenerate man wills them, to that extent they become evil, and the unregenerate man sins when he wills and desires even what is indifferent by its nature, because he wills it neither in the way nor for the end that he ought.

units.la: Nunc de statu regenerationis quaeritur, an homo renatus habeat hanc voluntatis libertatem? Resp. Si libertatem definias potentiam in utrumlibet, primùm in rebus adiaphoris dicimus eum habere hanc libertatem: deinde in rebus quoque bonis & malis hanc libertatem illi non negamus: nam cum duplex sit actus, & duplex forma voluntatis hominis renati, forma sanctitatis, & forma corruptionis; primitiae novi hominis, & reliquiae veteris, necesse est duplex sit potentia etiam propinqua voluntatis ipsius: una quae est ad bonum, altera quae est ad malum: ut mihi videatur recepta haec definitio libertatis maximè competere in libertatem voluntatis hominis renati.
units.tr: Now it is asked concerning the state of regeneration, whether the regenerate man has this freedom of the will. Answer: If you define liberty as the power to either alternative, we say first that he has this liberty in things indifferent; and then we do not deny him this liberty in good and evil things too. For since the act is twofold, and the form of the will of the regenerate man is twofold, the form of holiness and the form of corruption, the firstfruits of the new man and the remnants of the old, it is necessary that there be a twofold proximate power of the will itself: one which is toward good, the other which is toward evil. So this accepted definition of liberty seems to me to apply most fully to the liberty of the will of the regenerate man.

units.la: Sin vero libertatem definias ex incoacta potentia, quae est ad bonum tantum, non etiam ad malum, profecto ne homo quidem renatus sic liber est: verùm progressum duntaxat facit ad libertatem suam, quae in altera demùm vita perfecta futura est.
units.tr: But if you define liberty by an unimpeded power which is toward good only, and not also toward evil, then certainly not even the regenerate man is free in this way; rather, he merely makes progress toward his liberty, which will be perfected only in the other life.

units.la: Postremò de statu glorificationis quaeritur, An homo cum in statu glorificationis erit, habiturus sit hanc voluntatis libertatem? Resp.
units.tr: Finally, concerning the state of glorification, it is asked: when man will be in the state of glorification, will he have this freedom of the will? Answer.

units.la: Si libertatem definias potentiam in utrumlibet, etiam in rebus bonis & malis, homo cum in statu glorificationis erit, non habebit eam: Nam potentiam propinquam ad bonum tantum habebit propter formam illam sanctitatis, vel gloriae potius, quàm tum induet ipsius voluntas. Non nego in eo quoque futuram potentiam remotam ad malum, propter necessariam creaturae mutabilitatem: verùm remota haec potentia, propinqua nunquam sutura est: quia Deus eum in aeternum confirmaturus est, & sustentarurus in illo gloriae statu. Sin verò posteriorem illam definitionem libertatis sequaris, profecto glorificatus demùm vere liber futurus est. Nam tantùm id quod bonum est, Deoq; acceptum volet, idque incoaté, & in aeternum. Libera voluntate fuit homo in statu innocentiae secundum imaginem divinae illius libertatis: verùm in statu glorificationis, in quo magis Dei sui imaginem referet, & gestabit imaginem caelestis illius hominis Christi, multò liberiori erit voluntate, & ad id quod bonum est tantù multò propensiori. Atq; haec de libertate voluntatis hactenus, hoc est, de voluntatis illa proprietate, sive insita qualitate.
units.tr: If you define liberty as the power to either alternative, even in good and evil things, then man, when he is in the state of glorification, will not have it. For he will have a proximate power only toward good, on account of that form of holiness, or rather of glory, which his will will then put on. I do not deny that there will also be in that state a remote power toward evil, on account of the necessary mutability of the creature; but this remote power will never become proximate, because God will confirm him for eternity and sustain him in that state of glory. But if you follow the latter definition of liberty, then indeed the glorified man will truly be free. For he will will only what is good and acceptable to God, and that perfectly and for eternity. Man was free in the state of innocence with a will free according to the image of that divine liberty; but in the state of glorification, in which he will more fully bear the image of his God and will carry the image of that heavenly man Christ, he will have a far freer will, and one far more inclined only to what is good. And so far concerning the liberty of the will, that is, concerning that property of the will, or innate quality.

units.la: Nunc dicendum est de libero arbitrio. Licet cet sint qui arbitrij verbum ad mentem referant, ut sit arbitrium nihil aliud, quàm mentis judicium, quod voluntatis functionem liberam antegreditur; liberi autem vocem, ad voluntatem pertinere dicant; tamen ego exi-stimo arbitrij nomine magis intelligendum esse voluntatis ipsius placitum, hoc est, accipiendum esse hoc nomine voluntatis functionem quaecunque ea sit, sive velit ipsa, sive nolit, sive eligat, sive repudiet. Huic voluntatis placito tribuitur libertas, & liberum dicitur, quemadmodum ipsa voluntas libera vocatur. Proprietas enim causae de effecto & actione ejusdem causae etiam praedicatur. Est itaque liberum arbitrium, nihil aliud, meo judicio, quàm placitum voluntatis, quod est citra coactionem, quodque profectum est à principio quodam voluntatis interno, non autem ab externo aliquo cogente.
units.tr: Now we must speak of free choice. Although there are some who refer the word arbitrium to the mind, so that arbitrium is nothing other than the judgment of the mind, which precedes the free function of the will, and who say that the word free pertains to the will; nevertheless I think that by the name arbitrium we should rather understand the very decision of the will, that is, that by this name we should take whatever function of the will there is, whether it wills or does not will, chooses or rejects. To this decision of the will liberty is ascribed, and it is called free, just as the will itself is called free. For a property of a cause is also predicated of its effect and action. Free choice is therefore, in my judgment, nothing other than the decision of the will, which is without coercion, and which proceeds from some internal principle of the will, and not from any external compelling force.

units.la: Quaeri potest, Annon cum liberè fungitur voluntas suo munere, in libere volendo aliquid vel nolendo; annon, inquam, hic sit meti locus aliquis? Respondeo, objectum illud quodcunque circa quod versatur voluntas, ipsiusque libera functio, primum monstrari & judicari à mente. Iudicium autem mentis duplex est: primum simplex & ἁπλοῦν, ut cum abscque discursu aliquo, & ratiocinatione judicat bonum esse, malum esse, sequendum esse, fugiendum esse. Mentis hoc judicium est de fine, & medio aliquo ad finem tendente, quod unicum est ac solum. Deinde judicium mentis est διαιρετικόν [?], quando cum discursu aliquid judicat bonum, malum, fugiendum, sequendum. Hoc judicium est in mediis, quae plura sunt, ex quibus, discursu mentis facto, unum eligitur, alterum repudiatur. Monstratum jam & aliquo modo judicatum a mente objectum, voluntas libere vult, vel non vult, eligit, vel repudiat: licet post hominis lapsum ea sequuta sit, ἀταξία facultatum in mente humana, qua fit ut voluntas saepenumero, quod tanquam malum judicatum est, vel quod improbatum est a mente, illud eligat, contraque quod tanquam bonum judicatum est, & approbatum a mente, illud repudiet.
units.tr: It may be asked: when the will freely performs its office, in freely willing or not willing something, is there not, I say, some place here for the mind? I answer that the object, whatever it is, about which the will is occupied and its free function, is first shown and judged by the mind. The judgment of the mind is twofold. The first is simple and single (ἁπλοῦν), as when it judges without any discursive reasoning that something is good, evil, to be followed, to be fled. This judgment of the mind concerns the end and some means tending to the end, and it is single and sole. Then there is the discriminating judgment of the mind (διαιρετικόν [?]), when with discursive reasoning it judges something to be good, evil, to be shunned, to be followed. This judgment concerns means, which are many, from which, after discursive reasoning, one is chosen and the other rejected. Once the object has been shown and in some way judged by the mind, the will freely wills or does not will, chooses or rejects it; although after the fall of man there followed a disorder (ἀταξία) of the faculties in the human mind, by which it happens that the will very often chooses what has been judged evil, or disapproved by the mind, and conversely rejects what has been judged good and approved by the mind.

units.la: De mente quoque potest quaeri, An possit boni judicium facere, vel bonum approbare, malum autem improbare? Haec quaestio solvenda est ex quadruplici illo hominis statu. Verùm cum quaeratur maximè de mente hominis corrupti, an ea possit bonum approbare malum autem improbare: de mente hominis corrupti responsio nostra erit maximè. Dici mus itaq; mentem hominis corrupti tantum posse approbare, quod malum est, si potentia intelligas propinquam, hoc est, eam, quæ formam consequitur: potest etiam approbare, id quod in se bonum est, sed non qua bonum est: cum neque eo modo, neque eo fine, quo debet, illud approbet, quemadmodum supra dictum est de voluntate. Ad bonum autem humanum approbandum, mens hominis corrupti est paulo propensior: à bono autem spirituali omnino aliena est. Nam teste Paulo spirituale bonum stultum judicat, ea enim quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, sunt ei stultitia. 1. Cor. 2.
units.tr: Concerning the mind also it can be asked: can it make a judgment of good, or approve good and disapprove evil? This question must be resolved from that fourfold state of man. But since the question is chiefly asked about the mind of corrupt man, whether it can approve good and disapprove evil, our answer will be chiefly about the mind of corrupt man. We say, therefore, that the mind of corrupt man can approve only what is evil, if you understand power as proximate, that is, the power which follows the form; it can also approve what is good in itself, but not as good, since it does not approve it in the way it ought nor for the end it ought, just as was said above about the will. But the mind of corrupt man is somewhat more inclined to approve human good; yet it is wholly alien to spiritual good. For, as Paul testifies, the spiritual good seems foolish to it, since the things of the Spirit of God are foolishness to it. 1 Cor. 2.

units.la: Atq; hæc de libertate voluntatis humanæ & libero arbitrio dicta sunto. Nunc de gratia Dei quæ libero arbitrio, sive naturæ contraria est, quæq; non modò principalis efficiens est fidei, spei, & resipiscentiæ, verùm etiam sola harum efficiens est: de gratia, inquâ, illa Dei, deinceps erit agendum.
units.tr: Let these things be said concerning the liberty of the human will and free choice. Now concerning the grace of God, which is contrary to free choice or nature, and which is not only the principal efficient cause of faith, hope and repentance, but is even the sole efficient cause of these: of that grace of God, I say, we shall now proceed to speak.

units.la: De Gratia Dei. Cap. 38.
units.tr: On the Grace of God. Chapter 38.

units.la: GRatia Dei est favor Dei immeritus: vel est, qua Deus favet creaturæ suæ absque creaturæ ipsius aliquo merito. Videtur Apostolus Ephes. 1. 9. gratiam & εὐδοκίαν Dei pro eodem fumere: Nam quod dicit eo versu, secundum gratuitam suam benevolentiam, sive ευδοκιαν, eodem sensu dictum esse videtur, cum eo quod dixit superius eodem cap. verf. 7. Secundum divitias gratiæ suæ. Videntur etiam gratia Dei, & Charitas, siue dilectio indifferenter accipi. Rom. 9. 13. Iacob dilexi: Hæc illa dilectio siue ευδοκια, siue gratia est qua, Iacobum ab æterno complexus est. Ephes. 3. 18. Vt in Charitate, inquit, radicati & fundati, &c. Hęc est illa gratia, quæ ab æterno nos prosequutus est Deus Tit. 3. 4. Gratia Dei erga homines in specie φιλανθρωπία appellata est.
units.tr: The grace of God is God's favour bestowed without merit: that is, it is the favour by which God shows kindness to his creature without any merit on the creature's part. In Ephesians 1:9 the Apostle seems to use grace and εὐδοκία [eudokia] of God as the same thing. For what he says in that verse, "according to his gratuitous benevolence" [εὐδοκίαν], seems to be said in the same sense as what he said earlier in the same chapter, verse 7: "according to the riches of his grace." Grace of God and charity or love also seem to be taken interchangeably. Romans 9:13: "Jacob have I loved." This love, whether called εὐδοκία or grace, is that by which he embraced Jacob from eternity. Ephesians 3:18: "That you, being rooted and grounded in love," etc. This is that grace by which God has pursued us from eternity. Titus 3:4: God's grace towards men is called by the special name φιλανθρωπία [philanthropia].

units.la: Porrò latius patere videtur gratia quàm misericordia, cum misericordia proprie miseros & peccatores respiciat, gratia vero patet ad omnes creaturas cujuscunq; sortis sint ec, tam ad Angelos beatos, quàm ad homines peccatores; unde in salutationibus, quæ habentur in prima & secunda ad Timotheum Epistola, Gratia primum vt quiddam latius patens, deinde Misericordia, vt angustius aliquid, & gratiam quasi restringens, optantur personæ salutatæ, Timotheo. Nam etsi in illis salutationibus gratia & misericordia metonymice accipiantur, pro beneficijs Dei, quæ ex gratia & misericordia conferuntur: tamen ex his ipsis satis liquet misericordiam Dei, quę causa est beneficiorum ipsius, angustius patere quàm gratiam: Sensus enim est, ac si dixisset Apostolus; Beneficia Dei gratuita, neque gratuita modò, hoc est, gratis ac immeritò collata, sed etiam ex misericordia erga miseros & mala omnia commeritos, multiplicentur vobis.
units.tr: Grace seems to extend more widely than mercy, since mercy properly regards the wretched and sinful, whereas grace extends to all creatures of whatever rank, to the blessed angels as well as to sinful men. Hence in the greetings in the first and second Epistles to Timothy, grace is wished to the persons greeted first, as something of wider scope, and then mercy, as something narrower which in a sense restricts grace. For although in those greetings grace and mercy are taken by metonymy for the benefits of God which are bestowed out of grace and mercy, yet from those very words it is clear enough that the mercy of God, which is the cause of his benefits, extends more narrowly than grace. For the sense is as if the Apostle had said: "May the benefits of God, freely given, be multiplied to you, freely given not only in the sense that they are gratuitous, that is, bestowed without merit, but also out of mercy towards the wretched and those who have deserved every evil."

units.la: Vt appareat Dei beneficia omnia ex hac gratia proficisci ad nos, doctrinæ de gratia initium paulò altius ex primis suis fundamentis repetemus. Deus ab æterno propositum glorificari imprimis in gratia sua. Rom. 11. 32. Conclusit Deus omnes in contumacia, ut omnium misereretur: quo loco vides ipsam justitiam Dei inservire ipsius misericordiæ & gratiæ: Eadem ratio est & aliarum Dei proprietatum, ut potentiæ, sapientiæ, &c. quę omnes inserviunt suo modo divinæ gratiæ & misericordiæ. Hinc primùm omnium ab æterno extiterunt decreta ex gratia, ad gloriam & laudem ejusdem gratiæ. Eph. 1. 6. & 12. Primum Dei decretum ex gratia fuit de Filio suo incarnando, & glorificando suo tempore, ad gloriam gratiæ suæ. De decreto de filio Christo vide Act. 2. 23. & 4. 28. de gratia erga Christum, vide Coloss. 1. 19. Quoniam in eo placuit patri, &c. vbi εὐδοκία patris vides causam esse cur plenitudo deitatis inhabitet in Christo corporaliter. Nam ex gratia fuit admirabili quod voluerit Deus carnem, hoc est, creaturam tam vilem, vniri cum Deo creatore gloriloso & incomparabili.
units.tr: So that it may appear that all God's benefits proceed to us from this grace, we shall trace the doctrine of grace a little further back, from its first foundations. From eternity God purposed to be glorified above all in his grace. Romans 11:32: "God has shut up all in disobedience, that he might have mercy on all." In this place you see that God's very justice serves his mercy and grace. The same reasoning applies to the other properties of God, such as power, wisdom, and so on, all of which in their own way serve his divine grace and mercy. Hence the first of all the decrees of God, from eternity, arose out of grace, to the glory and praise of that same grace. Ephesians 1:6 and 12: The first decree of God out of grace concerned the incarnation of his Son, and his glorifying at the appointed time, to the glory of his grace. On the decree concerning the Son Christ, see Acts 2:23 and 4:28; on grace towards Christ, see Colossians 1:19: "For it pleased the Father," etc., where you see the Father's εὐδοκία [eudokia] to be the cause why the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily in Christ. For it was out of grace, wonderful indeed, that God willed the flesh, that is, a creature so base, to be united with God the glorious and incomparable Creator.

units.la: Secundum decretum Dei ex gratia, fuit de homine primum creando ad imaginem suam, deinde post lapsum reparando in Christo filio suo, ad imaginem filij sui, hoc est, suo tempore in Christo filio suo, vocando, justificando, glorificādo homine, ad gloriā Christi pariter, & ad gloriam gratię suae. Summatim enim in his partibus posita est hominis post lapsum reparatio ac restitutio. Vide Eph. 1. 4. 5. Rom. 9. 11. Rom. 11. 5. 6.
units.tr: The second decree of God out of grace concerned man: first, that he should be created in God's image, and then, after the fall, be restored in Christ his Son, to the image of his Son. That is, at the appointed time, in Christ his Son, he should be called, justified and glorified, to the glory of Christ equally and to the glory of his own grace. For the restoration and re-establishment of man after the fall is summarily set out in these parts. See Ephesians 1:4–5; Romans 9:11; Romans 11:5–6.

units.la: Hinc sequuta est exequutio decretorum illorum ex eadem illa Dei gratia. Primum autē exequutio fuit decreti de homine; quod quidem naturae ordine secundum fuit: Nam quod primum fuit decreto & ordinatione, id secundum evasit exequutione, contraq; quod secundum fuit decreto & ordinatione, id primum factum est exequutione. Primum itaq; locū obtinuit exequutio decreti de homine, eaque fuit ex eadem illa Dei gratia, ad gloriam am ejusdem gratiæ.Exequutio igitur decreti de homine, vt de ea dicamus nonnihil, primùm fuit creatio hominis ad imaginem creatoris ex gratia ipsius, ad gloriam ejusdem illius gratiæ:Deinde fuit hominis post lapsum ex gratia reparatio in filio Christo, ad gloriam filij Christi, & ad laudé gratię Dei Patris. Reparatio hæc, quæ altera pars est executionis decreti de homine, plures habet in se partes, quæ & ipsę omnes sunt ex gratia, & ad gloriam Christi capitis ac mediatoris primùm tendunt, deinde ad laudem gratiæ Dei Patris. De hoc ordine vide 1. Cor. 3. 22. 23. Omnia vestra sunt: vos autem Christi: Christus autem Dei.
units.tr: From this followed the execution of those decrees, out of the same grace of God. The execution of the decree concerning man came first, though in the order of nature it was second. For what was first in decree and ordering became second in execution, and conversely what was second in decree and ordering was first in execution. Thus the execution of the decree concerning man held the first place, and it was from that same grace of God, to the glory of that same grace. Therefore, to say something of this execution: first came the creation of man in the image of the Creator out of his grace, to the glory of that same grace. Then came the restoration of man after the fall, out of grace, in the Son Christ, to the glory of the Son Christ and the praise of the grace of God the Father. This restoration, which is the second part of the execution of the decree concerning man, has many parts within it, all of which are also from grace, and tend first to the glory of Christ the head and mediator, and then to the praise of the grace of God the Father. On this order see 1 Corinthians 3:22–23: "All things are yours; and you are Christ's; and Christ is God's."

units.la: Sciendum de reparatione ista humani generis, priusquàm ad ejus partes accedamus, quòd tempore partim præcesserit exequutione decreti illius de Christo Dei filio, partim vero eam sequuta fit. Nam antequàm venit plenum illud tempus in quo Christus manifestatus est in carne, cœperunt homines reparari jam inde à lapsu, hoc est, vocari, justisicari, glorificari; idque virtute, partim decreti illius de Christo, quod inde ab æterno fuit, partim futuræ manifestationis ejusdem Christi. Postquam autem venit plenum illud tempus, pus,& Christus in carne jam manifestatus est, passus est, glorificatus est, reparatio eadem illa hominis evasit jam locupletior atque vberior. Christus enim jam exhibitus efficacior est ad reparationem nostri, hoc est, ad vocationem, justificationem, & glorificationem, quàm fuit idem jam olim, antequàm exhibitus est in carne. Ergo in mediam quasi reparationem hominis, sive exequutionem decreti de homine reparando incidit exequutio decreti illius de filio Dei Iesu Christo, quod primum fuit: Quamobrem nos quoque medio loco de ea agemus, vt hinc ad partes reparationis humani generis transeamus.
units.tr: Concerning this restoration of the human race, before we come to its parts, it must be noted that in time it partly preceded and partly followed the execution of that decree concerning Christ the Son of God. For before that fullness of time came, in which Christ was manifested in the flesh, men began to be restored from the fall onwards, that is, to be called, justified and glorified. This was by the power partly of that decree concerning Christ, which was from eternity, and partly of the future manifestation of the same Christ. But after that fullness of time came, and Christ was now manifested in the flesh, suffered and was glorified, that same restoration of man became richer and more abundant. For Christ, now revealed, is more effective for our restoration, that is, for our calling, justification and glorification, than he was before he was revealed in the flesh. So into the middle, as it were, of the restoration of man, or the execution of the decree concerning the man to be restored, falls the execution of that decree concerning the Son of God Jesus Christ, which was first. Wherefore we too shall treat of it in the middle place, so that from there we may pass on to the parts of the restoration of the human race.

units.la: Exequutio igitur decreti illius de filio Dei Iesu Christo, posita est in ejus incarnatione, passione, & glorificatione, & quidè ex gratia Dei, quæ partim fuit erga carnè ipsam Christi mediatoris, partim fuit erga nos, qui reparamur per eandem illā Christi carnem cum filio Dei ὑποστατικῶς vnitam. Ex gratia itaq; duplici fuit exequutio decreti de filio Dei Iesu Christo, & fuit quidem ad gloriam gratiæ ipsius Dei.
units.tr: The execution of that decree concerning the Son of God Jesus Christ therefore consists in his incarnation, passion and glorification, and this indeed out of the grace of God, which was partly towards the very flesh of Christ the mediator, and partly towards us, who are restored through that same flesh of Christ, hypostatically [ὑποστατικῶς] united with the Son of God. So the execution of the decree concerning the Son of God Jesus Christ was twofold in grace, and indeed it was to the glory of the grace of God himself.

units.la: Nunc redeo ad reparationem illam humani generis, sive exequutionem decreti de homine reparando: Ejus partes summatim sunt, vocatio, justificatio, glorificatio. Vocatio, vt de ea dicamus primùm, ex gratia Dei est, sive gratuita est, idque ratione duplici. Primùm enim in efficaci vocatione, promulgatio fœderis, sive Evangelij prædicatio, ex sola Dei gratia est: Vnde Ephef. 1. 9. Patefacto, inquit, nobis mysterio voluntatis suæ secundùm gratuitam suâ benevolentiam. Deinde fides, qua recipimus promissionem fœderis in Christo oblatam, ex mera Dei gratia est. Philip. 1. 29. Vobis, inquit, datum est in Christi negotio, non solùm in eo credere, &c. Ergo fides est donum Dei. Prior illa gratia in vocatione, dici potest gratia vocationis, & communis est quibuscunque vocatis, tam electis illis, quàm reprobis: Posterior verò gratia in vocatione efficaci dici potest gratia fidei, & ad electos proprie pertinet: nam solis ijs qui prædestinati sunt ad vitam æternam datum est credere. Sub gratia fidei comprehendo quoque spei & resipiscentiæ gratiam, quæ loco de vocatione efficaci subalternæ sunt.
units.tr: Now I return to that restoration of the human race, or the execution of the decree concerning man to be restored. Its parts, in summary, are calling, justification and glorification. Calling, to speak of it first, is from the grace of God, or is gratuitous, and this for a twofold reason. For first, in effectual calling the promulgation of the covenant, or the preaching of the Gospel, is from the grace of God alone. Hence Ephesians 1:9: "Having made known to us the mystery of his will, according to his gratuitous benevolence." Then faith, by which we receive the promise of the covenant offered in Christ, is from the pure grace of God. Philippians 1:29: "To you it has been given, in the cause of Christ, not only to believe in him," etc. Therefore faith is the gift of God. The former grace in calling may be called the grace of calling, and is common to all who are called, whether elect or reprobate. But the latter grace in effectual calling may be called the grace of faith, and properly pertains to the elect; for to those alone who are predestined to eternal life has it been given to believe. Under the grace of faith I include also the grace of hope and of repentance, which are subordinate to effectual calling.

units.la: Duplicem hanc in vocatione efficaci gratiam sequitur gratia justificationis; nam illa ipsa imputatio quæ sequitur fidem, fideique apprehensionem in vocatione efficaci, ex noua quadam Dei gratia est: Non enim nisi ex gratia est, quòd aliena justitia & satisfactio pro nostra censeantur. vnde Rom. 3.14. Iustificamur autem gratis, id est, ejus gratia, & alibi passim. Hanc gratiam perpetuò opponit Apostolus operibus, hoc est, merito nostro, & fidei in Christum, comitem eam ac sociaam facit: optime enim convenit gratiæ Dei cum merito Christi fide apprehéfo, non ideò tantùm quòd meritum illud non fit nostrum, sed Christi, hoc est ipsiusmet Dei, sed vel multò magis quòd Christi satisfactio & meritum illud alienum, ex Dei gratia fit, meraq; liberalitate: Non enim pepercit Deus Filio suo, sed pro nobis tradidit eum in mortem. Rom. 8.32. Atque hac de causa fit, vt in Christi illa satisfactione & merito ipsius magis eluceat gratia Dei, majorque appareat, quàm si fine vllo merito vel nostro vel alieno, quo satisfiat ipsius justitiæ, nos justificet. Optimè igitur consistit gratia, qua nos justificat Deus, cum merito illo, & λυτρῳ, quod ipse Deus de suo dedit. Quòd si autem λυτρον illud & precium redemptionis ab ipso Deo non dissoluéretur, tum profectò in merito illo ac λυτρῳ non adeò consipiceretur gratia. Quod verò ad meritum hominum attinet, affirmamus nullo pacto gratiæ Dei cum illo convenire posse.
units.tr: This double grace in effectual calling is followed by the grace of justification. For that very imputation which follows faith, and the apprehension of faith in effectual calling, comes from a certain new grace of God. It is only by grace that another's righteousness and satisfaction are reckoned as ours. Hence Rom. 3.24: "We are justified freely", that is, by his grace; and elsewhere everywhere. The Apostle always opposes this grace to works, that is, to our merit, and he makes it the companion and associate of faith in Christ. For the grace of God agrees well with the merit of Christ, received by faith, not only because that merit is not ours but Christ's, that is, God's own, but much more because the satisfaction of Christ and that alien merit come from the grace of God and from pure liberality. For God "did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all" (Rom. 8.32). And for this reason the grace of God shines forth more clearly in that satisfaction and merit of Christ, and appears greater, than if he justified us without any merit, ours or another's, by which his justice might be satisfied. Therefore the grace by which God justifies us agrees best with that merit and ransom which God himself gave from his own store. But if that ransom and price of redemption were not paid by God himself, then indeed grace would not be so conspicuous in that merit and ransom. As for the merit of men, we affirm that it can in no way be reconciled with the grace of God.

units.la: Gratiam justificationis sequitur gratia glorificationis sive regenerationis: vt enim sententiæ ipsa latio & dictio, est ex gratia; ita sententiæ latæ, dictæque exequutio ex gratia pariter est. Regeneratio enim, sive glorificatio, exequutio quædam est sententiæ justificationis quæ præcessit. De hac gratia vide r. Pet. 1.3. Qui ex multa sua misericordia regenuit nos in spem vivam. & Tit.3.5. Ex sua misericordia servavit nos per lavacrum regenerationis & renovationem Spiritus sancti, et Eph. 2.5.8. Gratia estis servati.
units.tr: The justification of grace is followed by the grace of glorification, or regeneration. For just as the very pronouncing and declaring of the sentence is from grace, so the carrying out of the pronounced and declared sentence is likewise from grace. For regeneration, or glorification, is a certain execution of the sentence of justification that has gone before. On this grace see 1 Pet. 1.3: "who according to his abundant mercy has begotten us again to a living hope"; and Titus 3.5: "according to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit"; and Eph. 2.5, 8: "By grace you have been saved."
