units.la: Notandum autem est, in ista humani generis reparatione ejusque partibus omnibus, unam eandemque reipsa Dei gratiam esse, quæ est principium omnium earum partium; nos vero eam ex effectis suis variis, variam aliquo modo facere, ac distinguere: non secus atque Spiritus sanctus qui unus est. 1. Cor. 12.4. ratione discriminis donorum & effectuum ipsius aliquo modo distinguitur, & ratione quadam, non reipsa, alius atque alius est. Rom. 8.15. Non enim accepistis Spiritum servitutis rursus ad metum, sed accepistis Spiritum adoptionis.
units.tr: It must be noted that in this restoration of the human race and in all its parts, there is in fact one and the same grace of God, which is the source of all these parts. We, however, from its various effects make it in a way various and distinguish it, just as the Holy Spirit, who is one, is in a way distinguished by reason of the difference of his gifts and effects, and is in a certain respect, not in reality, different and other. Rom. 8.15: "For you have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption."

units.la: Ex his quæ diximus nota quatuor esse quasi gratias in reparatione hominis ejusq; partibus. Nam cum in efficaci vocatione duplex sit Dei beneficium, primum, oblatio Christi cum beneficiis ipsius in fœdere gratuito sive Evangelio: secundum, fides quæ oblatum Christum recipit (sub Fide intelligo Spem & Resipiscentiam, quæ fidem consequuntur) ideo in efficaci vocatione duæ censentur gratiæ, gratia vocationis sive oblationis, gratia fidei sive receptionis. In justificatione est tertia gratia, quam gratiam justificationis nominare possumus. In glorificatione est quarta quam non inepte gratiam glorificationis vocabimus.
units.tr: From what we have said, it is to be noted that there are, as it were, four graces in the restoration of man and its parts. For since in effectual calling there is a twofold benefit of God: first, the offer of Christ with his benefits in the free covenant or Gospel; second, faith, which receives the offered Christ (by faith I understand hope and repentance, which follow faith); therefore in effectual calling two graces are reckoned: the grace of calling or offer, and the grace of faith or reception. In justification there is a third grace, which we may call the grace of justification. In glorification there is a fourth, which we not inappropriately call the grace of glorification.

units.la: Ex his vides primam gratiam, quam prævenientem vocant, esse eam qua nos primùm ad se vocat Deus per Evangelium suum, ultimam vero gratiam, & gratiæ quasi complementum, eam qua nos in cœlis una cum filio suo glorificat: nam gratiam ultimam inchoat in hac vita, per regenerationem ista inchoatam, absolvet autem eam in altera illa vita, per glorificationem. Hæc de reparationis partibus hactenus, quæ ex gratia sunt omnes, & ad gloriam gratiæ dirig untur.
units.tr: From these things you see that the first grace, which they call prevenient, is that by which God first calls us to himself through his Gospel, but the last grace, and as it were the completion of grace, is that by which he glorifies us in heaven together with his Son. For he begins the last grace in this life, which is begun through regeneration, and he completes it in that other life, through glorification. So far concerning the parts of restoration, all of which are from grace and are directed to the glory of grace.

units.la: Observandum in genere beneficia Dei omnia, tàm ea quæ ab æterno fuerunt, quàm ea quæ in tempore sunt, fundata esse pariter in sola meraque Dei gratia: neq; quoad gratiam discrimen esse aliquod inter illa quæ ante tempora sæcularia fuerunt beneficia, verbi gratia, præscientiam, prædestinationem, & hæc quæ in tempore sunt, verbi gratia, vocationem, justificationem, & glorificationem.
units.tr: It is to be observed in general that all the benefits of God, both those which were from eternity and those which are in time, are alike founded in the sole and pure grace of God; nor is there any distinction as regards grace between those benefits which were before the ages, for example foreknowledge and predestination, and those which are in time, for example calling, justification and glorification.

units.la: Hæc ipsa veritas est ac manet, invitis adversarijs & hostibus illis gratiæ ac crucis Christi, qui tamen libertatem nescio quam voluntatis nostræ, & opera nostra meritoria in vocatione nostri, justificatione & glorificatione volunt concurrere unà cum Dei gratia. Nam quod ad vocationem, quamvis illud verum esse fateantur, prævenientem nempe gratiam illam, quam dicunt, nos tum primùm nihil de gratia Dei cogitantes, non præparantes nosipsos ad gratiam recipiendam, etiam plane consopitos in peccato, præoccupare: tamè assensionem illam, quà nos fidei tribuimus, qua nimirùm assentimur gratiæ prævenienti, eamq; admittimus, libertati arbitrij nostri ascribunt: quasi verò voluntatis libertas aliqua fit actu, vel, ut loquuntur, potentia propinqua fit voluntatis ad gratiam Dei recipiendâ.
units.tr: This truth is and remains, though their adversaries and enemies of the grace and cross of Christ are unwilling, who nevertheless want some freedom of our will, I know not what, and our meritorious works, to concur with the grace of God in our calling, justification and glorification. For as regards calling, although they confess that it is true, namely that prevenient grace which they speak of comes first, anticipating us when we are not thinking at all about the grace of God, not preparing ourselves to receive grace, indeed plainly lying asleep in sin; yet they ascribe to the freedom of our choice that assent by which we give faith, namely by which we assent to prevenient grace and admit it. As if indeed there were some freedom of the will in act, or, as they say, a proximate power of the will to receive the grace of God.

units.la: Nos verò, ut non negamus libertatem sive potentiam voluntatis aliquam, qua fit ut ad bonum ipsa aliquo modo propendeat; potentia intelligo materiae: ita negamus plane libertatem voluntatis, quae actu fit: vel, quod idem est, propinquam ejus potentiam ad id quod bonum est, qua bonum est. Potentiam voluntatis propinquam, sive libertatem actu ad bonum definio, eam quae ex forma sanctitatis, vel imagine Dei voluntati impressa existit, ut patet ex doctrina de libero arbitrio jam a nobis tradita.
units.tr: We, however, as we do not deny some freedom or power of the will, by which it is inclined in some way toward the good, understanding power in the sense of matter, so we plainly deny freedom of the will which exists in act; or, which is the same thing, its proximate power toward what is good, as good. I define the proximate power or freedom in act of the will toward the good as that which arises from the form of holiness, or the image of God, impressed on the will, as is clear from the doctrine of free choice already set out by us.

units.la: Affirmamus itaque in prima gratia recipienda voluntatem nostram habere se tantum passive, non autem active: hoc est, dum praevenit eam Dei gratia, habere quidem ipsam potentiam ad bonum, sed eam materiae duntaxat, & passivam, quam remotam vocant; in actum autem redigi illam potentiam, & ex remota propinquam fieri, beneficio ipsius gratiae divinae nos praevenientis, hoc est, beneficio Spiritus Dei qui cum verbo Evangelij praedicato concurrit, & per illud ipsum verbum refingit atque renovat corda nostra, infpirando quasi in ea vitam illam Dei, a qua prius prorsus fuerunt abalienata, ut habetur Eph. 4. & creando in ijs quasi denuo amissam illam Dei imaginem, quę in sanctitate & justitia cernitur. Quod vero ad justificationem attinet, cum duplicem statuant justitiam; primam, quam vocant habitualem, & secundam, quam actualem nominant: ad primam justitiam præparari nos dicunt libertate arbitrij nostri, tanquam principali agente, & gratia cooperante. Secundam vero collocant in operibus à libertate arbitrij nostri, & à prima justitia, quâ infusam gratiam appellant, profectis. Iustitiæ hujus secundæ quæ est in operibus liberi arbitrij, & infusæ, quam vocant, gratiæ, hujus (inquam) justitiæ merito adscribunt vitam æternam.
units.tr: We affirm, therefore, that in receiving the first grace our will has itself only passively, not actively: that is, while the grace of God goes before it, it has indeed the power itself for the good, but only as a power of matter and passive, which they call remote; and that this power is brought into act, and from remote becomes proximate, by the benefit of the grace of God itself going before us, that is, by the benefit of the Spirit of God, who concurs with the Word of the Gospel preached and through that very Word refashions and renews our hearts, breathing into them, as it were, that life of God from which they were before utterly alienated (as is stated in Eph. 4), and creating in them, as it were anew, that lost image of God, which is seen in holiness and righteousness. But as regards justification, since they establish a twofold righteousness, the first which they call habitual, and the second which they name actual, they say that we are prepared for the first righteousness by the freedom of our choice, as the principal agent, and grace cooperating. The second they place in works that proceed from the freedom of our choice and from the first righteousness, which they call infused grace. To this second righteousness, which is in works of free choice, and to the infused grace, as they call it, I say, to the merit of this righteousness they ascribe eternal life.

units.la: Ex quibus vides eos nullum ex his beneficium, non vocationem, non justificationem, non glorificationem, nullum denique ex his omnibus beneficijs spiritualibus, quæ in tempore in nos conferuntur, soli Dei gratiæ tribuere: verùm ea inter gratiam Dei, & libertatem nostram, operaque nostra meritoria partiri. Imò verò, si comparatio Dei & nostri fiat, in his beneficijs conferendis, plus eos videbis tribuere nobis, libertati nostræ, operibus nostris, quàm gratiæ divinæ. Sed de his jam antea diximus nonnihil, in capite de Vocatione, in capite de resipiscentia, & in capite de libero arbitrio: ideoque lectorem ad
units.tr: From these things you see that they assign to the grace of God none of these benefits, neither calling, nor justification, nor glorification, nor finally any of all these spiritual benefits which are conferred upon us in time; but they divide them between the grace of God and our freedom and our meritorious works. Indeed, if a comparison of God and ourselves is made in conferring these benefits, you will see them attribute more to us, to our freedom and our works, than to divine grace. But we have already said something of these things before, in the chapter on Calling, in the chapter on Repentance, and in the chapter on free choice; and therefore we refer the reader to those places. And now we bring this doctrine to an end.

units.la: [Some words in the body of the text are obscured by an ink blot near "inter gratiam".] ad ea loca remittimus: Atque nunc huic doctrinæ finem imponimus.
units.tr: to that place we refer the reader. And now we bring this doctrine to an end.

units.la: Hactenus itaque dictum sit de loco Vocationis efficacis, qui, quòd subalternos plures sub se comprehendat, inter generalissimos doctrinæ Theologicæ locos, merito potest numerari.
units.tr: So much, then, has been said concerning the locus of effectual calling, which, since it comprehends many subordinate heads under it, may rightly be counted among the most general loci of theological doctrine.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.

units.la: DE MODIS QVIBVSDE
units.tr: Concerning the Modes by Which

units.la: VS AB INITIO FOEDVS suum utrumque, humano generi revelavit.
units.tr: God from the beginning revealed both of his covenants to the human race.

units.la: Q. Vot sunt omnino modi quibus Deus iam inde á principio universam voluntatem suam, hoc est, utriusq; fœderis, & operum, & gratiæ, doctrinam, humano generi revelavit?
units.tr: Q. What are all the modes by which God, from the beginning, revealed to the human race his entire will, that is, the teaching of both covenants, of works and of grace?

units.la: R. Duo sunt.
units.tr: R. There are two.

units.la: Q. Quinam illi?
units.tr: Q. What are they?

units.la: R. Primus est viva vox; secundus scriptio
units.tr: A. The first is the living voice; the second is writing.

units.la: Q. Quid appellas vivam vocem?
units.tr: Q. What do you call the living voice?

units.la: R. Primum revelationis modum, quo Deus, partim per suiipsius, partim per aliorum os, universam utriusque fœderis doctrinam Ecclesiæ suæ subindè revelavit.
units.tr: R. The first mode of revelation, by which God, partly through his own mouth and partly through the mouths of others, repeatedly revealed to his Church the whole teaching of both covenants.

units.la: Q. Quorum fuit viva vox iam inde à principio?
units.tr: Q. Whose living voice has there been from the beginning?

units.la: R. Primū fuit viva vox Dei ipsius, qui modò per filium suum sub specie humanæ formæ, patribus apparente, modò dò per Spiritum suum intus in animo loquutus est: Deinde fuit viva vox Angelorum: Tertiò fuit viva vox hominū, primùm Patrum, tum Mosis & Prophetarū, postea Iohannis Baptiftę ad Christum usque: hinc fuit viva vox ipsius Christi jâ in carne manifestati: postremò viva vox fuit Apostolorum Christi Q. An modus hic revelationis qui fuit per vivam ipsorum omnium, quos dixisti, vocem, plane θεοπνευστος & ab erroribus prorsus libera fuit?
units.tr: A. First there was the living voice of God himself, who spoke sometimes through his Son under the appearance of a human form to the fathers, and sometimes inwardly to the mind through his Spirit. Next there was the living voice of the angels. Third there was the living voice of men: first of the Fathers, then of Moses and the prophets, afterwards of John the Baptist up to Christ. From there came the living voice of Christ himself, now manifested in the flesh; lastly, the living voice of the apostles of Christ. Q. Was this mode of revelation, which was through the living voice of all those you have named, plainly divinely inspired [θεόπνευστος] and wholly free from errors?

units.la: R. De viva voce Dei ipsius, Christi, & Angelorum nulla quæstio est. Quod ad homines attinet, quorum viva voce usus est Deus inde à mundo condito in revelanda voluntate sua Ecclesiæ suæ, illi quidem etsi homines peccatores erant omnes, & ex parte tantùm regeniti, tamen in tradenda veritatis & fœderis utriusq; doctrina, sic extra ordinem gubernati sunt & afflati Spiritu Dei sancto, ut errare nequaquam potuerint.
units.tr: A. There is no question about the living voice of God himself, of Christ, and of the angels. As for the men through whose living voice God has made known his will to his Church from the creation of the world onward, although all of them were sinful men and only partly regenerate, nevertheless, in delivering the doctrine of truth and of both covenants, they were so governed beyond the ordinary course and inspired by the Holy Spirit of God that they could in no way err.

units.la: Q. Vis ergo omnes quotquot fuerunt inde à mundo condito, per quorum os loquutus est Deus Ecclesiæ suæ, extraordinarios exstitisse homines, donis Spiritus sancti extraordinâdinariis instructos, & miraculis confirmatos?
units.tr: Q. Do you therefore maintain that all who have existed from the creation of the world, through whose mouth God has spoken to his Church, were extraordinary men, furnished with extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit and confirmed by miracles?

units.la: R. Volo: Non enim libidine hominis allata est olim prophetia, sed acti à Spiritu sancto loquuti sunt sancti Dei homines. 2.Pet.21. -
units.tr: R. I do. For prophecy was never brought forth by the will of man, but holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit. 2 Pet. 21.

units.la: Q. Quo tempore cæpit viva vox in Ecclesia?
units.tr: Q. At what time did the living voice begin in the Church?

units.la: R. Cœpit in prima hominis creatione
units.tr: A. It began at the very creation of man.

units.la: Q. Quamdiu duravit in Ecclesia viva vox Dei, & hominum, qui in veritatis doctrina tradenda errare non potuerunt?
units.tr: Q. How long did the living voice of God and of men, who could not err in teaching the doctrine of truth, last in the Church?

units.la: R. Duravit inde à mundo condito ad Apostolorum usque decessum, quo toto tempore nulla fere ætas fuit, in qua nō extra ordinem excitatus est, saltē unus aliquis sanctus Dei homo, qui in tradenda veritatis doctrina errare non potuit.
units.tr: A. It lasted from the creation of the world until the death of the apostles. Throughout that whole time there was hardly any age in which at least one holy man of God was not raised up beyond the ordinary course, who could not err in teaching the doctrine of truth.

units.la: Q. Cur addis fere? Anne fuit aliqua intermissio?
units.tr: Q. Why do you add "hardly"? Was there some interruption?

units.la: R. Fuit quidem: Sed ego intermissiones aliquot insigniores, quæ ex Scriptura sacra colligi possunt duntaxat tibi recensebo. Primùm temporibus Patrum observatur fuisse intermissio ætate Terachi qui pater fuit Abrahami: Nam is, etsi quædam fundamenta veritatis retinuit à Patribus suis sibi tradita, tamē apostasiam fecit, & evasit Idololatra, ut constat ex historia. Deinde intermissio fuit quo tempore populus in Ægypto ageret: nam à morte filiorũ Iacobi usq; ad exitũ ex Ægypto testatur Ezechiel cap. 20. populum vniversum à Deo ad Idola Ægyptiorum defecisse: denique intermissio fuit à Malachia Prophetarũ ultimo, ad Iohannem Baptistam, quo toto temporis spatio nullus Propheta est excitatus: Continuatum tamen est verbum Dei in populo Iudaico per Pōtifices & ministerium ordinarium; verũ non sine corruptelis, adeo ut in adventu Christi magna ex parte jam corrupta fuerit veritatis doctrina.
units.tr: A. There was indeed. But I will recount for you only the more notable interruptions, which can be gathered from Holy Scripture. First, among the fathers, an interruption is observed in the time of Terah, the father of Abraham. For although he retained some foundations of truth handed down to him by his fathers, he nevertheless fell away and became an idolater, as is clear from history. Next there was an interruption during the time the people lived in Egypt: for Ezekiel, chapter 20, testifies that from the death of the sons of Jacob until the exodus from Egypt the whole people fell from God to the idols of the Egyptians. Finally there was an interruption from Malachi, the last of the prophets, to John the Baptist, during which whole span of time no prophet was raised up. Nevertheless the word of God was continued among the Jewish people through the priests and the ordinary ministry, but not without corruptions, so that by the coming of Christ the doctrine of truth was for the most part already corrupted.

units.la: Q. Annon oportet in Ecclesia Dei durare vivam vocem errori non obnoxiam ad reditum usque Christi: dixisti enim durasse vivam vocem in Ecclesia ad Apostolorum duntaxat tempora?
units.tr: Q. Ought not a living voice, not liable to error, to endure in the Church of God until the return of Christ? For you said that the living voice lasted in the Church only as far as the time of the apostles.

units.la: R. Durat quidem, fateor, in Ecclesia christiviva vox; sed nō durat viva vox, vel Dei, vel hominum extraordinariorum, quales erant Patres, Prophetæ, & Apostoli: verùm hominum duntaxat ordinariorum, Pastorum, & doctorum, qui & errare possunt, & errant reipsa quandocunque à verbo scripto Prophetico & Apostolico vel tantillū recedūt.
units.tr: A. I grant that the living voice of the Christian Church does endure; but it is not the living voice of God or of extraordinary men, such as the fathers, prophets and apostles were, that endures. It is only the voice of ordinary men, of ministers and teachers, who both can err and actually err whenever they depart even slightly from the written prophetic and apostolic Word.

units.la: Q. Atqui dedit Deus Ecclesiæ suæ quæ nunc est sub Christo, Spiritus sui sancti maiorem mensuram, quàm unquam dedit veteri Ecclesiæ: Ergo si in veteri Ecclesia vt vox fuit quæ errare non potuit, quantò magis in Christi Ecclesia viva vox erit, quæ errare non poterit.
units.tr: Q. Yet God has given to his Church, which now exists under Christ, a greater measure of his Holy Spirit than he ever gave to the ancient Church. Therefore, if in the ancient Church there was a voice which could not err, how much more will there be in the Church of Christ a living voice which will not be able to err?

units.la: R. Verum quidem est, cum plena hac revelatione, quæ scriptis Apostolicis continetur, datum esse Spiritum pleniorem Ecclesiæ Christi quæ nunc est, quàm qui datus est veteri populo: Sed non ex eo sequitur ita nunc gubernari illo Spiritu vel Ecclesiam, vel pastores, & doctores in Ecclesia, ut in veritate tradenda nō possint omnino errare: hoc enim donum est Spiritus sancti extraordinarium & temporarium. Spiritus autem donum quod Ecclesiæ Christi datū est post Apostolorum tempora, ordinariū est & perpetuum, utpote sanctificationis, illuminationis, & regenerationis donum.
units.tr: A. It is indeed true that, with the full revelation contained in the apostolic writings, a fuller Spirit has been given to the present Church of Christ than was given to the ancient people. But it does not follow from this that the Church, or the ministers and teachers in the Church, are now so governed by that Spirit that they cannot altogether err in delivering the truth. For this is an extraordinary and temporary gift of the Holy Spirit. The gift of the Spirit, however, which has been given to the Church of Christ after the times of the apostles, is ordinary and perpetual, being the gift of sanctification, illumination and regeneration.

units.la: Q. Deteriori igitur loco videtur esse Ecclesia ecclesia quæ nunc est, quàm fuit vetus illa Ecclesia quæ habuit vivam vocem Dei, & hominum, quæ errare non potuit?
units.tr: Q. Is the Church which now exists, therefore, seen to be in a worse condition than that ancient Church which had the living voice of God and of men, which could not err?

units.la: R. Non sequitur: nam Scriptura hæc Prophetica & Apostolica, quam nunc habet Ecclesia, & non errat in docendo, & plenissimam clarissimamque continet revelationem.
units.tr: A. It does not follow. For this prophetic and apostolic Scripture, which the Church now has, neither errs in teaching and contains the fullest and clearest revelation.

units.la: Q. Ut concedam tibi conditionem Ecclesiæ nostræ meliorem esse, quàm fuit veteris illius quæ ante Mosis tempora exstitit, quaeque solam habuit vivæ vocis traditionem, eamque imperfectam admodum & obscuram: non tamen video qui non fuerit meliori conditione Ecclesia illa quæ post Mosen duravit ad Christi usque adventum, ut quæ non modo traditionem & vivam vocem, sed etiam Scripturam habuerit Propheticam, tanquam lucernam in obscuro loco splendentem?
units.tr: Q. Grant that I concede to you that the condition of our Church is better than that of the ancient Church which existed before the time of Moses, and which had only the tradition of the living voice, and that a very imperfect and obscure one. Yet I do not see how that Church which lasted from Moses until the coming of Christ was not in a better condition, since it had not only tradition and the living voice but also prophetic Scripture, shining like a lamp in a dark place?

units.la: R. Habuit quidem illa Ecclesia utrumque, & traditionem vivæ vocis, & scriptionem, sed neutrum perfectum ac plenum. Scriptura autem ista, quam solam habet nostra Ecclesia, plenissimam continet revelationem: Præstantiorem autem oportet esse, vel unam aliquam revelationis formam quæ perfectam & plenam conticōtinet revelationem;quàm duas,quarum neutra cōtinet plenam perfectamque revelationem.
units.tr: A. That Church did indeed have both, the tradition of the living voice and writing, but neither of them perfect and complete. The Scripture, however, which our Church alone has, contains the fullest revelation. Now, one form of revelation which contains a perfect and complete revelation must be superior to two, neither of which contains a full and perfect revelation.

units.la: Q.[?] At nemo est qui non dicat melius actum iri cum Ecclesia nostra, quæ hodierno die est, si haberet vivam aliquam vocem, quæ in docendo & respondendo ad omnes controversias errare non posset?
units.tr: Q. But is there anyone who does not say that it would go better with our Church today if it had some living voice which could not err in teaching and in answering all controversies?

units.la: R. Habent Mosem, Prophetas, & Apostolos, hoc est, Mosis, Prophetarum, & Apostolorum scripta, & ea quidem non sufficientia tantùm, sed perfectissima: ex quibus quidem si veritatem, & omnium controversiarum decisionem nō didicerint, profectò ne ex viva quidem alicujus extraordinarij hominis voce informationem aliquam accipere potuerunt, ut de hoc nihil dicam quod jam priùs respondi, vivam vocem tantisper locum habuisse in Ecclesia quantisper aliquid desiderabatur ad plenam mysterij Christi manifestationē. Quod si igitur nunc locus esset vivæ voci, vel Dei vel hominis extraordinarii in Ecclesia Christi; profectò id palam argueret, nondum perfectam esse atque impletam veritatis ac mysterij Christi revelationem.
units.tr: A. They have Moses, the prophets and the apostles; that is, the writings of Moses, the prophets and the apostles, and these are not merely sufficient but most perfect. If from these they have not learned the truth and the decision of all controversies, then certainly they could not have received any information even from the living voice of some extraordinary man. To say nothing more on this, which I have already answered: the living voice had a place in the Church only so long as something was still lacking for the full manifestation of the mystery of Christ. But if there were now room for the living voice, either of God or of an extraordinary man, in the Church of Christ, that would certainly prove that the revelation of the truth and of the mystery of Christ is not yet perfect and complete.

units.la: Ergo concludis post Apostolos nullam vivam audiri in Ecclesia vocem, quæ non errèt?
units.tr: Q. So you conclude that after the apostles no living voice that could err is heard in the Church?

units.la: R. Concludo.
units.tr: A. I conclude.

units.la: Cur toto illo tempore quod fuit ab Adamo ad Apostolos duravit in Ecclesia viva vox errori non obnoxia?
units.tr: Why, throughout the whole period from Adam to the Apostles, did a living voice not liable to error endure in the Church?

units.la: R. Ut de voluntate Dei nihil dicam quæ vel sola debemus esse contenti, durationem hanc postulavit: primùm Ecclesiæ conditio, deinde revelationis mensura.
units.tr: A. Setting aside God's will, which alone we ought to be content with, this duration was required first by the condition of the Church and then by the measure of revelation.

units.la: Cur Ecclesiæ conditio?
units.tr: Why the condition of the Church?

units.la: R. Quia Ecclesia visibilis toto illo tempore, quod fuit ab Adamo ad Apostolos, & loco angustior fuit, utpote vel una familia, vel una gente conclusa, & ætate minor ac immaturior fuit: nam Ecclesia ante Christum, vel puer fuit, ut sic dicam, vel adolescens.
units.tr: A. Because the visible Church during that whole period from Adam to the Apostles was narrower in place, confined to a single family or a single nation, and was smaller and less mature in age. The Church before Christ was, so to speak, either a boy or a youth.

units.la: Quid tum?
units.tr: So what?

units.la: R. Ad Ecclesiam loco angustiorem, & sanctos numero pauciores facilius extendit sese viva vox: & Ecclesia adhuc rudior per ætate, & immaturior, opus habebat viva docentis voce, nõ secus atq; pueri opus habent viva voce
units.tr: A. A living voice extends itself more easily to a Church that is narrower in place and has fewer saints. The Church, still cruder and immature in age, needed the living voice of a teacher, just as children need a teacher who stammers along with them.

units.la: Magistri qui cum ipsis quasi balbutiat. Postquàm autem in adventu Christi jam latis est crudita per vivam Christi & Apostolorum voce, Ecclesia, & jam virilem attigit ætatem; non amplius audita est viva aliqua vox, vel Dei, vel hominum extraordinariorum.
units.tr: But after Christ came, the Church was already instructed through the living voice of Christ and the Apostles and had reached manhood. From then on no living voice, of God or of extraordinary men, was heard any more.

units.la: Q. Cur id postulavit revelationis mensura?
units.tr: Q. Why did the measure of revelation require this?

units.la: R. Quia toto illo tempore, quod fuit ab Adamo ad Apostolos, restabat adhuc aliquid clarius & manifestius revelandum, & singulis ætatibus facta est continuo manifestior ejusdem, quod ad substantiam attinebat, doctrinæ revelatio: Quamdiu autem fuit aliquid clarius revelandum, tamdiu oportuit durare vivam vocem: Novam enim revelationem quamcunque oportuit primum fieri per vivam vocem.
units.tr: A. Because throughout that whole period from Adam to the Apostles something clearer and more manifest still remained to be revealed, and with each age the revelation of the doctrine, as far as its substance went, became continually more manifest. As long as something clearer remained to be revealed, the living voice had to endure, for any new revelation had to come first through the living voice.

units.la: Q. Postquam facta est revelatio ultima & plenissima per vivam Christi & Apostolorum vocem, an amplius audita est viva vox, vel Dei vel hominis cuiusquam extraordinarij?
units.tr: Q. After the final and fullest revelation was made through the living voice of Christ and the Apostles, was a living voice of God or of any extraordinary man heard any more?

units.la: R. Nulla.
units.tr: A. None.

units.la: Q. Nunquid ex his quæ dixisti de causis duratio-
units.tr: Q. Do you infer from the reasons you have given for the duration of

units.la: rationis viva vocis in Ecclesia, colligis ipsius usum, qui fuerit aliquando in Ecclesia?
units.tr: the living voice in the Church what its use was at any time in the Church?

units.la: R. Colligo: usus enim ejus fuit primum respectu ipsius Ecclesiae, ut eam, & loco angustiorem, & cognitione rudiorem, doceret: deinde respectu revelationis ut eam subinde clariorem traderet.
units.tr: A. I do infer it. Its use was first, with respect to the Church itself, to teach it, both as narrower in place and cruder in knowledge; then, with respect to revelation, to hand down from time to time something clearer.

units.la: Q. Ex hoc quem dicis viva vocis usu videtur sequi revelationis eum modum, qui suit per vivam vocem, simpliciorem, magisque familiarem, adeoque imperfectiorem fuisse, utpote & personis & rebus imperfectioribus convenientem?
units.tr: Q. From this use of the living voice that you mention, does it seem to follow that this mode of revelation which was through the living voice was simpler and more familiar, and so more imperfect, as suited to persons and matters that were more imperfect?

units.la: R. Est ita ut dicis.
units.tr: A. It is as you say.

units.la: Q. De viva voce audivi hactenus: nunc velim de eius subiecto aliquid ex te discere: Quid igitur traditum fuisse dicis, viva voce toto illo temporis spatio?
units.tr: Q. I have heard so far about the living voice. Now I should like to learn from you something about its subject. What, then, do you say was handed down by the living voice during that whole span of time?

units.la: R. Omnibus & singulis aetatibus, & una eademque, & tota veritatis doctrina per vivam vocem tradita fuit.
units.tr: A. The whole doctrine of truth, one and the same, was handed down by the living voice in each and every age.

units.la: Q. Cur igitur dixisti aetate demum Apostolorum impletam perfectamque mysterii revelationem?
units.tr: Q. Why then did you say that the revelation of the mystery was completed and perfected only in the age of the Apostles?

units.la: R. Plenitudinem illam ac perfectionem intellexi, non de substantia ipsius doctridoctrinæ,sed de qualitate, hoc est, unius ejusdemq; Doctrinæ claritate. Mysterium enim Christi fuit in Ecclesia, & certo quodam modo manifestatum fuit inde ab Adamo ad Christum & Apostolos: sed si fiat temporum comparatio, clausum fuit & absconditum omnibus sæculis adventum Christi antecedentibus.
units.tr: A. I understood that fullness and perfection not of the substance of the doctrine itself but of its quality, that is, of the clarity of one and the same doctrine. The mystery of Christ was in the Church and was in a certain manner made manifest from Adam to Christ and the Apostles. But if a comparison of times is made, it was closed and hidden in all the ages that preceded the coming of Christ.

units.la: Q. An per vivam vocem satis confervata fuit Doctrinæ cælestis puritas?
units.tr: Q. Was the purity of the heavenly doctrine sufficiently preserved through the living voice?

units.la: R. Historia satis docet Doctrinam viva voce traditam, subinde corruptam fuisse & adulteratam.
units.tr: A. History teaches well enough that the doctrine handed down by the living voice was from time to time corrupted and adulterated.

units.la: Q. Quomodo tum instaurata est?
units.tr: Q. How was it then restored?

units.la: R. Visum est Deo per novas deinde revelationes puritatem verbi sui collapsi restituere, confervare, & pleniorem ejus declarationem addere.
units.tr: A. It pleased God to restore and preserve the purity of his fallen Word by further new revelations, and to add a fuller declaration of it.

units.la: Q. An sic satis esset conservata doctrinæ puritas?
units.tr: Q. Was the purity of the doctrine sufficiently preserved in this way?

units.la: R. Ne sic quidem: ideoque visum est Deo tandem ad vivam vocem addere scriptionem.
units.tr: A. Not even so. So it pleased God at last to add writing to the living voice.

units.la: Q. An non sunt alia præterea addita scriptionis causæ?
units.tr: Q. Were no other causes for adding writing given besides these?

units.la: R. Sunt: scriptionem enim vivæ voci adjungendam postulavit primum Ecclesiæ conditio, deinde revelationis mensura.
units.tr: A. There were. The condition of the Church first required writing to be joined to the living voice, and then the measure of revelation.

units.la: Q. Cur Ecclesiæ conditio?
units.tr: Q. Why the condition of the Church?

units.la: R. Quia ætate demum Mosis, Ecclesia cœpit esse & loco amplior, vtpote diffusa in totam gentem, & ætate major atque provectior: Nam à Mose ad Christum vsq;, fuit quasi Ecclesiæ adolescentia.
units.tr: A. Because only in the age of Moses did the Church begin to be larger in place, spread through a whole nation, and greater and more advanced in age. From Moses until Christ it was, as it were, the adolescence of the Church.

units.la: Q. Quid tum?
units.tr: Q. So what?

units.la: R. Vtrique & loci amplitudini, & ætati provectiori ac maturiori convenit scriptio: Nā & vniversa aliqua gens facilius scripto docetur, quàm viva voce, & ætas quæ paulò provectior est, capax est doctrinæ quæ scriptione, hoc est, revelationis modo qui non ita familiaris est & simplex, traditur: atque ex scripto mentem alicujus facilè deprehendit.
units.tr: A. Writing suits both the wider extent of place and the more advanced and mature age. A whole nation is taught more easily by writing than by the living voice, and an age somewhat more advanced is capable of doctrine handed down in writing, that is, in a mode of revelation that is not so familiar and simple. Such an age also readily grasps a person's mind from what is written.

units.la: Cur scriptionem adjungendam postulavit revelationis mensura?
units.tr: Q. Why did the measure of revelation require writing to be added?

units.la: R. Quia, cum ante Mosem revelatio fuisset exigua & obscura admodum, non dum visum est Deo eam statim scripto committere, quo quidem ipsa posteritati conservaretur. Cum verò ætate Mosis coepisset multo clarior esse revelatio, quàm antea; tum visum est Deo scripto eam committere, quò posteritati ipsa cōservaretur: Quod enim perfectius est & plenius, id solemus nos scripto tradere, ad hoc ut & nobis ipsis & posteris conservetur: Quod vero imperfectius est, non putamus illud dignum quod scripto commendetur & conservetur posteritati.
units.tr: A. Because before Moses revelation had been scanty and very obscure, so it did not yet please God to commit it at once to writing, by which it might be preserved for posterity. But when in the age of Moses revelation had become much clearer than before, then it pleased God to commit it to writing so that it might be preserved for posterity. We are accustomed to commit to writing what is more perfect and fuller, so that it may be preserved both for ourselves and for posterity. What is more imperfect we do not think worthy to be entrusted to writing and preserved for posterity.

units.la: Q. Priusquam longius abeas, velim mihi explices Ecclesiæ illas, quarum non semel meministi, ætates?
units.tr: Q. Before you go further, I should like you to explain those ages of the Church which you have mentioned more than once.

units.la: R. Explicabo.
units.tr: A. I will explain.

units.la: Q. Quotuplicem igitur statuis Ecclesiæ Dei ætatem?
units.tr: Q. How many ages, then, do you reckon for the Church of God?

units.la: R. Triplicem. Prima fuit ab Adamo ad Mosem usque, quæ infantia simul & pueritia Ecclesiæ fuit. Secunda a Mose ad Christum, quæ adolescentia Ecclesiæ fuit. Tertia a Christo & Apostolis ad finem usque, quæ virilis Ecclesiæ ætas dici potest, si modo comparetur cum præcedentibus illis ætatibus: alias enim non nisi cum in cœlis cum capite nostro Christo colligendi sumus viri evademus.
units.tr: A. Three. The first was from Adam to Moses, which was at once the infancy and childhood of the Church. The second was from Moses to Christ, which was the adolescence of the Church. The third, from Christ and the Apostles to the end, may be called the manhood of the Church, if it is compared with the preceding ages. Otherwise we shall not become fully men until we are gathered in heaven with our head, Christ.

units.la: Q. Vis ne igitur Deum trium istarum ætatum in agendo cum Ecclesia sua perpetuò rationem habuisse?
units.tr: Q. Do you mean, then, that God has always taken account of these three ages in dealing with his Church?

units.la: R. Volo. Nam ut sic dicam, proportionaliter ad Ecclesiæ tres istas ætates attemperavit hæc tria, nempè primò revelationis mensuram. Secundò Spiritum suum sanctum. Tertiò revelationis modum.
units.tr: A. I do. For, so to speak, he has proportioned these three things to the three ages of the Church: first, the measure of revelation; second, his Holy Spirit; third, the mode of revelation.

units.la: Q. Explica quæso particulatim quod dixisti?
units.tr: Q. Please explain particularly what you have said.

units.la: R. Ecclesiæ infantiæ & pueritiæ accommodavit minimam revelationis mensurâ: scilicet 1. Prima dūtaxat doctrinæ elementa. 2. Spiritus sancti portionem minimam, eam nempè, quæ revelationi proportionalis erat. 3. vnicum tantùm revelationis modum qui fuit per vivam vocem, vt qui sit infantibus ac rudioribus docendis erudiendisque aptior.
units.tr: A. To the infancy and childhood of the Church he adapted the smallest measure of revelation: (1) only the first elements of doctrine; (2) the smallest portion of the Holy Spirit, namely that which was proportioned to the revelation; (3) only one mode of revelation, the living voice, as being more suitable for teaching and training infants and the cruder.

units.la: Q. Intelligo quæ dixisti de prima Ecclefiæ ætate: Nunc velim dicas de media, quam adolescentiam dixisti, & hæc quæ tradidisti tria ei pariter accommodes?
units.tr: Q. I understand what you have said about the first age of the Church. Now I should like you to speak of the middle age, which you called adolescence, and to fit these three things to it in the same way.

units.la: R. Ecclesiæ ætati mediæ accommodavit primùm majorem revelationis menmensurâ. Secundò maiorem Spiritus fanêti, vt sic dicam, portionem. Tertiò denique duplicé reuelationis modum, viuam vocem & Scriptionem: Viuam vocem, inquâ, quia adhuc rudior fuit: Scriptionem verò quia ætate fuit proueêtior, atque ideò capax fuit aliquo modo doêtrinæ scriptæ. Temperavit enim Deus inter fe duos revelationis modos, & ex vtroque medium quoddam revelationis genus constituit, pro ætatis ratione, quæ media fuit & quasi temperata.
units.tr: A. To the middle age of the Church he adapted, first, a larger measure of revelation; second, a larger portion, so to speak, of the Holy Spirit; third, a twofold mode of revelation, the living voice and writing. The living voice, I say, because it was still cruder; writing, because it was more advanced in age and so was in some measure capable of written doctrine. For God tempered the two modes of revelation with each other, and from both constituted a certain middle kind of revelation, suited to the nature of that age, which was middle and, as it were, tempered.

units.la: Q. Dixisti de prima & secunda Eccle- sia ætate: Nunc de tertia dicas velim?
units.tr: Q. You have spoken of the first and second ages of the Church. Now I would like you to speak of the third.

units.la: R. Ad tertiam denique Ecclesiæ ætatem, quâ virilem appellavi, accommodavit primùm plenâ revelationis mensuram. Secundò plenum Spiritus sanêti donum. Tertiò denique vtrumque illum revelationis modum, & eum quidem plenam jam perfestamque revelationem comprehendentê. Viva quidem voce eam docuit certo aliquo tempore: Hinc adjecit scriptionem Apostolicam: Postquàm autem viva voce primùm mysterium esset plenè revelatum, deinde scriptioni plena illa revelatio mandata esset, jam finis impositus est vivæ voci. Manet autem quod scriptum est, primùm per Prophetas, deinde per Apostolos solum, absque viva voce quæ errare non potest.
units.tr: R. To the third age of the Church, which I have called manly, God first gave the full measure of revelation; secondly, the full gift of the Holy Spirit; and thirdly, both of those modes of revelation, the one which embraces revelation already complete and perfect. He taught it by living voice for a certain time; then he added Apostolic writing. Yet once the mystery had first been fully revealed by living voice, and that full revelation had afterwards been committed to writing, the living voice was brought to an end. What remains is what has been written: first through the Prophets, then through the Apostles alone, without a living voice, which cannot err.

units.la: Q. Unde sumus initium tertiæ ætatis Ecclesiæ?
units.tr: Q. From what point do we date the beginning of the third age of the Church?

units.la: R. Non tam ab adventu Christi & missione Apostolorum ad omnes gentes, quàm ab eo tempore quo desierunt Apostoli loqui viva voce, tam Iudæis, quàm Gentibus: Tum enim Ecclesia Catholica virilem attigit & incepit ætatem, ac tum cœpit Ecclesia mentem Dei ex solo scripto, utpote accuratiori & perfectiori quodam revelationis modo, duntaxat intelligere ac discere. Tempus igitur quod fuit ab adventu Christi ad discessum usq; Apostolorum, transitus quasi erat à media ad tertiam & virilem Ecclesiæ ætatem.
units.tr: R. Not so much from the coming of Christ and the sending of the Apostles to all nations, as from the time when the Apostles ceased to speak by living voice, both to Jews and to Gentiles. For then the Catholic Church reached and began its manly age, and then the Church began to understand and learn the mind of God from Scripture alone, as from a more exact and perfect mode of revelation. The time, therefore, which lay between the coming of Christ and the departure of the Apostles was, as it were, a transition from the middle to the third and manly age of the Church.

units.la: Q. Habeo de causis addita ad vivam vocem scriptionis, deque singulis Ecclesiæ ætatibus: Nunc de scriptione velim mihi ordine tradas aliquid?
units.tr: Q. You have given me the reasons for adding writing to living voice, and about the individual ages of the Church. Now I would like you to tell me something, in order, about writing?

units.la: R. Faciam.
units.tr: R. I will.

units.la: MODI REVEL. FOED.
units.tr: THE MODES OF REVELATION AND COVENANT

units.la: Q. Quid igitur vocas scriptionem?
units.tr: Q. What, then, do you mean by writing?

units.la: R. Scriptionem voco, secundum revelationis modum quo Deus, vel per suam ipsius, vel per aliorum hominum, scilicet, extraordinariorum manus ea revelavit, quae jam priùs viva voce, hoc est, primo illo revelationis modo sunt tradita.
units.tr: A. By writing I mean the mode of revelation by which God, either by his own hand or by the hand of other men, that is, extraordinary persons, has set down those things that were earlier delivered by word of mouth, that is, by the first mode of revelation.

units.la: Q. Quinam igitur fuerunt, qui iam inde à principio scripserunt?
units.tr: Q. Who, then, were those who began to write from the very beginning?

units.la: R. Primum ipse Deus, deinde homines, Moses, Prophetæ, & Apostoli.
units.tr: A. First God himself, and then men: Moses, the Prophets, and the Apostles.

units.la: Q. An modus hic revelationis qui fuit per scriptionem erori non est obnoxius, perinde ut modus ille qui fuit per viuam vocem?
units.tr: Q. Is this mode of revelation, which was by writing, not liable to error, just as that mode which was by the living voice was not?

units.la: R. Ita est, nam de Dei ipsius scriptione nulla quæstio est: Homines vero sic extra ordinem afflati sunt & gubernati Spiritu sancto, ut in scribendo errare nequaquam potuerint.
units.tr: A. It is so. For there is no question about the writing of God himself. But men were so inspired outside the ordinary course and so governed by the Holy Spirit that they could in no way err in writing.

units.la: Q. Quando demùm coeptum est scribi?
units.tr: Q. When, at last, did writing begin?

units.la: R. Ætate Moses.
units.tr: A. In the age of Moses.

units.la: Q. Quamdiu duravit in Ecclesia scriptio?
units.tr: Q. How long did writing last in the Church?

units.la: R. Duravit quidem scriptio, hoc estipse scribendi actus à Mose ad Apostolos usque: quo toto tempore nulla feré ætas fuit in qua non extra ordinem excitatus est, saltem unus aliquis, qui in tradenda per scriptum veritatis doctrina, errare non potuit.
units.tr: A. Indeed writing lasted, that is, the very act of writing, from Moses down to the Apostles. Throughout all that time there was scarcely any age in which at least one man was not raised up outside the ordinary course who could not err in delivering the doctrine of truth in writing.

units.la: Q. Aliter sentis de ipsa Scriptura atque descriptione sive scribendi actu?
units.tr: Q. Do you think otherwise about Scripture itself than about the act of writing?

units.la: R. Sentio: nam Scriptura ipsa, siue id quod jam scriptum est à Mose, Prophetis, & Apostolis, etiamnū durat in Ecclesia, & durabit ad secundum usqj Christi adventum.
units.tr: A. I do think otherwise. For Scripture itself, that is, what has already been written by Moses, the Prophets, and the Apostles, still endures in the Church and will endure until the second coming of Christ.

units.la: Q. An igitur non sine intermissione duravit scriptio in Ecclesia à Mose ad Apostolos?
units.tr: Q. Did writing, then, endure in the Church from Moses to the Apostles without any interruption?

units.la: R. Ita quidem est: nam constat toto illo tempore, quod fuit à Malachia ad Iohanne Baptistam nullum excitatum fuisse, vel Prophetam, vel scriptorem aliquem θεοπνευστον, nam Machabæorum scriptura θεοπνευστος non est, vt postea videbimus.
units.tr: A. It did. For it is agreed that throughout the whole period from Malachi to John the Baptist no one was raised up, either a Prophet or any writer who was theopneustos [θεόπνευστος, God-breathed]. For the writing of the Maccabees is not theopneustos, as we shall see later.

units.la: Q. Dixisti scriptionem durasse ad Apostolorum tantùm tempora, an non oportet eam durare in Ecclesia ad finem vsque.
units.tr: Q. You have said that writing lasted only to the time of the Apostles. Ought it not to endure in the Church to the end?

units.la: R. Vt post Apostolos nulla auditur cur viva vox in Ecclesia, quæ sic per Spiritum sanctum gubernatur ut omninò errare non possit: ita post Apostolos nihil scribitur in Ecclesia quod {θεοπνευστον} merito vocari potest.
units.tr: A. Just as after the Apostles no living voice in the Church is heard that is governed by the Holy Spirit in such a way that it cannot err at all, so after the Apostles nothing is written in the Church that can rightly be called theopneustos [θεόπνευστος].

units.la: Q. Quid igitur sentis de tot scriptis hominum piorum & doctorum, qui post Apostolorum illa tempora, in Ecclesia usum non mediocrem subinde in luce exiverunt?
units.tr: Q. What, then, do you think of the many writings of pious and learned men which, after the time of the Apostles, have from time to time come to light in the Church and been of no small use?

units.la: R. Idem plane sentio de scriptis Pastorum & Doctorum in Ecclesia, quod sentio de eorundem viva voce: nempe, utrumque erroribus obnoxium esse, & neutrum sic gubernari à Spiritu sancto, ut in tradenda veritate errare omninò non possit.
units.tr: A. I think exactly the same of the writings of ministers and teachers in the Church as I think of their living voice: namely, that both are liable to errors, and neither is so governed by the Holy Spirit that it cannot err at all in delivering the truth.

units.la: Q. Ergo videtur Ecclesiæ conditio quæ est post Apostolorum tempora, non ita bona esse: ut quæ neque viuam vocem, ut iam prius dixisti, neque scriptionem habeat, ut nunc dicis, hominum certè eorum qui in tradenda veritate errare non possunt?
units.tr: Q. So it seems that the condition of the Church after the time of the Apostles is not so good, since it has neither the living voice (as you said earlier) nor writing (as you now say) of men who certainly cannot err in delivering the truth?

units.la: R. Habet Scriptura Propheticam & Apostolicam, quæ, quoad substantiam revelationis, plena est: quoad verò qualitatem modi revelationis, {θεοπνευστος} est & errori non obnoxia: ex qua
units.tr: A. Scripture has the Prophetic and Apostolic writings, which, as regards the substance of revelation, are full; and as regards the quality of the mode of revelation, they are theopneustos [θεόπνευστος] and not liable to error. From this Scripture

units.la: Scriptura quicunque non discunt omnia quæ ad fidem & salutem sunt neceffaria, profecto illi ne ex ore quidem Dei ipsius, coram loquentis & vivam edentis vocem, doctrinam fidei & salutis essent excepturi.
units.tr: whoever do not learn all that is necessary for faith and salvation would certainly not have received the doctrine of faith and salvation even from the very mouth of God himself, speaking in person and uttering a living voice.

units.la: Q. Cur toto eo tempore, quod fuit à Mose ad Apostolos, duravit in Ecclesia scriptio?
units.tr: Q. Why did writing endure in the Church throughout the whole period from Moses to the Apostles?

units.la: R. Durationis eædem causæ sunt quæ scriptionis ad vivam vocem addite: Nam durationem illam postulavit, & Ecclesiæ conditio, & revelationis mensura.
units.tr: A. The reasons for its duration are the same as those for writing being added to the living voice. For both the condition of the Church and the measure of revelation demanded that duration.

units.la: Q. Cur Ecclesiæ conditio?
units.tr: Q. Why the condition of the Church?

units.la: R. Quia Ecclesia continuò âudior facta est, & numero, & cognitione.
units.tr: A. Because the Church became continually larger, both in number and in knowledge.

units.la: Q. Quid tum?
units.tr: Q. And what follows?

units.la: R. Major hominum numerus & cognitio maturior postulant scriptionem.
units.tr: A. A greater number of people and more mature knowledge call for writing.

units.la: Q. Cur revelationis mensura?
units.tr: Q. Why the measure of revelation?

units.la: R. Quia revelatio subinde clarior evasit ad Christi & Apostolorum usque tempora, quibus demum temporibus perfecta est & completa. Oportuit autem scripto mandari clariorem & pleniorem quamque revelationem ad hoc vt firmiter conservaretur, & posteris traderetur.
units.tr: A. Because revelation became ever clearer down to the times of Christ and the Apostles, and in those times it was at last made perfect and complete. Moreover, it was fitting that each clearer and fuller revelation be committed to writing, so that it might be firmly preserved and handed down to posterity.

units.la: Q. Ex his colliges scriptionis in Eccle-sia continuata vsum?
units.tr: Q. Do you gather from these points the use of writing as continued in the Church?

units.la: R. Colligam.
units.tr: A. I do.

units.la: Q. Quis igitur vsus fuit?
units.tr: Q. What, then, was its use?

units.la: R. Vt nihil de puritatis conservatione dicam, vsus fuit primùm respectu ipsiusEcclesiæ, vt eam jam ampliorem loco,& cognitione perfectiorem doceret, Deinde respectu revelationis ipsius vt eam plenioré & clariorem comprehenderet atque conservaret.
units.tr: A. Not to speak of preserving purity, its use was first, with respect to the Church itself, to teach it, now larger in place and more perfect in knowledge; and secondly, with respect to revelation itself, to embrace and preserve it more fully and clearly.

units.la: Q. Ex hoc, quem tradis, Scripturæ vsu videtur sequi revelationis hunc modum, qui est per scriptionem, perfectiorem esse aliquato & sublimiorem, vtpote & personis & rebus perfectioribus convenientem?
units.tr: Q. From this use of Scripture that you set out, it seems to follow that the mode of revelation which is by writing is somewhat more perfect and more excellent, as befitting more perfect persons and things?

units.la: R. Est quidem ita vt dicis.
units.tr: A. It is indeed so, as you say.

units.la: Q. De ipsa scriptione audivi: Nunc velim de subiecto scriptionis, et de re ipsa scripto tradita, aliquid mihi exponas?
units.tr: Q. I have heard about writing itself. Now I should like you to explain to me something about the subject of writing and about the very matter delivered in writing.

units.la: R. Idem scriptum est quod viva prius traditum fuit.
units.tr: A. What was delivered in writing is the same thing that was earlier delivered by word of mouth.

units.la: Q. Velim mihi ordine dicas de subiecto scriptionis, primùm Dei, deinde hominũ, Mosis, Prophetarum, & Apostolorum.
units.tr: Q. I should like you to tell me in order about the subject of writing: first God, then men, Moses, the Prophets, and the Apostles.

units.la: R. Di.
units.tr: A. I will.

units.la: MODI REVEL. FOED.
units.tr: The Modes of Revelation of the Covenant

units.la: R. Dicam.
units.tr: A. I will say.

units.la: Q. Quid igitur scripsit Deus?
units.tr: Q. What, then, did God write?

units.la: R. Summam doctrinæ fœderis operum & legis, quam ipsam primùm viva voce tradiderat Patribus, & Mosi.
units.tr: A. The sum of the doctrine of the covenant of works and of the law, which he had first delivered by word of mouth to the Fathers and to Moses.

units.la: Q. Quid scripsit Moses?
units.tr: Q. What did Moses write?

units.la: R. Totam doctrinam cœlestem, quâ partim à Patribus per traditionem acceperat, partim à Deo ipso loquente ipsi ore ad os (vt cum Scriptura loquar) audiverat: partim à Spiritu sancto per afflatum internum didicerat: partim denique quæcunque sibi & populo toto vitæ suæ tempore per annos 120. contigerant: hæc omnia in literas redegit, & populo exhibuit.
units.tr: A. The whole heavenly doctrine. Part of it he had received from the Fathers by tradition, part he had heard from God himself speaking mouth to mouth (to use the words of Scripture), part he had learned from the Holy Spirit through inward inspiration, and finally part was whatever had happened to him and to the whole people during his life of 120 years. He committed all of this to writing and gave it to the people.

units.la: Q. An igitur à Mose scriptum est quicquid doctrinæ veræ traditum fuerat iam inde à mundo condito?
units.tr: Q. Did Moses, then, write down everything of true doctrine that had been handed down from the creation of the world?

units.la: R. Nihil omissum est à Mose veræ doctrinæ, quod unquam traditum fuerat, vel de fide, vel de bonis moribus. Nam inde ab initio tradita fuit omnibus ætatibus una eademq; & tota, quoad substantiam, veritatis doctrina. Discrimen tantum fuit in revelationis mensura, hoc est, in accidente: Hæc autem doctrina eadē & tota,à Mose primùm viua voce tradita est apertiùs & clariùs, quàm vnquam antea, deinde scripto commissa est.
units.tr: A. Moses omitted nothing of true doctrine, whether of faith or of good morals, that had ever been handed down. From the beginning, one and the same doctrine of truth, complete in substance, was delivered to all ages. The only difference lay in the measure of revelation, that is, in the accident. This same and whole doctrine was first delivered by Moses by word of mouth, more openly and clearly than ever before, and afterwards committed to writing.

units.la: Q. Quid scripserunt Prophetæ post Mosem excitati, singulí suo tempore atque ordine?
units.tr: Q. What did the Prophets write, raised up one by one in their own time and order, after Moses?

units.la: R. Idem & totum quoad substantiam quod ante ipsos Moses scripserat; tantū in hoc discrime fuit, quòd quisque ex divina revelatione addebat interpretationem illustriorem, prout Lucifer ille novi Testamenti magis magisque appropinquabat.
units.tr: A. The same and whole thing, in substance, that Moses had written before them. The only difference was that each, by divine revelation, added a clearer interpretation, as that morning star of the New Testament drew ever nearer.

units.la: Q. Quid scripserunt post Prophetas Apostoli?
units.tr: Q. What did the Apostles write after the Prophets?

units.la: R. Idem & totū quod inde à condito mundo omnibus ætatibus ante ipsos, & viua voce traditum, & scriptum fuerat, primùm viva voce tradiderunt, deinde scriptis commendarunt.
units.tr: A. The same and whole thing that had been handed down by word of mouth and written in all ages before them from the creation of the world. First they delivered it by word of mouth, then they commended it in writings.

units.la: Q. Nullum ne statuis discrimen inter scripta Prophetica & Apostolica?
units.tr: Q. Do you not make any distinction between the prophetic and the apostolic writings?

units.la: R. In re & substantia nullum, in rei claritate & accidente magnum: Continet enim Scriptura Apostolica revelationem mysterij, inde à mundo condito multò clarissimam & plenissimam.
units.tr: A. None in the thing and substance; a great one in the clarity of the thing and in the accident. For apostolic Scripture contains the revelation of the mystery, which from the creation of the world was far clearer and fuller.

units.la: Q. Audiui de vtroque revelationis modo extra comparationem spectato: Nunc velim inter se vivam vocé & scriptionem compares, vt ex hac comparatione appareat vtra maioris sit dignitatis atque authoritatis?
units.tr: Q. I have heard about each mode of revelation considered apart from comparison. Now I would like you to compare the living voice and writing with each other, so that from this comparison it may appear which of them has greater dignity and authority?

units.la: R. Comparationem duorum modorum inter se faciam. Comparantur viva vox & scriptura vel in substantia & in reipsa quæ his modis revelatur, vel in ipsis revelationis modis. Si comparatio fiat in re, jam vtriusque æqualitas est, cum res sit eadem vtrobique: Sin revelationis modos inter se compares, profectò non potest negari vivæ voci locus priorac dignior, cum viva vox & antiquior tempore fuerit, & organis prior fit (os enim organon prius ac dignius est manu) & magis accómoda fit ad captum rudiorum, ac familiarior docendi ratio. Quamquam sunt quoque in quibus scriptio vivam vocem antecellat: est enim perfectior & accuratior quidam revelationis modus perfectioribus docendis conveniens, & firmior veritatis custos. Non est negandum in-
units.tr: A. I will make a comparison between the two modes. The living voice and writing may be compared either in the substance and in the thing itself that is revealed by these modes, or in the modes of revelation themselves. If the comparison is made in the thing, then the two are equal, since the thing is the same in both. But if you compare the modes of revelation with each other, it certainly cannot be denied that the living voice has the more worthy place, since it is both earlier in time and prior in its instruments (for the mouth is a prior and more worthy instrument than the hand), and it is better suited to the grasp of the less learned and a more familiar method of teaching. Yet there are also cases in which writing surpasses the living voice. For there is a more perfect and accurate mode of revelation, suited to teaching the more advanced, and a firmer guardian of truth. It must not be denied that

units.la: te rea vtrumq; inter se parem esse aliis respectibus: idem enim loquuti sunt, & scripserunt, eodem modo, nempe acti a spiritu sancto, atq; inspirati a Deo. 2 Pet. 1. 21. 2 Tim. 3. 16. Denique postquam jam cessavit viva vox & Dei voluntate, scriptio in ejus locum est surrogata, adeo ut tota illa dignitas quae vivae vocis fuit, rat jam merito scriptionis sit habenda.
units.tr: in other respects the two are equal: for they spoke and wrote the same things, in the same way, namely moved by the Holy Spirit and inspired by God (2 Pet. 1. 21; 2 Tim. 3. 16). Finally, since the living voice has now ceased by the will of God, writing has been substituted in its place, so that all the dignity that belonged to the living voice must now rightly be attributed to writing.

units.la: Q. Visne igitur scriptionem hanc Propheticam & Apostolicam a nobis eodem dignitatis loco habendam quo a superioribus aetatibus habita est, ipsa viva Dei hominum extra ordinariorum vox?
units.tr: Q. Do you therefore want this prophetic and apostolic writing to be held by us in the same place of dignity in which it was held by earlier ages, namely the living voice of God itself, speaking through extraordinary men?

units.la: R. Volo, & in hac revelationis modo solo tanquam θεοπνευστῳ lubens acquiesco, tantisper dum vocem illam Christi servatoris viram, longeq; suavissimam audiero in illustri ipsius adventu, cum dicet iis qui ad dexteram ipsius erunt: Venite benedicti Patris mei, possidete regnum paratum vobis a jactis mundi fundamentis. Huic sit omnis gloria in omnia secula. Amen.
units.tr: A. I do, and I gladly rest in this mode of revelation alone, as God-breathed, until I hear that living and by far the sweetest voice of Christ our Saviour at his glorious coming, when he says to those who are at his right hand: "Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world" (Matt. 25). To him be all glory for ever and ever. Amen.
